### *NOTICE TO THE READER*

*During the printing of the present work, several modifications were made to the territorial extent and administrative organization of the colony of Upper Senegal-Niger: an order from the Governor-General of the A.O.F. <note>A.O.F. stands for Afrique Occidentale Française, or French West Africa, a federation of eight French colonial territories</note>, dated June 21, 1911, has separated the district <note>The original French "cercle" refers to the primary administrative unit used by the French colonial government</note> of Gao from the Military Territory and attached it to the colony of Upper Senegal-Niger proper; a decree of September 7, 1911, has placed the Military Territory of the Niger, thus diminished by the district of Gao, under the direct command of the Governor-General of the A.O.F.; finally, for reasons of hygiene, the administrative center <note>The French "chef-lieu" refers to the capital or administrative seat of a district</note> of the district of Koury has been transferred to Dédougou, a short distance south of Koury and on the right bank of the Black Volta.*

*It must be clearly understood that the territorial limits and the statistics relating to the population given in the course of this volume apply to the territory of the colony as it was constituted before the order of June 21, 1911.*

# PREFACE

When I took over the administration of <term>Upper Senegal-Niger</term> <note>original: "Haut-Sénégal-Niger"; a colonial territory in French West Africa that existed under this name from 1904 to 1921.</note> in May 1908, among the documents I consulted to study the new Colony for which I was responsible were district monographs established by order of my predecessor in 1903. These works, generally interesting, no longer corresponded to reality; documents of this kind age quickly in a colony as young and as vibrant as the <term>Sudan</term> <note>Refers to the French Sudan, roughly modern-day Mali.</note>. This led to the plan to revive my predecessor’s idea and obtain a status report on Upper Senegal-Niger in 1909; I completed this with an inquiry similar to the one I had undertaken in the Ivory Coast in 1901 regarding the <term>customary law</term> <note>original: "droit coutumier"; the traditional legal systems and social rules of the local ethnic groups.</note> of the <term>Indigenous people</term> <note>original: "Indigènes"; the standard term used in the colonial era to refer to the local populations.</note>. The two questionnaires that served as the basis and framework for this consultation will be found further on.

First of all, it is only right to acknowledge the eagerness and conscientiousness with which, almost unanimously, the <term>Circle Commanders</term> <note>original: "commandants de Cercle"; the primary administrative officers in charge of a "cercle," which was the basic colonial administrative district.</note>, whether civilian or military, set about responding to the double questionnaire addressed to them. I am happy to be able to thank them once again.

Finding myself in possession of this truly considerable mass of documents—of somewhat unequal value, but almost always interesting—it appeared to me that there was something better to do than simply keeping them in our archives to be consulted in case of need.

But a full publication of all these reports was not to be considered; by their very nature, their juxtaposition would have resulted in a quantity of redundant double-work, in which the lost and weary reader would have had great difficulty finding essential information, and from which they could have extracted neither

<summary>Governor Clozel explains that upon taking office in 1908, he commissioned a comprehensive update of district reports and a study of indigenous customary law to replace outdated 1903 records.</summary>
<keywords>Governor Clozel, Upper Senegal-Niger, colonial administration, customary law, Circle Commanders, ethnography, 20th-century history</keywords>

## HAUT-SÉNÉGAL-NIGER

...overviews or clear assessments. A work of restructuring and coordination was therefore necessary.

After adopting the framework that seemed most suitable for presenting a complete picture of our Sudan, it remained to find men who combined the writing talent necessary for such a task with a deep enough knowledge of the country and its inhabitants to correct detailed errors and accurately place the historical, economic, and geographical facts that constitute the life of many peoples, while distilling their general data and essential characteristics.

**M. Delafosse** <note>Maurice Delafosse (1870–1926), a famous French ethnographer and colonial administrator who became a pioneer of African studies.</note>—as his numerous previous works attest—is, of all Frenchmen, the one who best knows the languages, traditions, customs, and manners of the <term>Indigenous people</term> of West Africa. While his strong general education and prior studies prepared him better than most to learn, it was not only through books but through sixteen years of African life, in permanent contact with the people and nature, that he acquired his erudition.

**Assistant in the <term>Supply Corps</term> Méniaud** <note>original: "L'Adjoint à l'Intendance"; the branch responsible for the colony's logistics and financial administration.</note> is completing his third stay in the Sudan; he has managed its finances and carefully studied its needs and resources. Prepared by the high level of culture provided by the <term>Polytechnic School</term> <note>original: "École Polytechnique"; a prestigious French elite institution.</note> and the specialized studies required for admission into the Supply Corps, he has, moreover, traveled through the entire colony from Senegal to Lake Chad during numerous missions. Everywhere, he examined on-site the products of the soil, resources of all kinds, means of transport, and the economic life of the country in both its details and its entirety.

**M. Brévié** <note>Jules Brévié (1880–1964), who would later become the Governor-General of French West Africa and French Indochina.</note> has been in the Sudan since graduating from the <term>Colonial School</term> <note>original: "École Coloniale"; the training ground for administrators of France's overseas empire.</note>; after becoming initiated into the life and administration of the country by serving in the most diverse districts, he has been placed at the head of the <term>Political Bureau</term> <note>original: "bureau politique"; the office responsible for monitoring political stability and local relations.</note> of the Government for nearly five years. There, he has demonstrated a talent for exposition and qualities that, until now, only his hierarchical superiors have been able to appreciate, and he has above all acquired the most complete knowledge of the political and administrative life of the Colony.

It is to these three collaborators that all the merit will belong...

He justifies their selection based on their long-term field experience and prestigious educational backgrounds.</summary>
<keywords>Maurice Delafosse, Jacques Méniaud, Jules Brévié, French Sudan, colonial administration, ethnography, colonial economy, West Africa</keywords>

# PREFACE

of the work; in case of success, I claim only the merit of having chosen them.

---

The task was indeed vast enough and complex enough to exceed the competence of a single person. Unlike most African colonies, whose past—as virgin as their forests—is reduced to the history of the effort of European explorers to penetrate them, the <term>Sudan</term> <note>In this context, "Sudan" refers to the French Sudan (Soudan Français), a vast territory in West Africa that encompasses modern-day Mali and parts of neighboring countries.</note> has a history. It is a history little known and imperfectly documented, but real, and capable of taking shape and rewarding the labor of whoever will unravel its obscurities and uncertainties.

In the times of Greece, Carthage, and the ancient Egyptian dynasties, the Sudan was in commercial relations with the Mediterranean, the cradle of ancient civilizations. Those caravans of old had to cross a Sahara that was very probably less sterile and less inhospitable than that of today.

The Sudan was touched by the Arab conquest; from its mysterious borders emerged the <term>Almoravids</term> <note>A Berber imperial dynasty that ruled the Maghreb and Al-Andalus (Spain) in the 11th and 12th centuries.</note> who conquered the <term>Maghreb</term> <note>The region of Northwest Africa, including present-day Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia.</note> and Spain; it saw the founding and disappearance of great Black empires; Moroccan armies invaded and dominated certain of its provinces for more than a century. Finally, the account of the French conquest, begun in 1880 and only recently completed, remains to be written. This epic, misunderstood and poorly judged because it is too close to us, has lacked its Bernal Diaz <note>Bernal Díaz del Castillo (c. 1492–1584), a soldier and chronicler who wrote a famous first-hand account of the Spanish conquest of Mexico.</note> and its Heredia <note>José-Maria de Heredia (1842–1905), a French poet known for his work "The Trophies," which celebrated the exploits of explorers and conquerors.</note>.

One would admire first of all the continuity of designs and effort, from the distant plans traced with such remarkable foresight by the likes of Bouët-Willaumez and Faidherbe, to the uninterrupted series of military expeditions begun by Brière de l'Isle and Borgnis-Desbordes, continued by Frey, Galliéni, Humbert, Archinard, Combe, Audéoud, de Trentinian, Gouraud... I pass over many other excellent men.

There, one would see enterprises of the maddest temerity, conducted with the coldest intrepidity, justifying by their success the most daring philosophical theories on the power of the will. General Combe, in the campaigns against <term>Samori</term> <note>Samori Ture (c. 1830–1900), the founder of the Wassoulou Empire and a primary leader of resistance against French colonial rule in West Africa.</note>,

<summary>Governor Clozel argues that unlike other African regions, the Sudan possesses a deep, documented history involving ancient trade and medieval empires. He highlights the need for a definitive historical account of the region, especially regarding the recent French military conquest led by figures like Faidherbe and Archinard.</summary>

<keywords>French Sudan, Almoravids, West African history, Trans-Saharan trade, French colonial conquest, Samori Ture, colonial administration</keywords>

### UPPER SENEGAL-NIGER

General Archinard at Nioro, Ouossébougou, and Djenné, and General Audéoud at Sikasso renewed the exploits of <term>Cortez</term> <note>Hernán Cortés, the Spanish conquistador who led the expedition that caused the fall of the Aztec Empire.</note> and <term>Pizarro</term> <note>Francisco Pizarro, the Spanish conquistador who led the conquest of the Inca Empire.</note>, as well as those more recent exploits of other Frenchmen, like Francis Garnier and his few companions during the first conquest of <term>Tonkin</term> <note>The northernmost part of modern-day Vietnam, which became a French protectorate in the 1880s.</note>.

Alongside the most famous leaders and battles, how much obscure heroism, how many fatigues and sufferings: the climate, the fevers, the privations, the boredom of distant exiles, and the depressing inaction during the bad seasons! Pain seems inseparable from every human birth; thus is justified once more the poet's verse:

> ... *Such a great labor it was to found the Roman race.* <note>original: "Tantæ molis erat romanam condere gentem," from Virgil’s Aeneid, Book I, line 33.</note>

Of all these perils, those of combat were always the most cheerfully faced. It seems that war possesses a peculiar and singular virtue, at least from an aesthetic and moral point of view, since men whom I otherwise knew to be quite ordinary—sometimes even vulgar—and our simple Black soldiers themselves <note>Likely referring to the *Tirailleurs Sénégalais*, West African colonial infantry units of the French Army.</note>, when they fall with weapons in hand, know how to die beautifully, with a stoic nobility and a purely classical bearing.

---

Among these soldiers, many were excellent organizers and administrators. The Colony still operates within the administrative frameworks established by Generals Archinard and de Trentinian. It would be unjust, however, to forget Governor Grodet, whose circulars and instructions—especially in financial matters—have lost none of their value. The controversies, now forgotten, which his time in the Government of the Sudan provoked, have caused this solid and unassailable part of his work to be too often neglected.

From 1900 to 1908, my immediate predecessor, Governor General Ponty, worked with the most enlightened spirit and the keenest practical sense toward the development of the young Colony. From the whole of his work, two facts stand out with particular prominence and will long perpetuate the mem—

### PREFACE

...come from his Government: the liberation of the captives and the creation of the administrative center of Koulouba <note>Koulouba is a hill in Bamako, Mali, where the colonial administration built its headquarters; it remains the seat of the presidency today.</note>.

While everyone agreed on the energetic repression of the <term>slave trade</term> <note>original: *traite*. This refers to the active trafficking and sale of people, as distinguished from the state of "domestic" slavery.</note>, the immediate suppression of captivity made even the best minds hesitate. All indigenous societies in every Colony within the group permitted slavery; its existence was thus intimately linked to the economic and social life of the entire country. The abrupt suppression of such an essential gear in the existence of our pagan or Muslim subjects could rightly be seen as a leap into the unknown, carrying the most unfortunate consequences for the tranquility and prosperity of our Colonies. One might have felt all the more encouraged to proceed gradually because the question of humanity did not generally present itself as it was believed to in France. It was, in effect, a gross error to view African captivity through the memories of Mrs. Beecher Stowe's novel <note>A reference to *Uncle Tom's Cabin* by Harriet Beecher Stowe.</note>. The misfortunes of the virtuous Uncle Tom had nothing in common with the lives of African captives in Africa. Their life was truly not very harsh, and their condition was generally not much more painful than that of free men <note>The author reflects a common colonial viewpoint of the era, which argued that "domestic slavery" in Africa was more akin to serfdom or kinship-based dependency than the chattel slavery of the Americas.</note>. With the slave trade rigorously suppressed, it seemed wiser to let time take its course, proceeding with partial liberations whenever any specific incident warranted them.

Governor Ponty had the merit of allowing no such delays. As soon as Governor-General Roume <note>Ernest Roume, Governor-General of French West Africa from 1902 to 1907.</note> had decided upon the complete and absolute suppression of slavery, he proceeded resolutely. And not only were the disturbances caused by this liberation of more than 300,000 captives in less than two years completely insignificant, but the prosperity of the country actually increased. The former masters, dispossessed of their slaves, set themselves to work; the liberated captives did the same on their part, and, certain of henceforth keeping all the fruit of their labor, they displayed a much greater activity than in the past. The success of a measure so debated and so debatable does the greatest honor to Governor-General Ponty.

<summary>This page discusses the colonial administration's decision to move from merely suppressing the slave trade to the total abolition of domestic slavery under Governor-General Ponty, arguing that the transition was economically successful despite initial fears of social collapse.</summary>
<keywords>William Ponty, Ernest Roume, abolition of slavery, Koulouba, slave trade, colonial economics, Uncle Tom's Cabin, French West Africa</keywords>

# UPPER SENEGAL-NIGER
<meta>catchword: pla-</meta>

The idea of establishing the administrative center of the Colony at Koulouba belongs to General de Trentinian <note>General Louis-Alexandre de Trentinian (1851–1942) was a French colonial officer who served as the Lieutenant-Governor of French Sudan from 1895 to 1899.</note>. This man, possessed of such a sharp and far-sighted mind, often had the misfortune during his time in the Government of Sudan of being right a few years too soon. Many of his projects, taken up by his successors, have succeeded or are currently in the process of succeeding; others still await a realization that they will undoubtedly find in the more or less near future.

It was obvious to General de Trentinian, and to anyone willing to take the trouble to study a map of French Sudan, that Kayes—while a necessary base of operations during the conquest, a transit town, and the Colony's port on the Senegal River—was far too <term>eccentric</term> <note>In this historical and geographical context, "eccentric" means located far from the center; peripheral or off-center.</note> to remain its political capital. Furthermore, the temperature there is particularly hot and difficult for nearly the entire year. Upper Senegal, of which Kayes and Médine are the principal towns, is moreover a rather poor country: chains of rocky and sterile hills and <term>laterite</term> <note>A red, iron-rich soil common in tropical regions that often forms a hard, crusty surface, making it difficult for farming.</note> plateaus leave truly fertile land only in the narrow valleys watered by the various streams forming the upper basin of the Senegal River. The population there is neither very dense nor very wealthy. Finally, the decree of October 17, 1899—which attached the <term>circle</term> <note>original: *cercle*. The standard administrative district used in French colonial government.</note> of Bakel to the Colony of Senegal and the circles of the Upper Niger closest to Kayes to Guinea—further emphasized the peripheral position of this town and more clearly shifted the axis of the Colony toward the Middle Niger.

The climate of the Niger Valley, much less grueling for Europeans than that of Upper Senegal, and the river itself—a natural access route toward Timbuktu and Niamey where all the land routes of the immense plateau encircled by the Niger Bend met—all argued in favor of a transfer of the administrative center. General de Trentinian began the movement by stationing the main portion of the troops on the hills of Kati, 12 kilometers from Bamako. Already, he pointed to the plateau of Koulouba (Point "F") as the site for the future capital, which towers 161 meters above the plain where the village and the post of Bamako are built. On a pla-

# PREFACE

...plateau nearby at a slightly higher altitude (Point G), the Colony's central hospital was to be built. Before leaving Sudan <note>The "French Sudan," a colonial territory in West Africa that roughly corresponds to modern-day Mali.</note>, the General had a small house built at Koulouba, a modest marker of the future city.

In 1903, Governor General Roume <note>Ernest Roume (1858–1941), a key figure in the organization of French West Africa.</note>, traveling to Timbuktu, visited Point F and Point G; captivated by the magnificent view from the top of these rocky plateaus—true cliffs overlooking the river and the Niger valley—and appreciating the many advantages they offered in terms of ventilation and healthiness, he used his high authority to approve the plans of General de Trentinian. Once free to act, Governor Ponty, assisted by Commander Digue and Captain Lepoivre of the Engineering Corps, set to work immediately. In less than five years, he oversaw the construction at Koulouba of the most beautiful and successful colonial capital to be found in West Africa, including foreign colonies—British or German—as well as French ones.

Having arrived at Kayes on May 10, 1908, when the work was nearly finished, I moved the seat of Government there ten days later.

The hospital at Point G has been under construction since last year and will likely be operational from the first days of 1912.

Pumping machines and water pipes provide for all the requirements of modern hygiene and comfort at these two locations; Bamako-Koulouba and the hospital will be lit by electricity next year. In Koulouba rise the Government House, the Secretary General's residence, and three large buildings housing the Treasury, the Archives, and various offices. All these structures, built in an <term>Hispano-Moorish</term> <note>An architectural style blending North African and Spanish motifs, frequently used by French architects in Africa to provide both aesthetic flair and practical heat management.</note> style that is somewhat heavy but perfectly suited to the climate, form an ensemble that lacks neither harmony nor a certain majesty. Twenty-five houses, smaller but all well-ventilated and provided with large verandas, house the Government printing press and the officials employed in the Colony's central administration. It is also at Koulouba that the head of the Public Works department is established, along with his...

### HAUT-SÉNÉGAL-NIGER

offices, the Director of Agriculture, and the head of the Animal Husbandry Service.

In Bamako, several departments have established themselves in buildings constructed since 1909: the management of the Kayes-Niger railway, a Justice of the Peace with extended jurisdiction <note>A colonial judicial official who handled both civil and minor criminal cases over a large area.</note>, the State Lands Department, and the Directorate of Posts and Telegraphs. The two towns—separated by 1,500 meters "as the crow flies" and 5 kilometers by the carriage road that links Bamako in the plain to Koulouba on the mountain—are destined to merge in the near future. This will likely occur once the Thiès-Kayes railway is completed, finally providing Upper Senegal and Niger with the reliable, permanent outlet to the sea that has been lacking for its economic development until now.

The central organization that has functioned at Koulouba for two years is, as I have mentioned, still the one created by Generals Archinard and de Trentinian <note>Louis Archinard and Louis-Gustave Binger de Trentinian were high-ranking French military officers and colonial administrators pivotal in the conquest and early organization of this region.</note>. The local decree of June 19, 1908, the text of which appears later in this work, aims solely to clarify and refine the specific duties of each official.

The Governor, assisted by his Cabinet and his military office, has under his immediate direction the four government bureaus: Political Affairs, Economic Affairs, Finance, and Supplies. The Secretary General has specific authority over the latter two bureaus; it is he who presents their work for the Governor's signature, while the heads of the first and second bureaus report directly on the matters entrusted to them. This constitutes the daily routine. Additionally, the heads of the technical services—the Kayes-Niger Railway and Navigation, Public Works, Posts and Telegraphs, Agriculture, etc.—hold a weekly conference with the head of the Colony.

9,000 kilometers of telegraph lines put the capital in communication with the twenty-nine <term>cercles</term> <note>The "cercle" (circle) was the primary administrative district in French West Africa, governed by a "Commandant de cercle."</note> of the Colony. These are: Kayes, Bafoulabé, Kita, Bamako, Nioro, Goumbou, Sokolo, the residency of Kiffa, Satadougou, Bougouni, Sikasso, Bobo-Dioulasso, Gaoua, Ségou, Koutiala, San, Djenné, Mopti, Issa-Ber or Niafounké, Bandiagara, Ouahigouya, Koury, Ouagadougou (or the Mossi region), Dori, and Fada-N’Gourma; to which, since...

# PREFACE

On January 1, 1911, the former Timbuktu region and the lands on the right bank of the Niger were added. These had been detached from the Military Territory to be placed under the direct orders of the Governor, albeit with a special organization (decrees of **June 22, 1910**) necessitated by current circumstances; these areas now form the districts of Timbuktu-Sedentary and Timbuktu-Nomadic, Gourma, and Say. <note>These administrative districts were divided based on the lifestyles of the inhabitants—stationary farmers versus migratory pastoralists—to better manage their specific social and economic needs.</note>

The Military Territory, with its own special budget and relative autonomy, now extends from the Niger River to Lake Chad. It comprises a semi-Saharan frontier <note>original: "marche," a term for a border region or frontier zone, often militarized for defense</note> approximately 1,500 kilometers long, serving as a link between French Equatorial Africa and French West Africa. On that same date, January 1, 1911, the capital was moved from Niamey to Zinder, which is closer to its geographic center. From there, the Colonel Commanding the territory can exert more effective control over the seven districts <note>The "administrative circle" (cercle) was the primary unit of French colonial administration.</note> under his authority: Gao, Niamey, Madaoua, Zinder, N'Guigmi, Agadez, and Bilma. A telegraph line of 800 kilometers already connects Niamey to Zinder and joins the colony’s general network via Timbuktu-Gao and Dori. In 1911, this line will be extended to N'Guigmi and, following an agreement with the Governor General of French Equatorial Africa, prolonged to Mao, the nearest post in the Congolese colony.

Due to its semi-desert location, its military obligations for protection against Saharan nomads, and the considerable transport costs that burden its administration, the Military Territory of the Niger cannot survive or organize itself solely with the approximately 1,200,000 francs generated by local taxes. A variable subsidy (300,000 francs in 1911), allocated from the budget of Upper Senegal and Niger, supplements its insufficient resources each year. The Governor of the Colony directs and monitors the administration of the Military Territory and exercises his authority there through the Colonel Commandant.

Such is the overall organization that allows us, with barely 500 French officers or officials and an armed force of about 4,500 Black soldiers in total—including regular troops,

Beyond maintaining order, a necessary condition for any progress, we ensure the execution of works useful for the economic development of the country, medical assistance to the indigenous people, and the spread of education among the primitive populations <note>In the colonial context of the early 20th century, 'primitive' was a standard term used by administrators to describe non-industrialized societies, reflecting the paternalistic view of 'civilizing' missions.</note> whose tutelage <note>original: "tutelle." My experience as a **Colonial Governor** is not very old, but it allows me to observe that the number of reports, accounting records, and documents of all kinds to be provided to the General Government or the Ministry has tripled in less than ten years. While the rapid development of our young African colonies can, to a certain extent, justify part of this increase, it cannot be invoked for the whole. It is even to be feared that this excess of solicitude may eventually paralyze the progress of our African possessions; it already has the result of delaying by one or more years the resolution of many affairs and the execution of numerous works, without the advantages of this anxious control appearing very clearly in most cases. # PREFACE

This is not the place to study the reforms to be brought to our colonial administration.

---

The second series of this publication, devoted to the economic situation of the Colony, will demonstrate, I hope, that the heroism of our soldiers, the labor of our officials, and the efforts of our merchants have not been squandered on a vain endeavor.

The French Sudan <note>The French Sudan (Soudan Français) was a colonial territory in French West Africa; it corresponds largely to the borders of modern-day Mali.</note> is certainly no Eldorado <note>A mythical city of gold; the author uses this to temper expectations of easy wealth.</note>, if there are still any Eldorados left in the world. There, as elsewhere, if we wish to harvest, we must cultivate our garden <note>original: "cultiver notre jardin." This is a famous allusion to the final line of Voltaire's *Candide*, suggesting that one should focus on practical work and the improvement of one's own domain rather than optimistic dreaming.</note>. But while in many parts of this vast Colony, the African soil appears hostile and ungrateful, it is already fertile enough to allow us to predict a flourishing future.

The number and diversity of exploitable products—a consequence of the country's extent and the variety of its landscapes—ensure solid foundations for this prosperity. I say "exploitable" and not "exploited"; until now, only one, rubber <note>In the early 20th century, wild rubber was a major colonial export, though its collection often involved harsh conditions for the local population.</note>, has been seriously exploited; two or three others (peanuts, wool, cotton, mineral wealth, livestock) are only just beginning to be. Finally, we have the Niger.

The Middle Niger valley <note>The section of the Niger River flowing through modern Mali, featuring a massive inland delta that floods seasonally.</note> is, of all the African countries I know, the one whose agricultural future seems to me the most vast and certain. When, about fifteen years ago, following the conquest of Timbuktu, young enthusiastic officers compared the Niger to the Nile, many—myself included—smiled at what seemed to us an excusable exaggeration, but a bit much nonetheless. Since then, I have seen, and I believe, or at least I understand.

The Middle Niger valley, from Sansanding to Timbuktu, with its vast periodic floods, its multiple branches, and its lakes acting as reservoirs, is undoubtedly as fertile and certainly much more extensive than the Nile Delta. However, it is a "brand new" Nile, which lacks 3,000 or 4,000 years of ancient civilization, not to mention modern [irrigation] works. That it could become one of the granaries of the world <note>original: "greniers du monde," often translated as "breadbaskets."</note> is probable. But

<summary>The author highlights the economic potential of the French Sudan, arguing that while it is not a land of easy riches, the Middle Niger valley possesses agricultural potential rivaling that of the Nile Delta.</summary>

### UPPER SENEGAL AND NIGER

this granary is 1,800 kilometers from the nearest port, and not much can leave it because the methods of transport are expensive and still quite imperfect.

However, modern civilization possesses mechanical means that the ancient world lacked. The Guinea railway is now complete, and the Thiès-Kayes <note>The Thiès-Kayes railway was a vital link connecting the Senegal River to the coast, facilitating the export of goods from the interior.</note> line will be finished in a few years. On that day, despite the forced increase in rates on our African railways, many things will become possible that are not today. It will probably not take 3,000 years for our engineers to study the floods of the Niger, to canalize them, to direct them, and to make them yield their maximum useful output. But will men not be lacking for this task? And by that, I mean the natives <note>original: "indigènes." In this 1911 context, the term refers to the local African population under colonial rule.</note> forming the bulk of the industrial and agricultural troops for whom we will provide the leadership—troops indispensable for the development of all these latent riches. In the Sudan, especially on the banks of the river, the population is undoubtedly less sparse than in most other regions of intertropical Africa; but it is still quite insufficient. These countries have not passed through centuries of internal wars and barbarity with impunity. And by this, we are brought back to the native question which dominates all others. I wrote this as early as 1902:

> "One cannot
> "repeat too often that, in French West Africa, the native
> "is the foundation of all prosperity, the pivot of all progress."

In the Sudan, the French peace <note>original: "paix française." Modeled after the "Pax Romana," this term refers to the period of relative stability imposed by French colonial authority after the initial conquest.</note> reigns; internal wars, looting, and massacres have definitively ceased, but the work of assistance is barely begun; we already perform more than 100,000 vaccinations per year, but we must perform 500,000 to fight against smallpox <note>Smallpox was a devastating disease in West Africa; the French colonial administration viewed mass vaccination as both a humanitarian act and a way to ensure a stable labor force.</note>. And we have other scourges to combat to preserve for our native races all their vitality and their power of growth. This is the duty prescribed at the present hour, even more by our interest than by humanity. The possibilities for wealth exist: the more men we have to develop them, the wealthier we will be, and the better we will have worked for the grandeur and strength of France.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Koulouba, January 1, 1911, <note>Koulouba is a hill in Bamako, Mali, which served as the seat of the colonial government.</note> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; CLOZEL.

# UPPER SENEGAL AND NIGER

### II. — Circular regarding the study of indigenous customs

***The Governor of the Colonies, Lieutenant-Governor of Upper Senegal and Niger, to the Administrators and District Commanders <note>original: "Commandants de Cercles"; the "cercle" was the primary administrative unit in French West Africa, governed by a colonial official.</note> of Upper Senegal and Niger and to the Commander of the Military Territory of Niger.***

->Gentlemen,<-

The decree of November 10, 1903, regarding the reorganization of the Judicial Service in the Colonies of the General Government of French West Africa, had the essential goal of unifying the Administration of Justice—which was previously subject to regimes that varied according to the administrative divisions of our great West African possession—and of guaranteeing to the indigenous people under our control and direction the maintenance of their customs, provided they are not contrary to our essential principles of humanity and civilization. These customs form the foundation of a private law appropriate to their mentality and social state.

In his instructions of April 25, 1905, regarding the application of Article 75 of this decree, which summarizes the legislator's dominant objective in a few lines, Governor General Roume <note>Ernest Roume (1858–1941) was a high-ranking colonial official who served as Governor General of French West Africa from 1902 to 1907.</note> expressed himself as follows:

> "I call your attention particularly to the provisions of
> "Article 75, under the terms of which indigenous Justice shall apply
> "local customs in all matters, in everything that is not contrary
> "to the principles of French civilization.
> "The indigenous courts will have to judge either according to the rules
> "of Koranic law, Maliki rite <note>The Maliki rite is one of the four traditional schools of Islamic jurisprudence within Sunni Islam, characterized by its reliance on the traditions of Medina and widely followed in West Africa.</note>, more or less modified by usage and
> "accepted in fact throughout a large part of our territories, or according
> "to local traditions in regions that have not yet undergone
> "Muslim influence.
> "We cannot, in fact, impose upon our subjects the provisions of
> "our French law, which are clearly incompatible with their social state.
> "But we can no longer tolerate the maintenance, under the protection of our
> "authority, of certain customs contrary to our principles of humanity
> "and to natural law <note>A philosophical and legal concept referring to a body of moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note>.
> "In civil matters, customs are not the same across
> "the entire extent of our territories. Variable according to the regions, it even
> "happens that within indigenous groupings, though united by a
> "common origin or language, customs change from village to
> "village. There will therefore be a need to ensure that, under the cover of this
> "excessive diversity, which is sometimes difficult to control, the indigenous courts

The vital interest of this work—both from the point of view of the task of magistrates who are too often inexperienced or dependent on certain local influences, and from the point of view of the guarantees that will result for the litigants <note>original: "justiciables"; those subject to the jurisdiction of a court.</note>—cannot escape you.

With a view to successfully carrying out a work as complex as it is delicate, I have decided to entrust its realization to a commission which will be responsible for centralizing your work, coordinating it, and through comparison, reconciliation, or adaptation, elaborating for each indigenous group of the Colony the customary law code that shall be applicable to it.

### CIVIL LAW

#### SECTION I. — ON THE FAMILY

*Family organization.* — Is this organization based on the principles accepted by civilized peoples? <note>In 1909, "civilized peoples" was a legal and social category referring specifically to Western European nations and their legal codes.</note> Definition of kinship: is it established through the paternal line <note>original: "tige paternelle"</note>, through the maternal line, or through both? On alliance <note>Kinship created through marriage rather than blood.</note>. On the degrees of kinship and alliance from the perspective of their effects, notably regarding: 1° rights of guardianship and in particular the transfers from uncle to nephew; 2° impediments to marriage.

Note on the organization of the tribe and its relationship with the analogous institution observed at the dawn of civilizations (kin group <note>original Greek: "genos"</note>, clan <note>original Latin: "gens"</note>, clan, horde, etc.). Constituent elements of the tribe. Rights and duties of its members. Political and administrative organization of indigenous groups before our occupation. Current state. Ongoing evolution. Modifications to be made.

#### SECTION II. — ON MARRIAGE

*Monogamy or polygamy?* — Does polygamy have the legal character that it presents among certain primitive peoples? Consequences of polygamy.

French legislation distinguishes four types of guardianship: 1st, guardianship by the surviving father or mother; 2nd, testamentary guardianship, conferred by the last surviving parent; 3rd, guardianship by ancestors, granted to the closest relative; 4th, dative guardianship, granted by a family council. ### SECTION V. — ON PROPERTY

*General theory of property among the indigenous people.* — On the origin of the right of ownership. Is property collective or private, or both collective and private according to the nature of the assets? Is it the eminent domain <note>The ultimate power of a sovereign or state over all land within its jurisdiction.</note> of the chief or the sovereign? Is there a distinction between movable property <note>Personal belongings that can be moved.</note> and immovable property <note>Land and permanent structures.</note>? Does the right of ownership include the ability to use the thing and to dispose of it, as it is granted in ancient Rome and in current legislation?
*On personal servitudes or rights of usufruct, use, and habitation.* — How and upon which assets can a usufruct <note>The legal right to use and derive profit from property belonging to another, provided it is not destroyed.</note> be established? On the rights and obligations of the usufructuary and the bare owner <note>The person who owns the title to a property but does not have the right to use it or its profits.</note>. How does the usufruct end? On use and habitation: rights and duties of the user.
*On real servitudes or land services.* — How they are established, the rights they grant, and the causes for their termination.
*Note on the public domain.* — What are the conceptions of the indigenous people in this regard? Do there exist, among them, assets belonging in common to the village, the tribe, or to larger groupings? Can these assets be alienated <note>Sold or transferred to another owner.</note>? By whom and in what form? On the various dependencies of the public domain.

### SECTION VI. — ON SUCCESSIONS, DONATIONS, AND WILLS

*On the opening of successions and the vesting or investiture of hereditary assets for the benefit of the heir.* — On the qualities required to inherit. On the various orders of succession. Who inherits? Is it the children of the deceased, his ancestors, or his uterine <note>Siblings born of the same mother but different fathers.</note> brothers and sisters? Do women inherit and, if so, under what conditions? What about <note>original: "Quid"</note> the nephews of the deceased? What about the spouse? On the rights of the collective, village, or tribe, over the assets of the deceased. Forms of acceptance and repudiation of successions. Consequences of acceptance, particularly regarding debts. Consequences of renunciation. On the sharing of successions. On reports: can the heir combine their hereditary share with the amount of donations received from the <term>de cujus</term> <note>A Latin legal term referring to the deceased person whose estate is being settled.</note>?
A detailed note on the customs and practices regarding the ceremonies accompanying death (drums <note>original: "tams-tams"</note>, libations, burials, sacrifices, etc.) and on the time when the liquidation of successions occurs. On mourning.
*On inter-vivos donations and wills.* — Capacity to dispose of or receive by donation <note>Gifts given while the giver is still alive.</note> or by will. Is the matter of the disposable portion <note>The part of an estate that a person is legally allowed to give away to whoever they wish, regardless of the rights of protected heirs.</note> regulated? Forms and effects of the inter-vivos donation. Is it revocable? On the rules of form for wills. Legacies.

->Messieurs,<-

The monographs of the districts <note>original: "cercles" — the primary administrative subdivisions in French West African colonies, managed by a "Commandant de Cercle."</note> of Upper Senegal and Niger, which were established at the beginning of the year 1904 by the order and according to a plan outlined by the Acting Governor General Merlin, still constitute at the present time—and despite the imperfections or gaps in some of them—the most complete methodical collection that we possess...

<page-num>25</page-num>

...of the knowledge acquired at the time concerning the history, geography, ethnography, and economic value of our Colony.

However, over the last five years, the studies and projects undertaken by several of you, the investigations conducted by certain officers or officials on special assignment, and the increasingly meticulous censuses carried out in the <term>cercles<note>The "cercle" was the fundamental unit of French colonial administration in West Africa, governed by a district commissioner known as a "Commandant de cercle."</note></term>, have remarkably expanded the scope of our knowledge regarding the historical evolution of the populations placed under our tutelage—specifically concerning the origins, political formation, geographical distribution, and the significance of the ethnic groups that make up these populations.

Furthermore, the completion in 1905 of the Kayes-Niger Railway <note>A vital colonial infrastructure project connecting the Senegal River (at Kayes) to the Niger River (at Koulikoro), facilitating trade and military movement.</note> has considerably increased the economic wealth and productive power of a large portion of the Colony’s territories, which until then had remained unproductive.

Therefore, in order not to lose the fruit of the precious labor provided in 1904, and to maintain a complete and precise set of documentation kept up to date with all the progress achieved in the work of civilization we are pursuing in these lands, it is appropriate to resume the work of your predecessors. These records should be completed for each of your respective districts by adding information of every kind collected and recording new facts that have occurred during the last five years.

The purpose of this circular is to invite you to undertake this task, the interest and practical utility of which cannot escape you.

To facilitate your work and to give the reports you must establish and send to me before August 1st the necessary character of uniformity—making them easier to read and coordinate—I have had the attached outline prepared. This outline reproduces the essential provisions of the program originally adopted for the creation of the first <term>monographs<note>Detailed, descriptive studies focused on a single district, ethnic group, or subject.</note></term>, while setting aside a certain number of questions that have lost their relevance or now hold only a relative interest from our specific point of view.

I believe I have no special recommendations to make regarding the subjects that should particularly claim your attention or require more or less extensive development depending on their importance within your district. It is up to you to treat each of them according to the interest they present from a local perspective.

I know that I can count on your full devotion, and I do not doubt that you will take it to heart to bring all your care to the creation and drafting of the work I am entrusting to you.

Furthermore, I will not fail to take note of those among you who distinguish themselves by the manner in which they fulfill their task.

->Bamako, January 15, 1909.<-

# FOREWORD

The work entrusted to me by Governor Clozel,<note>François Joseph Clozel (1860–1918) was the Governor of Upper Senegal and Niger and later the Governor-General of French West Africa. He was a proponent of "associationist" colonial policy, which sought to rule through existing local structures.</note> which has provided the material for the present volume and the following one, relates only to the portion of the Upper Senegal-Niger colony administered directly by the Governor. That is to say, I have not concerned myself with the zone located between the Lower Niger and Lake Chad; this zone currently constitutes the Military Territory of the Niger and is the subject of the third series of this publication, written by Mr. Brévié.<note>Jules Brévié (1880–1964), like Delafosse, was a colonial administrator and researcher who later became Governor-General of French West Africa and French Indochina.</note>

I have divided the work into five parts.

The first — *the land* — is a brief study of the geography of Upper Senegal-Niger. I did not feel it necessary to engage in extensive considerations on a subject that falls outside my particular expertise and which, moreover, is about to be treated in a remarkable fashion by Assistant Administrator Henry Hubert in a book reproducing the results of his great geological mission.

The second part — *the peoples* — contains the nomenclature, classification, and distribution of the various ethnic groups that make up the indigenous population of the colony, along with a look at the probable origins and formation of each of them and a description of their most striking ethnographic characteristics.

The third part — *the languages* — is an attempt to classify the numerous idioms spoken in the French Sudan,<note>The term "idioms" (idiomes) here refers to distinct languages and dialects. At the time, "French Sudan" was a specific administrative region within the larger colony.</note> coupled with a quick overview of the specific character of each language family and an indication of the main publications relating to these languages.

<summary>In this foreword, Delafosse defines the geographic scope of his study—excluding the Military Territory of the Niger—and outlines the first three parts of his work: geography, ethnography, and linguistics.</summary>
<keywords>Upper Senegal-Niger, French Sudan, Governor Clozel, Henry Hubert, geography, ethnography, linguistics, colonial administration</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the work's structure, focusing on the fourth and fifth parts—history and civilizations—and detailing the diverse source materials and critical methodology employed by the author.</meta>

### FIRST SERIES

The fourth part — *history* — is an attempt to reconstruct the life of the indigenous states <note>original: "Etats indigènes"</note> that have succeeded or coexisted with one another from the most remote times to the contemporary period. This attempt is based both on the few written documents bequeathed to us by Arabic authors <note>Delafosse likely refers to major 16th and 17th-century chronicles like the *Tarikh al-Sudan* or *Tarikh al-Fattash*, which provided the first written histories of the Western Sudanic empires.</note> and European travelers, and on oral traditions collected in recent years across the various administrative districts <term>cercles: the primary administrative subdivisions of a colony in French West Africa, each managed by a "commandant de cercle."</term>. I have added to this a sort of table of the explorations that have made the lands of Upper Senegal-Niger known to us, a sketch of the French occupation from its beginnings to the present day, and finally a synthetic summary grouping the main facts in chronological order.

The fifth part — *civilizations* — consists of a study of the customs that constitute, in a sense, the indigenous civil code; the social and political organization that preceded our occupation of the country and which has survived, in its fundamental bases, through that occupation; the indigenous judicial organization as it existed before the decree of 1903 <note>The Decree of November 10, 1903, was a landmark piece of legislation that reorganized the justice system in French West Africa, officially establishing "customary courts" for the local population.</note> and as it has functioned since the application of that decree; and finally, the various religions currently practiced by our indigenous subjects, among which Islam <note>original: "l'islamisme"</note>, although the best known, is far from being the most widespread.

To treat these different subjects, I naturally made use of the monographs of the districts and the records of customary law <term>coutumiers: official compilations of local traditional laws and customs recorded by colonial administrators for use in the courts.</term> established in 1909 in accordance with the instructions of Governor Clozel, grouping the information they contain and coordinating them methodically and, where necessary, correcting them.

But I did not believe I could limit my documentation to these works alone: however excellent some of them may be, and however much a wealth of information most of them contain, they did not seem to me to constitute a sufficiently solid basis on their own, especially regarding the history of past times. Therefore, I have had recourse to a number of published works, the examination of which has allowed me more than once to complete or clarify points only touched upon in the reports of the district commanders. There, too, I felt I should not limit myself to a simple compilation: I have taken the liberty of performing a work of criticism, rejecting certain haphazard assertions...

# FOREWORD

3

...somewhat casually, to interpret others in the light of a new method, to compare written documents with oral traditions, and to derive from this comparison all the benefit one might expect from it.

The historical and geographical accounts of the Arabs, especially those of authors rightly considered the most conscientious, such as <term>Ibn Haoukal: A 10th-century Arab traveler and geographer whose work *The Face of the Earth* is a primary source for early West African history.</term>, <term>Bekri: Abu Ubayd al-Bakri, an 11th-century geographer from Al-Andalus who provided detailed descriptions of the Ghana Empire without ever visiting it.</term>, <term>Ibn Saïd: A 13th-century geographer and historian who expanded upon earlier works with new details on African kingdoms.</term>, <term>Ibn Batouta: The famous 14th-century traveler who personally visited the Mali Empire and provided eyewitness accounts of its court.</term>, <term>Ibn Khaldoun: The renowned 14th-century historian and philosopher of history who recorded the rise and fall of the North African and Sudanese dynasties.</term>, <term>Yakout: Yaqut al-Hamawi, a 13th-century geographer famous for his encyclopedic geographical dictionary, the *Mu'jam al-Buldan*.</term>, without forgetting <term>Sa'di: Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di, the Timbuktu-born author of the *Tarikh al-Sudan*.</term> and his *<term>Tarikh-es-Soudân: The "Chronicle of the Sudan," a vital historical record of the Songhai Empire and Timbuktu written in the 17th century.</term>*, have been of the greatest assistance to me. To tell the truth, their works had already been utilized more than once concerning the history of the <term>Soudan: Derived from the Arabic *Bilad al-Sudan* (Land of the Blacks), this term historically refers to the vast Sahelian region of West Africa, rather than the modern nation-state of Sudan.</term>, and it would seem at first glance that, after the commentaries provided by <term>Ralfs: Likely referring to Karl Friedrich Ralfs, a 19th-century German scholar of Arabic literature.</term>, <term>Barth: Heinrich Barth, the 19th-century German explorer and linguist whose multi-volume works laid the foundation for modern Central and West African studies.</term>, <term>Basset: René Basset, a French Arabist and specialist in Berber and African languages.</term>, <term>Binger: Louis-Gustave Binger, a French officer and explorer whose 1887-1889 journey mapped the regions between the Niger River and the Gulf of Guinea.</term> and so many others, there was not much unpublished material left to glean from this source of information. However, I believed I noticed that, despite the undeniable value of the translations we possess for most of these authors, there was a major interest in not sticking solely to these translations and in resorting to the Arabic text itself, particularly when it comes to reading or identifying names of people or places foreign to the Arabic language and country: the best translators, being little acquainted with the languages and geography of the Sudan and poorly aided by the often defective transcription system of the Arabic authors, have distorted many proper names which generally can only be read correctly by having recourse to the original text. Furthermore, some of these works relating to North Africa and, incidentally, to the Sudan, have not yet been translated into any European language, notably the precious geographical dictionary of Yakout, and for those, I was forced to stick to the Arabic text and translate the passages to be used myself.

Finally, it seemed necessary to me to take into account to a certain extent, especially concerning ethnography, sociology, and linguistics, my previous personal works and the notes and experience that I have been able to accumulate during my sixteen years of residence in <term>Afrique Occidentale: French West Africa, a federation of eight colonial territories administered by France from 1895 to 1958.</term>, including nine years spent in the Sudanese region. I also felt I should make use of information provided to me...

To facilitate the reading of certain chapters, I have accompanied them with plates of maps and sketches, each established specifically for the subjects treated in that chapter. These maps and sketches were executed, according to my instructions, by Mr. Meunier, cartographer for the Ministry of Colonies, who is also the author of the general map located at the end of the volume; among the recent documents used to create this general map, I must mention the maps provided in 1909 by the <term>district commanders: Known in French as "commandants de cercle," these were the primary administrative officers in the colonial districts.</term> at the same time as the monographs of their respective jurisdictions.

# CHAPTER ONE <note>original: "CHAPITRE PREMIER"</note> (1)

## Boundaries

**Extent and population.** — The colony of <term>Upper Senegal-Niger</term> <note>A vast administrative territory in French West Africa, existing under this name between 1904 and 1921; it covered much of what is now Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.</note>, including the Military Territory, has the following political and administrative boundaries: to the North, the Saharan territories falling under the General Government of Algeria; to the East, the Chad Territory, which forms part of the General Government of <term>French Equatorial Africa</term>; to the South, moving from East to West, the British colony of Northern Nigeria, the French colony of <term>Dahomey</term> <note>Now the Republic of Benin.</note>, the German colony of <term>Togo</term> <note>Germany held Togo as a protectorate from 1884 until it was divided between France and Britain after World War I.</note>, the British colony of the <term>Gold Coast</term> <note>Now the nation of Ghana.</note>, and the French colonies of the Ivory Coast and Guinea; to the West, the French colonies and territories of Senegal and Mauritania.

The whole represents an approximate surface area of **3 million square kilometers**, populated by **approximately 5,600,000 inhabitants**.

However, a notable portion of this area, about **1,200,000 square kilometers**, is composed of partly arid and desert lands that form the Military Territory of the Niger, which is populated by 800,000 inhabitants.

# THE LAND <note>original: "LE PAYS"</note>

The civil territory of the colony, or <term>Upper Senegal-Niger</term> <note>The administrative name for this region of French West Africa from 1904–1921.</note> proper, covers an area of approximately 1,800,000 square kilometers—more than triple the size of France—and contains roughly 4,800,000 inhabitants. This results in an average of **2 and a half inhabitants (exactly 2.66)** per square kilometer.

Reduced to this specific area, which is the sole subject of this volume, the colony of Upper Senegal-Niger corresponds roughly to the territories that, through long-standing habit, are still commonly called the *French Sudan* <note>A term often used colloquially or historically to describe the interior of West Africa before and during the colonial period; it eventually became the name of the modern Republic of Mali.</note>.

Its geographical boundaries remain imprecise to the Northwest, North, and Northeast, due to the desert nature of these regions and the more or less nomadic lifestyle of their inhabitants. One can, however, assign specific locations as the extreme limits of its Saharan marches: Tichit to the Northwest, Taodéni to the North, and Tessalit (situated across from and at the same latitude as Timiaouine) to the Northeast. At the first of these points, Upper Senegal-Niger touches the Mauritanian zone of influence; at the second, the Algerian zone of penetration; and at the third, the Saharan action zone of the Military Territory of the Niger. In reality, the zone of direct administration for the colony hardly exceeds the 17th parallel of north latitude to the West (approximately the Kiffa-Oualata line), while to the East it extends slightly north of the 19th parallel (the Araouâne-Bou-Djebiha line). North of this broken Kiffa-Oualata-Araouâne-Bou-Djebiha line, we primarily fulfill a role of policing and surveillance, and we maintain no fixed posts or permanent establishments.

**Boundary with Mauritania.** — The boundary between Upper Senegal-Niger and Mauritania, measured at the level of Tichit, is formed first by the extreme point of the <term>Djouf</term> <note>A vast, arid sedimentary basin in the Sahara, located between northern Mali and eastern Mauritania.</note>—a sandy region pushing between Tichit and Tidjikja—and then by a line following roughly the eastern edge of the heights encircling the <term>Tagant</term> plateau. It then curves westward around the southern part of these heights as far as the <term>Assaba</term> mountains, which serve as the starting point for the valley of the Gorgol-Noir <note>Literally "Black Gorgol," a river valley in southern Mauritania.</note>,

->### WESTERN BOUNDARY<-

From this point, the boundary turns quite sharply toward the Southeast, reaching the vicinity of Fété-Dioullé (to the Southwest of Kiffa) and joining the valley known by the names Tartafout, Bakhambora, and Karakoro. It follows this valley from Fété-Dioullé to its confluence with the Senegal River, located just upstream of the village of Kabou, between Ambidédi and Bakel.

The boundary with Mauritania is thereafter formed by the Senegal River itself, from the mouth of the Karakoro to that of the Falémé. From this latter point, the Senegal River leaves the colony of <term>Upper Senegal-Niger</term> <note>The administrative name for this region of French West Africa from 1904–1921; it was a precursor to the modern Republic of Mali.</note> entirely, giving its right bank to Mauritania and its left bank to the colony of Senegal.

**Boundary with Senegal.** — The boundary between Senegal and Upper Senegal-Niger is formed by the Falémé River (1), from its mouth in the Senegal River to a point located slightly upstream of Satadougou, where this river is formed by the junction of the Balinko and the Koundako. From this point forward, Guinea succeeds Senegal as the neighboring colony of Upper Senegal-Niger.

**Boundary with Guinea.** — The boundary between Guinea and Upper Senegal-Niger is formed as follows: first by the Balinko (or upper western Falémé), then by its tributary, the Kassaya, up to the hills from which the latter emerges; next, moving generally eastward through these hills, it follows the Dialako—which also originates there—to its confluence with the Koundako (or upper eastern Falémé). The boundary then descends the course of the Koundako to the point where this river meets the Kolounko; it then travels up the course of the Kolounko from its mouth to Mount Sagou, where the Kolounko begins. The border then crosses Mount Sagou and descends the Koroko stream from the eastern slope of the moun-

**Boundary with the Military Territory of Niger.** — From the mouth of the Mékrou, which is located level with the village of Boumba, the Niger River has formed the boundary between the Military Territory <note>The "Military Territory of Niger" was an administrative division of French West Africa created to manage the volatile frontier regions; it later became the Republic of Niger.</note> and the colony of Upper Senegal-Niger proper since January 1, 1911. This boundary ascends the <term>thalweg</term> <note>The deepest part of the river channel.</note> of the river to a point situated at approximately 17° North latitude and roughly halfway between Bourem and Bamba. At this point, the boundary leaves the Niger to follow a direction roughly North-Northeast up to 18° North latitude, then Northeast from this parallel to a location situated between Tessalit to the West and Timiaouine to the East at about 20°40' North latitude. This is drawn so as to leave the Tilemsi valley and the Adrar of the Ifoghas <note>A highland region in the Sahara, primarily in what is now northeastern Mali.</note> to the Military Territory, and the territory of the Kounta of Mabrouk <note>The Kounta are a prominent Arab-Berber tribal confederation of the Sahara.</note> to the civilian colony.

**Boundary with Algeria.** — From the region of Tessalit-Timiaouine, it is Algeria that becomes the neighbor of Upper Senegal-Niger. The boundary, which is entirely approximate, passes between the Tanezrouft to the North and the Adrar Timetrhine to the South, then between the Erg-ech-Châche to the North and, to the South, the heights (Djebel-el-Haricha) that overlook Taoudenni. # CHAPTER II (1)

## Hydrography. <note>Hydrography is the science that measures and describes the physical features of bodies of water, such as rivers and lakes.</note>

**Retrospective Hydrography.** — Before moving on to the study of the water systems <note>original: "régime hydrographique"</note> of Upper Senegal-Niger, it may be interesting to see what antiquity and the Middle Ages knew, or believed they knew, about the rivers of the Sudan, and how—quite recently—we arrived at a satisfactory understanding of the reality from these false or imperfect notions. This retrospective look could have been placed in the chapter on the exploration of French Sudan <note>The colonial name for the territory that now makes up much of modern Mali.</note>, but because the data we possess regarding a country’s water systems is of capital importance for its geographic understanding, I found it preferable to place this overview here.

It is likely that the mouth of the Senegal River was discovered as early as the 6th century BCE, around 570, by the Carthaginian navigator Hanno, when, having passed through the Strait of Gibraltar, he sailed South and advanced as far as the vicinity of present-day Sierra Leone. Unfortunately, the original account of his voyage, which he reportedly wrote in the Punic language <note>The language of ancient Carthage, derived from Phoenician.</note> and was preserved at Carthage, has never reached us; we only know it through a Greek translation made in Carthage by scholars whose names have not been revealed to us. Thus, the information provided by the oldest voyage accomplished along the western coasts of Africa only began to be utilized about two centuries after

However, whatever the extreme limit assigned to Hanno's maritime exploration, it is very probable—if the documents used by Ptolemy and other Greek geographers were not apocryphal <note>Apocryphal refers to writings of doubtful authenticity or questionable origin.</note>—that the Carthaginian admiral made landfall at the mouth of the Senegal River, and that it is this river to which he gave the name *Chretes* or *Khritis*.

A little later, around 550 BCE, some Phoenicians, by order of the Egyptian King Necho or Neko II, set sail on the Red Sea, traveled southward, and, three years after their departure, returned to Egypt via the Strait of Gibraltar and the Mediterranean. If this first circumnavigation of Africa, which Herodotus <note>A Greek historian often called the "Father of History."</note> made known to us, was truly carried out, it is possible that the Phoenicians who accomplished it also recognized the mouth of the Senegal; however, their voyage in any case left no traces in the geographical knowledge of their contemporaries.

The Greek historian Herodotus, who lived from approximately 484 to 410 BCE and who traveled in Egypt, Cyrenaica <note>A region in modern-day eastern Libya.</note>, and Libya, also tells us of another voyage of which he was a contemporary, as it was supposedly carried out under Xerxes, who reigned from 485 to 465 BCE. A relative of this king, named Sataspes, who had been condemned to death for violating a young girl, reportedly obtained a pardon through the intervention of his mother, the sister of Darius, on the condition that he sail around Africa. He departed from Egypt on a ship, passed through the Pillars of Hercules <note>The ancient name for the peaks flanking the entrance to the Strait of Gibraltar.</note>, then sailed southward for several months. He saw a land where the inhabitants dressed in palm leaves and from whom he took cattle to replenish his supplies. Then, terrified by the length of the journey remaining before him, he returned to Egypt by the same path he had followed on the way out. Xerxes, judging that he had not fulfilled the imposed conditions, had him crucified (2). The detail of the palm leaves is of a nature to make us believe that this Sataspes reached at least —

### HERODOTUS AND THE SUDAN

...at least Cape Verde, but that is all one is permitted to conjecture about this voyage.

Herodotus, moreover, does not speak of the Senegal; but it has been claimed that he was the first to reveal the existence of the Niger. To tell the truth, nothing is more doubtful. No doubt it is permissible, at a stretch, to suppose that it is the Niger he intends to speak of when he describes the *Cinyps*, "a country which bears the same name as the river by which it is watered" and which "can be compared with the best wheat lands: thus—Herodotus continues—it resembles in nothing the rest of Libya <note>In antiquity, "Libya" was the name used by the Greeks for the entire African continent known to them, or specifically the regions west of Egypt.</note>. It is a black earth watered by several springs: it has nothing to fear from drought, and, as excessive rains only serve to soak it, it suffers no damage. It does indeed rain in this part of Libya" (1). This description could certainly apply to the Niger valley, but as Herodotus gives us no indication of the situation of the *Cinyps*, other than it being part of "Libya," and as he gives this name of Libya to the entire region situated to the West of Cyrenaica <note>An ancient Greek and later Roman province in modern-day eastern Libya.</note>, from the Mediterranean to the limits of the then-known world, it is very difficult to assert that his *Cinyps* must be identified with our Niger.

Elsewhere (2) the same author recounts the famous adventure of the Nasamones <note>An ancient Berber people of North Africa.</note> in terms that have sometimes led to the supposition that the Niger had been the end point of this singular journey. Here is this story, as Herodotus learned it from several Cyreneans who, themselves, had heard it told by King Etearchus when they had gone to his country to consult the oracle of Ammon <note>The famous Oracle of Amun located in the Siwa Oasis.</note>. Five young Nasamones (3) of good family had made a bet to cross the deserts of Libya; having set out with supplies of water and food, they first crossed the inhabited lands of northern Libya, then a region filled with wild beasts, and then, heading westward, desert lands, waterless and very sandy. In my opinion (and assuming that the five young Nasamones did not abuse the credulity of their compatriots), the river mentioned cannot be identified with the Niger. If it were this river, the travelers would have reached it at the peak of its bend, since they found the "large river" immediately after leaving the desert, and it is unlikely that a people of pygmies <note>The original French uses "nains" (dwarves). In the context of historical African geography, this almost certainly refers to the various Pygmy ethnic groups.</note> ever existed in the region between Timbuktu and Gao. # FROM HERODOTUS TO PLINY

...was modified by tradition. On the other hand, it is fair to observe that Herodotus, assuming that the Nile crossed all of Libya <note>In ancient Greek geography, "Libya" generally referred to the entire African continent or the parts of it known to them west of the Nile.</note> before watering Egypt, implicitly identified its upper course with our Middle Niger.

And this is above all what is interesting from the perspective of the idea that the ancients could form of the hydrographic system of the Sudan <note>Historically, "Sudan" referred to the broad region of sub-Saharan Africa stretching from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, rather than the modern country of Sudan.</note>: for Herodotus, the South of Libya was crossed by a large river flowing from West to East which, upon reaching Nubia, became the Nile. And it is this idea, more or less modified, that would be accepted by all geographers until a relatively recent era.

However, the Greek philosopher Aristotle, who lived a century after Herodotus (384 to 322 BCE), adopts another theory which would also later have many supporters, among others Leo Africanus <note>A 16th-century North African diplomat and traveler whose descriptions of Africa were the primary source for Europeans for centuries.</note>: for him, from a common source located somewhere in the center of the Sudan, two large rivers flowed; one, heading East, then North, to empty into the Mediterranean, was the Nile; the other, flowing from East to West, went to empty into the Atlantic Ocean, thus corresponding to the Senegal. This second river is called *Chremetes* by Aristotle, and in this name one could strictly speaking find the *Chretes* of Hanno. Of the Niger, or a river corresponding to the Niger, there is no mention in Aristotle, who consequently confused it either with the Nile, or rather—by reversing its course—with the *Chremetes* or Senegal.

The Greek historian Polybius conducted a nautical reconnaissance along the western coast of the Maghreb around 130 BCE, by order of Scipio Aemilianus. Beyond the river *Darat* (Wadi Draa), he encountered Cape *Barce* (undoubtedly Cape Juby), then further south the river *Palsus* (perhaps the Saguia el-Hamra) and, further south still, the river *Bambotus*, which abounded in crocodiles and hippopotamuses and which, for that reason, people have believed could be identified with the Senegal.

### THE LAND

...distance from the Columns of Hercules <note>The ancient name for the peaks flanking the Strait of Gibraltar.</note>, he lost one of his ships and, in the face of his crew’s grumbling, was forced to turn back. Later, he organized a second expedition which was undoubtedly just as unfortunate but whose result, in any case, has always remained unknown. We owe the mention of these attempts to Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BC–24 AD).</note>, Pomponius Mela, and Pliny the Elder.

In short, after Aristotle, we must come to the Latin naturalist Pliny the Elder (23 to 79 AD) to find new information regarding the rivers of the Sudan <note>Referring here to the "Bilad al-Sudan" or "Land of the Blacks," the broad belt of territory south of the Sahara.</note>. This information is, moreover, not very explicit and quite confusing, but it is nonetheless interesting because it is to these accounts that the Niger owes its current name. Indeed, Pliny places a river in southern Libya <note>The ancient Greek and Roman term for the African continent.</note> that he calls the *Nigris* <note>original: "Nigris"</note> and which, very likely, corresponded in his mind to our Niger. Elsewhere, when recounting the expedition of Suetonius Paullinus in southern Morocco, which took place in 41 AD, Pliny tells us that a few miles south of the *Dyrin* mountains—that is to say, the Atlas—in a desert of black sand, the Roman general discovered a river called the *Ger* (pronounced "Guer"): this river was very likely the Guir of our maps, which flows out of the Bou-Denib region and heads toward the Touat under the successive names of Saoura and Oued Messaoud; but Pliny believed he could identify the *Ger* discovered by Suetonius Paullinus with a river he knew from what had been said shortly before him by King Juba II of Numidia <note>An ancient Berber kingdom in North Africa.</note>, who lived from 25 BC to 22 AD. Juba’s informants called this river **Niger** (pronounced "Niguer"); they described it as emerging from a lake called *Nilis*, located not far from the Atlantic, from where it flowed eastward, only to be lost underground and reappear much further away, emerging from a source called *Nigris*; then, taking the name *Astapus*, it formed one of the branches of the Nile.

Certainly, the river encountered by Suetonius Paullinus was not our Niger, nor, very probably, Juba’s Niger. But Pliny’s theory becomes easy to understand if one refers to the one later developed by Ptolemy and if one conjectures that Pliny identified Suetonius Paullinus’s *Ger* with a watercourse relatively close to the Guir and of course...

### THEORIES OF PLINY AND JUBA

...similar, at least in its beginnings—that is to say, with one of the branches of the Oued Ziz <term>Oued: A North African riverbed that remains dry except during the rainy season.</term>: *currently*, after watering the Tafilelt region, this river seems to lose itself south of that province in the sands of the Erg Iguidi <term>Erg: A vast area of shifting sand dunes.</term>, near Gourara; but in the past, it may have continued as far as the Faguibine depression through a series of temporary riverbeds whose traces can still be found today. In any case, it does not seem absurd to suppose that in a distant era, the Niger possessed a Saharan branch with a general North-South direction. This branch would have originated in the Atlas Mountains north of Tafilelt, near the sources of the Guir, passed west of Taodéni and Araouane, and eventually joined the Sudanese branch (coming from the mountains of Guinea) near the current site of Timbuktu—or rather, just to the west of it (1).

It is highly possible that this upper course of a hypothetical "Saharan Niger"—something like the modern Oued Ziz—was what Pliny confused with the *Ger* <note>original: "Ger"</note> mentioned by Suetonius Paullinus, and that he further sought to identify it with the *Niger* <note>original: "Niger"</note> of the Berber king, Juba.

As for this king <note>Juba II, the Roman-educated King of Mauretania (c. 48 BC – 23 AD).</note>, we can assume that through his Saharan countrymen, he possessed some knowledge of the Niger proper, or at least of its existence. The information he provided, which Pliny utilized, aligns with ancient beliefs regarding the river systems of the Sudan: his lake *Nilis* <note>original: "Nilis"</note> might correspond to the marshy lake region stretching from Lake Débo to Faguibine, where the Niger indeed begins to flow eastward. Since the lower course of the river was likely completely unknown to the Numidians <note>An ancient Berber people of North Africa.</note>, Juba supposed that, shortly—
