...around modern-day Gao, the waters of the Niger were lost underground—a hypothesis justified by the knowledge he likely had of several Saharan *oueds* <term>Oued: A North African riverbed that remains dry except during the rainy season.</term> with underground courses, such as the Oued Rirh; perhaps he also had a vague notion of the existence of the Tilemsi <note>The Tilemsi Valley is a major prehistoric riverbed in eastern Mali.</note> and took it for an overflow of the Niger's waters into the land. His *Nigris* <note>original: "Nigris"</note>, the point where the river supposedly reappeared at the surface, could correspond to Lake Chad, from which, according to general belief, he believed one of the upper branches of the Nile emerged under the name *Astapus* <note>original: "Astapus," likely referring to the Blue Nile or the Sobat River</note>.

In any case, what deserves to be remembered from the indications provided by Pliny—and what has indeed been remembered—is the name *Niger* <note>original: "Niger"</note> given to an important and somewhat mysterious river that watered the unknown lands located beyond the Libyan desert. This name has come down to us, and we apply it to a river that may not belong to the basin glimpsed by Suetonius Paullinus <note>The first Roman to lead an army across the Atlas Mountains into the Sahara (c. 41 AD).</note> nor to the one suspected by Juba, but which, in any case, is indeed—at least in one of its parts—the river that Pliny had surmised.

What is most remarkable in this entire matter is that the name “Niger” could apply perfectly to the river encountered near the Atlas Mountains by the Roman general, and that it applies even better to the now well-known river that passes near Timbuktu and waters Gao. In the Berber language, the syllable *gher* or *ghir* is a root expressing the idea of “moving water” and designating either the sea or a river, much like the word *bahr* <term>Bahr: An Arabic word used for both seas and large rivers, such as the Nile.</term> in Arabic. This is why, even today, the name *Ghir* (Guir) is given to the river of Igli, and why the Oulmidden <note>A major confederation of Tuareg people living in the Niger River valley.</note> call the river at Gao *egheriou-n-igheriouan* or *gher-n-igheren*, which is to say “the river of rivers”—an expression that could easily be translated by a traveler ignorant of Berber as “the Niger River.” And, regardless of the degree of accuracy in the information gathered by Pliny, this is indeed the etymology of the name Niger; it has no connection to the skin color of those living along its banks <note>The Latin word for "black" is "niger," which led to the long-standing mistaken belief that the river was named for the race of the people living there.</note>, just as the derivatives *Nigrites*, *Nigritae*, and *Nigritia* <note>original Latin/Greek terms for the inhabitants and the region of the Niger.</note> that the Greeks and Latins derived from it simply meant “the people of the Niger” or “the region of the Niger.” It was only at...

### THEORIES OF PTOLEMY

It was only in a relatively recent era (the 16th century) that the ignorance of certain cartographers turned "Nigritia" into a synonym for "Sudan"—that is to say, "land of the Blacks"—and that equally ill-informed ethnologists invented a "Nigritic race" to be contrasted with the white race. In reality, the *Nigrites* of the ancients were "Nigerians," a group including white Berbers as well as Black people, and "Nigritia" is the absolute equivalent of the name *Nigeria* given by the British to their colony along the banks of the Niger (1).

The Greek mathematician and geographer Ptolemy, who lived a century after Pliny the Elder and composed his geography around 150 AD based on earlier documents—and particularly those of Pliny and Marinus of Tyre <note>Original: "Martin de Tyr." The author likely refers to Marinus of Tyre, the Phoenician geographer whose work served as the foundation for Ptolemy's *Geography*.</note>—gave us a relatively extensive description of the course of the Niger. He cites a number of cities near or bordering this river and even provides the astronomical position of one of them, which he calls *Thamondakana*. Unfortunately, Ptolemy’s latitudes and longitudes, obtained by estimating distances based on days of travel, are rarely accurate, especially when dealing with countries far from his base of operations and about which he possessed little information; such was the case for the Niger regions.

Ptolemy clearly distinguishes the *Nigher* or *Nighir* from the *Gher* or *Ghir*, but it appears that his Niger—at least in its upper portion—was the same one described by Pliny, interpreting in his own way the accounts of Suetonius Paullinus <note>A Roman general who led an expedition across the Atlas Mountains.</note>; that is to say, the Oued Ziz <term>Oued: A riverbed in North Africa that is often dry except during rainy seasons.</term>. Indeed, he has one of its northern branches emerging from Mount *Sagapola*, which he also identifies as the source of the *Subus*—the Sebou river that passes through Fez—and the other from Mount *Usargala*, near which he also places the source of the *Ghir*. This latter was undoubtedly the true *Ger* of Suetonius Paullinus and very likely our modern Oued Guir (2).

# THE COUNTRY

These two northern branches corresponded well with the two main branches of the Oued Ziz <note>A river in Morocco that flows from the High Atlas mountains into the Saharan desert.</note>.

On the other hand, he claimed the main branch of his Niger originated from Mount *Mandros*, which he also gave as the source for the *Salathos*—likely representing the Tensift or the river of Marrakech—and for the *Massa* (Pliny’s *Masatat*), which is undoubtedly the modern-day Souss. This would suggest that Ptolemy’s Niger was formed by the joining of the Oued Ziz with the Dades, or the upper branch of the Dara (the Oued Draa), which is obviously impossible. However, one should not place too much confidence in Ptolemy's information, even regarding regions near the Mediterranean: indeed, does he not claim that Mount *Usargala* is the source for the *Nighir* (assuming this Nighir is the Oued Ziz), the *Ghir*, and the *Bagradas*, even though this last river is surely the Bedjerda or Medjerda, which empties into the Gulf of Tunis and has its source in the Aurès <note>A mountain range in eastern Algeria.</note> nearly a thousand kilometers from the Moroccan Atlas? Furthermore, does he not tell us that the Dara (the Oued Draa of our maps), which he calls the *Daras* or *Darados*, flows from a Mount *Kaphas* near his mounts *Sagapola* and *Usargala* and is located like them in the Moroccan Atlas—which is correct—yet elsewhere states that the same river is an outflow of his *Nighir*?

In any case, this *Nighir* or Niger, once formed by the union of the three branches coming out of the Moroccan Atlas, headed South toward a Mount *Thala* (?) and ended at a Nigritic lake, which could very well correspond to the current lake region of Timbuktu (Pliny's *Nilis*); from there, it flowed East to form the Libyan lake (undoubtedly Pliny's *Nigris*, meaning probably Lake Chad). Here we find once again the theory of the *Niger flowing toward Lake Chad, and then toward the Nile.*

# THE COUNTRY

...that is to say, the Soninké <note>A West African ethnic group known as the founders of the Ghana Empire and for their extensive trade networks.</note>, who had more contact than others with travelers coming from the Maghreb <note>The region of Northwest Africa, primarily modern-day Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia.</note>. It is also not unlikely that Ptolemy situated these mines further north than they actually are, placing them on the northern bank of the Senegal instead of the southern bank, and that he viewed the river that waters the Ouangara (the Senegal) as a simple branch of the Niger: this same theory was later adopted by Arab and European geographers. But this is merely a hypothesis.

The rudimentary sketch of Sudanese geography <note>In this context, "Sudanese" refers to the *Bilad al-Sudan* (Land of the Blacks), the vast region south of the Sahara, rather than the modern nation of Sudan.</note> drafted by Greek and Latin scholars remained for eight centuries in the state Ptolemy had left it. We must look to the Arabs to see it develop and become more precise, albeit within limited bounds. In the 10th century AD, Ibn Hawqal completed a journey to the northern border of the land of the Blacks and saw part of the middle course of the Niger, which he named the *Nile* <note>original: *Nil*</note>, assuming that it flowed East as far as Nubia and merged there with the river of Egypt, just as Pliny and Ptolemy had supposed. Al-Bakri, who lived in the 11th century and who—likely thanks to the excellence of the documents he was able to use—is certainly the best and most accurate of all Arab geographers concerning the northern Sudan, provides us with the first information on the course of the Senegal and completes Ibn Hawqal's data regarding the Niger. Unfortunately, he confuses these two rivers under the single name of the *Nile*, although he nonetheless distinguishes them implicitly by describing the *Nile* of Tekrur <note>An ancient state located along the lower Senegal River.</note> as flowing into the Atlantic and the *Nile* of Ras-el-Ma <note>A location near Lake Faguibine in modern-day Mali, once an important crossroads.</note> as flowing toward the East. Al-Idrisi, who lived in the following century, did little more than reproduce Al-Bakri's indications with much less accuracy and precision; in his work, too, there is only mention of the *Nile*, sometimes flowing from East to West in the region of Tekrur and emptying...

# THE NAME OF SENEGAL

...into the Atlantic (Senegal), at other times flowing from West to East in the region of Gao (Niger), only to merge in Nubia <note>A region along the Nile river, encompassing northern Sudan and southern Egypt.</note> with the Nile of Egypt.

The famous geographer *Yaqut* <note>Yaqut al-Hamawi (1179–1229), a Greek-born geographer and biographer known for his comprehensive geographical encyclopedia, the *Mu'jam al-Buldan*.</note> (13th century) likewise sticks to the name *Nile* for the Senegal, the Niger, and the true Nile; however, he seems to have had a premonition that the Nile of Gao (the Niger) was not the same river as the Nile of Egypt, which he describes as originating from the "Mountains of the Moon" <note>An ancient term for a legendary mountain range in East Africa thought to be the source of the Nile.</note>. *Ibn Sa'id* <note>Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi (1213–1286), a geographer from the Maghreb who traveled extensively through the Islamic world.</note>, who died in 1286, deliberately creates a single river basin for the Niger, Lake Chad, and the Nile, encompassing the whole under the everlasting name of *Nile*; *Abu al-Fida* <note>An Arab geographer and historian (1273–1331) from the Ayyubid dynasty.</note> does the same at the beginning of the 14th century: these two geographers seem to have been unaware of the Senegal. The same is true of the famous traveler *Ibn Battuta* <note>Often called the "Marco Polo of the Muslim world," Ibn Battuta (1304–1368) was a Moroccan explorer who traveled more than 75,000 miles across Africa, Asia, and Europe.</note> who, around 1352, visited part of the upper Niger slightly upstream from Segou and described the course of this river downstream as far as Nupe <note>A historical state located in central Nigeria.</note>: for him, too, this river was the Nile and, from Nupe, he has it going toward Dongola <note>An important city on the Nile in modern-day Sudan, capital of the medieval kingdom of Makuria.</note>.

At the time when *Ibn Battuta* was making his journey, Norman, Spanish, and Italian navigators had already begun to sail along the western coast of Africa and had rediscovered—about two thousand years after the Carthaginian admiral *Hanno* <note>A 5th-century BC explorer from Carthage whose "Periplus" describes an expedition down the West African coast.</note>—the mouth of the Senegal: it was they who gave this river the name it still bears. It is commonly said that this name comes from the fact that the *Zenaga* or *Sanaga* Berbers lived on its northern bank, but it is quite possible that this etymology is inaccurate and that the Senegal received its name from the country through which its lower course flows: this country is called *Senegana* or *Sangana* by *Al-Bakri* <note>An 11th-century Andalusian-Arab geographer who wrote the "Book of Roads and Kingdoms" based on reports from merchants.</note>, who seems to apply this term to a region or a tribe occupying roughly the territory shared today by the *Trarza* Moors and the *Wolof*, that is to say, straddling the lower Senegal. This name *Senegana* certainly has nothing to do with that of the *Zenaga*: first, because the spelling adopted by *Al-Bakri* for the two words is completely different; second, because the Moors have preserved this term even today, in the form *Isongán*, to designate the Wolof bank of the lower Senegal, and they pronounce and write this latter word in a very distinct way...

### ANCIENT IDEAS ABOUT THE NIGER

...name, that the map of Livio Sanuto <note>An Italian cosmographer (1540–1576) whose work *Geografia* was published posthumously in 1588.</note> (1588) indicates the *Zanhagæ populi* <note>original: "Sanhaja people"</note> and the *Çanaga fluvius* <note>original: "Senega river"</note>. Marmol <note>Luis del Mármol Carvajal (c. 1520–1600), a Spanish chronicler who wrote a detailed description of Africa.</note> (late 16th century) tells us indeed that the river watering the kingdom of Gualata (Oualata) was momentarily called the "river of the Senecas" <note>meaning the Zenaga or Sanhaja Berbers</note>, but he undoubtedly meant by this the Niger and not the Senegal; in any case, he informs us that the lower river—here, he is indeed referring to the Senegal—was called *Senedec* by the Senegues (Zenaga) and *Senega* by the Portuguese because a navigator of that nation—specifically Lancelot du Lac, who visited the Senegal in 1447—had given the river the name of a kingdom whose prince he had first traded with (1): the inhabitants of this kingdom, probably Wolofs, themselves called this river *Ovidech*. It seems permissible to conclude from all this that the name of the Senegal comes, rather than from that of the Zenaga, from the word *Senegana* or *Senegan*, which formerly designated the Wolofs and their country and which still designates today, at least among the Moors, the part of the Senegal valley inhabited by the Wolofs.

Cadamosto <note>Alvise Cadamosto (c. 1432–1488), a Venetian slave trader and explorer hired by Prince Henry the Navigator.</note>, who visited the coast of Senegal in 1455 and 1457, considers this river, the Niger, and the Nile to be the same watercourse coming from the interior of the continent and sending one branch toward Egypt and another (the Niger) toward the Atlantic, where it emptied through two channels, the Senegal and the Gambia. Ramusio (1550) established—based on indications provided by Leo <note>Referring to Leo Africanus (c. 1494–1554), a diplomat and author famous for his descriptions of African geography.</note>—a map on which the Niger, at the height of Timbuktu, begins to form a delta whose main branches are the Senegal, the Gambia, and the Rio-Grande. Thevet (1575) reproduces on his "Map of Africa" the indications from Ramusio and gives three mouths to the Niger: the Senegal, the Gambia, and the Rio-Grande; the main novelty of his map consists in the literal translation he made of the word "Niger": he deliberately writes **Black River** <note>original: "Noir Fl." (Fleuve Noir)</note>. As for Marmol, who is primarily inspired by Barros in his *General Description of Africa* published from 1573 to 1599, he supports the theory of the delta formed by the Senegal and the Gambia; he informs us elsewhere that his "Niger-Senegal" bears, from Timbuktu to the Ocean, the successive names of *Oued-Nichar* (Niger River) among the Arabs, *Yça* or *Iza* among the people of "Tombut" <note>Timbuktu</note>, *Zimbala* or *Zimbale* among the people living to the east of "Tocror" <note>Takrur, an ancient state in the Senegal River valley</note>, *Colle* among the "Saragoles" <note>The Sarakollé or Soninke people</note>, *Maye* among the "Turcorons" or "Tucorons" or "Tucorols" <note>The Toucouleur people</note>, *Dengueh* among the "Ialofes" or "Gelofes" <note>The Wolof people</note>, and *Senedec* among the "Sénègues" <note>The Zenaga Berbers</note>, the name *Senega* being given by the Portuguese to the end of its lower course; he adds that the confluence of the "white river" (Bakhoy) and the "red river" (Baoulé) is called *Busitemba* by the "Saragoles" (1).

# THE NIGER IDENTIFIED

Livio Sanuto (1588) departs from his predecessors by listing three nearly parallel rivers flowing from East to West and emptying into the Atlantic, with distinct sources, courses, and mouths; these rivers are, from North to South: the *Çanaga*, which moreover represents both the middle Niger and the Senegal, the *Gambia*, and finally the *Niger*, which in reality corresponds to the Rio-Grande.

At the end of the 17th century, the Dutch geographer Dapper <note>Olfert Dapper (1636–1689), a Dutch physician and writer famous for his detailed geographical works, though he never traveled to Africa himself.</note> still confused the Niger and the Senegal into a single river and attributed to it an East-West course with a multiple delta. He carelessly identifies the *Sanaga* with the *Daras* of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian mathematician whose maps influenced geography for over a millennium.</note> — which was the Dara or Wadi Draa, as I mentioned above — and reproduces Marmol's indications on the origin of the name given to the Senegal by the Portuguese, as well as on the different names of this river and the Niger along their course, adding only that the word *Zimbala* is used among the *Baganes*, that is to say, no doubt the Mandé people of Bagana or Baghena.

Four years after Dapper's work had been translated into French, in 1690, the Sieur La Courbe, Inspector General of the Senegal Company, pushed a reconnaissance as far as the Félou Falls (near and upstream from Médine) and was the first to assert that the Senegal and the Niger could not be one and the same river.

However, geographers were still some time before admitting the truth: Guillaume Delisle first shared the old error and, in his maps published from 1700 to 1707, also confused the Senegal with the Niger; but in 1722, he assigned a distinct basin to each of the four rivers to which he gave the names Senegal, Gambia, Rio-Grande, and Niger. Finally, d'Anville <note>Jean-Baptiste Bourguignon d'Anville (1697–1782), a French cartographer who revolutionized the field by removing speculative features from maps.</note>, in the second half of the 18th century, returned to the theory of the great Arab geographers and had the Niger flow toward the East, achieving real progress over the Arabs, since he clearly distinguished its basin from that of the Senegal;

...*bala*, which means "place of the great water" and which is given today to part of the Niger's flood zone. As for *Busitemba*, this term can be compared to *Badoumbé*, which means "red river" in Soninke <note>A Mande language spoken by the Soninke people of West Africa.</note>.

<header>THE COUNTRY</header>

...but he was still unaware of the lower course of the Niger and had it ending in the interior of the Sudan <note>The "Sudan" here refers to the vast "Bilad al-Sudan" region of West Africa, rather than the modern nation-state.</note>.

It was not until 1830 that the problem of the Niger’s mouth was definitively resolved. When Mungo Park set out on his first voyage in 1795, he was convinced that the Niger flowed into the Congo; at that time, he was only able to descend it as far as a short distance downstream from Sansanding. In 1805, he made a new attempt which ended the following year with his death and that of his last companions in the Bussa Rapids, such that the lower Niger still kept its secret. Furthermore, Mungo Park, by lending credence to the legend of the Mountains of Kong <note>A non-existent mountain range that appeared on maps of West Africa for nearly a century until proven mythical in the late 1880s.</note> based on erroneous reports, contributed to the persistent ignorance regarding the hydrography of the Niger Bend, particularly the upper course of the Volta—an ignorance that only ended in 1889 with the exploration of Mr. Binger. However, in 1817, James Riby, anticipating later discoveries, asserted that the Niger, after describing the arc of the circle that was already known, eventually flowed into the Gulf of Guinea. The following year, Mollien, without identifying the exact location of the sources of the Senegal and the Gambia, provided good indications of the region where the high tributaries of these two rivers originate, and definitively debunked the legend of connections between these rivers or between one of them and the Niger. Four years later (1822), Gordon Laing indicated the approximate location of the sources of the Niger. Shortly after (1824), Denham, Clapperton, and Oudney demonstrated that the Niger and Lake Chad constituted two entirely different basins. Finally, in 1830, Richard Lander—formerly Clapperton's servant, who had already reached Bussa in 1826 with his master shortly before the latter's death at Sokoto—reached the river at that same point in Bussa which had been the tragic terminus of Mungo Park’s journey. He descended it by canoe to the Gulf of Benin: the entire course of the great Sudanese river, at least in its broad outlines, was definitively known, eighteen centuries after Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author who provided some of the earliest, albeit vague, European accounts of African geography.</note> had first spoken of it. There remained only to determine the exact location of its sources, one of the prin-

There remained the Volta, to which, due to the belief in the famous chain of the Mountains of Kong <note>A legendary mountain range that appeared on maps for a century until it was proven to be a myth in the 1880s.</note>, was accorded only a very limited extent. **Comoé Basin.** — The watercourses that irrigate Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A former administrative territory of French West Africa existing in the early 20th century.</note> all belong to the basins of four rivers of varying importance, which are, in order of length, *the Niger, the Volta, the Senegal, and the Comoé* (2).

---

(1) The Volta owes its name either to the sinuosities <note>twists and turns</note> of its lower course, which supposedly led the Portuguese to name it so <note>From the Portuguese "volta," meaning "turn."</note>, or to the name the indigenous people give to its mouth, which, according to what I have been told, is *Folita*. Like all great African rivers, it does not carry a specific name in local languages, and each riverside tribe designates it by a word that, in their idiom, means nothing other than "the river" (*Mâné* among the Dagari, *Miro* among the Lobi, *Môrhe* among the Nunuma, etc.). The same is true for the Senegal and the Niger, as Marmol and Dapper <note>Luis del Mármol Carvajal and Olfert Dapper, 16th and 17th-century geographers.</note> had already observed. However, the Mande-speaking peoples often designate the Niger—besides the word *ba* which simply means "river"—by the more particular name *Bâba* (the great river) or *Dioliba* <note>original: "Dioliba"</note>, which means "the river of the *Dieli*," that is to say, the "griots" or professional singers and musicians; likewise, the Hausa call it either *Baba-n-goulbi* (the great river), or *Kwara*, a word for which I do not know the etymology.

(2) Contrary to the indications given by certain maps, the Bandama basin is entirely outside of Upper Senegal-Niger: the watercourses originating near Ngorho (district of Bobo-Dioulasso) and sometimes listed as upper tributaries of the Bandama are in reality some tributaries of the Bagbé (Niger basin), and others tributaries of the Léraba (Comoé basin). The surveys carried out in the Korhogo district from 1904 to 1907, notably those of Mr. Terrasson de Fougères, demonstrated that the Bandama took its source south of the road from Korhogo to Tombougou, crossed this road, and circled Korhogo to the north before heading south.

# THE LAND

64

is only of moderate interest to Upper Senegal-Niger, for it only waters the territory through the upper reaches of its furthest branches: the Léraba (River of Léra) or upper western Comoé, and the *Komonoba* (River of the Komono) or upper eastern Comoé, along with a few of their tributaries. These branches or tributaries, often dry or nearly so during part of the year, are never navigable—not even for canoes. Far from contributing to the fertility of the land they water, they instead render it partially uninhabitable due to the vast, unusable, and unhealthy marshes that border them during the high-water season. It is well known, moreover, that the lower course of the Comoé is itself unsuitable for navigation; it is frequently broken, up to about 60 kilometers upstream from its mouth, by rapids that the smallest steamers and often even canoes cannot cross. Additionally, it is deprived of sea access due to the Grand-Bassam sandbar <note>A "barre" is a dangerous accumulation of sand at a river's mouth, common along the West African coast, which creates violent surf and hinders ship entry.</note>.

Let us note, for the record, that the Léraba and the Komonoba (also called the Baoulé) both take their source a short distance from one another in the country of the Tagba or Tagoua (within the district of Bobo-Dioulasso), between Sifarasso and Ouorodara, roughly at the same latitude as Bobo-Dioulasso and to the west of that city.

**Senegal Basin.** — The Senegal River is quite another matter. Not only does this river—from its most remote source, that of the Bafing, to its mouth—measure approximately 1,500 kilometers in length (double that of the Comoé), but its width, its water flow, and its relative depth even at the lowest water levels in its lower course make it far superior. Its clearly defined banks are less prone to flooding, and there is the possibility for ships—though not continuously and often with difficulty—to cross the Saint-Louis sandbar and pass directly from the Ocean into the river. Finally, and most importantly, the 700 kilometers from Saint-Louis to Kayes are navigable in all seasons for barges, for five months of the year for steamers with a 1.3-meter draft <note>The "draft" is the vertical distance between the waterline and the bottom of the ship's hull; it determines the minimum depth of water required for a vessel to float.</note>, and for two to three months for high-tonnage ships with a 4-meter draft. These factors make the Senegal a precious transport route for the colony of Upper Senegal-Niger.

# SENEGAL

65

5

Although the irregularities of navigation do not provide complete satisfaction, and we find ourselves forced to bypass, in a way, the Senegal River by using the railway currently under construction from Kayes to Thiès-Dakar, it is no less true that the Senegal has been, until now, the only access route to the French Sudan <note>A colonial territory in French West Africa, roughly corresponding to modern-day Mali.</note>. It will always remain, even after the completion of the Thiès-Kayes line, an excellent and economical transport route during part of the year.

The Senegal River proper is formed at Bafoulabé (the "meeting of two rivers") by the joining of the *Bafing* (Black River) and the *Bakhoy* or *Badié* or even *Bagoué* (White River); the latter owes its importance to its tributary, the *Baoulé* (Red River), which it receives between Toukoto and Badoumbé. The *Bafing* takes its source in Guinea, not far from Timbo and the Koumi pass, in the same mountain massif from which the *Tinkisso* flows—one of the branches of the upper Niger. The *Bakhoy* also originates in Guinea, some distance to the northwest of Siguiri. As for the *Baoulé*, its basin is entirely contained within Upper Senegal-Niger: it is originally formed by several streams that take their source in the hills running along the Niger between Kangaba and Bamako, one of which flows from Kati, only twelve kilometers from the Niger. This indicates how narrow the zone is that separates the upper basin of the Senegal from the upper valley of the Niger.

The Senegal only becomes navigable downstream of Kayes, after receiving on its right bank a fairly significant tributary, the *Kolembiné* (Black River), which comes from the region of the pools <note>original: "mares"</note> neighboring Nioro. A little beyond Ambidédi, another tributary also flows into its right bank: this is the *Karakoro* <term>marigot</term> <note>A West African term for a seasonal stream, side channel, or creek.</note>, which serves as the boundary between Upper Senegal-Niger and Mauritania. Finally, just before reaching Bakel and at the moment it leaves Upper Senegal-Niger, the Senegal receives—on its left bank this time—a very important tributary, the *Falémé*. This river takes its source on the border of Guinea, not far from the source of the Gambia River, and serves as the boundary of Upper Senegal-Niger from its upper course to its mouth, with the exception of a small portion of its lower course, near—

## The Volta Basin

**The Volta** is slightly longer than the Senegal, as it measures more than 1,600 kilometers from the furthest source of the Black Volta to the river's mouth in the Gulf of Guinea. However, regarding Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A massive French colonial territory in West Africa existing under this name from 1904 to 1921.</note>, it is of much less interest than the Senegal River. First, its mouth is located in a British colony (Gold Coast <note>Modern-day Ghana.</note>) and its lower course is entirely in foreign territory, sometimes flowing through the British colony, sometimes serving as the border between the latter and the German colony of Togo. Furthermore, its mouth is in much the same situation as that of the Comoé; that is to say, it is obstructed by a sandbar <term>barre: a ridge of sand at a river's mouth that makes navigation dangerous or impossible for large ships</term> impassable for ships. Finally, the lower reach <term>bief: a specific stretch or section of a river</term>, where vessels of a certain tonnage can circulate, only begins after the river has entered the Gold Coast, near the confluence of the Black Volta and the White Volta.

In truth, one can utilize a portion of the Black Volta flowing through French territory—from Koury to the confluence of the Bougouriha and even, if necessary, to where it meets the 10th parallel of north latitude (approximately 330 kilometers)—for navigation using flat-bottomed barges <note>original: "chalands"</note> of 2 to 5 tons. However, these transports, having no outlet to the South or the North, can only be of purely local interest. They would only be called upon for any significant development if the Black Volta were connected either to the Bani River by a railway from Koury to San, or to the future extension of the railways of the Ivory Coast, Guinea, or Upper Senegal-Niger. Additionally, while it is generally easy to descend the Black Volta by barge, it is sometimes very difficult to travel back up against the current. Finally, the lack of depth upstream of Koury, the frequency of rapids downstream of the 10th parallel north, and the violence of these rapids from the point where the Volta enters the Gold Coast restrict the extent of this relatively navigable reach far too much.

The branches and major tributaries of the upper Volta, like those of the upper Comoé, have excessively marshy banks and

# THE VOLTA

67

Generally uninhabitable for a width of 2 to 5 kilometers on each bank, both because of the presence of tsetse flies <note>Flies that carry parasites causing "sleeping sickness" (trypanosomiasis) in humans and livestock.</note> and because of the clayey nature of the soil, which turns into thick mud during floods and hardens when the waters recede. These floods are generally due not to the overflowing of the rivers—the Black Volta, in particular, has very high banks—but to the lack of drainage for rainwater. This water accumulates along the river in a sort of basin <note>original: "cuvette"</note> lower than the bank itself, which only connects at long intervals to the main branch via tributaries that, moreover, exhibit the same layout.

The *Black Volta* <note>original: "Volta Noire"</note> or Western Volta is the longest and most important of the two main branches whose meeting, near and to the west of Salaga, forms the Volta proper. It takes its source at Sifarasso, south of and near the road from Sikasso to Bobo-Dioulasso, very close to the sources of the Comoé. Due to a rather peculiar phenomenon, the Volta follows a course roughly parallel to that of the Niger, forming a loop certainly much more modest than that of the latter river but with an analogous curve and direction: after flowing toward the northeast as far as Koury—like the Niger as far as Timbuktu <note>original: "Tombouctou"</note>—it then bends toward the east, then toward the southeast, much as the Niger behaves between Timbuktu and the 11th parallel of north latitude. Beyond that same parallel, just as the Niger heads clearly south as far as Jebba <note>original: "Djebba"</note>, only to flow thereafter toward the east-southeast until the confluence of the Benue <note>original: "Bénoué"</note> and finally resume a southern direction to its mouth, the Volta similarly heads south during the entire part of its course that serves as the boundary for the French and English possessions, then east-southeast until the confluence of the Oti, and finally south to the sea.

The main tributaries of the Black Volta, in the portion of its course belonging to Upper Senegal-Niger, are: on its right bank, the *Poni* or *Bammasso*, which waters Gaoua, and the *Bougouriba*, which waters Diébougou; on its left bank, the *Sourou*, which rises not far from Ouahigouya, describes a loop in the opposite direction to that of the Black Volta, and ends at Koury; when the flood occurs...

The *White Volta* or Eastern Volta originates in the districts <note>original: "cercles," an administrative division used in French West Africa.</note> of Ouahigouya and Dori, via two branches taking their source to the Southwest and East of Djibo; it follows a noticeably North-South course. In the Gold Coast <note>The British colony that became modern-day Ghana.</note>, it receives a tributary of modest importance on its right bank called the *Red Volta*, the course of which begins near and to the west of Ouagadougou.

The third branch of the Volta, the *Oti*, is formed by the joining of the *Pépiénou*, which takes its source between Koupéla and Fada-n-Gourma, and the *Pendjari*, which originates in Dahomey <note>Modern-day Benin.</note> and traverses the district of Fada-n-Gourma in immense loops.

**The Niger Basin.** — With the Niger, we come to a hydrographic basin of much greater importance. From Tembi-Kounda (on the border of Guinea and Sierra Leone) to Akassa (the central point of the Niger delta), this immense body of water is no less than 3,800 kilometers long—almost exactly the combined lengths of the Volta, the Senegal, and the Comoé rivers put together.

After being enlarged by the Milo from the East and the Tinkisso from the West, the Niger enters Upper Senegal-Niger <note>original: "Haut-Sénégal-Niger," a French colonial territory in West Africa existing under this name from 1904 to 1921.</note> downstream from Siguiri. Opposite Kangaba, it receives the *Sankarani* on its right bank, then flows as far as Koulikoro through a rocky valley that is often very narrow and obstructed by powerful rapids between Bamako and Koulikoro. Among these rapids, one should mention those of Sotuba, near Bamako, where the most important branch of the river is not always thirty meters wide.

Downstream from Koulikoro, the valley widens; the hills that form it lower and gradually space further apart, rocks give way to sandbanks, the banks flatten out, and the riverbed is slowly transformed into a sheet of water whose extent is governed solely by the rise and fall of the floods. Starting from Ségou, the Niger is no longer a river in the strict sense, but a shallow valley...

# THE NIGER SYSTEM

This *Bani* (meaning "small river" in the Mande language) or *Mayèl-Balévèl* (meaning "black river" in the Fula language <note>original: "langue peule."</note>) is essentially the only important tributary of the Niger, but it constitutes a true river in its own right, with a main branch over 900 kilometers long. This main branch, called the *Bågbe* or *Bagoé* (meaning "white river") in its upper course, takes its source in the Ivory Coast, south of the road from Odienné to Tombougou, enters Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A French colonial territory in West Africa existing from 1904 to 1921.</note> between Tengréla and Ngorho, and is successively enlarged by the *Bâfing* (meaning "black river"), the *Bânigbe* (meaning "little white river"), and the *Baoulé* (*red river*), all three of which also originate in the Ivory Coast; it then receives the *Bânifing* (meaning "little black river"), becomes the Bani, passes by San and Djenné, and merges with the Niger at Mopti.

As I mentioned earlier, connections have already been established between the Niger and the Bani; or rather, as two valleys are no longer enough to carry the enormous quantity of water arriving from both sides of Djenné, the Niger transforms into a maze of channels which will soon be intermingled with lakes, forming an exceedingly curious and interesting system from Djenné to Timbuktu <note>original: "Tombouctou."</note>. In this region, recognizing exactly where the proper bed of the Niger lies is nearly impossible.

At Diafarabé, to the west-northwest of Djenné, the river forms a V-shape, one arm of which heads toward Mopti (which is called *Issa-ka* in the Songhai language, meaning "arrival of the river") and the other, known as the *Dia* or *Diaga*, toward Lake Débo. Downstream from Mopti, there is a new connection via a transverse channel between the two main channels, which reunite in Lake Débo after giving rise to a third channel, the *Kolikoli*, which heads toward Saraféré via Lake Korienza. At the outlet of Lake Débo, one of the two main channels, the *Issa-Ber* (meaning "great river" in Songhai), heads toward Niafounké, while the other, the *Bara-Issa* (meaning "river of the Bara"), joins the Korienza channel at Saraféré. [Oua]ledji, at the place called *Issa-fer* (meaning "river's divide" <note>original: "partage du fleuve"</note>), to form shortly after, by splitting once again, the island of *Koura*, a little downstream from Timbuktu <note>original: "Tombouctou."</note>.

Between Niafounké and El-Oualedji, the western branch serves several lakes, the main ones being *Lake Horo* and *Lake Fati*, and those of lesser importance being lakes *Tenda*, *Kabara*, *Soumpi*, *Takadyi*, and *Gaouati*; between El-Oualedji and Koura, it also serves the great lakes of Goundam and Ras-el-Ma—also known as *Hari-bongo* or *Issa-bongo* (words which mean, the first in Arabic and the other two in Songhay <note>original: "songaï"</note>, "head of the water" or "head of the river"): lakes *Télé*, *Faguibine* or *Fangabina*, *Daouna-korina*, and *Daouna-ber*, while the eastern branch serves lakes *Haribongo*, *Garou*, *Dô*, *Nangaï*, *Hagoundou*, *Koratou*, etc.

All this part of the middle Niger valley, contained generally between Sansanding and Timbuktu, is a true lacustrine <note>A region characterized by lakes.</note> region, whose appearance changes strangely according to the seasons and where, independent of the main branches and lakes just listed, there exist numerous diversion channels and temporary lakes or ponds. This region constitutes the Niger's flood zone, an area which, during periods of high flood, covers a width of 150 to 200 kilometers, from which nothing emerges but the hillocks where the villages are built.

It is easy to conclude from the preceding the importance of the Niger from the dual perspective of agriculture and transport facilities. The lands of the Niger valley, whose clayey nature is tempered by a sufficient quantity of sand, do not become hard and brittle like those of the Volta basin when the floodwaters recede. On the contrary, they become a wonderfully fertile soil, favorable for cultivation as well as the growth of grazing grasses. It is not bold to think that, now that the security guaranteed to the local inhabitants allows them to attach themselves more closely to their land, the middle Niger region will rapidly become the wealthiest in all the Sudan <note>Referring to the geographical "Sudan" region of West Africa, rather than the modern country of the same name.</note>.

Furthermore, the products harvested there will find...

# THE NIGER

71

...in the Niger itself, an economical and relatively constant transport route: shallow-draft steamers <note>Boats designed with a flat bottom to navigate shallow waters without running aground.</note> can indeed travel for six months of the year between Koulikoro and Gao, and for the rest of the time, barges can be used under satisfactory conditions. These barges can even, in January and February, continue beyond Gao as far as Niamey. The small section of the river where rapids prevent navigation, between Koulikoro and Bamako, has been bypassed by a railway line: so that, through the successive use of railways and rivers, there is currently a reasonably satisfactory transport route from the port of Dakar to Gao. This route will be further improved by the completion of the direct line from Dakar to Koulikoro via Thiès, Diourbel, and Kayes.

The upper reach of the Niger is also navigable for a good part of the year, though under less favorable conditions, between Bamako and Kouroussa, where the railway line starting from the port of Conakry arrived just a few months ago. One can also travel up several of the Upper Niger's tributaries by barge, reaching Kankan from Bamako and Siguiri via the Milo River, and traveling from Bamako to within 75 kilometers of Odienné via the Sankarani and its tributary, the Gouanhala—at least during the high-water season. The Bâni River allows for transport between Mopti and the Sikasso region via Djenné and San.

All this constitutes a navigable network that is certainly imperfect, due to the variation in water levels according to the seasons, but which has already been improved and could be further refined by the execution of certain works. As it exists today, it is very valuable in a country where waterways so rarely lend themselves to navigation and where routes and means of transport are generally rudimentary <note>original: "embryonnaires"</note> and expensive.

Downstream from Timbuktu <note>original: "Tombouctou"</note>, although dotted with islands and islets, the Niger forms a much more regular river than it does upstream. After crossing the sandy region extending from Timbuktu to Bourem, its bed becomes rocky again as it approaches Gao, and it is broken here and there by rapids, the main ones being those of Ayorou and Labezenga, but none of which constitutes...

It is only after leaving French territory that the Niger presents impassable rocky sills—in the Boussa region <note>Located in modern-day Nigeria, these rapids historically blocked inland access from the sea.</note>—which sharply separate the long middle reach from the maritime reach.

The right bank of the Niger, or more precisely the entire region located on the right bank between Lake Débo and Say, is known in the Songhay language as *Gourma* or *Hari-banda* (which we have spelled *Aribinda*); the lands on the left bank are grouped under the name *Haoussa* or *Aoussa*, whether at the level of Débo, Bamba, Gao, or Say (1). These names are often used as terms for orientation, but it is easy to see that they then take on multiple and very different meanings depending on where one is located: for example, from Débo to Timbuktu, *Gourma* designates the East and *Haoussa* the West; from Timbuktu to Bourem, *Gourma* designates the South and *Haoussa* the North; finally, downstream from Bourem, *Gourma* means the West and *Haoussa* the East. It is also easy to understand how inaccurate our application of some of these terms has been to specific localized regions of the Bend of the Niger <note>The "Great Bend" is the massive curve the river takes as it pushes north into the Sahara before turning south toward the ocean.</note>. For instance, we call the districts of Hombori and Fada N'Gourma "Gourma," and apply "Aribinda" to the country south of Timbuktu and west of Dori: in reality, the entire interior of the Bend of the Niger deserves these two names of *Gourma* or *Aribinda*.

It is perhaps not useless to speak here of the ports of Timbuktu. The principal one, in the sense that it is the most consistent, is *Korioumé*, located on the Niger itself. But at Korioumé, a canal branches off from the Niger and reaches *Daï*, 10 kilometers from Timbuktu, to rejoin the main river downstream. # LIMIT OF THE FLOODS

73

...Timbuktu. Finally, during the great floods, the current carves a path through the East of Kabara, reaching within 300 meters of the city of *Timbuktu* (1).

Timbuktu therefore actually possesses four ports: Korioumé, usable all year round and at all times; Dai, which is hardly usable except from September to April; Kabara, which becomes so from November to April; and finally one of the suburbs of Timbuktu, though access to this last port is only possible in years of great flood (about every three years) and only in the month of January.

The varying abundance of rains in the Sudanese region has, in effect, a considerable influence, not only on the extent of the flooded zone, but also on the limit reached by the waters in the lakes, depressions, and <term>canals</term> <note>The author refers to natural and semi-natural distributaries of the Niger.</note> originating from the Niger. Indeed, all these lakes and canals are merely <term>spillways</term> <note>original: "déversoirs"; these are outlets for overflow rather than tributaries.</note>: they do not feed the Niger, but are fed by it. When the flood has been exceptionally strong in the upper river, Lake Faguibine is filled as far as Ras-el-Ma, the Daouna depressions are transformed into lakes, and the water flows back toward the North into the Sahelian and Saharan diversion canals—which are also spillways rather than tributaries—such as the <term>creek</term> <note>original: "marigot," a term used in Francophone Africa for a seasonal stream or side channel.</note> of Niamina, the lower parts of the Tilemsi and Azaouag valleys, etc., and the meager rivers, such as the Gorouol and the Sirba, which cross the region of temporary ponds separating the Volta basin from the lower Niger near Dori. When, on the contrary, the flood has been weak, the water spreads very little outside the river itself and its main branches; the lakes become nothing more than ponds, and many pools or valleys remain dry for one or several years.

...basin <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of the Volta River basin.</note> [one] notes that, over the course of the last fifteen years, there has been a progressive decrease in Lake Faguibine and a drying up of the Daouna: the water, which reached Ras-el-Ma during the floods of 1894, reached no further than forty kilometers east of that point last year. He supposes that, independently of temporary climatic causes, this drying is due to a general and constant cause which would affect the entire North of the Sudan <note>In this 19th and early 20th-century context, "Sudan" refers to the "French Sudan" (encompassing modern Mali and surrounding areas), not the modern nation of Sudan.</note>. I do not believe I should share his opinion: in the 11th century, according to the testimony of Bekri <note>Abu Abdullah al-Bakri (c. 1014–1094), a famous Arab geographer and historian who provided some of the earliest written accounts of West African kingdoms.</note>, the point of Ras-el-Ma (meaning "head of the water" <note>original: "tête de l'eau"</note>) already deserved its name by its position at the extreme limit of the floods; it would be singular if, if a constant cause of drying truly existed, the limit of the floods had remained identical for at least nine centuries only to suddenly retreat afterward. It is much more likely that this limit varies and has always varied according to the years, or rather according to periods of several years each, in proportion to the quantities of rainfall, and that, if the maximum has always been at Ras-el-Ma—at least since the beginning of the historical period—the minimum has varied and will vary again from era to era; it is probable that before 1894 the extreme limit of the floods had already retreated many times as far as the minimum observed in 1910 and perhaps even further, and that after a series of rainy years, Ras-el-Ma will once again become the "head of the water."

# CHAPTER III (1)

## Orography <note>The study of the formation and physical features of mountains and hills.</note>

For anyone seeking high altitudes, the orographic system of the Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A territory of French West Africa existing from 1904 to 1922, encompassing much of modern-day Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.</note> would appear rather meager: it does not seem, in fact, that one encounters peaks exceeding one thousand meters within the colony, and even the number of those reaching this altitude is quite limited. They are found in the Hombori region (within the Niger Bend) and perhaps in the district of Satadougou, near the sources of the Falémé River, at the northernmost point of the massif known as the Fouta Djallon.

This latter massif actually extends from the sources of the Bandama and the *Bâgbê* (Ivory Coast) to those of the Gambia (Guinea), following a general South-East to North-West direction; it gives rise, on one hand, to all the small coastal rivers that empty into the sea between Grand-Lahou and Bathurst <note>Now known as Banjul, the capital of The Gambia.</note> (Bandama, Sassandra, Cavally, Nuon or Cestos, Saint John, Saint Paul, Makona, Sherbro, Rokel, Great and Little Scarcies, Konkouré, Rio Grande, Gambia) and, on the other hand, to the main branches of the Niger and the Senegal (Bâgbê, Baoulé, Sankarani, Milo, Tembiko, Tinkisso for the Bani and the Niger; Bafing and Falémé for the Senegal). The highest peaks of this massif are situated in the region where Guinea, Liberia, and the Ivory Coast meet (*Nimba* or *Nuonfa* at 1,644 m., *Momy* at 1,400 m., *Dou* at 1,339 m., *Soulou* at 1,121 m., *Gouékouma* at 1,026 m., according to the barometric observations of Mr. Aug. Chevalier in 1909 <note>Auguste Chevalier (1873–1956) was a prominent French botanist and explorer who documented much of West Africa's flora and geography.</note>). The massif seems to lower as it moves toward the North-West, and its final foothills in this—

There, they merge, so to speak, with another system—much less significant in terms of altitude and extent—which separates the upper valley of the Niger from the Senegal basin. On the slope where the Bakhoy, the Baoulé, and their tributaries originate, it extends into a series of hills, sometimes isolated and sometimes grouped or branching, which stretch westward. Due to their very isolation, these hills initially give the appearance of mountains, an impression that their actual altitude is far from justifying.

On the right bank of the Niger, between this river and the Bani, a third system appears. It merges toward the South, near Odienné (Ivory Coast), with the final eastern ramifications of the massif known as the Fouta Djallon. It follows the direction of the Niger, closing off its narrow valley on the eastern side much as the previously described system closes it on the western side, though with a less considerable relief. As is also the case for the range on the left bank, the range on the right bank is less steep on the slope that does not face the river; it extends on that side through branches that define the valleys of the upper reaches of the Bani (the Baoulé and Bâgbé), gradually fading away as it reaches the region of canals and floods. <note>This refers to the Inner Niger Delta, a vast area of lakes and floodplains in central Mali.</note>

We have seen that the course of the main branch of the Volta is essentially parallel to the course of the Niger and forms a loop nested inside the loop of the latter river: as a result of this phenomenon, the orographic system <note>An orographic system refers to the physical structure and arrangement of mountains and hills in a particular region.</note> we are currently considering generally takes the form of an arc, also parallel to the Niger valley, with the caveat that it follows the contours of the Volta basin more closely than those of the Niger. ## CHAPTER IV (1)

### Natural Regions

From the perspective of the landscape, the composition of the soil, and the flora and fauna, Upper Senegal and Niger <note>Upper Senegal and Niger (Haut-Sénégal-Niger) was a colony in French West Africa, existing under this name from 1904 to 1921, covering much of modern-day Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.</note> can be divided into three large natural regions. These regions or zones are not, moreover, clearly delimited: they overlap with one another at many points, and the following indications should only be accepted from a general and approximate point of view.

*The Sudanese Region.* — The southern part of Upper Senegal and Niger belongs to the African zone commonly called the "Sudanese region," however improper this designation may be from an etymological standpoint, as the word "Sudan" comes from the Arabic expression *Land of the Blacks* <note>original: "Blâd-es-Soudân"</note> and should therefore logically apply to the entire part of the African continent located south of the Sahara.

This zone begins where the final branches of the great dense forest of the Gulf of Guinea end and extends to the north—though very approximately—to just beyond the latitude of Bamako. It is appropriate to include within it, in the Senegal River basin, the lands located on the left bank of the river itself or watered by its main branches, the Bafing, the Bakhoy, and the Baoulé; and, in the Niger and Volta basins, the lands located south of a line passing roughly through Koulikoro, Segou, San, Koury, Ouahigouya, and Fada N’Gourma.

This region is, generally speaking, where the terrain is—

But the appearance of the Sahel changes little by little as one moves northward: initially not very different from the Sudan proper, it emphasizes its special character at the latitude of Sokolo and Bandiagara to identify more and more with the desert until one reaches the Sudanese Sahara. <note>The author uses "Sudanese Sahara" to describe the transitional steppe-desert zone.</note> The boundary between the Sahel and the Sudanese Sahara can be represented by a line passing about fifty kilometers north of Nioro and Goumbou, advancing nearly to Bassikounou, reaching the Niger at Mopti, heading from there to Hombori while passing north of Bandiagara and Douentza, then descending southward toward the vicinity of Djibo, finally taking an eastward direction to rejoin the Niger near Niamey via Dori.

It would not be accurate to say that the Sahel is arid: the vegetation there is sometimes even denser than in the Sudan, but in general, well-grown trees are rarer, and especially thorny shrubs appear in much larger quantities, outnumbering other species as one advances north, until they become almost the sole representatives of woody vegetation upon reaching the Sudanese Sahara. Savannas also exist, but the grasses are thinner and shorter than in the Sudanese savannas and, moreover, appear to constitute much better pastures. <note>Short-grass savannas in the Sahel are historically noted for their high nutritional value for livestock compared to the tall, coarse grasses of the wetter south.</note>

->### SAHEL AND SAHARA<-

one finds diversion channels where water overflows during the rains, forming a kind of intermediary between the Saharan wadis <note>original: *oueds* — seasonal riverbeds that remain dry except during the rainy season.</note> and the temporary streams of the Sudanese region. Generally, however, water only appears in the form of pools or ponds of varying sizes that fill up during the rainy season, several of which, moreover, never dry up completely. Most villages are supplied with water only by these pools or by wells.

As for the rocks that make up the terrain, they differ from those of the Sudanese region particularly in that limestone <note>original: *calcaire*</note> is found in the Sahel, whereas it is absent further south. Conversely, Sudanese laterite <note>A reddish clay soil rich in iron and aluminum, common in tropical regions, often used for building.</note> still abounds in the Sahel, while it is absent in the Sahara. From this point of view, as from many others, the Sahel represents the transition zone between the Sudanese region and the Sudanese Sahara.

Regarding the wildlife, one encounters roughly the same species in the Sahel as in the Sudan, minus the elephant, but with the giraffe and the ostrich in addition; the lion is also more common there. But above all, probably due to the vast uninhabited spaces and also the limited number of watering holes—each of which becomes a mandatory meeting point for wild animals—one sees much more game in the Sahel than in the Sudan, and hunting there is far more successful.

As for the human inhabitants, while in the Sudan the indigenous people are—with the exception of merchant tribes and castes of artisans and fishermen—almost exclusively farmers and belong solely to the black race, in the Sahel one finds a very notable proportion of semi-nomadic herders of the white race, more or less of mixed descent (Moors <note>original: *Maures*</note> and Fulani <note>original: *Peuls*</note>).

*Sudanese Sahara.* — The third natural region of Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A former administrative territory of French West Africa.</note> can be called the "Sudanese Sahara"; it is called by the natives *Hodh* or *Haoudh* in its western part, between Tagant and the lake region of Timbuktu, and *Azaouad* in its eastern part—that is, within the Bend of the Niger between Timbuktu and Tillabéry and to the north

The difference in appearance and climate between these two parts of the desert has been very clearly pointed out by Messrs. Gautier and Chudeau <note>Émile-Félix Gautier and René Chudeau were prominent French geographers and explorers of the Sahara in the early 20th century.</note>: while from the region of Timiaouine and In-Ouzel heading north, vegetation is absent outside of the wadi valleys <note>original: *oueds* — dry riverbeds that only flow during rare rains.</note> and depressions favored by occasional, albeit very rare, rainfall, the Sudanese Sahara—where it rains almost everywhere regularly every year—contains, except in particularly stony regions, vegetation that is certainly very sparse but nevertheless visible. First, the Niger inundation zone <note>The Inland Niger Delta, a vast area of lakes and floodplains.</note> between Mopti and Timbuktu should be set aside, as it shares more characteristics with the Sahel than the Sahara. In truth, the trees become more spaced out and decrease in height as one travels north; similarly, the pastures atrophy as one approaches the Sahara proper. However, it remains no less true that the appearance of the Sudanese Sahara as a whole is far less desolate than that of the Algerian Sahara south of the Oases.

The rest of the Sudanese Sahara—that is to say, nearly the entirety of this region—is inhabited or traversed by nomads or semi-nomads: shepherds of sheep and camels, traders, caravan workers, guides, and religious leaders. Some, in the Hodh and Northern Azaouad, are primarily Moors of more or less mixed Arab origin, accompanied by vassals of Berber origin and *Harratîn* <note>A social class in the Sahara, often sedentary farmers or servants of sub-Saharan African descent.</note> or serfs of Black origin. All of them—excluding, of course, the few sedentary inhabitants of the *ksour* <note>original: *ksour* (singular *ksar*) — fortified villages or settlements typical of North Africa and the Sahara.</note> or villages—live in tents and can be considered true nomads, moving their camps over often considerable distances depending on the year and the seasons. Others, on both banks of the Niger and within the interior of the Loop <note>The "Niger Loop" or "Niger Bend."</note>, are mainly Tuareg, along with some Peuls <note>Also known as the Fulani or Fula people.</note> who barely venture beyond the immediate surroundings of the northern limit of the Sahel. Both are accompanied by serfs of Black origin (*Bella* among the Tuareg, *Rimaïbé* among the Peuls). These groups live in huts rather than tents—Tuareg and Peuls alike—and possess actual villages; though these are temporary, they generally move only within a limited geographic radius.

The Sudanese Sahara contains a significant number of wells, created and maintained by the indigenous population; aside from these wells, the Niger, and the lakes and ponds fed by the river, there are no permanent water sources. A few modest valleys temporarily collect rainwater in the area located to the west of Araouâne, where a sort of Saharan branch of the Niger likely existed in the past. # THE REGION

wider and deeper [depressions] exist, which head toward the Tilemsi <note>The Tilemsi Valley is a large prehistoric dry riverbed in eastern Mali.</note>.

While the Saharan region of Upper Senegal-Niger <note>original: *Haut-Sénégal-Niger* — a former administrative territory in French West Africa.</note> is poor in water, it is, on the other hand, quite rich in salt: it is this region above all that supplied the land of the Black peoples with this precious foodstuff, until the day when improvements in our means of transport allowed us to bring salt from the Cape Verde islands or from Europe to the markets of the Sudan <note>original: *Soudan* — referring to the West African region, not the modern country of Sudan.</note> in a state to compete with Saharan salt. In the past, this latter salt came primarily from the salt works of Aoulil, located in present-day Trarza <note>A region in modern-day Mauritania.</note>, near the Atlantic coast north of Biakh, and from the mines of Teghazza, which are located about 120 kilometers north-northwest of Taodéni. The salt from Aoulil was brought partly by boat up the Senegal River and partly by caravans that reached the Sahel <term>Sahel</term> <note>term: Sahel — From the Arabic word for "shore" or "coast," referring to the semi-arid transition zone between the Sahara Desert and the more fertile Sudanese savanna.</note> by crossing the Tagant. Today, salt primarily reaches the Sudan from the Taodéni quarries, which have replaced those of Teghazza, via the Araouâne route, and from the Idjil salt mines, located north of the Mauritanian Adrar, via the Tichit route. Salt is also imported, though in much smaller quantities, harvested from a certain number of marshes in the Hodh, one of the most important of which is found near Tichit itself.

It has often been claimed that the Sudanese Sahara was formerly better watered and consequently more fertile than it is today. This hypothesis is not implausible, especially if one accepts that the "Niger" of Pliny and Ptolemy <note>Pliny the Elder and Claudius Ptolemy were ancient Roman and Greco-Egyptian scholars whose geographical works influenced European understanding of Africa for centuries.</note> actually drew a significant portion of its waters from the Moroccan Atlas, which, however, is far from being proven. But it is very probable that for a long time—undoubtedly since the beginning of our era and perhaps much earlier—the general appearance of the Sahara has not changed significantly. In the time of Herodotus—that is, more than four centuries before Christ—this part of Africa already stood out for its lack of water and vegetation, since this author tells us that south of the maritime coasts of Libya "one encounters Libya populated by wild beasts, beyond which is a sandy ridge extending from Thebes in Egypt to the Columns of Hercules <note>original: *colonnes d'Hercule* — the ancient name for the Strait of Gibraltar.</note>. In this sandy country, at intervals of ten days' travel...

# HAS THE SAHARA'S APPEARANCE CHANGED?

"...ten days [travel], large blocks of salt on hills (1); from the top of each of these hills, one sees a spring of fresh and sweet water gush out from the middle of the salt. Around this water, one finds inhabitants, who are the last ones on the side of the deserts" (2). It is worth noting, moreover, that this passage only concerns the Northern Sahara, since Herodotus <note>Herodotus (c. 484–425 BCE) was an ancient Greek historian often called "the Father of History."</note> places Augila, Germa (land of the Garamantes, Fezzan) and Ghadames (land of the Atarantes) there. As for the Sahara proper, here is what our author says about it: "Above this sandy elevation, toward the south and the interior of Libya, one finds only a frightful desert, where there is neither water, nor wood, nor wild beasts; no moisture is found there" (3).

The description by Herodotus could apply perfectly to the part of the Sahara located between the last oases of the Tuat <note>The Tuat is a natural region of central Algeria containing a series of small oases.</note> and Timiaouine <note>A border location in the Adrar des Ifoghas, currently on the border between Algeria and Mali.</note>, as it appears to our eyes today: if this portion of the desert has not changed for more than 2,300 years, there is little chance that the southern portion, which we call the Sudanese Sahara <note>original: *Sahara soudanais* — referring to the southern edge of the desert bordering the historical Sudan region, not the modern nation of Sudan.</note>, has changed significantly during the same span of time. Some valleys may have been filled with sand, but the rainfall patterns must be the same today as they have always been, and it would seem quite bold to suggest that the Sudanese Sahara once possessed actual rivers and forests that bushfires would have caused to disappear.

In the Sahel itself, the situation at the time of Yaqut <note>Yaqut al-Hamawi (1179–1229), a famous Arab geographer and scholar of Greek origin.</note>—that is to say, 700 years ago—was exactly as it is today: this author speaks to us, in fact, of waterless deserts that stretched between roughly the latitude of Oualata and the regions bordering the Senegal [River] where people went to buy the gold dust harvested in Bambouk <note>Bambouk is the traditional name for the region in eastern Senegal and western Mali, famous for its gold mines since antiquity.</note>, a desert where the drought was—

# DEFORESTATION

...despite their certain utility, have at all times constituted only one of the manifestations of land clearing <term>défrichement: the process of clearing land of its natural vegetation, usually for agriculture</term> and one of the most harmless ones regarding tree-like vegetation. The axe and the hoe, by proceeding with the uprooting of stumps and the stripping bare of unproductive rocks and clays, have had a far more significant impact; and yet, we cannot reasonably blame the Sudanese <note>In this 19th/early 20th-century context, "Sudanese" refers to the inhabitants of the "Sudan" region of West Africa (the Sahelian belt), rather than the modern country of Sudan.</note> for having transformed into productive fields the sterile forests where their ancestors led the wild and precarious life of the most distant primitives. 

We would, moreover, be poorly placed to reproach the natives for having deforested a part of the Sudan in order to survive—we who, in much larger proportions but fortunately in restricted areas, have deforested the banks of the Senegal and Niger Rivers in just a few years to fuel our steamboats, as well as the vicinity of the railways and cities created by us, to build our establishments, manufacture our furniture, and maintain our cooking fires.

## Climatology

*Climatic regions.* — The climatic regions of Upper Senegal and Niger <term>Haut-Sénégal-Niger: a former administrative territory in French West Africa, covering parts of modern-day Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger</term> correspond quite closely to the natural regions of which I have just given a brief and approximate description. Without discussing the Sahara for the moment, it is undeniable that the climate of the Sahelian region <term>Sahelian region: the semi-arid transition zone between the Sahara Desert to the north and the wetter savannas to the south</term> differs quite significantly from that of the Sudanese region <note>In this historical context, "Sudanese" refers to the "Sudan" geographic belt (the savanna zone of West Africa) rather than the modern nation of Sudan.</note>. More generally, one could say that the climate of Upper Senegal and Niger varies the further one moves from the equator.

In the south of the colony, rains are more frequent and more abundant, and the rainy season lasts longer; as a consequence of this pattern and the greater number of watercourses, the air is generally more heavy with humidity, even when it has not rained for a long time. Furthermore, the temperature is more constant from one end of the year to the other, and the thermometer's fluctuations within a single day are less significant. Barometric shifts are, conversely, more frequent and the average pressure is slightly lower; storms are more numerous and more violent, as are tornadoes accompanied by rain, while "dry tornadoes"—or dust storms <note>original: "ouragans de poussière"</note>—are rarer and milder.

In the Sahelian region, the rainy season is shorter, the hours of rain are fewer, and the amount of water falling in a given time is less on average: the air

->### THE SEASONS<-

The air is therefore drier, the sweat glands <term>sudoripares: the glands in the skin that produce sweat</term> function more easily, and the heat is more bearable. There are greater temperature fluctuations, especially during the dry season, during which the thermometer reaches maximums and minimums unknown—or at least exceptional—in the South; on the other hand, the average temperature is higher during the rainy season.

In the Sahara, even where annual rains exist, the rainy period is of a very short duration—only a few days—and, regardless of the amount of water that falls, it can be said that the dryness of the air is extreme throughout the entire year. Summer temperatures are very high, but by contrast, there is a noticeable winter, and the barometric pressure is generally constant.

*Seasons.* — The division of the year into climatic <term>climatériques: relating to specific climatic periods or cycles</term> periods is the same everywhere in the Sudan and the Sahel, in the sense that the same periods follow one another in the same order in the North as in the South; however, the dates on which each period generally begins and ends are not exactly the same.

These periods or seasons are four in number: the cold season or dry season proper, the hot season, the rainy season or "wintering" <term>hivernage: a term commonly used in West Africa to refer to the rainy season, distinct from the European concept of winter</term>, and the intermediate season between the rains and the cold.

The cold season lasts about three months: in the Sudanese region, it begins around December 1st and ends at the end of February. The name "cold season" applied to this period is only partially accurate: it is indeed the time of year when the thermometer drops to its lowest (8°, 5°, and even 2° centigrade above zero, depending on the year and the region), but, without reaching the maximums of the following season, it rises during this so-called "cold" season, even in the extreme South of the colony, up to 30° and 35°. It is during this period that the harmattan <term>harmattan: a dry, dusty trade wind that blows from the Sahara over West Africa</term> blows—a Northeast wind coming from the Sahara, which is the drying wind par excellence, causing leaves to yellow and fall, and peeling skin and chapping lips. Because of—

<header>THE COUNTRY</header>

[due to] the considerable radiation <note>The process by which the earth loses heat into space at night</note> caused by this wind during the night, the temperature is truly cold in the morning at sunrise; however, it rises rapidly, and it is not uncommon to observe a difference of about thirty degrees Celsius <note>A shift of about 54 degrees Fahrenheit</note> between 5:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m. Consequently, it would be more accurate to call this period the "season of cold nights."

The hot season that follows it fully deserves its name: it is, in fact, the time when the thermometer drops the least and rises the highest, so that the average temperature is higher during this season than during the rest of the year. It is rare to record less than 18°C <note>64.4°F</note> during this period in Bamako <note>The modern-day capital of Mali</note>, and temperatures of 40° to 45°C <note>104° to 113°F</note> are often read there at the same time. The maximum temperatures observed in Kayes and Ségou are even more considerable. In general, this season is more bearable in the far south of the Sudan <note>Referring to the French Sudan, a colonial territory encompassing much of modern Mali</note> than in the Sahelian region, but it is unpleasant everywhere. It begins roughly with the month of March and ends around June 15th. At the start, it is still connected to the dry season, but the wind is almost non-existent and there is virtually no nocturnal radiation; the temperature only begins to drop slightly toward midnight, only to rise again starting at 8:00 a.m. and becoming overwhelming in the afternoon. Sometimes, when the atmosphere is at its most stifling, the wind begins to blow suddenly, coming from the East with extreme speed and great violence, and swirls of red dust rush forward like a cyclone: these are the dry tornadoes <term>tornades sèches: in this context, these are not funnel-cloud tornadoes, but violent "line squalls" or dust storms common in West Africa</term>. Toward the end of the hot season, these dry tornadoes are generally followed by a violent storm and torrential rain of short duration, after which it seems even hotter than before.

The rainy season or "wintering" <term>hivernage: the West African term for the rainy season</term> generally begins in the Sudanese region around mid-June and lasts until the end of October, with a brief lull in the second half of August; but in the Sahel, it establishes itself a bit later and ends a bit earlier. It begins with rainy tornadoes brought by the East wind, just as during the pre-[ceding season...]

<header>THE RAINY SEASON <note>French: *L'hivernage*. In West Africa, this term refers to the rainy season rather than "winter" in the temperate sense.</note></header>

[from the] preceding [season], but which are not always preceded by **dry squalls** <note>original: *tornades sèches*; these are high-wind events that occur without precipitation</note> and which end in an ordinary rain following a shift in the wind. Starting in July, the rains last longer, brought by a Southwest wind, and are very often accompanied by violent storms, especially from July 15th to August 15th. The rains of September and October are generally more spread out, but often heavier. This is the season during which temperature fluctuations are the least pronounced; the average temperature generally remains around 22° or 23°C <note>71.6° to 73.4°F</note>, with 15°C <note>59°F</note> as the minimum and 30°C <note>86°F</note> as the maximum; it quite often happens that the average temperature is slightly lower in the Sudan than in France during the months of July and August. Despite this, this period is generally less appreciated by Europeans than the season of cold nights, due to the humidity of the atmosphere, though it is certainly less unpleasant than the hot season of March-April-May. The indigenous population, on the contrary, dread the cold season, during which—lacking the means to protect themselves against the chill of the nights—they frequently contract ailments of the throat or lungs; it should also be noted that it is during the dry season that contagious diseases, primarily **smallpox** <note>original: *variole*</note>, cause the most devastation, due to the greater ease with which morbid germs spread because of the dryness <term>siccity: the state of being dry or arid</term> of the atmosphere.

Despite the intensity of the rains that fall from late June to late October, Upper Senegal-Niger, even in its southern part, is far from being a country of humid heat like many tropical regions: indeed, the rains rarely last more than a few hours and it does not rain every day, even in the heart of the rainy season. The annual rainfall fluctuates around 1.50 meters in **Bamako**, 0.75 meters in **Nioro**, and 0.50 meters in **Niafounké**.

The fourth season, which is very short, lasts about one month: November; it is a sort of respite between the last rains and the time when the **harmattan** <note>A dry, dusty trade wind that blows from the Sahara</note> begins to blow. It presents roughly the same disadvantages as the hot season: in truth, the temperature is lower, but the wind is generally weak
