[or] absent, the still-humid air dries out only slowly, and the rain no longer arrives to refresh the atmosphere.

Regarding the various appearances that nature takes on according to the seasons, one can observe a relative correspondence between the Sudan <note>Referring to the "French Sudan," a colonial territory covering much of modern Mali</note> and our own country <note>The author is referring to France</note>. Although the rainy season is commonly given the name "wintering" <note>French: *hivernage*; in West Africa, this term historically refers to the rainy season</note>, this latter period has nothing that recalls our winter; on the contrary, the cold season—the duration of which corresponds roughly to our winter—presents many analogies with the latter: the suspension of vegetation, the falling of leaves, the hardening of the earth’s crust, etc. At the first squalls <note>French: *tornades*; in West African meteorology, these are high-wind storm cells or squall lines rather than vortex tornadoes</note> of the hot season, the phenomena characterizing spring manifest themselves around the same time as in our land: the trees cover themselves in new leaves, the grass grows back with a beautiful green color, and the first flowers appear. The rainy season is, like our summer, the period when grains and fruits reach maturity and the time of the harvest—at least for a portion of the cereals—while the intermediate season of November, marking the exhaustion of nature, corresponds in part to our autumn.

*General climate conditions.* — It was believed for a long time that the Sudanese climate must be more pleasant and healthier at high altitudes than in low-lying regions: it is indeed possible that this is so in theory, but in practice, while the summits—which are, moreover, modest—of the Sudan exist in better conditions of ventilation, it follows first that they are more exposed to squalls; furthermore, these summits, which are always bare and composed of rock, mostly constitute veritable reservoirs of heat, so that the nights there are frequently less cool than in the surrounding plains (1). Moreover, when these summits are

The latter, having spent a night at the summit of the mountain, observed that the cold there was notably less sharp than in the valley.

formed of layers of laterite <term>a reddish, iron-rich clay soil common in tropical regions that hardens when dry</term>, as is generally the case, rainwater lingers in the crevices, which thus become excellent breeding grounds for mosquito larvae.

All in all, the climate of Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A French colonial territory in West Africa (1904–1921), covering much of modern-day Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso</note> as a whole is certainly among the healthiest in West Africa and the easiest for Europeans to endure. To be sure, malaria prevails there, as in all tropical countries, but it causes far less devastation there than in the coastal colonies of the Gulf of Guinea; blackwater fever <term>a severe complication of malaria; original: "fièvre bilieuse hémoglobinurique"</term>, so frequent in those latter colonies, is rare in the Sudan and almost unknown in the Sahelian region.

As for the Sudanese Sahara, despite the many inconveniences presented by life in this disinherited land, it is—by the admission of all those who have traveled through it or resided there—the healthiest of all the regions of Upper Senegal-Niger for Europeans.

# CHAPTER VI (1)

## Population Distribution

We have seen above that the average population density was approximately 2.66 inhabitants per square kilometer for the entirety of the civil colony of Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A French colonial territory in West Africa (1904–1921). The "civil colony" refers to areas under civilian rather than military administration</note>. However, this density varies enormously depending on the region.

This is due to various causes, of which the nature of the soil and its relative fertility are only one factor. The upheavals brought about by the wars that followed one another for such a long time before our occupation of the country, the migrations that resulted from them, and the raids <term>original: "razzias"; these were organized pillaging and slave-raiding expeditions</term> that were their consequence, have enormously influenced the current distribution of the indigenous population. Now that security has been restored everywhere, it is very probable that regions which are fertile but depopulated or abandoned will be repopulated at the expense of other, less advantageous areas—areas which were only occupied by their current inhabitants or their ancestors because they could go nowhere else. We have an example of this in the district <note>original: "cercle"; the primary administrative unit in French West African colonies</note> of Bougouni. This area, which was almost completely deserted at the time we were hunting down the devastating bands of Samori <note>Samori Touré (c. 1830–1900), the founder of the Wassoulou Empire who resisted French colonial expansion for nearly two decades</note>, currently holds the 13<sup>th</sup> rank among the 29 administrative districts of the colony in terms of population density. On the other hand, it is quite possible that a certain region, though naturally disadvantaged, may one day become populous because a new industry has been created there or because a railway, by passing through it, will have profoundly modified its economic conditions.

# POPULATION DENSITY
->7<-

We cannot make any predictions on this subject that offer any degree of certainty, and we must be content with observing the current distribution of the population.

The region where the population density is most significant is—along with the surroundings of the town of San <note>A town in modern-day Mali, historically a significant commercial center</note>—the *Mossi*, or more precisely the district <note>original: "cercle"; the primary administrative unit in French West African colonies</note> of Ouagadougou. This area alone contains a quarter of the colony's total population, even though it contains no town worthy of the name, and the large settlements there are generally composed only of a greater or lesser number of hamlets scattered amidst the fields. The density of this almost exclusively agricultural and peasant population can be estimated at *16 inhabitants per square kilometer* for the district as a whole and rises to *35 in the Mossi region proper*.

The rest of the country included in the West and South of the *Niger Bend* <note>original: "Boucle du Niger"; the great curve the Niger River takes as it flows toward the Sahara before turning south</note> follows immediately after, with the Volta basin in the first rank. here, one encounters a certain number of towns, inhabited primarily by traders and artisans, amidst an indigenous population that is essentially agricultural and peasant and scattered like that of the Mossi, though sometimes with quite considerable gaps in settlement. The average density there varies from *13 to 7 inhabitants per square kilometer*.

The valleys of the Upper Niger and the Bani come only in third place, with a population of farmers less scattered than that of the Volta basin, a city-dwelling population composed of fishermen, traders, and artisans, and a wandering population of nomadic or rather semi-nomadic herders. Average density: *8 to 4 inhabitants per square kilometer*, with an exceptional average of *17 inhabitants per square kilometer* for the district of San.

The Senegal basin comes in fourth place, with small villages of farmers and hunters separated by large uninhabited expanses and a city-dwelling population of recent formation, mostly localized to the town of Kayes. Average density: *4 to 1.5 inhabitants per square kilometer*.

I have already had several opportunities to mention the names and locations of the 29 current administrative districts of the civil colony of Upper Senegal and Niger <note>At the time of writing, this massive colony encompassed much of the interior of West Africa, including modern-day Mali, Burkina Faso, and parts of Niger.</note>. # CHAPTER ONE (1)

## **Classification and Current Geographical Distribution of the Various Ethnic Groups**

**Difficulties of a Proper Classification.** — Establishing a precise and exact classification of the various ethnic groups currently living in Upper Senegal and Niger <note>A vast French colonial territory that existed from 1904 to 1921; it covered a massive area of West Africa, including much of modern-day Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.</note> is a very difficult task. Many bases can serve as a starting point for a classification of peoples, but no single method is free of serious drawbacks.

The anthropological method <note>The author is referring to "physical anthropology," a branch of science prevalent in the early 20th century that attempted to classify human races through physical measurements, such as "craniometry" (skull measurements).</note>, based on the comparative study of the physical characteristics of individuals and on the measurements of the living or of skeletons, is difficult to apply in the regions that concern us. Even assuming that one day a sufficient number of observations and measurements could be gathered to reach satisfactory averages—and that day has not yet come—the classification obtained this way would be purely artificial. Each of the groupings is composed of highly diverse elements regarding their origin, due to migrations, conquests, unions between individuals of different peoples, and the large number of slaves imported from distant lands, etc. While the results of the anthropological method present some interest regarding rural populations, among whom mixing is less extensive, they seem almost useless from a practical standpoint regarding the population of the towns.

The genealogical method, relying on the origins and ancestry of modern families, is a project that is nearly

Furthermore, one must consider two coefficients of error that are very difficult to determine exactly: the ignorance of most natives regarding the generations that preceded the current era, and the tendency of all Muslims to claim a Sharifian <note>Descended from the family of the Prophet Muhammad.</note> or at least an Arab origin. This tendency has always been noted among the Berbers and is found even among the most clearly Black peoples, such as the Mandinka <note>original: "Mandingues"; a major West African ethnic group, founders of the historic Mali Empire.</note>. Let us add to this that an individual questioned about the origins of his people or his tribe almost always responds by giving what he believes—or wants others to believe—is his own personal genealogy, the ancestry of his immediate family, and not that of the ethnic group to which this family belongs.

The ethnographic method <note>The study of human cultures through their material objects, social practices, and customs.</note>, based on the analogies and differences of material and social civilizations, is certainly much better and more fruitful than the two preceding ones <note>The author previously discussed physical anthropology (measuring bodies) and likely linguistic classification.</note>. However, it is not enough on its own to give entirely satisfactory results. The similarity between two civilizations may indeed stem from a common origin between the two peoples considered, but it can also arise either because these two peoples were influenced by an identical environment, or because one of them—subjected to the yoke of the other or, conversely, having conquered it and then allowed itself to be assimilated—adopted the customs of that other people and substituted them for its own. Many have already pointed out the errors one is destined to fall into when taking either scarification tattoos or *diamou* <term>clan names</term> as a basis for classification. For instance, a tribe living in contact with another may adopt the ethnic tattoo of the neighbor; slaves take the *diamou* of their master; and the natives we address in a language that is not their own translate their *diamou* into that foreign tongue. For example, many Dioula <note>original: "Dioula"; a Mande ethnic group known historically as long-distance traders.</note> wear the scarifications of their Senufo <note>original: "Sénoufo"; an ethnic group living primarily in modern-day Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso, and Mali.</note> neighbors, and a Senufo Soroo, questioned through a Mandé interpreter, will say that his clan name is Kouloubali <note>original: "Kouloubali"; a common surname across West Africa, often associated with the Bambara and Mande lineages.</note>, etc.

# METHODS OF CLASSIFICATION

The linguistic method finally, which considers only the degree or absence of kinship between the languages spoken by various groups, has an indisputable advantage: that of being based on data that is currently accurate, easy to verify, and which, once established, leaves no room for debate. Although the linguistic inventory of Upper Senegal and Niger <note>original: "Haut-Sénégal-Niger"; a major administrative territory in French West Africa, covering much of modern Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.</note> is far from complete and has generally not been carried out in a truly scientific or sufficiently precise manner, the classification of the peoples of this colony according to their idioms is certainly the one that offers the most guarantees and is the most practically usable. However, from an ethnic point of view, it cannot provide all the desired satisfaction: indeed, many peoples, for various reasons (conquest, geographical contact, etc.), have adopted the language of other peoples whose origin is very different from their own, without, for that matter, adopting their customs or character. Conversely, and for opposite reasons, two branches of the same people may speak two completely distinct idioms. Examples of this double phenomenon are numerous in West Africa: for now, I will limit myself to citing, on the one hand, that of the Fula <note>original: "Peuls"; a traditionally nomadic pastoralist group whose linguistic relationship with their neighbors has long interested ethnographers.</note> speaking the same language as the Toucouleur <note>original: "Toucouleurs"; a sedentary population of the Senegal River valley.</note>, and, on the other hand, that of the Soninke or Marka <note>original: "Soninké ou Marka"; the Soninke were the founders of the ancient Ghana Empire.</note> of the Niger Bend <note>The great curve of the Niger River flowing through modern-day Mali.</note> speaking generally not the language of their kin in Senegal, but that of the Dyula <note>original: "Dioula"; a Mande ethnic group known for their role as long-distance traders.</note>, and that of the Soninke of Djenné <note>original: "Dienné"; an ancient trading city in Mali known for its mud-brick architecture.</note> speaking the language of the Songhai <note>original: "Songai"; the people of the historic Songhai Empire.</note>.

## *Adopted method of classification.*

I have no pretension of opposing a new system to the scientific methods of classification whose difficulties and disadvantages I have just described; I have simply tried to call upon the simultaneous cooperation of these various methods and to classify the ethnic groupings of Upper Senegal and Niger, as they currently present themselves to our observation, by taking into account both the anthropological data <note>The study of human physical characteristics and evolution.</note> that are clearly certain, the most probable traditions relating to the origin of the different groups, the analogies observed in material civilizations, social state, and intellectual character and

This method might not have a very deep scientific foundation, but perhaps it possesses the merit of leading to a result that approaches practical reality as closely as possible, given the state of our current knowledge. I am, moreover, perfectly aware of the gaps and flaws in this classification, which I consider only provisional and which will need to be seriously revised—especially concerning the populations of the Bend <note>original: "Boucle"; referring to the great "Bend of the Niger," the region where the Niger River turns south, encompassing much of modern-day Mali and Burkina Faso.</note>—when we are in possession of more precise and abundant documentation.

I must first define the value and scope of the terms I use to designate each of the categories and units considered.

I reserve the name ***race*** <term>race: In the early 20th-century context of this manuscript, the author uses "race" to denote the broadest biological divisions of humanity, rather than specific ethnic groups.</term> for the major divisions of the human species, as they are commonly understood; that is to say, in this case, it will only concern two races: the white race and the black race. This term, applied to more restricted categories, seems to me inadequate for the meaning one would wish to give it, and it seems quite improper to me to speak of a "Fula race," a "Mandé race," a "Mossi race," etc.

I shall call ***family*** <term>family: A broad classification based on shared ancestry and general physical and cultural characteristics.</term> a group of peoples proceeding, in a general way, from the same origin, presenting the same major anthropological and ethnographic characteristics, and all speaking—with some exceptions—languages that belong to the same linguistic family.

A family understood in this way can be subdivided into several fractions to which I give the name ***groups***, and each of which is characterized by a special modality of the overall characteristics common to all groups in the family.

The division coming immediately after the group is the ***people***: I shall call a "people" an ethnic grouping characterized by common origins and history, and speaking—most generally—a common idiom that is sufficiently differentiated from neighboring idioms to deserve the name "language." It may happen that a people constitutes a group on its own, or at least that a given group is represented

Each people, in turn, is most often subdivided into *tribes*, each of which presents specific secondary characteristics and generally speaks a special "dialect" of the common language shared by the entire people; or, they may have simply become differentiated as a result of their distant geographical position.

Finally, a tribe may comprise several *sub-tribes*, not to mention social subdivisions such as castes, classes, or clans. It is not appropriate to take these into account in a purely ethnic classification, but they should nevertheless be mentioned when they are known to us.

The system adopted here having been thus explained, I can now move to the nomenclature of the various ethnic groupings—a nomenclature which, as will be seen, does not correspond exactly to the classification table of languages that will be provided later in the third part of this work. <note>The author distinguishes between ethnic identity (shared culture/origin) and linguistic identity, noting that they do not always overlap perfectly.</note>

**Nomenclature of the families, groups, and peoples of Upper Senegal-Niger.** <note>Upper Senegal-Niger was a massive administrative territory in French West Africa, covering much of modern Mali, Burkina Faso, and parts of Niger.</note> — The peoples currently inhabiting the civil administration territories of Upper Senegal-Niger number forty, without taking into account the few colonies of foreigners established among them (principally Wolofs and Hausas). They belong to **two races** (the white race and the black race) and are divided into *seven families*. Two of these are of the white race, more or less mixed (*the Semitic family* and the *Hamitic* or *Chamitic family*), and five are of the black race (the *Tekrurian* or *Toucouleur*, *Songhai*, *Mandé*, *Senufo*, and *Voltaic* families).

## **Different names given to the peoples of the Upper Senegal-Niger.**

The ethnic families and groups of West Africa do not know themselves by generic names, and often the various peoples who compose each family do not even suspect the ties of kinship that unite them. Most peoples each designate themselves by a specific name; however, it happens that certain peoples (the Senoufo, for example) do not use a term corresponding to the people as a whole and that only the tribes each designate themselves by a distinct term. On the other hand, it is not uncommon for a foreign people to use a special term to designate an entire family or an entire group which, as far as it is concerned, does not possess the corresponding word in its own language. Finally, the various ethnic groupings are known to us under very different names.

# THE NAMES OF THE MOORS

...depending on which group we were in contact with. Thus, it seemed necessary to me to indicate and, if needed, explain the various names given to each of these groups.

The terms *Semitic* and *Hamitic* <note>These terms derive from the biblical figures Shem and Ham, sons of Noah. In the era this was written, they were standard academic labels for linguistic and ethnic families in Africa and the Near East.</note>, borrowed from the biblical terminology of the children of Noah, are sufficiently well-known, as are the expressions "Arab group" and "Berber group"—or Libyco-Berber—that I do not need to dwell on them.

The name *Moors* <note>original French: "Maures"</note>, which we give to the Arab and Arab-Berber populations of the Azaouad <note>A dry, sandy basin in northern Mali.</note> and the Hodh <note>A natural region of southeastern Mauritania.</note>, was borrowed by us from the Romans, who themselves took it from the Greeks. The Greeks had formed it from the Punic word *Mahourim* (or *Maouharin*), which means "the Westerners" <note>original Punic: "Mahourim" or "Maouharin"</note> and is the exact equivalent of the Arabic term for "Westerners" <note>original Arabic: "Maghrebiyyin"</note>. In this way, "Mauritania" is quite simply a synonym for "Maghreb" <note>Maghreb is the Arabic term for the "West," referring to Northwest Africa.</note>. Among themselves, the Moors identify by the names of their different tribes; however, the Moors of the Hodh who claim an Arab origin give themselves the generic name of *Beni-Hassan* or simply *Hassan* (singular *Hassani*). Meanwhile, they designate those among them whose Berber origin is indisputable by the term *Zenaga* (singular *Zenagui*; in Berber *Iznaguen*, singular *Aznag*; in Fula *Senagabe*, singular *Tienagadio*). It should be added that the word Zenaga, in the mouth of a *Hassani*, carries a somewhat contemptuous meaning and has almost become a synonym for "tributaries" <note>In the social hierarchy of the Sahara, "tributaries" were groups who paid taxes or protection money to warrior tribes (the Hassane), despite often being scholars or farmers.</note>, even though it is the name of one of the most glorious branches of the ancient Berber nation—the one that gave birth to several famous empires, notably that of the Almoravids <note>A powerful Berber Muslim dynasty that ruled the Maghreb and Al-Andalus during the 11th and 12th centuries.</note>. The *Berabich* (singular *Berbouchi*) and the *Kounta* or *Kenata* (singular *Kounti*) know no other generic name than that of each of these two tribes. The Moors as a whole are called *Safalbe* (singular *Tiapado* or *Tiapato*) by the Fula <note>original: "Peuls"</note> and the Toucouleurs; the Songhai call them *Sourkou* or *Sourgou*; and the Mande call them *Soura-ka, Soula-ka, Soulaa-ka, Soularha-ka,* or *Soulurha*. The Tuareg owe this name, by which we usually designate them, to the appellation given to them by the Arabs: *Taouâreg* (singular *Targui*); the Arabs, great lovers of complicated etymologies always drawn from their own language, have attributed to this word the meaning of "renegades" <note>original Arabic: "Taouâreg," linked by folk etymology to the verb "taraka," meaning to abandon.</note> (from the Arabic verb *taraka* "to abandon"), under the pretext that the Tuareg supposedly renounced the Muslim religion twelve times before finally embracing it; some European authors have sought to translate Tuareg as "highway robbers" or more simply "tramps" <note>original Arabic: "thariq," meaning path or road.</note> (from the Arabic word *thariq* "path"), an etymology which, moreover, would not agree with the spelling used by the Arabs to write the name of the Tuareg. But it is much more likely to suppose that *Targui* (from which the plural *Taouâreg* was formed) is quite simply the singular form of the ethnic name *Targa*, a name formerly given to one of the tribes of the Sahara—perhaps that of the *Hoggar* <note>A highland region in the central Sahara, southern Algeria, home to the Kel Ahaggar Tuareg.</note> or that of the *Oulmidden* <note>A major Tuareg confederation located primarily in present-day Mali and Niger.</note>—and then, by extension, to all representatives of the same people (1). The Tuareg only designate themselves by the names of their various tribes or sub-tribes, but, within each tribe, they distinguish themselves into two classes: those of the *Imocharhen* (singular *Amocharh*) or "nobles" and those of the *Imraden* (singular *Amrad*) or "vassals." The Songhai <note>An ethnic group centered along the Niger River.</note> name the Tuareg *Sourkou* or *Sourgou*, as do the Moors, designating more specifically the *Imocharhen* by the term *Bourdâm* or *Berdâm* (2) and the *Imraden* by that of *Daga*. — The Tuareg have with them Black serfs generally designated under the name of *Bella*, who correspond to the *Harrâtin* of the Moors.

The Peuls <note>Also known as the Fula, Fulani, or Fulbe, a predominantly pastoralist group spread across West Africa.</note> call themselves *Foulbé* (singular *Poullo*), a word which, in their language, would mean "the dispersed, the scattered," according to Commander Gaden <note>Henri Gaden (1867–1939), a French colonial official and pioneering scholar of West African languages.</note>. It is the root of this word, pronounced *Peul* by the Wolof, that we have most generally adopted in France to designate this people. It is

# NAMES OF THE PEULS AND THE TOUCOULEURS

**Peuls, Toucouleurs, Foullânia, Foulldniyin, Ifouldn, Ifelldn, Foulani, Bafalatché, Fellata, Kanouri, Mossi, Diawambé, Laobé, Rimaïbé, Soninké, Halpoularen, Fouta, Tekrour, Songhai**

The Mossi <note>The dominant ethnic group of present-day Burkina Faso.</note> designate the Peuls by the name *Silmissé* (singular *Silmiga*). Among the Peuls there exist special castes, notably those of the *Diawambé* (singular *Diawando*) and the *Laobé* (singular *Labbo*), to whom the true Peuls do not apply the generic name of "Foulbé" <note>The endonym, or self-designation, of the Peul/Fulani people.</note>. In addition, they have among them, like the Moors and the Tuareg, Black serfs whom they call *Rimaïbé* (singular *Dimadio*): this word means roughly "those who are to become free," in allusion to the custom by which the descendants of slaves—who originally constituted the Rimaïbé—became free after a few generations; these Rimaïbé are called *Komongallou* by the Soninké.

The Toucouleurs refer to themselves by the term *Halpoularen* (singular *Halpoular*), "those who speak Pular" (1), or by that of *Foutankobé* or *Foutanké* (singular *Foutanko* or *Foutankédio*), meaning "those from Fouta" <note>Referring to Fouta Toro, a highland and riverine region in northern Senegal.</note>, or even by the names of their various tribes or subgroups. The Moors call them *Tekarir* (singular *Tekrouri*) and the Berber-speaking Zenaga call them *Itkariren* (singular *Etkarir*), all words deriving from the name of the ancient city or the ancient country of *Tekrour* <note>An ancient state that flourished in the Senegal River valley from the 9th to 13th centuries.</note>, a country that corresponded roughly to the current Senegalese Fouta and where the Toucouleur people was formed. This last name, which the French have adopted, comes quite simply from the way the Wolof <note>The largest ethnic group in Senegal.</note> pronounce the name of Tekrour and its inhabitants: *Tokoror*, *Tokorogne*, or *Tokolor*. The Mande give the Toucouleurs the name *Foutanka* (people of Fouta).

# THE PEOPLES

**Songhai.** They are divided into several classes, the most noble of which, that of the **Arma** (also called *Darbout* and *Haïdara*), claims descent from the Moroccan soldiers—Berbers, Arabs, and especially Andalusian renegades <note>European Christians, often from Spain, who converted to Islam and served in the Moroccan military.</note>—who, from approximately 1590 to 1650, participated in the conquest of the city of Timbuktu and the Gao Empire. These Arma derive their name from the Arabic word *râmi*, meaning "thrower of projectiles," and explain this etymology by saying that their Moroccan ancestors were the first to use rifles in the Niger region (1). The Arma give the name **Gabibi**, which means "black body"—that is to say, "negroes"—to the lower class of laborers and especially farmers, who constitute the vast majority of the Songhai people. By this, they mean to indicate that people of this class cannot claim white ancestry. A portion of the Songhai population, composed mainly of fishermen and boatmen, is designated by the special terms **Sorko** and **Kourteï**. The Tuareg call the Songhai *Ihattân* (singular *Ahatti*) and the Peuls call them *Diermabé* (singular *Diermadio*); it is this last word that we apply mainly, in the form **Djerma**, to the Songhai of the Dosso and Niamey region on the left bank of the Niger—a region also called **Saberma** or **Zaberma**—while the corresponding region on the right bank of the river and the Songhai who inhabit it are called **Dendi**.

The name **Mandé**, which we provide in the absence of a [general] designation—

---

(1) <note>original: "Cette étymologie peut à bon droit paraître douteuse..."</note> This etymology may rightly seem doubtful, as does the exclusively Moroccan origin of the Arma. The Arabic word *râmi* does not necessarily designate a "rifleman"; it actually refers more specifically to an "archer." Archers formed the bulk not of the Moroccan army, but of the indigenous army that sought to repel the Moroccans. As for the Arma themselves, they deserve the name "negroes" just as much as the Gabibi, at least currently, and are distinguished from the latter neither by color nor, especially, by language. It is probable that they descend primarily from Songhai nobles who held power and constituted the indigenous aristocracy long before the Moroccan conquest. Later, as Moroccan dominance weakened and they reclaimed their rank as masters, they likely wished to justify their replacement of the Moroccan *caïds* <note>Local governors or leaders in North African and Muslim administrative systems.</note> by creating a genealogy that traced their descent from the conquerors. Furthermore, it is quite likely that their claim was partially justified, as it is certainly from noble families that the Moroccans most readily took wives.

# MANDÉ, MANDING, AND MALI

indigenous, to the whole of the ethnic family comprising, among other peoples, the Soninké, the Malinké, and the Diallonké, is nothing other than the name of the mother-country of one of these peoples—that of the Malinké or Mandingos—and of this people themselves. Properly speaking, this name Mandé is no more suitable for the Soninké, the Diallonké, or even the Dioula and Bambara, than the name "English" is suitable for the Scottish and the Irish; but, since one must give a name to each ethnic family, there is ultimately no harm in conforming to a usage that is now accepted.

The country of origin of the Malinké has indeed always borne the name it still bears today: *Mandé* or *Mandeng*, *Mandï* or *Manding*, depending on whether dialectal pronunciations close the final vowel more or less, and whether they elide or exaggerate the nasalization. This name is often pronounced *Mané* or *Mani* by the people of Ouassoulou, *Malé* or *Mali* by the Soninké, and *Mallé* or *Malli*, *Mellé* or *Melli* by the Peuls <note>Also known as the Fula or Fulani people.</note>: this last pronunciation was adopted by several Arabic authors and by European authors who drew upon them, while others adopted the spelling *Mali* or the spelling *Mandé* or *Manding*; but all these forms are merely variants of the same word—variants perfectly in accordance with the laws of Sudanic <term>Sudanic: Referring here to the "Sudan" geographic belt of West Africa, stretching from the Sahara to the tropical forests, not the modern nation-state.</term> phonetics. Some have attempted to find a totemic etymology for this word and have translated *Mali* as "hippopotamus" and *Mandé* as "small manatee": both these etymologies are rejected by the natives of the country—that is, the Malinké—who state that *Mandé* or *Mali* is simply the name of their homeland and that they do not know its meaning (1), and who, moreover, have no national totem, neither the manatee nor the hippopotamus: only one of their clans—

<margin>(1) Furthermore, while the form *mali* may mean "hippopotamus" in certain dialects, this meaning cannot in any way be applied to the form *mandé*; conversely, if one can translate *mandé*, *mané*, *mani*, etc., as "small manatee," it would be very difficult to give the same translation to the forms *mali*, *mallé*, etc.; one could also propose the etymology "son of the master" <note>original: "fils de maître"</note>, but it would be equally doubtful.</margin>

*Soninké* is the name by which the Soninké people refer to themselves. It has been claimed that this word meant "the people or the partisans of the *Sonni*" and had been applied to those who, during the conquest of the Gao Empire by Ali Kolon, founder of the Sonni dynasty (in 1331), allegedly embraced the latter's cause; this etymology seems unacceptable to me for several reasons: first, the Soninké existed as a people and had even played a very significant role in the history of the Sudan <note>Referring to the "Bilad al-Sudan," the geographic belt across West Africa, rather than the modern country.</note> long before the beginning of the Sonni dynasty; furthermore, they seem to have had very little relationship with the Gao Empire, at least until the final years of the Sonni dynasty, and it would be strange if the entire people owed their name to the fact—which is, moreover, hypothetical—that a few of its members had taken the side of the founder of this dynasty. It is probable, moreover, that this word—of which I confess I am completely ignorant of the etymology—is not formed from an element *sonni* or *soni* followed by the suffix *ké* which, in Fula <note>original: "peul". The Fula (or Fulani) are a major ethnic group across West Africa.</note> rather than in Mandé (1), is the suffix of nationality: contrary to what exists in the words Malinké, Foulanké, etc., the syllable *ké* is undoubtedly, in Soninké, part of the root of the word; I find proof of this in the fact that the *k* was preserved by the Berabish Moors <note>A nomadic tribe of the Saharan region.</note> in the form they have given to this name: *Assouanik*. There has also been an attempt (2) to identify the name of the Soninké with that of the *Zenaga*, written *Sanhadja* by Arabic authors; this identification seems quite difficult to establish for me: first, it would be quite surprising if, the two names being identical, the Moors had preserved the form *Zenaga* to designate the Berbers living alongside them and adopted another form—*Assouanik*—to designate the Soninké; second, there are real phonetic differences between the two names, particularly regarding their first vowel,

### THE NAMES OF THE SONINKÉ

...which has always been written *a* and pronounced *a* or *e* by the Arabs in the name of the Zenaga (*Sanhadja*, *Sanaga*, *Zenaga*) <note>The Sanhadja were once one of the largest Berber tribal confederations of the Maghreb and Sahara.</note> whereas it is clearly pronounced *o* or *ou* in the name of the Soninké; finally, it is quite difficult to suppose that the Soninké—who are Black people, sometimes of mixed descent, but undeniably Black—descend from a fraction of the Berber Zenaga. What led Mr. Ch. Monteil <note>Charles Monteil (1871–1949), a French ethnologist and colonial administrator who specialized in West African cultures.</note> to this identification is a passage from the *Tarikh-es-Soudan* <note>original: "Tarikh-es-Soudan"; "The History of the Sudan," a vital 17th-century historical chronicle written in Arabic by Abd al-Sadi.</note> where Sa'di gives the name "Sanhadja" to the "Nono braid-wearers," who were almost undoubtedly a fraction of the Soninké people. In my opinion, there was either an error of information on Sa'di's part, leading him to mistake these Nono for Berbers, or rather an unconscious orthographic error that led him to transcribe into the form "Sanhadja"—well known to him—a form "Soninké" that he might have misheard, which in any case was not familiar to him, and which moreover shares a certain analogy with the form "Sanhadja" when pronounced "Senaga."

Whatever the case may be regarding the word *Soninké*, it is, by the admission of the Soninké themselves, their true name. As I mentioned earlier, the Bérabich <note>A group of Arabized Berbers from the Timbuktu region.</note> have transformed this word into *Assouanik* (singular *Souananki*) (1). The Moors also give the Soninké the name *Azer* or *Adjer*. # THE NAMES OF THE DIOULA

...and especially "traveling merchant, peddler": this is certainly inaccurate; "merchant" is said in Mandé as *diagolila* or *diaolila* <note>original: "diagolila" or "diaolila"; these terms are derived from the root for trade or commerce.</note> or in several other ways, all of which are derivatives of the verb *diago* or *diao* "to trade," but the word *Dioula* does not possess the meaning of "merchant" or "peddler" in any Mandé dialect. However, because the Dioula practice more than other peoples the trade of peddler, their name has become synonymous with "traveling merchant" in most of West Africa, in exactly the same way that the name of the *Auvergnats* <note>People from the Auvergne region of France, who were historically known in Paris as water-carriers and chimney sweeps.</note> was for a long time among us synonymous with "water-carrier" and that of the *Savoyards* <note>People from the Savoy region, traditionally associated with the trade of chimney sweeping in French cities.</note> synonymous with "chimney sweep," and with no more accuracy. Moreover, the Dioula themselves are very firm on this point and claim this word *Diula* or *Diaula* as the proper name of their people or tribe, adding that it means "from the foundation, from the root," that is to say, "those who are of noble origin, who have not been altered by the mixing of foreign blood."

Because the Dioula and the Soninké <note>A Mandé ethnic group often associated with the ancient Ghana Empire and widespread commercial networks.</note> are often confused together in the Niger Bend <note>The great curve of the Niger River in West Africa, a vital historical region for trade and the intersection of various cultures.</note> by religion (both are predominantly Muslim), by trade (merchants, weavers, dyers), and by the use of the same language (the Dioula dialect), they are also often confused under the same names: *Ouangarbé* among the Fula <note>original: "Peuls"; a major pastoralist and scholarly ethnic group spread across West Africa.</note>, *Ouangaraoua* among the Hausa, *Ouankoreï* among the Songhai, *Yarhsé* (singular *Yarhga*) among the Mossi of Ouagadougou, *Kambossé* (singular *Kamboga*) among the Mossi of Yatenga, *Sahersé* (singular *Saherga*) among the Nankana, *Yourou* among the Samo, *Sorho* among the Koulango, *Tiorho* among the Senufo, *Nzoko* among the Agni <note>Also spelled Anyi; an Akan people of Ivory Coast and Ghana.</note>, etc. The Dioula themselves often give the name *Dafing* (1) to those among them and to the Soninké who live in the region of Koury or Dafina (the land of the Dafing).

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic study of West African peoples, shifting from the specific terminology of the Dioula to the broader and often misinterpreted label of "Bambara," clarifying the distinctions between ethnic identity and religious affiliation.</meta>

# THE PEOPLES

According to the *Tarikh-es-Soudan* <note>original: "Tarikh-es-Soudan"; a 17th-century historical chronicle written in Arabic, documenting the history of the Songhai Empire and the middle Niger region.</note>; it is very possible that *Bambara* is nothing more than an alteration of the indigenous pronunciation *Banmana*; it is also possible that the word has another origin. Regardless, it is absolutely certain that, for the Muslims of the Sudan <note>The term "Sudan" here refers to the *Bilad al-Sudan* (Land of the Blacks), the historical geographic region stretching across West Africa, rather than the modern country.</note> in general and of the Niger Bend in particular, the word *Bambara* designates not a specific people nor a special tribe, but the collective of all Sudanese people living among or alongside Muslims who have remained faithful to their indigenous religion. For example, the Dioula of Sikasso and the Kong region call the Sénoufo "Bambara"; the Dioula and Soninké of Odienné call the non-Muslim Malinké <note>The Malinké, or Mandinka, are a major Mandé-speaking ethnic group.</note> who surround them "Bambara"; the Dioula of the Volta countries call the Gbanian and the Dagari "Bambara," and so on. Furthermore, in Sikasso, the expression *bambara-kan* means not the Mandé language nor the Mandé dialect of the Banmana, but rather the Sénoufo language. Consequently, the indiscriminate use of the word *Bambara* has led to unfortunate results; for instance, it has led people to believe that the Bambara-Minianka of the Koutiala district formed a single people with the Bambara of Ségou and Bamako, whereas the former are Sénoufo and the latter are Mandé. Therefore, I prefer to abstain completely from this expression of ambiguous value, and I shall always designate the people of Ségou, Bélédougou, etc., as they designate themselves—that is, by the word *Banmana* (1).

The *Khassonké*, as they call themselves—or *Kassouké*, as the Peuls <note>Also known as the Fulani or Fula, a large ethnic group spread across West Africa.</note> pronounce it—derive their name from that of their country of origin, the Khasso or Khasson (the Kayes region). They often share the name *Sossé* with the Soninké mixed with Malinké of Senegal and the Gambia.

---

(1) Some derive *Bambara* from the Mandé word *bamba* or *bamma* "crocodile" and give this term the meaning of "(those) of the crocodile," in allusion to the fact that the crocodile is a very widespread religious emblem among all the peoples whom the Muslims lump together under the nickname of "Bambara." As for the word *Banmana*, it signifies, according to the Banmana themselves, "refusal to the master" (*ban-ma-na*), in allusion to the legend according to which the Banmana left their country of origin (Ouassoulou) to escape the yoke of Malinké conquerors.

### VARIOUS MANDÉ PEOPLES

The *Malinké* call themselves ***Mandenka, Mandenga, Mandinga*** or ***Maninga*** depending on regional pronunciations; the Dioula prefer to say ***Manenga*** or ***Mandenga*** and the Banmana say ***Maninka***; the Peuls <note>Also known as the Fulani or Fula, a traditionally pastoralist ethnic group widespread across West Africa.</note> call them ***Mandinké, Malinké, Mellinké,*** or ***Mellenké*** (sing. *Mandinkédio, Malinkédio*, etc.) or else ***Mandinkobé, Malinkobé,*** etc. (sing. *Mandinko, Malinko,* etc.), and the Tuareg call them ***Imalan*** (sing. *Amali*): all these expressions have the same value, that of "people of the Mandé, Manding, Mali, Melli, etc.," that is to say, of the country shown on our maps under the name of "Manding," south of Kita and southwest of Bamako, which was indeed the land of origin of those whom we ourselves call *Mandingoes* or *Malinké*. Arab geographers often gave them the name *Wangara* <note>original: "Ouangara"; a historical term used by North African and Arab travelers for Mandé-speaking gold traders.</note> which, today, is mainly applied to the Soninké and the Dioula, as I mentioned just now.

The word *Foulanké* (in the Peul language) or *Foulanka* (in the Mandé language), sometimes used to designate the Peuls or the Toucouleurs <note>The Toucouleur (or Tukulor) are a sedentary ethnic group closely related to the Peuls, primarily living along the Senegal River.</note>, actually applies to populations that can currently be considered incorporated into the Mandé family and who speak only Mandé (the Malinké dialect), although they are certainly of Peul origin, at least in part; they are encountered in several provinces, all called in the Mandé language *Fouladougou* or *Fouladou* (land of the Foula or the Foulanka).

The *Diallonké* or *Diallonka* are, as their name indicates, the indigenous people of *Diallon* or *Fouta-Diallon* and the neighboring regions; they themselves claim the name *Susu* <note>original: "Soussou"; an ethnic group today found primarily in coastal Guinea.</note>, which we prefer to give to those among them who moved toward the Atlantic.

The *Sia* are commonly called *Bobo-Dioula*, although the expression is doubly improper since they are neither *Bobo* nor *Dioula*; it comes from the fact that some of their customs resemble those of the Bobo, while their way of dressing makes them look like the Dioula, whose dialect they have moreover partially adopted, while retaining their own language.

I see no observations to make on the names of other peoples or tribes of the Mandé family (*Bozo, Kâgoro, Samo*,

...Samorho, etc.), except that there are strong presumptions that *Samo* and *Samorho* are one and the same term, with the first form representing the Banmana <note>The Banmana are the people more commonly known to Europeans as the Bambara.</note> pronunciation and the second representing the Dioula pronunciation.

Most of the time, the Sénoufo only refer to themselves by the names of their various tribes (*Bamána*—whom the Mandé call *Minianka* and who should not be confused with the Banmana—*Siénrhè*, *Tagba*, etc.). However, they do possess a term to designate their people as a whole, although they use it very rarely and it is not known to all the tribes: this term is *Siéné* or *Siéna* (1) (in the plural, *Siénamana*). On the other hand, the Malinké and the Banmana, who are familiar with this word, use it to designate them in the forms *Siénéfo*, *Sénéfou*, *Sénofo*, or *Sénoufo*, meaning "(those who) speak *Siéné*," and it is the last of these forms that Europeans use most frequently. The Dioula commonly call the Sénoufo *Bambara* (see above) and sometimes *Nafana* (after one of their tribes in the Ivory Coast) or even *Pomporon* (a term that seems to be a nickname given primarily to the Folo tribe and some sub-groups of the Siénrhè). The Samorho call them *Sopi*; the Koulango call them *Gan* (2), and the Agni call them *Kanga*, a word that in their language has become almost synonymous with "slave" <note>Historically, this linguistic shift often occurred when a specific neighboring group was frequently targeted in slave raids.</note>; the Abron and Asante or Ashanti call them *Pantara* or *Ouandara*.

I have given the name *Voltaic* to the very important ethnic family whose members make up nearly half of the total population of Upper Senegal and Niger <note>A French colonial territory in West Africa that existed from 1904 to 1921.</note>; this name seemed justified to me by the fact that the territory of this family is largely located within the Volta River basin. To simplify the nomenclature, I have assigned to each of its seven groups the name of the primary or best-known people within that group, without intending to imply that this specific group is the ancestor from which the others originated.

The three peoples of the Tombo group (*Tombo* proper, *Dogom* <note>Known today as the Dogon.</note>, and *Déforo*) are commonly designated by the French of the Sudan <note>The "French Sudan" refers to the colonial territory that is now the Republic of Mali.</note> by the generic term *Habé* or *Habbé*, or else by that of *Kado* or *Kaddo*: these two terms are nothing more than the plural and singular forms of a Peul <note>Also known as the Fulani or Fula people.</note> word which is applied to all populations that are neither Arab, nor Berber, nor Peul—that is to say, to all Black Africans. Thus, the Peul of Nigeria call the Hausa *Habé*, just as the Peul of Massina call the highlanders of the Bandiagara escarpment *Habé*. This term (*Habé* or *Kado*) is therefore even more vague and improper than the term Bambara, and must be rejected. It seems indeed—though I cannot state it with absolute certainty—that the highlanders I have just mentioned refer to themselves by the word *Tombo*, while the two other peoples of the same group call themselves *Dogom* (or *Dom*) and *Déforo*. The Peul call the Tombo and at least a portion of the Dogom *Houmbébé* or *Hombobé* (singular: *Koumbédio* or *Kombodo*) (1), and they call the Déforo *Déforobé*. The Mossi reportedly call the Tombo proper *Kibsé* (singular: *Kibga*) and give the name *Suida* to the Tombo group as a whole, but I do not dare to make a definitive pronouncement in this regard.

The *Mossi* call themselves *Mô-sé* or, more rarely, *Mô-si* (singular: *Mô-rha* or *Mô-ga*); they call their country *Mô-rho* and their language *Mô-rhé*. All names of peoples or tribes ending with the suffix *sé* or *si* in the plural and *rha* or *ga* in the singular are borrowed from the language of the Mossi or a language of the same group. — The *Yansi* (singular: *Yanga*), so named by the Mossi, reportedly refer to themselves as *Kôssé*, but I assert nothing in this regard (2). — The *Gourmantché* (singular: *Gourmanga*), meaning "those of the Gourma, from the right bank of the Niger," reportedly call themselves *Bimba*.

### Composition of each group.

1º **Moors of the Azawad.** — I stated above that the Moors of the Azawad <note>Azawad is a large territory in northern Mali, traditionally inhabited by nomadic Tuareg and Moorish tribes</note> were divided into two tribes: the *Bérabich* and the *Kounta*.

Linked to the first of these tribes are the *Oulad-Slimân*, the *Oulad-Abderrahmân*, and the *Oulad-Ameur* and, at least from an ethnic perspective, the sub-tribes of the *Tormoz* (or Tourmous), the *Ousra*, the *Borrada*, the *Oulad-Noumou*, the *Oulad-el-hadj-el-Hassân*, the *Idao-Yata* (or *Doyata*), etc.

Among the Kounta, one includes the *Regaguida* from north of Bamba, the *Ahl-cheikh-sidi-el-Mokhtar* or *Bekkaï* of the Timbuktu region, and the *Oulad-el-Ouafi* of the Mabrouk region, as well as the *Chorfa* <note>singular: "Cherif" (Sharif); descendants, or those claiming to be such, of the family of the Prophet Muhammad</note>, plus vassals of Berber origin (the *Zakhoura*).

Furthermore, it is important not to forget that—however illogical it may seem regarding an ethnic classification—it is impossible for us to separate from the Moors the *Harratin* <note>The Haratin are a social group in the Sahara, often of sub-Saharan African descent, who historically occupied a lower social tier as sedentary laborers or freedmen within nomadic Moorish society</note> of various Black African origins who are, so to speak, incorporated into them. Consequently, independent of individuals whose Semitic blood has been deeply altered by a long history of ancestral alliances with Berbers and Black Africans, there exist among the Moors of the Azawad <note>Azawad is a large territory in northern Mali, traditionally inhabited by nomadic Tuareg and Moorish tribes</note> true Black Africans of pure Black race.

2nd **Moors of the Hodh.** — The Moors of the Hodh <note>The Hodh is a vast geographical depression located in present-day southeastern Mauritania and parts of western Mali</note> comprise, as I have already stated, two very different ethnic elements which are most often found side-by-side but are also sometimes mixed: an Arab element represented by the *Beni-Hassan* and a Berber element—likely more significant in number than the first—represented by the *Zenaga* <note>The Zenaga are a Berber-speaking group, often considered the original inhabitants of the region before the arrival of Arab tribes</note> and by families who call themselves Hassanides <note>descendants of the Beni-Hassan</note> but are nevertheless of Berber origin. It is worth noting that the maraboutic families <term>maraboutic: relating to a Marabout, a Muslim religious leader and teacher in West Africa</term>, who designate themselves by the generic name *Zaouïya* <note>original: "Zaouïya"; refers to people living in a religious fraternity or monastic-style center</note>, are for the most part of Berber origin, or at the very least the result of a mixture of Zenaga and Beni-Hassan—a mixture which many of the Beni-Hassan themselves have not escaped, even among those who claim pure Semitic origin.

Each of the seven great tribes listed above comprises several sub-tribes. Some are considered noble and are primarily composed of Beni-Hassan; others are regarded as vassals <note>in this context, tribes that paid tribute or were under the protection of "noble" warrior tribes</note> and are mainly composed of Zenaga; and others finally contain the maraboutic families. We thus have political and social divisions that are not always ethnic groupings. The most important sub-tribes of the Hodh are:

Among the *Idao-Aïch* or *Douaïch*, those of the *Ahl-Amar* (Arabs and Berbers, divided into the *Abakak* and the *Chrattit*), the *Tadjakant* (Arabs and Berbers), the *Ligouatit* and the *Louata* (Berbers), the *Laghlal* (Arabs), the *Ahl-Mokhtar* and the *Ahl-Soueïd* (Arabs and Berbers), the *Idao-Ali* (marabouts), and the *Ahl-Sidi-Mahmoud* or *Oulad-sidi-Mahmoud* (marabouts, linked to the Idao-el-hadj or Darmankor of the Mauritanian Adrar <note>The Adrar is a highland region in central Mauritania</note>);

Furthermore, certain Moors of the Hodh are descended from a very ancient mixture of Berbers with Fulani or Proto-Fulani: they are called *Massîn* or *Ahl-Massina* or even *Guirganké*, and in the Sahel <note>The semi-arid transition zone between the Sahara Desert and the Sudanian savanna</note> they are divided into "white Guirganké" and "black Guirganké," though this distinction is no more justifiable than that of the *Bobo* people into white, red, and black.

**3. Tuareg.** — The Tuareg of the noble families (*Imocharhen* <note>The warrior aristocracy of Tuareg society</note>) are, it seems, of nearly pure Berber blood, while many of those from the vassal families (*Imraden* <note>The social class of pastoralists who historically paid tribute to the noble lineages</note>) are more or less of mixed race as a result of unions with Black Africans or Fulani. Among the Tuareg, as among the Moors of the Hodh, there exist maraboutic families who have often allied themselves with...

---

(1) The *Nimadi* are said to be of Jewish origin and reportedly do not practice Islam; they are encountered in the Oualata region. <note>The Nimadi are a specialized group of nomadic hunters in the eastern Mauritanian desert</note>

(2) According to Mr. Gautier (*The Conquest of the Sahara*), the word *Harratin* likely means "plowmen" (from the verb *haratha* <note>original: "haratsa"</note>, though the usual spelling includes a *tha* [ث] and not a *tsa* [س]) and does not necessarily designate Black Africans or even people of servile status. However, in practice, this word applies to Black Africans who descend from former slaves and who have become the serfs of the Moors; it does not apply to the Black Africans of the Saharan towns whose ancestors occupied the land before the Berber domination—that is to say, the Azer or Soninke of Tichit, Oualata, etc.

<summary>This page details the specific sub-tribes of the Moors in the Hodh region and introduces the Tuareg, highlighting the complex social hierarchies and the racial blending between Arab, Berber, and Black African populations.</summary>
<keywords>Oulad-Mbarek, Mejdouf, Oulad-Delim, Nimadi, Harratin, Guirganké, Tuareg, Imocharhen, Imraden, ethnic mixing, Saharan social hierarchy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic survey of the region, moving from the Tuareg tribal structures to the Fulani people. It details the complex social hierarchies and caste systems that define these societies in the Upper Senegal and Niger territory.</meta>

<header>THE PEOPLES</header>

Arabs. Finally, as with the Moors, one must note the presence of numerous Black serfs (the *Bella*), who are so well integrated today with their masters that it is difficult to separate them, even in an ethnic classification. <note>The Bella are a servile caste of the Tuareg, historically composed of captured or tributary sedentary populations who adopted the language and culture of their masters.</note>

Each Tuareg tribe comprises several sub-tribes: some are noble, others are vassals, and others are maraboutic <note>maraboutic: religious lineages of scholars and teachers</note>. The principal sub-tribes in the civil territories of Upper Senegal and Niger are:

*Among the Iguellad*, those of the *Tagama* or *Kel-Haoussa* (nobles); the *Kel-Antassar* (1), *Kel-Nkounder*, and *Kel-Ncheria* (marabouts); and the *Kel-Tounloukouri*, *Inataben*, *Kel-Taberint*, *Kel-Dokoré*, *Kel-Rezzaf*, *Kel-Tinakaouat*, *Kel-Ouorodjel*, *Kel-Teguiaït*, and *Kel-Tountoun* (vassals);

*Among the Kel-Tadmekket*, those of the *Tenguéréguif*, the *Igouadaren*, the *Kel-Temoulaï*, and the *Irréganaten* (nobles); the *Chorfiga* or *Icherifen*, the *Zinmaten*, the *Ahl-sidi-Ali*, and the *Kel-es-souk* (marabouts); and the *Imededrhen* and the *Idnán* (vassals);

*Among the Oulmidden*, those of the *Kel-Gheress*, the *Oudalen*, and the *Tenguéréguédech* (nobles); and the *Kel-Oulli* and *Kel-Gossi* (vassals).

It is worth adding to this list the following vassal sub-tribes, whose attachment to a specific tribe is unknown to me: *Kel-Guerisouân*, *Kel-Tigouelt*, *Imakelketten*, *Ibourliten*, *Imetchas*, *Kel-Rîla*, *Déguésellen*, *Chemenama*, *Damossân*, and *Missiguender*.

## 4. <term>Peuls</term> or <term>Foulbé</term>. 
<note>Known in English as the Fulani or Fula, this widespread ethnic group is traditionally nomadic and plays a vital role in West African history and religion.</note>

— We shall see further on how many diverse elements comprise the current Fulani people, elements among which the Black race holds an undeniable place. Furthermore, we must consider as part of this people the specialized castes of the *Laobé* (singular *Labbo*, woodworkers and woodcutters), the *Abarbé* (singular *Gabardo*, jewelers and shoemakers), the *Ouaïloubé* (singular *Baïlo*, blacksmiths and potters), and the *Mabbé* (singular *Mabo*, <term>griots</term> and weavers). <note>Griots are traditional West African historians, storytellers, and musicians who preserve oral traditions and genealogies.</note>

---

(1) Some have attempted to link the name of the *Kel-Antassar* to that of the <term>Ansâr</term> <note>original: "Ansâr" — the "Helpers" or early supporters of the Prophet Muhammad in Medina</note>, but the spelling used by the best Arabic authors for the name of the *Kel-Antassar* (using the letter *sin* <note>س - a standard 's' sound</note> and not a *sad* <note>ص - a heavy, emphatic 's' sound</note>) requires that this etymology be rejected.

<header>FULANI</header>

...the *Ouambabé* (singular *Bambado*: musicians and griots <note>Griots are West African hereditary historians, storytellers, and praise-singers.</note>), the *Ouaouloubé* (singular *Baoulo*: beggars), the *Soubalbé* (singular *Tiouballo*: fishermen and boatmen), and the *Diawamhé* (singular *Diawando*: brokers and weavers). We must also classify among the Fulani <note>original: "Peuls"</note> certain highly mixed branches, such as the *Silmimossi*, who issued from unions between the Fulani and the Mossi, and even groups of pure Black African origin who have been incorporated into the Fulani: the *Rimaïbé*, who correspond to the *Haratin* of the Moors and the *Bella* of the Tuareg <note>The Rimaïbé were a servile class of sedentary farmers historically bound to the nomadic Fulani.</note>.

The Fulani, beyond their distribution into geographical tribes or branches, are further divided into a certain number of clans, each of which may be represented in several tribes at once. The most widespread clans in Upper Senegal-Niger are those of the *Ourourbé* (singular *Bourourdo*, *Balardo*, or *Boli*), the *Tôrobé* (singular *Tôrodo*) (1), the *Dialloubé* (singular *Diallo*), the *Yalalbè* or *Alaïbé* (singular *Galadia*), the *Irlabé* (singular *Guerladia*), the *Oualarbé* (singular *Balardo*), the *Salsalbé* (singular *Tialtialla*), the *Fitobé* (singular *Pitodo*), the *Daébé* (singular *Daédia*), the *Férébé* or *Férobé* (singular *Pérédio*), the *Sitigahé* (singular *Tyitigadio*), etc. Other clan names, borrowed from the Toucouleur or Mandé peoples, take the same form in both singular and plural; such are *Ba* or *Diakité* (the same clan as the Ourourbé), *Soumontara* (the same clan as the Dialloubé), *Bari* or *Sangaré* (the same clan as the Daébé), and *Sô* or *Sidihé* (the same clan as the Férobé), etc. Finally, it should be noted that many individuals bear, as a clan name, the very name of the Fulani people (*Poullo*) or that of the caste to which they belong (*Labbo*, *Diawanda*, etc.).

5º **Toucouleurs**. — The Toucouleurs or Foutanké, a people who are little inclined toward nomadism...

---

(1) The word *Tôrobé* does not mean, as is generally believed, "people originating from Toro"—an expression that in the Fulani language is *Toronké*, *Torankobé*, or *Toronâbé* (singular *Toronkédio*, *Taronka*, or *Toronâdio*). According to Commander Gaden, *Tôrobé*—or more accurately *Tôrodbé* or *Tôrobbé* (singular *Tôrodo*)—means "those who pray together" <note>The term literally translates to "those who supplicate," referring to the clan's historical role as a scholarly and religious elite.</note>; it is the name of a clan that could just as easily be considered a caste. This clan has numerous representatives in Toro, but no more there than elsewhere; there does not appear to be any more of a relationship between the region of Toro and the *Tôrobé* clan than between Diallon (Fouta-Djallon) and the *Dialloubé* clan.

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic survey of the peoples inhabiting the Upper Senegal-Niger region, moving from the general introduction of the Toucouleur people to their specific regional subgroups and clans, followed by an overview of the Songhai people.</meta>

<header>THE PEOPLES</header>

The Toucouleur, who are numerous throughout the Upper Senegal-Niger region, are divided into four fractions depending on whether they originate from **Dimar** (west of Toro), **Toro** (the province of Podor, known as the *Toronké* or *Torondbé*), **Fouta** proper (the province of Saldé, the *Foutanké* proper, including the *Foutanké* of Lao, the *Foutanké Irlâbé*, the *Bosséabé*, the *Ebiâbé*, and the *Koliâbé*), or **Damga** (the province of Matam, including the *Dénianké*, the Toucouleur of Ganar, and the *Aéranké*).

Furthermore, like the Fulani <note>original: "Peuls"</note>, they are divided into a certain number of clans, the principal ones being those of the *Ba* or *Boli*, the *Ka*, the *Si* or *Bari*, the *Sô* (1), the *Li*, the *Fal*, the *Tal*, the *Sal*, the *Diao*, the *Kane*, the *Diko*, etc. (2).

6° **Songhai**. — The *Songhai* people, as they appear today, include the *Arma*, the *Gabibi*, and the *Sorko* or *Kourteï*, which are classes or castes whose composition we have seen above <note>The Arma are descendants of 16th-century Moroccan invaders; the Sorko are traditional fishermen of the Niger River.</note>. I have also mentioned that it is appropriate to link them to the southeastern fractions known by the names **Dendi**, **Djerma**, and **Zaberma**. In Timbuktu, the class of *alfa* or Muslim doctors is usually ranked among the Songhai (*alfa* is said to be the abbreviation of the Arabic *al-faqih* <note>original: "le jurisconsulte"</note> meaning "the legal scholar"): in reality, these *alfa* are of multiple origins and are composed of people belonging to very diverse ethnic groups.

The Songhai are divided into clans, like the Fulani, the Toucouleur, and all the peoples of the Sudan (excepting the Moors and the Tuareg), but I possess very little information regarding their clan names; I only know that one finds among them the clans of the *Meïga* and the *Haïdara*—the latter including the *Arma* who claim a Sherifian origin <note>Descendants of the Prophet Muhammad</note>—and that the *Sorko* caste is divided between two great clans, that of the *Faran* or *Faram* and that of the *Fono*.

---

(1) Barth <note>Heinrich Barth (1821–1865) was a German explorer of West Africa.</note> says that the name for the collective body of Fulani-speaking people appeared to him to be *So*: perhaps he confused this with the Toucouleur clan of the *Sô*, which was very widespread among the princely families of the Sokoto Empire at the time of his journey.

(2) Many Toucouleur also carry clan names with singular and plural forms identical to those of the Fulani: the *Tôrobé* clan in particular has many representatives among the Toucouleur. Finally, one finds among the latter the same castes as among the Fulani, with the same names.

# BOZO AND SONINKÉ

7º **Bozo**. — The Bozo have sometimes been identified with the Sorko on one hand and the Somono on the other; from an ethnic perspective, this is an error. To be sure, there is indeed a common trait among these three groups: all three engage in fishing and navigation. However, the Sorko and the Somono engage only in this dual profession, or rather, this trade is, in a sense, the privilege of their caste. They form—the former among the Songhai, the latter among the Bambara <note>original: "Banmana"</note>—a caste analogous to that of the *Soubalbé* among the Fulani <note>original: "Peuls"</note>, a caste of fishermen and boatmen. The Bozo, on the contrary, do not constitute a caste, at least at the present time, and are not exclusively fishermen and boatmen; some inhabit villages quite far from the river and engage in agriculture there. The Sorko are Songhai, and the Somono are Bambara; the Bozo form a distinct people. I have no information on the clan names carried by the Bozo, except for those of the *Diennépo*, *Sétao*, and *Karapata* clans, cited by Mr. Ch. Monteil <note>Charles Monteil (1871–1949) was a French ethnologist and colonial administrator who wrote extensively on the history of Djenné.</note>.

8º **Soninké**. — I include within the Soninké people, at least from an ethnic point of view, the *Nono* tribe and those of its current representatives commonly called the *Diennenké* <note>meaning "the people of Djenné"</note> because they constitute almost the entire population of Djenné. I also include the *Diawara* (*Sagoné* or *Sahonéra* and *Dabo*), a hybrid group partaking at once of the tribe, the caste, and the clan, which seems to correspond among the Soninké to the *Diawambé* group among the Fulani.

The clans proper are numerous among the Soninké. The most widespread in the Upper Senegal-Niger are those of the *Diakaté*, *Diakhaté*, *Diaghaté* or *Niakaté*; the *Sissé*; the *Silla*; the *Didbi* or *Didbira*; the *Sakho*; the *Tounkara* <note>original: "(1)"</note>; the *Daramé*; the *Kamara*; the *Sissokho*, *Soussokho* or *Sossé*; the *Niarè*; the *Touré* (of which the *Daraoué* are a part); the *Doukouré*; the *Diarisso* or *Diaressi*; the *Koromakha* or *Koromaga*; the *Soumaré*; the *Souaré*; the *Sibi*; the *Bakili* or *Simbara* or *Sempré*; the *Gourseï*; the *Kounaté* or *Kounaré*; the *Taraoré*; the *Diabouraga*; the *Gaoudéra*; the *Kanndé* or *Kannté*; the *Koumma* or *Koumba*; the

---

<note>original: "(1)"</note> The *Tounkara* present themselves as being of royal stock and derive their name from *tounka*, meaning "king."

# THE PEOPLES

*Kaba*, *Fofana*, *Ouagui*, *Dikéné*, *Bérété*, *Diagouraga*, *Soma*, *Koné*, *Séméga*, *Maréga*, *Mokhassiré*, *Tiléra*, *Gakou*, *Sarambaunou*, *Yatéra* or *Yaté*, *Timéra* or *Timété*, *Fadé*, *Nambaunou*, *Goundiémou*, *Galadyi*, *Baradyi*, *Soudouré*, *Kalé*, *Mana*, *Koussata*, *Samunra*, *Mangara*, etc. The Soninké who claim sharifian origin <note>meaning they claim descent from the family of the Prophet Muhammad</note> take the name of *Sirifé* or, in the Djenné-Timbuktu region, that of *Haïdara*.

From an ethnic perspective, I consider as Soninké all the *Marka* <note>a term often used by neighboring groups like the Bambara to refer to the Soninké</note> of the Niger Bend and the Bambara <note>original: "banmana"</note> and Malinké countries, although most no longer use their original language and have adopted the speech of the Dioula, the Bambara, or the Malinké depending on the region, just as the Soninké of Djenné have adopted the Songhai language. The *Dafing*, or Muslims of Dafina, are often identified as Marka—that is to say, Soninké; in reality, the Dafing are composed, from the perspective of their origin, partly of Soninké and partly of Dioula.

9º **Dioula**. — The Dioula are not distributed into tribes; perhaps it would even be more accurate to consider them as a tribe rather than a people, at least from a linguistic point of view. However, they are divided into clans, the principal ones being those of the *Ouatara*, *Konaté* or *Kounaté*, *Sissé*, *Konndé* or *Koné*, *Kouloubali* or *Kouroubari*, *Sarhandorho* or *Sarkanorho*, *Kamara* or *Kamaya*, *Sinngaré* or *Sinnari*, *Diabi*, *Fofana*, *Touré*, *Daa*, *Dagnorho*, *Dosso*, *Barho*, *Timété*, *Kangoté*, *Garamvoté*, *Tondossama* or *Samatondo*, *Siya*, *Nanaya*, *Dérébo*, *Daramé*, *Karidioula*, *Sissouma*, *Bérété*, *Sorkoba*, *Dembélé*, *Koïta*, *Somarha*, *Koro*, *Taraoré*, *Bamba*, *Kérou*, *Sarha*, *Sanou*, etc. One also encounters *Sirifé*, who claim sharifian origin.

I felt I should attach the small tribe of the *Boron* or *Bolon* to the Dioula; they have representatives in the districts of Bobo-Dioulasso (8,000) and Koury (450).

# THE BANMANA

10° **Kågoro.** — The Kågoro people—or tribe, if one prefers—has the *Kågorota*, *Fofana*, *Kané*, *Tounkara*, *Magaza* or *Makassa*, *Konaté*, and *Touré* as its principal clans.

11° **Banmana.** <note>Today more commonly known as the Bambara, the Banmana are the largest ethnic group in modern-day Mali.</note> — The *Banmana*, like the *Dioula*, the *Kågoro*, the *Khassonké*, the *Malinké*, and the *Foulanké*, could be considered, especially from a linguistic point of view, as forming a single tribe rather than a distinct people. They are divided into several political and geographical subgroups (*Kaartanka*, *Bélédougouka*, *Ségouka*, *Baninkoka*, etc.). Their principal clans are those of the *Kouloubali* (of which the *Massassi* are a part) (1), the *Taraoré* or *Travélé* (of which the *Dembélé* or *Dambélé* are a part), the *Doumouya* or *Doumbouya* (of which the *Kourouma* are a part), the *Diara* (of which the *Konnté* or *Koné* and the *Sinngaré* are a part), the *Fofana*, the *Konaté* or *Kounari*, the *Koussata*, the *Tangara*, the *Kanté* or *Kané*, the *Niarè*, the *Touré*, the *Dansira* (2), the *Mariko*, the *Sanorho*, the *Sissé*, the *Samakè*, the *Kamara*, the *Bouaré*, etc.

As I mentioned above, I link the *Somono* caste (fishers and boatmen) to the Banmana. Other castes also exist among the Banmana: the *Noumou* (blacksmiths and potters), the *Lorho* (copper jewelers), the *Koulè* (woodworkers), the *Diéli* (griots <note>traditional oral historians, musicians, and praise-singers</note>), the *Founè* or *Founérkè* (religious griots and magicians), and the *Donzo* or *Lonzo* (hunters); these various castes are not unique to the Banmana people: they are found under the same names among other Mande peoples and, under different names, among most of the peoples of the Sudan <note>In this historical context, "Sudan" refers to the *Bilad al-Sudan* or the West African Sahel region, specifically the area of former French Sudan, not the modern nation of Sudan.</note>. Within any given people, the members of these castes are not designated by the locals by the name of the people, but by the name of their respective castes; however, from an ethnic perspective, it is appropriate to incorporate them into the people as a whole.

***

(1) The *Massassi* (from *massa* “king” and *si* “descendants” <note>original: "massa « roi » et si « descendance »"</note>) are the Kouloubali of the senior branch.
(2) According to Father Brun, the name *Dansira* would be given to women of the Dembélé clan; without wishing to contradict this very well-informed missionary, I must say that I have known men who bore this name and gave it as that of a specific clan.

# THE PEOPLES

12° *Khassonké*. — The Khassonké, who are quite few in number, include the clans of the *Sissokho* (also known as *Sousokho* or *Sossé*), the *Séga*, the *Sambala*, the *Diala*, the *Fali*, the *Diakité* (or *Diakhaté*), the *Sangaré*, the *Sidibé*, the *Diallo*, etc.

13° *Malinké* or Mandingues. — The Mandingue people—or tribe—is divided into several sub-tribes which are primarily geographical branches. Regarding the Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A former administrative territory in French West Africa, covering parts of modern-day Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso</note>, these branches are those of *Manding* proper, *Bambougou* (or *Bambouk*), *Gangaran*, *Ouassoulou*, etc.

The principal clans are those of the *Keïta* (which include the *Mansaré* (1), the *Kanessi*, and the *Batassi*), the *Diara* (which include the *Konnté* or *Koné*), the *Kouloubali* (which include the *Bamba*), the *Taraoré* (which include the *Dembélé*), the *Doumouya* (which include the *Kourouma*), the *Diarassouba*, the *Kamissorho*, the *Sissé*, the *Sarhanorho*, the *Kamara* or *Kamaaté*, the *Diabaaté* or *Diawaté*, the *Konaté* or *Koyaté*, the *Kannté*, the *Tounkara*, the *Fané* or *Fani*, the *Samaké*, the *Fofana*, the *Diomansi* or *Diomandé*, the *Sissoko* (comprising the *Maga* and the *Koromaga*), the *Barhayorho*, the *Mariko*, the *Doukouré*, the *Béré* (also *Béréya* or *Bérêté*), the *Mété* or *Mérité*, the *Souko*, the *Demba*, the *Sakiliba* (2), etc. To these must be added a few *Sirifé* of alleged Sherifian origin <note>Claiming descent from the Prophet Muhammad</note>.

14° *Foulanké*. — The Foulanké are, as I mentioned above, descendants of Peuls <note>also known as the Fulani or Fula people</note> with a very heavy Mandingue intermixture. In their customs and language, they are hardly distinguishable today from the Malinké proper. They are recognized primarily by their clan names, which are almost exclusively *Diakité*, *Sankaré* (or *Sangaré*), *Sidibé*, and *Diallo*.

15° *Diallonké*. — The principal clans of the Diallonké of the Upper Senegal-Niger are those of the *Monékata*, the *Kessékho*, the *Dagnokho*, the *Dao*, the *Kontaga*, the *Touré*, the *Diatara*, the *Danvoko*, the *Bamba* (or *Bambaya*), the *Siré* (or *Siréya*), the *Kelléma*, etc.

---

(1) *Mansaré* means, like *Massassi*, "of royal stock."
(2) According to Father Brun, *Souko* is the name given to women of the Keïta clan, *Demba* to women of the Sissoko clan, and *Sakiliba* to women of the Doumouya clan.

# SENUFO AND VOLTAIC PEOPLES

16th, 17th, and 18th *Samo*, *Samorho*, and *Sia*. — I do not possess sufficiently certain information regarding the clans of these three peoples, nor on those of the tribes of doubtful classification that neighbor them (*Blé*, *Natioro*, *Ouara*, and *Sembla*). Most individuals belonging to these peoples or tribes, when questioned about their clan, respond with a Dioula <term>diamou</term> <note>clan name</note> (or a Mossi one in the case of the Samo); however, it is highly probable that this Dioula or Mossi <term>diamou</term> is merely a sort of translation of their national <term>diamou</term>.

19th *Senufo*. — I previously provided a list of ten Senufo tribes whose presence has been confirmed in the Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A former administrative territory in French West Africa, covering parts of modern-day Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso</note>. I should add that the sub-tribe of the *Niéné*, which has representatives in the district of Bougouni, is attached to the *Siénérhè* tribe. I am only aware of five Senufo clans: the *Soroo*, *Yéo*, *Siluè*, *Tuò*, and *Sékongo*, but others likely exist. For instance, among the Senufo of the Koutiala district, the *Malé*, *Péné*, and *Ounogo* clans have been reported. Like the Samorho and the Sia, the Senufo frequently adopt Dioula, *Bambara*, or *Malinké* clan names (*Kouloubali*, *Ouatara*, *Koné*, *Diarassouba*, *Touré*, *Dagnorho*, *Kamara*, *Sànou*, *Dembélé*, *Fofana*, etc.).

The same castes exist among the Senufo as among the *Mande* and the *Fulani*; I do not know the names these castes take among the Senufo, except for that of the *Sono* or *Sonon* caste, which corresponds roughly to that of the *Founè* among the Mande (<term>griots</term> <note>West African oral historians, musicians, and praise-singers</note> who are religious and magical in nature).

I also know that all the peoples of the Voltaic family <note>A group of languages and peoples primarily located in the savanna regions of West Africa, such as the Mossi and Lobi</note> are divided into clans, but most of the time we only know the Mande equivalent of their national <term>diamou</term> or <term>sondré</term> <note>terms for clan names or surnames</note>.
