### Numerical distribution of the peoples of Upper Senegal-Niger by race, family, and religion. — The white race—including, however illogical it may be, not only the Moors, the Tuareg, and those Fulani <note>original: "Peuls"</note> most mixed with Black blood, but also the pure Black people who live with them (*Harratin*, *Bella*, and *Rimaïbé* <note>These groups historically lived in various states of dependency or servitude to nomadic Saharan peoples</note>)—comprises, within the current civil territories of Upper Senegal-Niger, 566,175 representatives. All are Muslim, with the exception of 35,646 animist Fulani (2). Dividing these 566,175 indigenous people between the two families, Semitic and Hamitic <note>19th-century linguistic and racial categories that have since been largely discredited or redefined</note>, would be very difficult.

The remainder of the 4,800,000 inhabitants of the colony (3), or **4,233,528**—the vast majority, in a word—belongs to the *Black race* and includes only 608,642 Muslims at most, compared to **3,624,886** animists. The distribution of Black indigenous people among the five families is as follows:

---

(1) To complete this nomenclature—which is, moreover, very imperfect—of the clan names of Upper Senegal-Niger, I provide below the <term>diamou</term> or <term>santa</term> <note>clan names</note> most frequently used by the Wolof settled in this colony: *Ndiaye*, *Diop*, *Diouf*, *Tiam*, *Diang*, *Sar*, *Tièp*, *Niang*, *Ngom*, *Diao*, *Boye*, etc.
(2) I use the term *animism* to refer to the set of beliefs common to all non-Muslim populations of West Africa—beliefs involving a mixture of monotheism, dynamism <note>The belief in impersonal spiritual forces</note>, and animism proper, but which manifest through a nearly exclusively animist cult. I will explain later (Part V) why I adopted this term and why I rejected the completely improper—though commonly used—expressions "paganism" and "fetishism."
(3) 4,809,053 or 4,799,703, according to the various census tables provided to me.

They disappear toward Mopti as one travels up the Niger: Djenné, which is quite wrongly considered to be a Songhai city, contains only three families with Songhai ancestors, and the vast majority of its inhabitants are of Soninké origin; it is true that these Soninké now speak the Songhai language, but this is a phenomenon due to political and economic reasons which we will discuss later, and which has nothing to do with the origin of the *Diennenké* <note>The people of Djenné</note>. Thus, when one relies on the physical characteristics of the people of Djenné to demonstrate the so-called Egyptian or Libyan origin of the Songhai (1), the same error of principle is committed as when relying on the architectural style of the houses in Djenné to prove the same origin; this style in no way represents Songhai architecture and is, moreover, of Moroccan and not Egyptian importation. <note>The author is refuting 19th-century theories that West African civilizations must have been imported from North Africa or the Middle East.</note>

<header>THE PEOPLES</header>

As seen in the preceding table, the *Bozo* (15,394, all of whom are Muslim) are located in the <term>circles (cercles)</term> <note>The "circle" was the primary administrative district in French colonial Africa, governed by a district commander.</note> of Djenné, Mopti, and Bandiagara, with a few representatives in San; the *Soninké* (243,392, including 231,578 Muslims and 13,814 animists) are primarily represented in the <term>Sahel</term> <note>The semi-arid transition zone between the Sahara Desert and the Sudanian Savanna.</note> (the circles of Kayes, Nioro, Goumbou, Sokolo, Niafounké, Mopti, and Djenné) and in the part of the Sudanese region bordering the Sahel (Northern Bamako circle, Northern Ségou circle, the San district, and Northern Koury circle), with some colonies in the Saharan towns (Tichit, Taoudenni, Oualata, Néma, etc.), while the rest of Upper Senegal-Niger contains only a tiny number; finally, the *Dioula* (227,270, including 147,786 Muslims and 79,484 animists) are all found in the South and Southwest of the Niger Bend (principally the circles of Ouagadougou, Ouahigouya, Koury, Bobo-Dioulasso, and Sikasso). As we shall see further on, almost all the Soninké living in the Niger Bend have abandoned their own language to adopt the speech of the Dioula.

# DISTRIBUTION OF THE MANDÉ

Banmana <note>The Banmana are more commonly known today as the Bambara, the largest ethnic group in modern-day Mali.</note> (among whom the Somono <note>A group of specialized river-dwellers and fishermen along the Niger River.</note> form the greatest number), 4,285 Khassonké, 3,380 Malinké, and 8,589 Foulanké <note>A group historically resulting from the linguistic and cultural mixing of Fula (Peul) and Mandé populations.</note>. The *Kâgoro* are all animists <note>Adherents of traditional indigenous religions rather than Islam or Christianity.</note>.

The *Kâgoro* form only small groups scattered for the most part in the South of the western <term>Sahel</term> <note>The semi-arid transition zone between the Sahara Desert and the Sudanian Savanna.</note>. The *Banmana*, who constitute one of the most numerous peoples of Upper Senegal-Niger and alone form about two-thirds of the Central Mandé and nearly half of all Mandé from the three groups combined, appear as a compact mass straddling the Niger River (the <term>circles</term> <note>The "circle" (cercle) was the primary administrative district in French colonial Africa.</note> of Bamako, Ségou, and Bougouni) with very significant colonies in the Sahel on one hand and to the East of the Bani River on the other. The *Khassonké*, who are very few in number, inhabit the Khasso region and its dependencies (the circle of Kayes) and a portion of the Sanga (the circle of Nioro). The *Malinké* <note>Also known as the Mandinka or Maninka.</note> are, of all the Mandé in Upper Senegal-Niger, those whose habitat is the most compact and presents the least interruption; generally speaking, this habitat extends South of the Senegal River from the Falémé to the Bakhoy (Bambouk and Gangaran), then South of the railroad from the Bakhoy to the Niger (Manding), and finally, East of the Niger, South of the Banmana country (Eastern Ouassoulou) (1). The *Foulanké*, on the contrary, are found scattered in the Ganadougou (circle of Sikasso), in the Birgo (circle of Kita), and in the various Fouladougous (circles of Bougouni, Kita, and Bafoulabé).

The preceding table shows that the Voltaic family is clearly clustered within the Volta River basin and the surrounding highlands; their territory is occupied almost exclusively by them, with the exception of a certain number of <term>Peuls</term> <note>Also known as the Fula or Fulani people.</note> scattered here and there, and primarily urban colonies populated by Northern Mandé (<term>Soninké</term> and <term>Dioula</term>). The *Tombo* <note>The "Tombo" and "Dogom" mentioned here are subgroups of what is known today as the Dogon people, famous for their cliffside villages and complex cosmology.</note> prefer to inhabit the summits or the slopes of the cliffs known as Bandiagara, Douentza, Hombori, etc. The *Dogom* are found in roughly the same regions, but they live instead on the plains or at the edge of the mountains. As for the *Déforo*, they are primarily spread across the Aribinda region (between Djibo and Dori).

# DISTRIBUTION OF THE VOLTAIC PEOPLES

Mossi. The Nankana live near the Red Volta, straddling the French-English border. The Gourmantché occupy most of the Fada-n-Gourma <term>Circle</term><note>A "Circle" (Cercle) was a primary administrative district used in French West Africa, governed by a district commander.</note>, as well as the far south of the Dori Circle and the tip of the Say Circle that extends between the two aforementioned districts. The Nioniossé are found alongside or among the Mossi in the regions of Yatenga, Yâko, and Ouagadougou, and in more compact groups in the Kipirsi (the triangle formed by Koury, Boromo, and Yâko). The Nounouma inhabit the area west of the Black Volta at the level of Boromo (north of the Oulé) and east of the same river, south of the Nioniossé and north of the Dagari proper. The Sissala live east of the Nounouma and west of the Nankana, with the junction point of the Nounouma and Sissala coinciding with the town of Léo. The Boussansé are located between the White Volta and the Fada-n-Gourma Circle, starting from Tenkodogo and moving south.

<meta>This page continues the ethnographic survey of the Voltaic family, specifically completing the description of the Bobo subgroups and moving into the Lobi, Koulango, and Bariba groups within the Upper Senegal and Niger colony.</meta>

->THE PEOPLES<-

The *Kian* are the westernmost of the Bobo and are found spread not far from the right bank of the Bani River, between Mopti and San, but are especially numerous around the latter town. The *Tara* follow them toward the East, between San and Koury. The *Boua* live to the south of the Kian and the Tara. The *Niénigué* are found to the east of the Boua, situated between them on one side and the Dagari-Oulé and Nounouma on the other.

E. — **Lobi group** (74,650 representatives).
This group is located in the <term>Circle</term><note>A "Circle" (Cercle) was a primary administrative district in French West Africa.</note> of Gaoua, at least regarding the colony of Upper Senegal and Niger, for it has some representatives in the Ivory Coast (Bouna district). In Upper Senegal and Niger, it includes: 62,050 *Lobi* proper, living mostly in the Gaoua region and to the west of that <term>post</term><note>A "post" refers to a smaller colonial administrative or military station.</note>; 5,950 *Dian*, forming the bulk of the population of Diébougou and its surroundings; 5,550 *Pougouli*, spread mainly along the Pougouliba or Bougouriba River—which owes its name to them—upstream from Diébougou; and finally 1,100 *Gan*, living in Lorhosso in the southwest of the Circle.
All are animists <note>Followers of traditional indigenous religions</note>, with the exception of 1,000 Muslim Dian in the town of Diébougou.

F. — **Koulango group** (4,000 representatives).
This group, which is quite numerous in the Ivory Coast, contains only 4,000 individuals in Upper Senegal and Niger from the *Lorho* tribe. All are animists, living alongside the Gan in the Lorhosso region, to which they formerly gave their name (Gaoua Circle) (1).

G. — **Bariba group** (5,037 representatives).
This group, which is very important in Dahomey <note>Modern-day Benin</note>, is represented in Upper Senegal and Niger only by 4,497 *Bariba* proper and 540 *Soumba* of the Takamba tribe. All are animists and live in the south of the Fada-n-Gourma Circle, in the Atakora mountains.

10. **Tribes of uncertain classification (19,035 representatives).**

---

(1) Many of these Lorho are copper jewelers: it is probable that they constitute a caste among the Koulango similar to the one called Lorho among the Mandé, and that it is the latter who, for this reason, gave them the name by which we know them.

->POPULATION COMPOSITION OF THE CIRCLES<-

These tribes, which undoubtedly belong either to the Senufo family or the Voltaic family, form a total of 19,035 indigenous people, all animists <note>Followers of traditional indigenous religions</note>, of whom 500 belong to the <term>Circle</term><note>A "Circle" (Cercle) was the primary administrative district in French West Africa.</note> of Gaoua (*Padorho*) and 18,535 to the Circle of Bobo-Dioulasso (specifically 10,045 *Toussia*, 3,700 *Dorhossié*, 2,790 *Vigué*, and 2,000 *Tiéfo*).

11º *Miscellaneous Foreigners* (4,096 representatives).

The main foreign colonies are composed of *Wolof* (3,205, all Muslims except for a few Christians, including 1,116 in the Circle of Kayes, 1,054 in the Circle of Nioro, 500 in the Circle of Bamako, 433 in the Circle of Sikasso, and 102 in Timbuktu). There are also 802 non-Muslim foreigners of various origins (445 in Kayes and 357 in Bamako) and 89 Muslim *Hausa* in the Circle of Ouagadougou; in reality, the number of Hausa established in the civil territories of Upper Senegal and Niger—particularly in the Mossi region and the East of the Niger Bend—is certainly much larger, but most were included during the censuses with the Soninké or the Dioula <note>A Mandé-speaking ethnic group known for trade</note> because of the similarity of their occupations and their religion.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Chapter II, transitioning from the geographic distribution of tribes discussed in the previous section to an investigation into the historical origins and formation of these ethnic groups. It establishes the difficulty of the task due to the lack of reliable historical and scientific data.</meta>

## CHAPTER II (1)

### **Origins and formation of modern ethnic groups**

**General Observations.** — While the naming and classification of modern ethnic groups <term>groupements ethniques: social units defined by shared culture, language, or heritage</term> presents many difficulties, it is even more challenging to determine their origins and explain their formation. Indeed, it is no longer enough to document facts that are obvious to the observer; it becomes necessary to untangle the always-muddled threads of a cloudy past that the few historians of the Sudan <note>The "Sudan" here refers to the Western Sudan, a historical geographical region in West Africa, not the modern country of Sudan.</note> have often obscured more than they have clarified.

Our sources of information are meager and their value is frequently poor.

I have stated above how precarious the data provided by anthropology, ethnography, and linguistics are, given the current state of our knowledge. History is no more fruitful regarding the subject of this chapter. Medieval Arab authors have provided us with little information except on the origin of the peoples with whom they were in immediate contact—that is, in relation to our subject, the origin of the Berbers—and their contradictions as well as their imaginative fantasies leave the reader who consults them perplexed. It is rare that they have transmitted precise facts concerning the origins of more distant peoples and, when they have done so, they generally held their information only at second or third hand; moreover, the problem is...

### THE PEOPLES

...further complicated by the difficulty we encounter in identifying the names of the Sudanese <note>In this context, "Sudanese" refers to the peoples of the Western Sudan, a historical region spanning the Sahel and Savannah of West Africa.</note> peoples cited by Arab authors.

The accounts of the locals, gathered on site by ancient and modern travelers, are rarely clear or explicit. Most of the time, as I observed earlier, when a Black person <note>The author uses "le Noir," reflecting the colonial-era terminology of the early 20th century.</note> is questioned about the origins of his people, he responds by simply giving the origin of his family or his village, or that of the ruling family (1); even then, he only provides it with some precision regarding the two or three generations that preceded him. For more distant times and for the origin of groupings of some importance, there really exists only one source of information: I refer to the historical and epic legends which constitute one of the most curious forms of popular literature in the Sudan—legends that are transmitted orally from father to son and have thus reached us.

Unfortunately, like all legends, these purely oral traditions are subject to revisions and interpolations <note>Later additions or changes made to a text or story</note> that successive storytellers do not fail to introduce into the narrative bequeathed to them. Furthermore, one must take into account the "marvelous" <note>Supernatural or mythical elements</note> aspect of many of these stories—not to reject it as a useless addition, but to extract the symbol it most often contains and translate it in a rational way. On the other hand, it is appropriate to be very cautious whenever a legend tends to give the people it concerns a particularly noble origin and to attribute its birth to a migration from Asia or Egypt. There is not, I believe, a single Sudanese tribe with even a slight exposure to Islam, even among those that are most clearly Black, that does not claim to descend from Abraham or from Himyar <note>The legendary ancestor of the Himyarite Kingdom in ancient Yemen</note> and does not claim as its cradle the Hejaz <note>The region of western Saudi Arabia containing Mecca and Medina</note> or Yemen—unless it is Egypt, Tunisia, or Morocco. Yemen is the object of a marked preference, a preference which...

# INDIGENOUS TRADITIONS

...is reflected in the considerable number of localities called *Yamina* or *Niamina*, which is the Sudanese <note>In this historical context, "Sudanese" refers to the peoples and cultures of the Western Sudan, a vast region in West Africa, not the modern nation of Sudan.</note> pronunciation of the name *Yemen*.

Here again, however, without taking the legends literally, one can discover a symbol that merely needs to be interpreted with common sense. Everyone knows that in the Sudan—as in many other regions for that matter—country names are frequently used to express the cardinal points; thus, near Bamako, the South is called *Ouorodougou*, named by the Mandé after the region where kola nuts <note>A caffeine-rich nut native to tropical forests, a major trade commodity in West Africa.</note> come from, a region which is indeed located to the south relative to Bamako; *Sourakadougou* (land of the Moors) is likewise used there to designate the North, and *Bâkô* (beyond the river) to designate the East; I mentioned above that *Sahel*, *Hausa*, and *Gourma*—words which actually represent countries, with the *Sahel* being the southern edge of the Sahara, *Hausa* the left bank of the Middle Niger, and *Gourma* its right bank—serve commonly to express directions of orientation. Everything leads me to believe that the same applies to *Yemen* for the Muslims of the Sudan, and that by translating this word as "East" in the legends that indicate it as the country of origin for a tribe or the founder of an empire, one has a great chance of not making an error (1).

From all that precedes, it follows that, while we do not totally lack documents regarding the origins of the Sudanese peoples, and while we possess some historical data that sheds light on the main phases of their formation, we cannot derive positive affirmations from them: at most we have the right to build plausible hypotheses, operating moreover with the greatest circumspection and guarding against...

---

(1) The word *yemen* in Arabic properly means "the right." <note>original: "le mot yemen en arabe signifie proprement 'la droite'"</note> Like many Easterners and also most Black Africans, the Arabs orient themselves by facing the rising sun; consequently, "right" becomes for them a synonym for "South," and this is how the people of the Hejaz <note>A region in the west of present-day Saudi Arabia, containing Mecca and Medina.</note> gave the name Yemen to the country located to the south of theirs. Just as Gourma designates the South at Bamba and the East at Niafounké, so Yemen—having become a country name after being a simple name for a direction—designates the South in Mecca and the East or North-East in the Sudan.

<header># THE PEOPLES</header>

...the spirit of system and generalization. This is what I have attempted to do in the following pages, not with the pretension of presenting absolute truths, but only with the hope of pointing out probabilities that might perhaps serve as a basis for future research.

Among these probabilities, there is one that should be noted right now, before moving on to the study of each of the peoples of whom we must speak. Of the seven ethnic families currently represented in Upper Senegal-Niger <note>Upper Senegal and Niger (*Haut-Sénégal-Niger*) was a major administrative territory in French West Africa between 1904 and 1921, encompassing parts of modern-day Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.</note>, four seem to have come from the outside through successive immigrations, some of which date back to a high antiquity: these are the *Semitic, Hamitic, Tekrurian* <note>Referring to the people of the ancient state of Tekrur, located in the Senegal River valley.</note>, and *Songhai* families.

This fact is indubitable concerning the *Semitic* family. Regarding the Hamitic and Songhai families, it is possible that, from the most remote times, tribes belonging to each of these two families were settled on a small portion of the territories that today form the civil colony of Upper Senegal-Niger, but in any case, they could only have been on the extreme borders of these territories, whereas now these two families are established in the very heart of the colony: they can therefore be considered immigrants. As for the Tekrurian family, it is possible on the contrary that its original domain extended further East—just as it is almost certain that it extended well to the North of its current domain—and that, consequently, at least a fraction of this family was indigenous to a part of the current Upper Senegal-Niger; but, as we possess no certain evidence on this subject and as, as far as our documentation reaches, the domain of the Tekrurian family appears localized beyond the borders of the colony, we must also consider as immigrants the representatives of this family whom we encounter today in the basins of the Upper Senegal and the Niger.

The three other ethnic families—*Mandé, Senufo*, and *Voltaic*—are, on the contrary, indigenous, though in various capacities. It seems quite certain that the northern group of the Mandé family had its cradle in Western Massina or Diagha...

The Senufo family seems to have occupied from all time the territories it still occupies today: I do not know if its primitive cradle should be placed in the Ivory Coast or in Upper Senegal-Niger, but in any case, its domain does not seem to have ever undergone very noticeable modifications and, if it did carry out migrations, we can find no serious trace of them.

The Voltaic family, finally, is likely indigenous also in its current territory: at most, one can suppose that this territory formerly extended further North and Northwest, that it suffered retreats in these two directions under the pressure of the Berbers, the Songhai, and the Mandé and that, conversely, it gained a little ground toward the Southwest...

Of course, when I speak of indigenous families, I do not go back further than the historical period. As for me, I prefer to take as a starting point an era in which Black peoples were already undoubtedly where they are currently found, at least in a general sense, and I believe that, if I could retrace even just to the beginning of our era the probable origins of the peoples of Upper Senegal-Niger, I would have done enough on my part.

## **I. Moors of the Azawad.** <note>The Azawad is a large desert region in northern Mali.</note>

**1. <header>ORIGIN OF THE BERABISH</header>

Berbers of various tribes (Messoufa and Lemta among others). It is probable that they had become more or less "Berberized" through contact with these groups; one can, nonetheless, recognize an Arabic origin for them.

It was undoubtedly the first Muslim expeditions into southern Morocco or the upheavals brought about by the founding of the Idrisid dynasty <note>The Idrisids (788–974) were the first Arab dynasty to rule the western Maghreb, marking the beginning of the Moroccan state.</note> in 788 that encouraged the Berabish to seek territories further south where they could maintain their independence. They left the Dara <note>The Draa River valley in southern Morocco.</note> in two groups, one led by Inis-ben-Yais and the other by Yaish; later they were joined by two other Arab families from the Dara, the Awlad-Abderrahman and the Awlad-Ameur <note>original: *Oulad-Abderrahmân* and *Oulad-Ameur*</note>. They were likely not yet Muslims at that time, in all probability, and were only converted around the beginning of the 17th century by Kounta marabouts <note>Marabouts are Muslim religious leaders and teachers in West Africa; the Kounta are a highly influential clerical tribe.</note>, following the capture of Timbuktu by the Moroccans.

The attraction of the profits they could derive from exploiting the salt mines of Teghaza <note>original: *Teghazza*</note> was likely a factor in their exodus; indeed, they became masters of these mines, which were previously owned by Messoufa Berbers. While leaving the actual labor of mining to the Soninke <note>A West African ethnic group that formed the basis of the ancient Ghana Empire.</note> who were already established there and whom they made their vassals, they established themselves as guides and transporters for the "Sudanic" caravans <note>Caravans coming from the sub-Saharan savanna regions.</note> that came to fetch salt at Teghaza, as well as for Moroccan caravans which, passing through this same point, traveled to the Walata-Timbuktu region to seek slaves and gold dust. It was in this way that their roaming grounds gradually extended as far as the Niger River and Ras-el-ma; Arawan <note>original: *Araouân*</note>, which only gained its full importance around 1690, became their geographic center and main base of operations from the 18th century onward. When Taoudenni <note>original: *Taodéni*</note> replaced Teghaza in 1596, the Berabish retained their monopoly, and they have kept it to this day.

Upon their arrival in the Sudanese Sahara, they found there—as I have just mentioned—Messoufa Berbers and Black Soninke peoples; it seems quite certain that unions were formed between these two elements and the Berabish—

**2° Kounta.** — The Kounta are also of Semitic origin. They trace the genealogy of their tribe—or at least the noble families of their tribe—back to the conqueror Uqba ibn Nafi <note>original: *Okba-ben-Nafi*</note> who, appointed in 670 as governor of Ifriqiya <note>original: *Ifrikia*; the historical Arab name for the region comprising Tripolitania (Libya) and Tunisia.</note> by the first Umayyad caliph Mu'awiya <note>original: *Moaouiya* (r. 661-680)</note>, campaigned in Tunisia against the Romans and the Berbers. He was reportedly joined there by relatives and friends of the same Arabic descent as himself, and also, very probably, by members of the Jewish colony that had been all-powerful in the Touat until then, but which

Nevertheless, as with the Berabish, it is the Arab type and blood—or at least Semitic—which seem, even today, to dominate among the Kounta.

## II. Moors of the Hodh.

In any case, these Berbers—this seems well established—belonged to the great Zenaga <note>Also known as the Sanhaja, one of the three major medieval Berber confederations.</note> branch, specifically the *Goddala*, *Lemtouna*, and *Messoufa* tribes, and came from the Mauritanian Adrar by way of the Tagant (*Goddala* and *Lemtouna*), as well as from Southern Morocco by way of Taodéni (*Lemtouna* and *Messoufa*). For a very long time, the Lemtouna had undoubtedly occupied the Adrar, having the Goddala between them and the Ocean and the Messoufa to the North and Northeast. They had settled there after coming from Morocco. Searching further back for their original point of departure would be very difficult: it would amount to settling the question of the origin of the Berbers, which has been resolved, it is true, but in various and often contradictory ways.

Is this group of the Hamitic <note>An 18th–20th century term for a historical branch of the Caucasian race and the associated language family, now largely replaced by the term Afroasiatic.</note> family indigenous to North Africa or did it come there from the Arabian Peninsula? I do not see the necessity of answering this question here, as it exceeds the limits of my modest competence and would lead us too far from our subject. Let it suffice for me to recall that the presence of the Libyans, who are manifestly identical to the Berbers, in Cyrenaica, present-day Tunisia, and the Maghreb was noted as early as the 5th century B.C. by Herodotus, who seemed to consider them the oldest and only inhabitants of almost the entirety of these regions. The Berbers are none other...

# ORIGIN OF THE BERBERS

...indeed, that the Libyans, the Gaetulians, and the Numidians of classical antiquity, to whom the Latins gave—because they proved rebellious to Roman civilization—the nickname *Barbari* (from the Greek *Barbaroï* <note>meaning "foreigners" or "those who do not speak Greek"</note>), which the Arabs transformed into *Berber*. They did so while also deriving it from an Arabic word meaning "to murmur" or "to speak in an incomprehensible way," following their habit of finding an etymology in the language of Muhammad <note>the Arabic language</note> for all names of places and peoples (1).

---

(1) Among Greek and Latin authors, we find the names of Berber tribes that still exist today: thus, it has been possible to identify the *Libyans* proper (*Loubim* <note>original: *Loubim*; a biblical term for the people of Libya</note> of the Bible, *Lebataï* of Procopius <note>a prominent 6th-century Byzantine historian</note>) with the *Lewwata* or *Louata*; the *Gaetulians* with the *Goddala*, *Djedala*, or the *Guezoula*; the *Serangaï* of Ptolemy <note>an influential Greco-Roman geographer of the 2nd century</note> (placed by him in the Sous <note>a region in modern-day southern Morocco</note>) with the *Zenaga*; and the *Maxyes* of Herodotus (*Mazikes*, *Masices*, *Mazices*, and *Mazax* in the works of Lucretius, Suetonius, Ptolemy, Ammianus Marcellinus, Corippus, and Cassian) with the *Imazighen* <note>original: *Imazirhen*</note> or *Imocharhen* <note>original: *Imocharhen*</note>—that is to say, with the Berbers of noble stock. 

Here now is a summary of the principal Arabic theories concerning the origin of the Berbers. Yaqut <note>original: *Yakout*; Yaqut al-Hamawi (1179–1229), a famous biographer and geographer of the Islamic world</note> (12th–13th centuries) tells us that *Berber* is the name of numerous tribes inhabiting the mountains of the Maghreb <note>Northwest Africa</note> from Barka <note>Cyrenaica, in modern-day Libya</note] to the Atlantic and extending South to the land of the Blacks <note>original: *pays des Noirs*; a reference to Sub-Saharan Africa</note>. He adds that the Berbers generally trace their origin back to Shem <note>original: *Sem*; the eldest son of Noah in the Bible</note> and claim that their ancestors emigrated from Arabia to Africa. Their primitive language—which would have been a Semitic language—was supposedly corrupted through contact with the language of the indigenous people of the Maghreb (who were these indigenous people? Yaqut does not tell us) and became the Berber language. 

Some, Yaqut specifies, say that the Himyarite <note>referring to an ancient kingdom in Yemen</note> king *Ifrikos*, having come from Yemen to lead an expedition into Ifriqiya <note>historical North Africa, specifically modern-day Tunisia and eastern Algeria</note>, founded a settlement of Yemenites there whose descendants are the Berbers. In his list of the principal Berber tribes, Yaqut cites several whose names are still carried today by Moorish sub-tribes of the Hodh and the Azawad (for example, the Louata, whom one encounters among the Idaw Aïsh, and the Sakhoura, who are undoubtedly the same as the Zakhoura, vassals of the Kounta). 

According to Ibn Khaldun <note>original: *Ibn-Khaldoun*; a 14th-century North African scholar often considered the father of modern sociology and historiography</note> (14th century), who appears better informed than Yaqut and who, above all, is gifted with a true critical spirit lacking in the former, the Berbers descend from Ham <note>original: *Ham* or *Cham*; another son of Noah</note> through Canaan and Mazigh <note>original: *Mazigh*; the source of the name *Imazighen* still used today by noble families</note> and a man named *Berr*. One of Berr’s sons, *Madghis*, was supposedly the ancestor of the *Zenata* and their cousins the Louata, the Zouaoua, the Maghraoua, etc. His other son, *Bernès*, was supposedly the ancestor of the *Zenaga* (the children of Zenag, son of Bernès, comprising the Messoufa, the Goddala, the Lemtouna, the Maddassa, the Wareli, etc.) and of their cousins the Lemta, the Hawwara, and the Guezoula.

<header>THE PEOPLES</header>

We know that the Berbers were formerly divided into several large groups, the two most important of which were called *Zenata* and *Zenaga*. The Zenata generally remained in North Africa, while the Zenaga, though leaving many representatives in the Maghreb <note>the western part of the Arab world, specifically North Africa</note>, sent out—from a very distant era—some of their sub-tribes into the Sahara and present-day Mauritania: the *Messoufa*, the *Djedala* or *Goddala*, the *Lemtouna*, the *Maddassa*, and the *Ouareth* were the principal of these Zenaga sub-tribes of the desert; the *Hoouara*, the *Lemta*, and the *Guezoula*, closely related to the Zenaga, if not Zenaga themselves, participated in the same movement. All distinguished themselves early on from their brothers who remained in the Mediterranean basin by adopting the veil, which later earned them the Arabic nickname *Molettemin* <note>original: *Molettemin*; meaning "the veiled ones," from the word *litham*, the desert veil</note> and which, today, is only worn by those among them who escaped the Arab conquest and became the Tuareg.

The *Lemta* and the *Hoouara* moved primarily into the central Sahara, where they are found under the barely transformed names of Oulmidden (*Lemta*) and Hoggar or Ihaggaren <note>the noble class of the Tuareg in the Ahaggar Mountains</note>.

> “A nation like that of the Berbers, formed from a multitude of peoples and filling a considerable part of the earth, could not have been transported there from another place, and especially from a very limited region. For a long succession of centuries before Islam, the Berbers have been known as inhabitants of the country and the regions that belong to them today.” (*History of the Berbers*, translation by Slane <note>William Mac Guckin de Slane, a 19th-century Irish Orientalist</note>, Vol. 1, page 183).

Procopius <note>a prominent 6th-century Byzantine historian</note> (6th century) had already supported the theory tracing the Berbers back to the Hamites originating from Canaan who were driven from Palestine by the Hebrews when the latter settled there upon returning from Egypt.

### THE LEMTOUNA

(Hoouara). The Messoufa remained for a long time stationed in the South of Morocco in the Tindouf region, then advanced toward Taoudenni and the Azaouad. The Maddassa also moved toward the northern course of the Niger River. As for the Lemtouna and the Goddala, accompanied by several families of the Guezoula and the Ouareth, they went to settle in the Mauritanian Adrar and in the Tirs or Tiris <note>arid, stony desert plains</note>, then in the Tagant, generally living side by side, although the Goddala later moved further toward the Southwest and the lower course of the Senegal River.

It is probable, as I mentioned earlier, that from the final centuries preceding our era until approximately the 7th century after Christ, the Lemtouna of the Adrar, crossing the Tagant, conducted raids into the Hodh <note>a large natural depression and region in southeastern Mauritania</note>, undoubtedly going to demand or take from the Soninke farmers and later from the Judeo-Syrian pastoralists the food supplies they lacked. Starting from the 8th century, they began to spread in more significant numbers into the lands today belonging to Upper Senegal-Niger and perhaps even had their capital there in the 9th and 10th centuries at *Aoudaghost*. This city must have been located not far from Kiffa, or at the very least was situated in the part of eastern Tagant neighboring Kiffa, likely a little to the north of that locality (1). Sometimes acting as overlords to the Black populations of the country, and sometimes paying them tribute, the Berbers must have, from this era onward, intermixed quite heavily with Black African blood, especially among the sedentary groups.

In all likelihood, they were Christians (2) at the time the sect of the Almoravids <note>from the Arabic *al-Murabitun*, "those from the ribat" or fortified monastery</note> was born among them (1052), or at least the majority were, since the principal goal of the foundation of this sect was the conversion—

(2) This is based at least on the testimony of the Arabic writer al-Zuhri (12th century), according to whom the Berbers of the Sudan <note>historical term for West Africa, from the Arabic *Bilad al-Sudan* or "Land of the Blacks"</note> only abjured Christianity and embraced Islam around the year 1075.

2. *The Arab Element.* — The Arab element, regarding the Moors of the Hodh, was provided almost exclusively by the *Beni Hassân*: its introduction is relatively recent.

The Beni Hassân, who claim to be descendants of the family of the Quraysh <note>original: *Koreïch*; the noble merchant tribe of Mecca to which the Prophet Muhammad belonged</note>, originate from the most important of the Arab immigrations that took place in North Africa, known as the Hilalian invasion. The Hilalian Arabs—descendants of Adnan and categorized by Ibn Khaldun <note>a famous 14th-century North African historian</note> as "Berberizing" Arabs <note>original: *barbarisants*; meaning those who adopted the lifestyle or mingled with the Berbers</note>, that is to say, mixed—moved into Africa toward the beginning of the 11th century; they were primarily nomads. In reality, the Beni Hassân (also known as the Idao-Hassân or Doui-Hassân) were not Hilaliens; they belonged to a group originating from the Maqil <note>original: *Makil*</note>, who claimed descent from Jafar, son of Abu Talib, son of Hashim, the great-grandfather...

<header>THE BENI HASSAN</header>

of Muhammad, but, according to Ibn Khaldun <note>a famous 14th-century North African historian and philosopher</note>, descended instead from the Arabs of Yemen via the Kodâa, grandsons of Himyar.

Be that as it may, the Beni Hassan followed the Hilalians <note>the Banu Hilal, Arab Bedouin tribes who migrated to North Africa in the 11th century</note> in their migration and, after crossing all of North Africa, settled with them in the Sous, the Noul or Noun, and the Dara or Draa <note>regions in modern-day southern Morocco</note>, between the Atlantic and the Tafilelt, toward the end of the 13th century. From there, they sent their herds to graze as far as the Saharan regions inhabited by the Messoufa, the Lemtouna, and the Goddala.

They were comprised of several branches: that of the *Beni Hassan* proper, or descendants of Hassan, son of Mokhtar, son of Mohammed, son of Makil; that of the *Chebanât*, or descendants of Chebana, brother of Hassan (including the Beni-Tâbet or Idao-Aïch, descendants of Aïch-ben-Talha, and the Ahl-Ali or Idao-Ali); and finally, the very important branch of the *Oulad-Delim* which, in reality, formed a sub-tribe distinct from the Beni Hassan proper.

Starting in the 14th century, according to the testimony of Ibn Khaldun, the territory of the Beni Hassan extended from the Sous to the border of the land of the Blacks <note>referring to Sub-Saharan Africa</note>, which is to say at least as far as the Mauritanian Adrar. Toward the end of the 16th century, a great number of Beni Hassan, after definitively conquering the Adrar, spread from there to the banks of the Senegal River, then into the Tagant, and finally into the Hodh (1), subjugating the Berbers, definitively converting them to Islam, and making them their vassals. The Beni Hassan proper and the Chebanât constituted the Arab and simultaneously the warrior element among the Regueïbât, the Idao-Aïch, the Ahl-Tichit, the Oulad-Mbarek, the Oulad-Nasser, and the Mejdouf; the Oulad-Delim, pushing further toward the East, contributed to the formation of the sub-tribes of the Oulad-Daoud, the Oulad-Allouch, etc.

The current Moors of the Hodh are therefore, in short, Arabized Berbers rather than Arabs. It is quite certain in any case that the Arab element was, in their formation, much smaller—

Finally, the <term>maraboutic</term> families <note>religious or scholarly lineages</note> almost always turn out to be—regardless of the genealogies they fabricated after the fact—either purely Berber or at least primarily Berber in their origin.

If one adds to this the infusions of Black African blood that occurred constantly among the Berbers first, and among the Beni Hassan thereafter, as well as the sometimes considerable mixing due to unions with the **Peuls** <note>also known as the Fulani, a major pastoralist ethnic group</note> (notably among the Guirganké (1) and the Allouch), one can understand how inaccurate it would be to say that the Moors of the Hodh are of Arab origin.

### III. The Tuareg.

The Tuareg of the civil territories of Upper Senegal and Niger are divided today, as we have seen, into three major tribes or groups. On the whole, they were formed by five great currents of Berber immigration, to which must be added some mixing of Arab, <term>Peul</term> <note>also known as the Fulani, a widespread pastoralist group</note>, and Songhai origin. The five great Berber immigrations that contributed to their formation are, in probable chronological order: those of the Lemta and Houuara from Tripolitania <note>the coastal region of modern-day Libya</note>; the Messoufa; the Saghmara or Kel-Tadmekket; the Goddala and Lemtouna; and finally the Oulmidden. Generally speaking, the current Oulmidden sub-tribes emerged from the first and last waves; the Kel-Tadmekket tribe from the third; and the Iguellad tribe and its related sub-tribes from the second and fourth.

---

(1) While relatively numerous in Mauritania, Moors speaking <term>Zenaga</term> <note>the southwestern Berber language</note> are exceedingly rare in the Hodh.

(2) In addition to the Beni Hassan, several other Arab families contributed to strengthening the Semitic <note>referring to Arab ancestry</note> element in the Hodh. For instance, the Kounta, coming from the Azaouad, settled in several places in this region, notably at Tichit, during their movement toward the Tagant and the Adrar. At different times, Arabs or Arabized Berbers came from Morocco to these same regions: such is the case of the Taleb-Mokhtar, whose ancestors, driven from southern Morocco following obscure events, are said to have settled in Massina. From there, fleeing before the conquest of <term>El-Hadj Omar</term> <note>the founder of the Toucouleur Empire</note>, they reportedly migrated toward Goumbou and Oualata to join the Mejdouf under the leadership of Mohammed-Fadel. Meanwhile, other branches of their family pushed as far as Mauritania with Saad-Bou, and later into the Saguïet-el-Hamra with Ma-el-Aïnin <note>a prominent Saharan religious and political leader</note>.

### 1. *Lemta and Houara Immigration.*

— As I mentioned earlier, during the remote era when the Berbers first began to penetrate deep into the Sahara, the Lemta went to establish themselves to the west of the Aïr <note>a mountainous region in modern-day northern Niger</note>. We still find them there today under the name Oulmidden, a name which seems clearly derived from the same root as the word *Lemta* used by Arabic authors. These Lemta came, at least in part, from present-day Tripolitania <note>the coastal region of modern-day Libya</note>, where they had left many of their compatriots, as well as in the Touat <note>an oasis region in the Algerian Sahara</note> and southern Morocco. A fraction of the Lemta who remained in the North—very probably of the Christian faith—fled the first Arab conquest of Ifriqiya <note>the medieval Arabic name for the territory comprising modern Tunisia, eastern Algeria, and western Libya</note>. Around the year 670, they left Tripolitania with a large number of Houara (another Berber tribe that was half-Christianized and then settled in the same areas). The Houara settled mainly in the mountainous region of the central Sahara and became the Hoggar <note>the Kel Ahaggar Tuareg</note>. As for the Lemta, accompanied no doubt by several Houara families, they went to join the members of their tribe already settled further south.

These earlier settlers, who had very likely remained faithful to the ancient Libyan religion <note>the indigenous polytheistic beliefs of North Africans before the arrival of Christianity and Islam</note>, looked upon these new Christian arrivals with a rather jaundiced eye; above all, they feared they would have to compete with them for the meager fare they struggled so painfully to obtain. These latest immigrants, poorly received by their own compatriots, continued their movement further still. They finally arrived, in a quite miserable state, on the banks of the Niger River, at the site where the Songhai village of *Gounguia or Koukia* then stood, populated mainly by Sorko fishermen. This village—at least, so I believe—must have been located on the island known today by the name Bentia, between Gao and Tillabéry (1).

Better welcomed by the Sorko than they had been by their own compatriots, the Lemta of Tripolitania managed

---

(1) It has sometimes been believed that Koukia could be identified with Gao, but, as we shall see in the fourth part of this work when dealing with the history of the Empire of Gao, such an identification is physically impossible. I would point out that *goungui* means "island" in the Songhai language; in the same language *goungui-yo* would mean "the islands," *goungui yé* "the seven islands," and *goungui yaha* "the eight islands."

Naturally, they did not remain fixed at Koukia <note>an ancient city on the Niger River, considered the early capital of the Songhai Empire</note> and, while maintaining it at least temporarily as the capital of their empire, they spread throughout the East of the Niger Bend. They remained there even after supremacy was taken from them by the Black populations (the Songhai led by the Soninké) in 1493, at which point they shifted from being the overlords of the latter to being their vassals. Still Christian at the time of their arrival in Koukia, they began to embrace Islam around the year 1009 CE, during the reign of their fifteenth emperor, Dia Kossoï.

2. *Messoufa Immigration.* — Toward the beginning of the 8th century, doubtless following the first Arab conquests in the Maghreb <note>the region of Northwest Africa</note>, some Messoufa established in southern Morocco in the region of Tindouf moved southward and seized the salt mines of Teghazza <note>a major source of rock salt in the Sahara</note>. Dispossessed around the 9th century by the Bérabich, as we have previously seen, they became the latter’s vassals; some remained at Teghazza, while others accompanied the Bérabich on their treks across the desert or, like them, became caravan guides. It is possible that the Messoufa did not wait for the arrival of the Bérabich to push as far as the Timbuktu region; in any case, the Berber *Maddassa*, mentioned in the 11th century by Bekri <note>Al-Bakri, a famous Andalusian geographer and historian</note> as inhabiting the north shore of Lake Faguibine and the Niger, and who were already Muslim at that time, were very likely a branch of the Messoufa.

3. *Saghmara or Kel-Tadmekket Immigration.* — In the Tilemsi Valley, about 300 kilometers north-northeast of Gao, the Berbers who first emigrated into the Sahara had founded, doubtless before the birth of Christ, a city

...which they called *Tadmekket* (1) and which, much later, the Arabs named *Es-souk* (the market) because it was the sole commercial center for the entire central Sahara and the meeting point for caravans traveling from Tripolitania <note>modern-day western Libya</note> and the Touat <note>a region in central Algeria</note> toward the Nigerien lands <note>the regions surrounding the Niger River</note>. This location seems to have been flourishing, if indeed such an epithet could ever be applied to a Saharan town; however, everything is relative, and what would be a common village in a fertile and populated country easily takes on the appearance of a brilliant metropolis in the desert. It is possible, moreover, that the first Berber settlers of the *Tilemsi* <note>a seasonal river valley in Mali</note> were able to take advantage of the lands in this valley and that *Tadmekket* was once a prosperous oasis.

Regardless, it enjoyed great renown and, from the first centuries of the Hegira <note>the Islamic era, beginning in 622 CE</note>, it attracted Muslims from *Ifrikia* (2), who were likely Berbers like its founders. They came there to preach Islam and formed the maraboutic <note>religious or holy</note> faction known today as the *Iforhass* <note>ancestors of the modern Kel Ifoghas</note>, while the general Berber populations gravitating around Tadmekket bore the name *Saghmâra*.

The nomadic *Oulmidden* <note>a powerful Tuareg confederation</note>, who pitched their tents between *Tadmekket* and the *Aïr* <note>a mountainous massif in northern Niger</note> and who likely shared the same primary origin as the *Saghmâra*—both groups were probably *Lemta*, at least for the most part—repeatedly attacked the people of *Tadmekket* for reasons that are not entirely clear to us, though the main cause was likely greed. By at least the 10th century, they had forced some of the maraboutic families to retreat into the region of stony hills that we call the *Adrar des Iforhass* <note>the Adrar des Ifoghas in modern Mali</note> and some of the

Saghmâra to descend the Tilemsi valley <note>a seasonal riverbed in modern-day Mali</note>, with the hope of finding other favorable lands on the banks of the Niger. The Saghmâra, colliding near Bourem with the Oulmidden <note>a powerful Tuareg confederation</note> of the Gao region, veered toward the West, reached the river near Bamba, and spread across both its banks. They occupied the right bank especially, from the heights of Bamba to the lakes located south of Timbuktu. When the Iguellad Tuareg came to settle in this region, they gave them the name *Kel-Tadmekket* (people of Tadmekket) because of their origin; they were also called *Kel-es-souk* <note>Tuareg for "People of the Market"</note>, which amounts to the same thing. However, this latter name was preferably reserved for the maraboutic <note>religious or holy</note> branch that had followed the Saghmâra exodus instead of settling with the other religious families in the Adrar of the Ifoghas <note>a mountainous massif in northeastern Mali</note>.

Al-Bakri <note>an 11th-century Arab geographer and historian</note> notes the presence of the Kel-Tadmekket (under the name Saghmâra) on the right bank of the Niger, across from Gao, in the 11th century. Their exodus was therefore much earlier than the destruction of the city of Tadmekket by the Oulmidden, a destruction which reportedly took place around 1640. But it seems established, on the other hand, that the final ruin of Tadmekket resulted in a new Saghmâra immigration to the banks of the Niger toward the middle of the 17th century.

4° *Goddala and Lemtouna immigration.* — I mentioned earlier, when tracing the origins of the Moors of the Hodh <note>a region in southeastern Mauritania</note>, how, toward the 11th century, a certain number of Lemtouna and especially Goddala <note>two of the primary Sanhaja Berber tribes</note>, coming from the Mauritanian Adrar, had advanced as far as Timbuktu. There, they escaped the Arab conquest of the Beni-Hassân who, toward the end of the 16th century, subjugated their compatriots who had remained in the Hodh. They were eventually joined at the end of the 17th century by the Arab immigration of the Bérabich, and in the 15th century by that of the Kounta. There were then mixtures between them and the Arabs, the result of which is still visible today, primarily in the maraboutic tribe of the Kel-Antassar (1). But

Unlike in the Hodh <note>a region in present-day southeastern Mauritania</note>, there was no Arab conquest here; the Goddala and Lemtouna of the lakes and the Azawad <note>an arid region in northern Mali</note>, who became the Iguellad, were not Arabized and kept their language and their veil <note>the *tagelmust*, the traditional indigo veil worn by Tuareg men</note>, only adopting the Muslim religion preached to them by the Kel-Tadmekket and later the Kounta <note>an influential Arabo-Berber tribal group known for their religious scholars</note>.

5° *Oulmidden immigration*. — I prefer to give the name Oulmidden <note>one of the largest and most powerful Tuareg confederations</note> here to the Lemta who settled in the Sahara before the arrival of those who, after joining them, pushed as far as Koukia <note>an ancient city on the Niger, likely the early capital of the Songhai Empire</note>, in order to distinguish them from the latter.

One can assume that when they saw the degree of prosperity of the Lemta in Gounguia or Koukia, the Oulmidden remaining in the Sahara sought to reconnect with them. The roles were reversed: once cumbersome guests and "useless mouths" <note>a French idiom for people who consume food without contributing labor</note>, the former immigrants from Tripolitania <note>the western region of modern-day Libya</note> had become powerful figures whose strength was to be feared and whose alliance was to be sought. Thus, the Oulmidden certainly did not fail to go and pay them respects and even recognize their suzerainty; in return, they obtained the right to take their share of the harvests grown by the Songhai <note>an ethnic group living along the Niger River</note> along the Niger. However, it does not appear that they crossed the river or entered the territories currently belonging to the civil colony of Upper Senegal-Niger <note>a former colony in French West Africa, covering parts of modern Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso</note> during the era of Berber hegemony in Songhai country.

It was only at the end of the 15th century, when the Lemta empire of Gounguia and then of Gao was replaced by the Soninke-Songhai empire of Gao and when this latter city became both a great market and an important Muslim center, that the Oulmidden—attracted even further toward the Niger—began to cross the river and partially settle within the Bend <note>referring to the "Great Bend" of the Niger River</note>, in the direction of Gao to Hombori, near the families that had previously come from Gounguia. It was also at this time that the Oulmidden of the Gao region must have embraced Islam, which was already practiced by the other Tuareg of the Niger valley.

<header>FORMATION OF THE TUAREG</header>

They were all Berbers who contributed to forming the branch of the Tuareg people that today occupies the northern Niger Bend and the left bank of the river in the region between Ras-el-ma <note>a location at the western tip of Lake Faguibine</note> and Bourem. Furthermore, some secondary elements exist whose importance does not seem very significant and which have not profoundly altered the original Berber type.

To begin with, it seems probable that the current territory of the Tuareg in Upper Senegal-Niger <note>a colonial administrative territory in French West Africa, covering parts of modern Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso</note>—excepting the riverbanks themselves—was largely uninhabited when the first Berber migrations arrived. Even along the Niger, the Songhai likely had not yet advanced far upstream from Gao; perhaps they did not pass Bourem. However, there is no doubt that, having first been vassals of the Lemta and later overlords of all the Niger Tuareg, they must have intermingled with them to a significant degree. Later, the Fula <note>original: *Peuls*; a major migratory ethnic group in West Africa</note> who settled in the Hombori and Dori regions introduced a degree of intermixing, at least on the periphery of their settlements, which should not be overlooked. In the Timbuktu region, unions certainly occurred between Arabs and Tuareg, but as the Arabs were fewer in number, they were the ones most influenced by these unions. As for the Moroccans who conquered Timbuktu at the end of the 16th century, their influence was felt primarily among the Songhai, as we shall see shortly (1).

<header>THE PEOPLES</header>

# IV. The Fula. <note>Original: *Peuls*; a major ethnic group spread across West Africa, known for their pastoral lifestyle and complex history.</note>

## 1st. *The Problem of Fula Origins.*

The question of the origin of the Fula has provided material for extensive discussions, and yet it is far from being resolved. This is a multifaceted problem that, to be treated with any precision, requires simultaneous examination from its various aspects. No one disputes that at least a significant portion of the current Fula people does not originally belong to the Black race: one only needs to observe the pastoral Fula encountered almost everywhere in the Sudan <note>The author uses "Sudan" in the historical sense of the *Bilad al-Sudan* or "Land of the Blacks," referring to the Sahelian region of West Africa, not the modern nation-state.</note> to be convinced. Among them, alongside individuals clearly mixed with Black African blood, one notices people whose skin tone and facial features absolutely recall the appearance of the Bedouins of Egypt and especially Palestine. Alongside this, the Fula language is spoken by a considerable number of individuals who are, just as incontestably, well-characterized Black people.

From this arise two theories: one considers the Fula a mixed-race people, while the other sees them as a collection of people—some of the White race, others of the Black race—who have nothing in common but their language. But here again, there is a divergence of opinion: some maintain that the Fula language was the original tongue of the White-raced element, while others think that the latter instead borrowed it from the Black-raced element.

I will state immediately that my opinion, based on long and patient research, leans toward the latter hypothesis: in my view, the so-called Fula language is a Black African language, originally spoken by a Black people completely different from the Fula—a people whose current representatives are none other than the Toucouleurs <note>An ethnic group primarily from the Senegal River valley, closely related to the Fula but traditionally more sedentary and agricultural.</note>—and this language was adopted, following circumstances I am about to recount, by a people of the [White] race...

...[protec]ted against their persecutors, they piously preserved it without ever parting from it. They forgot their language (Arabic) as a result of their incorporation with the Berbers and adopted the language of the latter. The Tuareg are said to be the descendants of these veiled Zenaga, who were supposedly driven into the desert by a faction among them, the Almoravids <note>A powerful Berber dynasty that formed an empire in the 11th century covering the Maghreb and Al-Andalus.</note>. It is noteworthy that most Arabic authors attribute this half-Yemeni, half-Berber origin to all the Zenaga and to certain closely related tribes, such as the Lemta, among others.

of the white race and of Judeo-Syrian origin, whose current representatives are the Foulbé or Peuls proper. <note>The author is distinguishing between the "pure" ethnic Fula (Foulbé) and groups like the Toucouleur who share the language but have different ethnic roots.</note>

To be thorough, I must add that long cohabitation has produced easily perceptible mixtures between the Toucouleurs and the Peuls, just as the scattering of the Peuls across vast territories populated by various Black peoples has profoundly altered the original Semitic type of the Foulbé. Finally, we must not forget that the latter have numerous Black serfs with them, the Rimaïbé, who speak the language of the Toucouleurs like their Fula masters, without being Toucouleurs or Fula themselves.

Before presenting the facts that make my hypothesis plausible, it seems appropriate to me to summarize and briefly discuss the main theories among the many put forward by my predecessors.

### 2nd. *Various theories concerning the origin of the Fula.*

If one identifies the Fula with the tribe of *Phut* <note>Original: *Fouth* or *Foudh*</note> mentioned in the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible.</note> and in the writings of several biblical prophets (Ezekiel, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Nahum)—a tribe whose name is also written as *Pul* <note>Original: *Foul*</note> by Isaiah (1)—one must recognize that this people has been mentioned since the earliest antiquity. I do not claim that this identification can be presented as a certainty, but in any case, it is not absurd. If it is accepted, it would seem to lead to attributing a Hamitic origin to the Fula; since *Phut* or *Foudh* is listed as one of the sons of Ham, along with Cush <note>Original: *Chous*, father of the Ethiopians or Kushites</note>, Misraim <note>Original: *Misraïm*, father of the Egyptians</note>, and Canaan. <note>Original: *Chanaan*</note>

---

(1) The word *Phut*, in the versions of the Bible in Semitic languages, ends with an emphatic *t* or *th* (*tav* <note>The Hebrew letter *Tav* (ת)</note> of the Hebrews, *tha* <note>The Arabic letter *Thāʾ* (ث)</note> of the Arabs), a letter which is rendered in the Fula language by a special *d* or *dh* that frequently changes into *l*. In this way, the *Phut* of the Bible can perfectly well be considered as originating from a root identical to that of the syllable *pul* <note>Original: *foul*</note>, which is the root of the name for the Fula people. On the contrary, the name of *Fouta* <note>The Fouta Djallon or Fouta Toro, mountainous and plateau regions in West Africa inhabited by the Fula.</note> is written in Arabic with an ordinary *t* and seems to come from a different root. — This term *Phut* or *Pul*, in European translations of the Bible, has often been replaced by "Africa" or "Libya," but without any valid reason.

(father of the Libyans or Berbers) (1); but there is no need to dwell on this point, as the Bible—like Arab authors—often confuses the descendants of Ham with those of Shem (2). <note>Shem and Ham are two of the sons of Noah in biblical tradition, representing the traditional ancestors of Semitic and Hamitic peoples respectively.</note>

Regardless, the Biblical Prophets constantly represent the tribe of Phut, Phoudh, or Pul <note>original: "Fouth, Foudh ou Foul"</note> as neighboring the Ethiopians, Egyptians, and Berbers. Ezekiel says that the Ludim <note>original: "Loudim"</note> (a group descended from the Mizraim <note>original: "Mesraïm"</note> or Egyptians) and the Phut served in the army of Tyre (XXVII, 10); that the ruin of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon (588 BC), will lead to that of Ethiopia, Phut, Lud, etc. (XXX, 5); that the army of "Gog"—no doubt Alexander—includes Ethiopians and the Phut (XXXVIII, 5). Jeremiah, also speaking of the defeat of Pharaoh Necho <note>original: "Néchao"</note> (Necho I) by Nebuchadnezzar, mentions among the Egyptian troops the Ethiopians, the Phut armed with shields, and the Ludim archers (XLVI, 9). Isaiah mentions the people of Pul <note>original: "Foul"</note> among the nations far to the South and West (LXVI, 19). Finally, Nahum, in his prophecy against Nineveh (III, 9), asks this city if it believes it is stronger than Alexandria, which the support of the Ethiopians, Egyptians, Phut, and Lubim <note>original: "Loubim"</note> (Libyans) failed to protect.

One could conclude from this, without too much boldness, that the Hebrews considered the Phut, Phoudh, or Pul as a people originating from Mesopotamia, Syria, or Palestine, but who, after long contact with the Egyptians and Ethiopians, had settled in Africa by the 6th century BC at the latest, in the neighborhood of Egypt and not far from the sea—since they provided contingents to the armies of Tyre and that of Alexander—probably in Cyrenaica. <note>Cyrenaica is the coastal region of what is now eastern Libya.</note>

...at least I believe—from the 14th century of our era. Al-Maqrizi <note>A famous Egyptian historian (1364–1442) known for his detailed descriptions of the Mamluk Sultanate and African history.</note> (1364–1442) speaks of an embassy sent around the year 1300 by the Emperor of Mali to the Emperor of Bornu, which included two individuals who spoke the Fula language (*foulânia*). A little later, toward the middle of the 15th century, Cadamosto <note>Alvise Cadamosto, a Venetian explorer who sailed for Prince Henry the Navigator of Portugal.</note> mentions the presence of a king of the Peuls (*rey dos Fullos* <note>Portuguese: "King of the Fulas"</note>) on the Senegal River. In the following century, Joao de Barros <note>An early Portuguese historian and explorer.</note> also speaks to us of the Peuls, but like Maqrizi and Cadamosto, he does not provide us with information regarding their origin.

The first work that discusses the Peuls at some length and offers at least a few words on their origin is, it seems to me, the *Tarikh al-Sudan* <term>Tarikh al-Sudan: An Arabic-language chronicle written in Timbuktu, providing a vital history of the Songhai Empire and the surrounding regions.</term>, which was written during the first half of the 17th century; its author, Abd al-Rahman al-Sa’di, had some Fula blood in his own ancestry, as he tells us that his great-grandmother was named Aïchat-el-Foulânia <note>Arabic: "Aishat the Fula woman"</note> and belonged to the Sonfontir clan of the Peuls, which should likely be identified with the Soumontara or Dialloubé clan (1). He hardly dwells on the history of the Peuls, except concerning the ruling family of Massina <note>An area in the inner Niger Delta of modern-day Mali.</note>, whom he claims came from Senegal; however, he seems to link them to the Wolofs <note>original: "Ouolofs"</note>, stating that the latter are far superior, in character and customs, "to the other Fula" <note>original: "Foulâni"</note>. No doubt we should simply understand from this that he considered the Wolofs and the Peuls as forming a single nation, because he knew that the Peuls of Massina came from Fouta, and that Fouta bordered the land of the Wolofs and had been part of the Jolof <note>original: "Diolof"</note> Empire.

In the early years of the 19th century, Grey Jackson, the British consul at Mogador <note>The coastal city of Essaouira in modern-day Morocco.</note>, learned from the Moroccans of the Sous region that a tribe of Israelites lived in Melli, or the land of the Mande. Although Jackson does not mention the name of this tribe, it seems very likely that his informants meant the Peuls (2).

<header>BARTH’S THEORIES</header>

of the Peul words <note>The Peuls, also known as the Fula or Fulani, are a major ethnic group spread across West Africa.</note> that he cites, one will not find twenty whose root is actually close to a corresponding Malay or Polynesian root; since the morphology and syntax of the two languages are, moreover, completely different, one can boldly state that these are pure phonetic coincidences, such as could be found between any two languages chosen at random among the most dissimilar.

Barth <note>Heinrich Barth (1821–1865), a German scholar and explorer of Africa.</note> seems to assume that the Peuls came from Southern Morocco and the Touat <note>An oasis region in the central Saharan desert of modern-day Algeria.</note> toward Ghana <note>The medieval Ghana Empire, located in parts of modern-day Mauritania and Mali, not the modern nation of Ghana.</note> and from there spread into the Sudan <note>The historical "Bilad al-Sudan" region, referring to the belt of territory south of the Sahara.</note>. His theory appears confirmed at first glance by a legend collected in 1857 by C.-J. Reichardt, according to which the Peuls of Fouta-Diallon <note>A highland region in Guinea.</note> originated from Arab families coming from Fez (1) to the Diaka or Diaga (Massina) <note>A region in the Inland Niger Delta of modern-day Mali.</note>, under the leadership of two chiefs named Sidi and Séri; these men were supposedly welcomed in the Diaka by a holy man named El-hadj Salihou Souaré, leader of a Mandingue tribe (or more accurately Soninké, based on his clan name: Souaré), who directed them toward Fouta-Diallon, where they became the ancestors of the two families of the Sidianké and the Sérianké. Not everything in this legend should be rejected: the arrival of the Peuls’ ancestors in the Diaga region, already occupied by the Soninké, followed by their migration toward the Senegalese Fouta and from there toward Fouta-Diallon and elsewhere, are facts that seem to me very close to being historically established. However, regarding the Moroccan and especially the Arab origin of these Peul ancestors, I can only consider it highly doubtful; it is not impossible that some families from which the Peuls are descended came to Ghana from Morocco, and it seems well-proven that some came from the Touat; but, in my opinion, these families were not Arab, and the Touat was only one of the intermediate stages where a fraction detached from the great immigration movement stopped momentarily—a movement which very probably had its starting point in Syria or Palestine (2).

Among the theories on the origin of the Peuls <note>Also known as the Fula, Fulani, or Fulbe, these are a major ethnic group across West Africa.</note> cited by Dr. Bérenger-Féraud, I must recall the one that has them descending from the ancient Egyptians. This is argued both because of anthropological affinities—which, it must be said, remain to be proven—and because of the resemblance of their name (*Foulbe*, *Foulan’*, *Foula*, *Fellata*, etc., depending on the language) to that of the *Fellah* of modern Egypt. It is well known that *fellah* in Arabic means "laborer" or "plowman" and that this term is applied by city-dwellers in all Arabic-speaking countries—no more in Egypt than in Algeria or Arabia—to the people we would call "peasants" in English (1). I do not need to highlight the absurdity of linking the name of a Sudanese people with the Arabic name of a profession that is not particularly Egyptian and is in no way an ethnic designation. However, I must admit that this unintentional pun has done more to establish the theory of the Egyptian origin of the Peuls than the actual work of anthropologists.

We must place in the same category—the "lighthearted" category—the etymology given by Bérenger-Féraud for the word *Toucouleur* <note>An ethnic group closely related to the Peuls, primarily found in the Senegal River valley.</note>, which he derives without hesitation from the English *two colours*. He does so under the pretext that the Foutanké <note>People from the Fouta region.</note> were supposedly the result of a mixture of peoples of "two colors," of Whites and Blacks (2).

<header>OPINIONS OF THALY AND FAIDHERBE</header>

Bérenger-Féraud also cites—though without sharing it—the opinion of Dr. Thaly, according to whom the Peuls were Indo-Europeans having the same origin as our Bohemians or Gipsies <note>The author refers here to the Romani people; "Bohemians" was a common French term for them at the time.</note>. According to this theory, they were driven from their country in the 15th century by the Mongols and took the route to Egypt by way of Syria, only later plunging into the center of Africa. Unfortunately for this theory, the presence of the Peuls in the Sudan <note>The "Sudan" here refers to the *Bilad al-Sudan*, the broad geographic belt south of the Sahara, rather than the modern nation-state.</note> as early as the beginning of the 14th century is confirmed for us by Al-Maqrizi <note>A 14th-century Egyptian historian and geographer.</note>, and as early as the middle of the 15th century, Cadamosto <note>A Venetian explorer who sailed for Portugal.</note> encountered them firmly established for a long time in the Senegal basin. For my part, I believe that there were already Peuls on the lower Senegal around the 11th century of our era at the very least, and perhaps before then. In any case, the language they currently speak—which Dr. Thaly links to the language of the Romanichals <note>Another term for the Romani people.</note>—was already spoken in Senegal by the Toucouleurs *at the very least* as early as the 11th century. This is proven by a passage from Al-Bakri <note>An 11th-century geographer from Al-Andalus.</note> describing the hippopotamuses of the Bakel region under the name *gabou*, which he says was the name given to these animals by the natives of the country (1).

General Faidherbe <note>Louis Faidherbe (1818–1889), a French colonial administrator and linguist who was Governor of Senegal.</note> spoke in favor of the theory that the Peuls came from the East, bringing with them the humped cattle <note>The zebu.</note> of Asiatic origin to Africa. At the same time, however, he pointed out the affinities that their language shares with several idioms of the far West of Africa, and in particular with Serer. I believe that here, as on many other occasions, General Faidherbe was correct; had he possessed the time or the means to delve deeper into the question, he would undoubtedly have resolved it in the right way. His theory, though incomplete, seems accurate to me: the Peuls originated from an immi—

...Asian migration which, having reached the Senegalese Fouta <note>The Fouta Toro region in northern Senegal, a historical center of Peul and Toucouleur culture.</note>, adopted the language of the indigenous Toucouleurs and then carried it, during its counter-migration from West to East, from the lower Senegal to the upper Nile basin.

Grimal de Guiraudon made himself look ridiculous through his pretentiousness, his eccentricities, and the rudeness with which he treated his predecessors, even the most illustrious; yet, beneath these somewhat whimsical appearances, he was nonetheless the first to see clearly regarding the Peul <note>Commonly known today as the Fula, Fulani, or Pulaar speakers.</note> language. His system is sometimes poorly supported, it is incomplete, and it contains inaccuracies, but we must nevertheless recognize that de Guiraudon possessed an undeniable merit in establishing it. Regarding the origin of the Peuls—and although he relied on facts, several of which are erroneous—it currently (1) appears to me that he provided the correct solution by leaning toward their connection to the Jewish people and their migration from Palestine to the Sudan by way of Egypt. Above all, he was correct in asserting that the people of the Peul language do not form a people of <term>métis|A historical term used here to describe people of mixed racial or ethnic ancestry.</term> but are constituted by two very distinct ethnic groups: one of the white race (the Peuls properly so-called) and the other of the black race (the Toucouleurs).

Professor Verneau attributed a Semitic or Hamito-Semitic <note>A linguistic and ethnic classification formerly used to group various peoples of North Africa, the Horn of Africa, and the Middle East.</note> origin to the Peuls; his conviction stems from the comparison of a few Peul skulls—whose origin, moreover, was only moderately certain regarding the ancestry of their owners—with Ethiopian skulls.

To complete this sort of summary of theories regarding the origin of the Peuls, I must say a word about the opinion expressed by various authors—Barth <note>Heinrich Barth (1821–1865), a renowned German explorer and scholar of African languages and history.</note> among others—according to which the Peuls were the *Leucoethiopes* <note>original: "Leucœthiopes"; literally "White Ethiopians."</note> or White Ethiopians mentioned by Pliny and Ptolemy. But it should be noted that, just as Ptolemy's *Darados* likely corresponds to the Dara or Draa <note>A river in modern-day Morocco.</note> and not to the Senegal, the *Stachir* must correspond to the Saguia el-Hamra or some river near Cape Bojador rather than to the Gambia. Furthermore, it is in the heart of the Sahara, between the Libyo-Egyptians and the Nigrite Ethiopians living along the Nigris or Niger, that Pliny locates the *Leucoethiopes*; the same author places tribes he calls the *Pharusii* and *Perorsi* to the west of the *Darates* Getulians <note>A Berber people of North Africa in antiquity.</note> or Getulians of the Dara. These may be the *Phetrusim* of the Book of Genesis, the ancestors of the Philistines, whom he also describes as "Ethiopians" and who were clearly Berbers and not Peuls. The ancients gave the name "Ethiopians" to all inhabitants of Southern Libya, to the nomads of the southern Sahara as well as to Black Africans; they only distinguished the former from the latter by the epithets "white" and "black."

The Philistines were a Hamitic people <note>A historical term used to describe descendants of Ham, son of Noah, often used in the 19th century to categorize various North African and Middle Eastern peoples.</note> originating from Canaan, whose migrated descendants in the Maghreb <note>The region of Northwest Africa, including modern-day Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia.</note> supposedly became the Libyans or Berbers. It is for these reasons that I prefer to give these various Semitic immigrations—occurring before the Arab immigrations and invasions from Yemen and the Hijaz <note>The region in the west of present-day Saudi Arabia, home to the cities of Mecca and Medina.</note>—the title "Judaeo-Syrian" rather than "Jewish," as the latter would have too narrow a meaning.

The first of these Judaeo-Syrian immigrations of which memory has been passed down to us seems to have taken place during the third millennium BC. Certain Egyptologists place it around the year 3000 BC; others believe it to be much more recent and place it only toward the year 2000 BC. This latter estimate is the most generally adopted.

Genesis <note>The first book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament.</note> teaches us that Joseph, one of the sons of Israel or Jacob, having been sold by his brothers to Arab merchants, was taken by them to Egypt (1) and resold to Potiphar, who commanded the Pharaoh's army. Later becoming the confidant and all-powerful minister of the King of Egypt, Joseph sent for his father, who went to Egypt with his other sons, "all his offspring" (2) and all his herds.
