The Bible does not mention that other Hebrew immigrants took another direction or remained in Egypt, but it is likely that, if their numbers were truly so great, Moses could not have taken all the Israelites with him; the Book of Exodus, moreover, hints at this by emphasizing the precautions he had to take to prevent many Hebrews from staying behind or returning to Egypt; finally, we are familiar with the tradition regarding the "lost tribes" of Israel.

Whatever share of truth one should accord to the somewhat marvelous and legendary accounts of Genesis and Exodus, it seems quite certain that there was, in a very ancient era, a very considerable Judaeo-Syrian immigration into Egypt, that the Judaeo-Syrians made a prolonged stay in that country, acquired great influence there, and were finally expelled following a revival of nationalist sentiment. But it seems difficult to admit that all of them took the path by which their ancestors had come; on the contrary, it is likely that an appreciable number of them dispersed either toward the South, in the direction of Ethiopia, or toward the West, in the direction of Cyrenaica <note>An ancient Greek and later Roman province on the North African coast, in modern-day eastern Libya.</note>. These Judaeo-Syrians who remained in Africa, not having received the teachings of Moses, must have practiced the religion of Abraham, which was undoubtedly heavily permeated with beliefs and rites borrowed from the Egyptian religion.

...provide others whose close parallelism with the former only serves to confirm them: I am referring to the information regarding the Hyksos <note>The Hyksos were a people of mixed Semitic and Asian origin who immigrated into the Nile Delta and ruled Northern Egypt for over a century.</note>. Almost all scholars who have dealt with the question of the Hyksos lean toward identifying their invasion of Egypt with the Israelite immigration, or at the very least think that the latter occurred thanks to the Hyksos coming to power, they too having come from Mesopotamia, Syria, and Palestine; so that the Israelite immigration and the exodus led by Moses would be merely episodes of the Hyksos invasion and their eventual dispersal.

The Hyksos invaded Egypt toward the end of the 14th^th^ dynasty, that is to say, toward the end of the first Theban Empire. Having seized power, they formed the 15^th^, 16^th^, and 17^th^ dynasties, and were expelled by the 18^th^ dynasty, which constituted the second Theban Empire. Lepsius <note>Karl Richard Lepsius (1810–1884) was a pioneering German Egyptologist who attempted to synchronize Egyptian chronology with biblical history.</note> gives 2136 and 1626 BCE as the probable dates of their arrival and departure; others push these dates back by a thousand years: in any case, these dates correspond singularly well with those given by biblical commentators for the arrival of Israel and the departure of Moses (2000 and 1570 according to some, 3000 and 2570 according to others).

According to the Egyptian historian Manetho <note>Manetho was an Egyptian priest who lived in the 3rd century BCE and wrote a history of Egypt in Greek, which remains a primary source for the chronology of the Pharaohs.</note>, the Hyksos—who were, like the Israelites, shepherds—returned to Asia, their country of origin, upon their departure from Egypt. However, just as it is permissible to suppose that a portion of the Israelites did not follow Moses, it is likewise possible to think that the Hyksos—first persecuted by their Theban victors, then left free to carry out their retreat peacefully (according to Manetho’s testimony)—did not all take the same route, and that many dispersed toward Cyrenaica <note>The coastal region of eastern Libya.</note> or Upper Egypt.

Later, Jews of the Mosaic religion are said to have emigrated to Yemen and from there to Abyssinia <note>Historical name for Ethiopia.</note>, during the reign of Solomon (10th^th^ century BCE) and would have been the ancestors of the Falasha <note>Now more commonly known as the Beta Israel, the Jewish community of Ethiopia.</note>. But it does not seem that this immigration spread west of the Nile, and it offers little interest for the question at hand. The same applies to the Phoenician immigrations which...

But around 320 BCE, following the capture of Jerusalem by Ptolemy Soter <note>Ptolemy I Soter (reigned 303–282 BCE) was a companion of Alexander the Great and the founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt.</note>, many Jews were deported to Cyrenaica <note>An ancient Greek and later Roman region on the coast of modern-day Libya.</note>. It is to this population that I believe I can trace back the ethnic origin of the Peuls <note>Also known as the Fula, Fulani, or Foulbé; a major ethnic group spread across West and Central Africa, traditionally known for pastoralism.</note>, or at least those of their branches that have not been too transformed by unions with Black Africans.

Before exploring how the Judaeo-Syrians of Cyrenaica may have become the Peuls, I would like to report some legendary traditions current among the Peuls themselves which serve, in part, to justify my hypothesis.

According to all the traditions gathered at various times among the Peuls of different regions of the Sudan <note>The author uses "Sudan" in its historical geographical sense: the *Bilad as-Sudan*, meaning the "Land of the Blacks," referring to the broad savanna belt south of the Sahara.</note>, the Foulbé <term>Foulbé: the plural form of the word for a Fula person; singular: Pullo</term> tribes—stretching from the lower Senegal and Fouta-Djallon in the West to the countries between Chad and the Nile in the East—unanimously declare that they came from the Senegalese Fouta or from Mali, that is, from the regions located between the Atlantic and the Upper Niger. But all of them also claim that their ancestors from the West were themselves descended from earlier ancestors who came from the North or the East, and especially from the North-East. The vast majority of these traditions assign the country of *Sam* or *Cham*—that is, Syria <note>original: "Sâm" or "Châm". According to indigenous traditions, they first came into the country of *Tôr* (the Sinai Peninsula) (1), then from the country of *Tôr* into that of *Missira* (Egypt) and from Egypt into the country of *Soritou* (no doubt *Sort* or *Syrte* <note>The region of Sirte or the Gulf of Sidra.</note>, *Cyrenaica*), from where, much later, they reached the country of *Diaka*, *Diaga*, or *Dia* (western *Massina* <note>An area in the Inner Niger Delta of modern-day Mali.</note>), where we will find them a little further on.

Those among the Fula who have been deeply Islamized have blended recollections from the history of Islam with their national traditions. Thus, many claim that their first ancestors were still in Sinai after the death of Muhammad when, in 639, the Caliph Omar-ben-el-Khattâb <note>Umar ibn al-Khattab, the second Caliph of Islam, who reigned 634–644 CE.</note> (634–644) sent an army from the Hejaz <note>The western region of Saudi Arabia, home to Mecca and Medina.</note> across the Red Sea, commanded by Amrou-ben-el-Assi <note>Amr ibn al-As, the Arab commander famous for the conquest of Egypt.</note>, with the goal of converting the Jews and infidels of Sinai and Egypt. Amrou is said to have landed a portion of his troops, led by a man named Okba-ben-Yasser, in the country of Tôr (Sinai); the latter reportedly converted the majority of the Jews of Sinai to Islam, while those who refused to renounce Mosaism <note>The religion of Moses; Judaism.</note> were massacred. When Amrou, returning from his expedition in Egypt, stopped in Sinai to observe the results obtained by Okba, the King of Tôr begged the Arab general to leave someone in the country capable of completing the religious instruction of the new converts; Amrou therefore left Okba in Sinai and resumed his route toward Medina, where Caliph Omar resided. Okba, having remained in Sinai, married Tadiouma, the daughter of the King of Tôr, who bore him four children: three daughters (Daa or Daadou, Ouol, and Noussou) and one boy (Raabou or Raarabou). It was there that the birth of the tribes, clans, and castes that still exist today likely took place, a short time later.

However, among those Fula who have been only slightly affected by Islamic influence, and especially among those who have escaped it entirely, the national legend is presented in a different light and likely stays closer to the truth. Here is a sample, which summarizes various traditions collected from the Fula of the Sahel <note>The semi-arid transition zone between the Sahara Desert and the Sudanian savanna.</note>.

The first ancestors of the Fula are said to have been *Yakouba* (Jacob), son of *Issiraïla* (Israel) (1), son of *Issihaka* (Isaac), son of *Ibrahima* (Abraham), and a man named *Souleïman* <note>Solomon</note>. The first, having departed from the land of *Kenana* (Canaan), reportedly came by way of *Tor* <note>Mount Sinai, referred to in Arabic as Jabal at-Tur</note> into the land of *Missira* (Egypt), where his son *Youssoufou* (Joseph) was then reigning. Joseph, having previously come to Egypt, had married the daughter of the king of the country and had succeeded him on the throne. The second ancestor, *Souleïman*, had come from the land of *Sam* (Syria) at the same time as Joseph and had settled near him.

The children of Jacob, as well as those of Solomon, supposedly formed the stock from which the Fula people would later emerge. They were all grouped together under the name *Banissiraïla* <note>Banu Israel, or the Children of Israel</note>. After the death of Joseph (2), the Egyptians wanted to shake off the yoke of the *Banissiraïla* and entrusted the scepter to a man of the country named *Firaouma* (Pharaoh).

(1) Jacob and Israel, in the Bible, are one and the same character.
(2) Doubtless several generations after this death.

### PRE-ISLAMIC TRADITIONS

The latter <note>Referring to the Pharaoh, mentioned on the previous page as the ruler in power during this era.</note>, jealous of the numbers, the power, and the wealth in herds of the *Banissiraïla* <note>The Children of Israel or Israelites.</note>, overwhelmed them with taxes of all kinds; the *Israelites*—or rather the *Judeo-Syrians*—then fled from Egypt. One part of them returned to *Kénana* (Canaan, Palestine) and *Sâm* (Syria) under the leadership of a chief named *Moussa* (*Moses*). The others crossed the Nile under the leadership of a descendant of Joseph and a descendant of *Souleïmân* <note>Solomon.</note>, heading toward the setting sun. *Firaouma* <note>Pharaoh.</note> pursued them, but, as he was crossing the Nile, the boat carrying him *capsized* and he drowned; his warriors then abandoned the pursuit of the *Judeo-Syrians* who, with their herds, came to settle in the land of *Soritou* (*Cyrenaica*) (1) and from that moment, "in memory of their flight," took the name *Foudh* or *Fouth* (2).

Later, a fraction of them, taking the southwest route, went to *Touat* <note>A region in the central Sahara, in modern-day Algeria.</note>; but another fraction headed south and reached *Bornou* (or rather *Aïr* <note>A mountainous region in northern Niger.</note>, as we shall see further on), under the leadership of two chiefs named *Gadia* and *Gaye*, the former a descendant of Israel and the second of *Souleïmân*. *Kara* or *Karaké*, son and successor of *Gadia*, and *Gama*, son and successor of *Gaye*, led their compatriots from Bornou to *Diaga* or *Massina* <note>Regions in the Inner Niger Delta, in modern-day Mali.</note>, where they were favorably received by the *Sébè* (*Soninké*) (3).

(2) The root *foudh*, with the meaning of "to flee," is found in Demotic Egyptian <note>The late stage of the ancient Egyptian language used for everyday documents.</note> in the form *pout* (with a *t* pronounced as *d*) and in Coptic <note>The final stage of the Egyptian language, written with the Greek alphabet.</note> in the form *fôt* (with a *t* pronounced as *d* in the south of the Delta). In the Semitic languages, one finds no analogous root having the meaning "to flee." This would suggest that, during their stay in Egypt, the *Judeo-Syrians* had adopted the Egyptian language or at least that their primitive language—probably Aramaic <term>Aramaic: A Semitic language that served as the common tongue of the Near East in antiquity.</term>—had been strongly influenced by Egyptian, which is not at all improbable. Similarly, later on, during their stay in Fouta, they were to adopt the language of the Toucouleurs <note>An ethnic group living along the Senegal River.</note>. As for the Hebrews who followed Moses, they could very well also have spoken Egyptian at the time of their departure from Egypt, but, having returned to a Semitic country, they must have quite quickly resumed the language of their ancestors.

THE PEOPLES

### 4. *Formation of the Fula people.*

We have seen how very important Judeo-Syrian colonies were formed in Cyrenaica <note>A coastal region in modern-day eastern Libya.</note>, both during the period of Moses and the Hyksos <note>A group of people from Western Asia who took over the eastern Nile Delta, ending the Middle Kingdom of Egypt.</note>—the *Foudh*, likely speaking the Egyptian language or at least a Semitic language strongly influenced by Egyptian (1)—and toward the end of the 4th century BCE. This population undoubtedly practiced partly the religion of Abraham and partly the Mosaic faith.

In the year 40 of our era, Saint Mark, who was himself a Jew from Cyrenaica, came to evangelize his homeland and was the first to preach Christianity in Africa. He made a number of converts <term>proselytes</term> among his compatriots; however, in contact with this new doctrine, religious fervor redoubled among the Jews who remained faithful to the religion of their ancestors, and old hatreds, previously dormant, were reawakened between pre-Mosaicists, Mosaicists, and the orthodox. Jewish priests devised a way to unify the different cults and preached a sort of reform of Judaism, seeking to bring it back to its primitive purity. Internal wars followed; Rome, which was not yet frightened by Christianity, took offense at these reformed Jews. Both because of the persecutions they suffered at the hands of imperial authorities and the kind of condemnation <term>réprobation</term> they faced from their compatriots, these supporters of a return to ancient doctrines—who were none other than...

---

<insert>
With the [arrival of] Judeo-Syrians in Massina <note>The Inner Niger Delta region in modern Mali.</note>, we almost enter the realm of history; we will see in the fourth part of this work what became of Kara and Gama. I must point out that the Soninké <note>An ethnic group from West Africa, known for founding the Ghana Empire.</note> of the Sahel have appropriated this tradition and present it as explaining their own origin; they have even introduced their own clan names to make it more plausible. But, in my opinion, the legend is indeed a Fula tradition, and the Soninké can only claim it as giving the partial origin of those families descended from the mixture of Judeo-Syrian immigrants with the original inhabitants of Massina.

# JEWISH MIGRATION TOWARDS THE AÏR

doubt that the *Foudh*, those pre-Mosaicists <note>Followers of a form of Judaism predating the laws of Moses.</note> who came from Egypt during the dispersion of the *Hyksos* <note>A group of Northwest Semitic people who ruled northern Egypt for a time.</note>—began, around the year 80, to migrate toward the South.

At that time, a Roman officer named Julius Maternus, acting on the orders of the Emperor Domitian, set out in search of the famous gold mines of the Sudan <note>Historically, the "Sudan" referred to the broad "Land of the Blacks" across the Sahel, rather than the modern nation-state.</note>; guided by Berbers from Djerma or the Fezzân (the Garamantes), whom Cornelius Balbus had subdued sixty years earlier, he ventured south of Tripolitania. After a very long and arduous journey, and without having encountered anything resembling a gold mine, he reached a country where he saw rhinoceroses and whose name has been transmitted to us by Latin historians in the form Agisymba; he then returned to the coast. It has been thought, not without reason, that this country must have been the Aïr <note>A mountainous region in modern-day northern Niger.</note> and that Agisymba corresponded to Asben or Agadez.

In all likelihood, this was the route followed by the *Foudh* or pre-Mosaic Judeo-Syrians, whether their exodus preceded the expedition of Julius Maternus by a few months—with the latter following in their tracks—or whether, having met in Phazania <note>The Latin name for the Fezzan region of modern Libya.</note>, they took advantage of the military apparatus of this expedition to complete their migration in total safety. Whatever the case, they certainly reached the Aïr, but it is unlikely they pushed further South, and it is undoubtedly the Aïr that is designated by the name Bornu in the legend I reported above (1). In the Aïr, where they must have stayed for some time, they gathered more precise information than Julius Maternus possessed regarding the location of the famous gold mines of the Sudan, or at least regarding the countries from which the gold originated. Continuing, perhaps unconsciously, the route that Maternus had only sketched out, they arrived—via Takedda and Tadmekket—at the banks of the Niger River, in the region located between Timbuktu—which did not yet exist—and Dia or Diaga—which already existed, at least as a province.

(1) The Aïr was, at one point, a political dependency of Bornu, or at least of Kanem <note>The Kanem-Bornu Empire was a major state in the Chad Basin from the 9th to 19th centuries.</note> during the time when the latter empire encompassed Bornu.

# THE PEOPLES

Undoubtedly, they had remained above all the quintessential pastoralists that their Israelite ancestors had been, bringing their herds with them. After having crossed the Sahara, they could not fail to be struck by the abundance of the pastures in the Massina <note>A flood-prone savanna region in the Inner Niger Delta of modern-day Mali.</note>. Considering this region as the land eternally promised to their traditionalist mysticism, they settled there. The country was inhabited by <term>Soninké</term> <note>A Mandé-speaking people known for founding the Ghana Empire.</note> farmers and <term>Bozo</term> <note>An ethnic group of the Niger River known as "masters of the water" for their fishing skills.</note> fishermen, but livestock must have been rare there. The indigenous people must, at least at first, have welcomed these white shepherds of mysterious origin, who lived mainly on dairy, did not seem to harbor designs of conquest, and brought with them a considerable element of wealth.

The story of Joseph in Egypt began anew on the banks of the Niger, though on a smaller scale, it is true. After a short time, the Judeo-Syrians became the advisors, then the masters of the Soninké of Massina, until the latter—weary of a guardianship that, in the long run, seemed heavy to them—wished to take their revenge by dispossessing these foreigners who had become wealthier than the locals. In doing so, they did not realize they were killing the goose that laid the golden eggs. What had happened in the time of Moses happened again: the Judeo-Syrians, who were no strangers to an exodus, moved away from the banks of the Niger. In their migration, they were protected by a Soninké patriarch who has become, in modernized legends, the Muslim cleric El-hadj Salihou Souaré <note>The legendary 12th-century founder of the Suwarian tradition of peaceful Islamic teaching, here synchronized with much earlier events by the author.</note>. Reaching more desert-like regions—which for that very reason must have been less inhospitable to them—they headed toward the northern extremity of the Bagana <note>A historical region located between the Niger River and the Sahara.</note>, toward Néma, where no doubt the Soninké had already long ago made scattered attempts at colonization. They established themselves in the Aoukar <note>A dry basin in southeastern Mauritania, once much wetter than it is today.</note> around the middle of the 2nd century of our era. Berbers must have been nomadizing in the region since that time, but no doubt their home base was further west—or rather, to the northwest—in the Mauritanian Adrar.

The *Foudh* were soon to be joined in the northern Bagana by another group of Judeo-Syrians from Cyrenaica <note>A region on the coast of modern-day Libya.</note>, who had come by a different route. Indeed, the departure of the pre-Mosaicists had not provided a sufficient solution to the question

### JEWISH MIGRATION TOWARD THE TOUAT

religious; if Christianity was still making only fairly slow progress in Cyrenaica <note>A coastal region in eastern modern-day Libya.</note> and did not show itself hostile to the established powers, the same was not true of the various Jewish sects. These eventually put an end to their internal quarrels and united in a common hatred of the Romans. In the year 115, a general revolt of all the Judeo-Syrian communities seriously threatened Roman authority in Cyrenaica; the emperor's representatives had to mobilize all their troops and call upon the Berber populations to fight the rebellion, which lasted two full years. Finally, in 117, the Judeo-Syrians, definitively defeated by the Romans, emigrated en masse—this time numbering several thousand.

Having reached Southern Tripolitania <note>The northwestern region of modern-day Libya.</note>, they did not take the route to the Aïr <note>A mountainous region in northern Niger.</note> like their predecessors, but, skirting the northern edge of the Sahara, they headed toward the oases of the Touat <note>A region in central Algeria composed of several oases.</note>. A great number of them remained there (1). Others pushed further west and went to found colonies in Southern Morocco that still exist today. Finally, others, and not the least numerous, went to join their compatriots in the Aoukar <note>A dry basin in southeastern Mauritania.</note> who had arrived there via the Aïr and the Massina. These easily forgot the religious quarrels of the past in the joy of seeing this new element of strength and wealth arrive; the newcomers were incorporated into the fraction already settled, and together they formed a single community.

They practiced the Hebrew religion in the broad sense of the term; from this group, about a century later, the Empire of Ghana was to emerge.

Towards the end of the 8th century, the Soninké <note>An ancient West African ethnic group, the founders of the Ghana Empire.</note> of the Diaga or Massina <note>An area in central Mali.</note>, drawn by the prosperity acquired by their colonies in the Aoukar—specifically Ghana—under the suzerainty of the Judeo-Syrians, moved there in large numbers and stripped the latter of their political supremacy. For the *Foudh*, this was the signal for a new dispersion and a fresh exodus.

Some of them, however, accepted Soninké rule and remained in the country; these belonged mostly to families from the first wave of immigration. They had intermarried with the Soninké during their stay in Massina and since their settlement in the Aoukar, and it was natural for them to want to remain near their relatives by marriage. It is the descendants of these Judeo-Syrians, more or less intermixed with the Soninké, who were called the *Massin* or *Ahl-Massina* <note>Arabic: "People of Massina."</note>, in memory of their stay in Massina before their arrival in Ghana. They are still found today in Oualata and Néma; they have adopted the Arabic language and, for this reason, they are associated with the Moors.

A few families of Judeo-Syrian *Massin*, accompanied by Soninké from Ghana, moved westward and founded *Chétou*, whose name was later transformed into *Tichit* by the Berbers. Tradition relates that their leader was a blind old man; God had promised him in a dream to lead him to a country destined to be his new homeland, which the old man would recognize by a specific scent emanating from the soil. Every day, upon reaching a stopping point, the blind man would have a handful of sand brought to him and would hold it to his nostrils. Finally, having reached the place where Tichit stands today, he recognized the guiding fragrance and chose this spot to establish his residence and that of his companions. Later, some of the Massin of Tichit emigrated to the Tagant <note>A plateau region in central Mauritania.</note>; attacked there by Berbers, they were partially massacred. The survivors took refuge in Diara, near Nioro, and finally in Akor, near Goum- <note>The text breaks off mid-word, likely referring to Goumbou.</note>

# THE JUDEO-SYRIANS BECOME THE PEULS

Once again, we are going to see the eternal story of the Jews in Egypt unfold in Fouta, though in a new form and with new consequences. Ismaïl, having become the confidant and the minister of the emperor of Tekrour, married his daughter *Diouma Sal* (1) and, upon the death of his father-in-law, he was chosen as sovereign by the Toucouleurs. After a few generations, the Semitic immigrants who had come from Ghana <note>This refers to the ancient Wagadu Empire, not the modern nation of Ghana.</note> had multiplied, without however equaling the indigenous Toucouleurs in number, with whom they had undoubtedly contracted frequent and fruitful unions. Perhaps their religion also underwent a rather profound modification, though this is less certain. To prevent Mahmoud from returning the children to their parents, his brother employed a method as radical as it was barbaric: he had them all killed during the night. 

When day broke, the fathers of the hostages—still unaware of what had occurred—went to see Mahmoud and begged him to return their children, swearing that his mercy would bring him good fortune. Mahmoud, allowing himself to be moved to pity, sent a messenger to his brother to reclaim the hostages. His brother sent back the reply that he had just put them to death. When the news became known to the Toucouleur chiefs, they spread it immediately throughout the country, calling for a bloody vengeance: all the indigenous people of the Fouta took up arms and fell upon the Judeo-Syrian <note>The author uses this term to describe the ancestors of the Peul/Fulani, following a historical theory that they migrated from the Levant; modern scholarship views Fulani origins within Africa.</note> herdsmen dispersed among them, massacring those they could reach and putting the others to flight. 

A Toucouleur named *Ouar Diabi*, *Ouar Diadié*, or *Ouar Ndiaye* seized power. Mahmoud and all the members of his family were killed. Indeed, from that point on, the Peuls must have shown themselves resistant to Islamization, since even today, a significant number of them are still “infidels”—in the Muslim sense of the word—even among the groups that remained in the vicinity of the Fouta (notably in the Ferlo) and especially among the families where the original Semitic type has remained the purest and who are the least mixed with Black African blood.

### 5° *Peul migrations.*

From the first years following the death of Mahmoud II, the vast majority of the Peuls of the Fouta Toro likely moved toward the South, into the region which was then uninhabited but favorable for livestock raising, known today as the Ferlo, and which at that time must have depended, more or less theoretically, on the Empire of Tekrur. ### MIGRATION OF THE PEULS TOWARD THE EAST ###

Tekrur <note>Tekrur was an ancient state located in the Senegal River valley, often considered one of the earliest West African centers of Islam.</note>, according to the testimony of al-Bakri, and the Soninké who already possessed colonies there must have been vassals of the Toucouleurs. Some Peul families must have, from this era, crossed to the right bank of the Senegal River near Kayes and rejoined in the Diomboko the descendants of the Judeo-Syrians who had remained there after arriving from Ghana.

It is this Peul colony of Galam, Khasso, and Diomboko that, most likely, al-Bakri points out to us under the name of *Al-Fâmân* — one could strictly read *Al-Fellân* <note>original: "Al-Fellân"; this is a significant variant as it closely resembles "Fellata," a common name for the Peul or Fulani.</note> in one of the manuscripts — and which he locates to the Southeast of the country of the Toronka (the Toucouleurs of Toro), in the region of Silla **(1)**, adding that these Al-Fâmân belong to the same race as the Honeihîn <note>The Honeihîn are mentioned in medieval Arabic texts as a light-skinned group associated with the early history of the Ghana Empire.</note> of Ghana. Certain families of this colony later united with the Mandé (principally the Soninké and Kâgoro) and gave birth to the current *Khassonké*.

According to indigenous traditions, this Peul colony of Galam chose a king from the Diallo clan whose title has been transmitted to us in the various forms of *saltigué, silatigui, fondokoï*, and *ardo* **(2)**. When the Soninké of Ghana, defeated and hunted by the Lemtuna <note>The Lemtuna were the dominant Berber tribe within the Almoravid confederation.</note> Berbers during the Almoravid movement, began to settle in large numbers in the Guidimaka and the Gadiaga or Galam (at the end of the 11th century), the Peuls, under the leadership of their *ardo*, for the most part left these regions and advanced toward the East through the Diomboko and the Kaarta, leaving at each of their stops families who, by uniting—

---

**(1)** Silla, according to the Arab geographers of the Middle Ages, was located on the Senegal River between Tekrur — which must have corresponded approximately to Podor — and Galambou (the chief town of Galam), which was likely situated near the confluence of the Falémé and the Senegal; Silla was much closer to Galambou than to Tekrur, since al-Bakri tells us there was only a day's journey (by land or water) between Silla and Galambou, so that this city (Silla) must have been located very near our current post of Bakel.

**(2)** This is indeed a title and not a name: in Wolof and Serer, *saltigué* designates a band leader; *silatigui*, in Mandé, means a guide or a leader of migration (the "master of the road"): it is the equivalent of *fondokoï* in Songhai and — at least in meaning — of *ardo* in Peul (which means "leader" or "conductor"). The early European travelers all referred to the emperor of Tekrur by the title of *silatigui, siratiki*, or *siratique*.

Having arrived in Kaniaga **(1)**, a southern province of Bagana, the main body of the migration remained there longer than in its previous stopping points. It appears that, having left Galam toward the end of the 11th century or the beginning of the 12th, the Peuls <note>Also known as the Fulani or Fula people.</note> had not significantly moved beyond Kaniaga by the end of the 14th century; no doubt the efforts of the Soninké Sossé or Sosso to conquer Ghana from the Sissé <note>The Sissé were the ruling dynasty of the Ghana Empire at its peak.</note>, followed by their struggles with the Mandingues and the raids that followed the final victory of the latter, had maintained a state of insecurity along the left bank of the upper Niger that did not favor eastward migrations. At the beginning of the 14th century, however, Diawambé Peuls <note>The Diawambé are a specific subgroup of the Peul, often associated with trade and diplomacy.</note> had moved into the Kingui and founded Nioro.

But at the beginning of the 15th century, the Peul exodus resumed its momentum in a decisive manner, following circumstances that indigenous traditions recount as follows. A *silatigui* <note>term: silatigui (a Mandé-influenced title for a leader or "guide of the way")</note> or *ardo* <note>term: ardo (a traditional Peul title for a chief or military leader)</note> named *Yogo*, son of Sadio or Sadia Diallo, residing in Kouma or Toi in Kaniaga, died around 1400, leaving a widow and two brothers, the eldest of whom was named *Diâdié* and the youngest *Maga* (or Maghan) or Atiba. *Diâdié* wished to marry Yogo’s widow, but she refused his advances; Maga went to her to urge her to accept his brother's hand: however, the woman persisted in her refusal, and enemies of Maga presented his brother's actions to Diâdié in a bad light, claiming that it was Maga who had pushed Yogo's widow to reject Diâdié's proposals with the goal of marrying her himself. A quarrel followed between the two brothers who, after exchanging hurtful words, separated.

# THE PEUL IN MASSINA

...without [delay], walking straight ahead of him toward the North. Having reached the center of the Bagana <note>A historical region in what is now Mali and Mauritania.</note>, near Kala (Sokolo), he encountered a herd of stray cattle. Driving them before him toward the East, he arrived in Diaga or Massina <note>The Inner Niger Delta region of Mali.</note>, near a pond adjacent to a village of Soninké Nono <note>A branch of the Soninké people, who were the founders of the Ghana Empire.</note>. Maga asked them for hospitality and established his camp near their village; he then went to greet the official who governed Bagana on behalf of the Emperor of Mali and received from him the official investiture as chief (*<term>ardo</term>* <note>original: "ardo"; a traditional title for a Peul leader or commander</note>) of the Peul families who had followed him, with authorization to reside in Massina. Later, other Peuls from Kaniaga, belonging to the Daédio or Bari clan, joined Maga, as did people belonging to the castes of the Mabbé (or Maboubé) <note>A social caste of weavers.</note> and the Diawambé <note>A social group often acting as intermediaries, advisors, or merchants.</note>; <term>Rimaïbé</term> <note>original: "Rimaïbé"; descendants of enslaved populations who were integrated into Peul society</note> (1) serfs, descended from Black slaves acquired by the Peuls during their crossing of the Senegal basin, further increased this core group, which gave rise to the very important group of the Massina Peuls and the secondary branches that later branched off from them.

Diâdié himself had headed toward the North-West and settled in Bakounou, between Goumbou and Nioro, with several families belonging to the clans of the *Irlâbé*, the *Yalâbé* (or *Alaïbé*), the *Oualarbé*, the *Férôbé*, and the *Ourourbé* (or *Boli*) (2).

# THE PEOPLES

From Massina, the Peul soon spread across the Niger Bend and beyond, although the bulk of their nation is still established today in the region where the Dia or Diaka waterway <note>A seasonal stream or branch of the Niger River in the Inner Niger Delta.</note> forms a sort of center. As early as the 15th century, the Oualarbé, the Ourourbé, the Salsalbé, and the Tôrobé clans moved toward the North, into the current district of Niafounké, along with a large number of Diawambé <note>A social group often acting as advisors or merchants.</note>. Others crossed the Niger and the Bani rivers and, filtering through the lands of the Tombo <note>An older term for the Dogon people.</note> and the Mossi, reached Liptako (the region of Dori), where they founded a prosperous colony that could almost rival that of Massina. Here again, we have numerous indigenous traditions relating to the various exoduses that together constituted this important migration.

The Peul clan of the *Tôrobé*—for there are both Peul Tôrobé and Toucouleur Tôrobé—had settled mainly North of Lake Débo, between Niafounké and Saraféré, following the great migration from Fouta toward Massina. Legend says that the exodus of the Tôrobé had been led by three brothers named Sambo, Paté, and Yoro. A portion of them, leaving the region of Saraféré, went to camp at Gorou, North of Douentza. There, they were joined by four members of their clan (Hamadi, Dembo, Dello, and Diobo), all four descendants of a man named Siré who was said to be the father of Sambo, Paté, and Yoro and who allegedly remained in Fouta with part of his family during the exodus of the latter three. The four emissaries came from Fouta in the...

...against the Emperor of Gao, El-Hadj Mohammed (the first <term>Askia</term> <note>original: "askia"; the title of the rulers of the Songhai Empire's Askia Dynasty</note>), who had become master of the majority of the former dependencies of Mali. In 1511-1512, El-Hadj Mohammed undertook an expedition against Tindo, whom he defeated and killed at Diara, near and to the Northeast of Nioro. *Koli*, the son of Tindo, then took command of the Peuls of Bakounou who resisted the sovereign of Gao; accompanied by Goro (or Gara), chief of the Oualarbé, Diko, chief of the Fêrôbé, and Nima, chief of the Ourourbé, he emigrated to Fouta Toro which, like all of ancient Tekrour, was then subject to the Emperor of Jolof. This Koli, aided by the Serer people and by the Toucouleur clan of the Denianke, reportedly succeeded in killing the Emperor of Jolof, freeing the Toucouleurs from the suzerainty of the Wolofs, and founding a new independent empire in Tekrour, of which he was the first sovereign. According to the testimony of Sa'di <note>Abderrahmane es-Sa'di (1594–1656), a chronicler from Timbuktu and author of the Tarikh al-Sudan.</note>, his descendants were still reigning in Fouta toward the middle of the 18th century.

The latter remained in Téma and married a Mossi man; the five sons came to settle in Kalsaka, in Yatenga, and married Mossi women there. It is the descendants of these unions between Peul and Mossi who are called *Silmimossi* by the Mossi, while the pure Peul are called *Silmissi*. These Silmimossi are linked more to the Peul than to the Mossi, but in reality, they share the heritage of both peoples: they speak both the Peul and Mossi languages simultaneously and are at once herders and farmers; however, among them, it is the men who milk the cows, and not the women as is the case among the true Peul <note>In traditional Peul culture, the management of milk is typically a female responsibility; this shift highlights the cultural blending of the Silmimossi.</note>.

The *Dialloubé* also provided a fairly large contingent to the Peul migrations that spread throughout the Niger Bend. One of their chiefs, Hamân, left Massina in the 17th century and settled in Gomboro, in western Yatenga, within the Samo country <note>The Samo are an ethnic group living primarily in northwestern Burkina Faso.</note>. Guibril, the current chief of the Dialloubé of Yatenga, is said to be the fourteenth successor of Hamân, from whom he is separated by nine generations.

(1) The Dénianké were those Toucouleurs who had helped the Peul leader Koli Galadio seize Tekrour <note>An ancient kingdom in the Senegal River valley.</note> at the beginning of the 16th century (see above, page 229, note 2). At the beginning of the 18th century, a Toucouleur marabout <note>A Muslim religious leader or teacher in West Africa.</note> named Abdoulkader Tôrodo preached a holy war against the "infidels" and overthrew the Peul dynasty of Koli’s descendants; power thus passed to the Tôrobé, who were all Muslims. The Dénianké, although they then converted to Islam, lost all influence in Fouta Toro and partially emigrated. Even today, a distinction is made between the Peuls and the Toucouleurs in Fouta Djallon by giving the former—who are very few in number—the name *Poulli* and the latter—who are heavily mixed with Mandé—the name *Foula*.

### 6. Conclusions.

Let us summarize in a few lines the conclusions to be drawn from all the preceding information regarding the origins and formation of the Peul people.

In a very ancient era, we find a Semitic population of Judeo-Syrian origin, speaking an Egypto-Aramaic or perhaps Berber language, practicing a pre-Mosaic or Mosaic religion <note>Referring to religious practices predating or following the laws of Moses, suggesting an ancient Middle Eastern influence.</note>. Having come from Cyrenaica <note>The eastern coastal region of modern-day Libya.</note> by way of Aïr and Touat <note>Oasis regions in the Saharan desert (modern Niger and Algeria).</note>, they established themselves west of Timbuktu, then emigrated in large part to the Senegalese Fouta. There, they encountered a Black population speaking a language that we call Peul today; without mixing intimately with this Black population, they nonetheless fell under its influence, adopted the language following long contact, and became the "primitive" Peul people.

Due to various circumstances, the majority of this people left the Fouta to head East, with the intention—so says the legend—of returning to Asia, their country of origin. However, for multiple reasons, they did not go that far and were content to push as far as Darfur. This led Arabic authors to give the name <term>Tekrour</term> <note>Originally the name of a small kingdom on the Senegal River, it became a generic term used by Arab geographers to describe the Islamic lands of West Africa.</note>—through a process of geographic extension that is easy to understand—to this entire vast region where they had introduced the Tekrurian language. All along this immense itinerary, groups of Peuls established themselves as shepherds among the Black populations; some completely lost their original physical type to become Black themselves, while others, having settled in sparsely populated areas, preserved their original Semitic type more purely while continuing to speak the language they took from the <term>Toucouleurs</term> <note>The Tukulor people, closely related to the Peuls but generally sedentary and early converts to Islam.</note>.

Sometimes dominant and powerful, they most often accept the laws of the countries willing to welcome them and live in a state of semi-vassalage, and occasionally as pariahs, among the Black populations. It appears that their conversion to Islam is quite recent and, for most of them, does not date back much further than the Toucouleur conquests of the 18th and 19th centuries; many, moreover, especially among those who have most purely preserved the characteristics of the race—

<summary>This page concludes that the Peul are a people of Semitic origin who adopted a local African language in the Senegal region before migrating back across the continent toward Sudan. It frames their history as a tension between preserving their original ethnic identity and assimilating into the cultures they encountered during their nomadic travels.</summary>

<keywords>Peul origins, Semitic hypothesis, Tekrour, Toucouleur, migration, Islamization, Darfur, West African ethnography</keywords>

white, still practice to this day a religion that does not seem to differ greatly from what must have been the religion of their primitive ancestors, and they piously preserve traditions that have a striking analogy with the oldest Jewish traditions.

### V. The Toucouleurs.

The extensive detail I felt necessary to give regarding the question of the origin of the Peuls will allow me to be brief concerning that of the Toucouleurs, since I have already explained that the latter, though speaking the same language as the Peuls, cannot in any way be linked to them by ancestry.

If the Peuls undeniably descend from a population of the white race, the Toucouleurs just as undeniably belong to the Black race. In my view, they are indigenous to the region they still inhabit today—the Senegalese Fouta <note>A highland region in northern Senegal, historically the heart of the Toucouleur and Peul kingdoms.</note>—but their primitive country, when it still bore the name of <term>Tekrour</term> (1), must have spanned both banks of the Senegal River (2) and contained not only the ancestors of the Tou—

---

(1) This name, which could well be of Berber origin, was given both to the empire of the Toucouleurs and to its capital, which, as I suggested above, must have roughly corresponded to the current location of Podor. Ibn-Saïd (13th century) places the city of Tekrour on the Senegal (Nile) <note>Medieval Arab geographers often referred to the Senegal River as the "Nile of the Blacks," believing it was connected to the Egyptian Nile.</note> at 5° planimetric longitude west of Aoudaghost, which corresponds very exactly to the position of Podor. For Mohammed Bello <note>A 19th-century Sultan of the Sokoto Caliphate and a prolific scholar.</note>, Tekrour designates the whole of the Muslim Sudan and more particularly the countries subject to kings of the *Tekrourïa* language (that is, the Peul-Toucouleur language); he includes Darfur, Wadai, Baguirmi, Hausaland, etc. This meaning of the word Tekrour is frequent among Arabs who did not specifically deal with West Africa. Lieutenant Desplagnes believed he could identify Tekrour with an island in the backwater of Dia (Massina) which he calls Tekrour-Rundee, but which maps generally designate under the name of Togoro-Koumbé: his hypothesis is supported only by a vague phonetic resemblance.

(2) Aboulfeda (died 1331) <note>A Syrian geographer and historian.</note> tells us that the greater part of Tekrour is found north of the Senegal (Nile), the part south of the river being much less extensive (translation by Reinaud and de Slane, volume II, page 220). The same author had perfectly grasped the difference between the Toucouleurs and the Peuls, since he divides the peoples of Tekrour into two fractions: one sedentary and the other nomadic (*Ibid.*, p. 208) <note>original: "l'une sédentaire et l'autre nomade." This distinguishes the settled Toucouleur farmers from the migratory Peul herders.</note>.

The pressure from the Berbers towards the South must have forced the Serer, from the 11th to the 14th centuries, to retreat into the lands of the Wolof first and then into the Sine <note>A pre-colonial kingdom located in what is now west-central Senegal.</note>, to the south of the latter; but the language they still speak is living proof of their very ancient and very intimate contact with the Toucouleurs.

The arrival of the Berbers on the right bank of the Senegal River also forced the Toucouleurs to settle on the left bank; the conquests of the Wolof to the West and those of the Soninke to the East further restricted the ancient territory of **Tekrour**. But it seems that, although their domain decreased little by little from approximately the 11th century until the 16th, they only began to move out and spread abroad starting in the 18th century, during which conquest carried them to Fouta Djallon and Bundu. At the beginning of the 19th century, they powerfully supported the revolt of the Peuls <note>Also known as the Fula or Fulani people.</note> of Gober against the Hausa and provided, it seems, a very significant contingent to the conqueror **Usman dan Fodio**, founder of the Sokoto Empire. Finally, in the second half of the same century, under the leadership of **El Hadj Umar** <note>El Hadj Umar Tall (c. 1797–1864), a West African political leader and Islamic scholar who founded the Toucouleur Empire.</note>, they spread—always through armed conquest—into several regions of Upper Senegal-Niger where they are found today.

But, while they have always constituted a strong and powerful nation, and while they became remarkable conquerors in recent times, they have never been a migratory people and they have not had a significant influence on the formation of the ethnic groupings of West Africa.

Let us not forget, on the other hand, that their linguistic and religious influence was the most considerable that we are permitted to record in the history of the **French Sudan** <note>A former territory in French West Africa, roughly corresponding to modern-day Mali.</note>, since, on one hand, they succeeded in having their language adopted by a people—the Peul people—who then spread it from the Atlantic to beyond Lake Chad and, on the other hand, having been converted to Islam as early as the 11th century, before other Black peoples, before a large portion of the Berbers, and long before the Peuls, they contributed more than any other African nation to the Islamization of the Wolof, certain Mandinka groups, and the Susu,

### DISPARATE ORIGINS OF THE MODERN TOUCOULEURS ###

While the Toucouleurs are not Peul, it is nevertheless highly probable that after the departure of the latter from the **Senegalese Fouta** <note>A highland region in the Senegal River valley, often called Futa Toro.</note>, relations continued between the two groups. When, much later, the Toucouleurs began their conquests, it is remarkable that they always moved toward regions where they knew they would find Peul populations. No doubt they expected to find natural allies in those who spoke their language and shared their ancestral lands; however, reality did not always justify their hopes—notably in **Massina** <note>A 19th-century Peul empire located in the Inner Niger Delta, in modern-day Mali.</note>, where the Toucouleurs encountered no enemies more fierce than the Peul.

The original physical type of the Toucouleurs was certainly greatly altered by successive mixing—first and foremost with the Judeo-Syrians or "Proto-Peul" <note>The author refers here to a historical theory, popular in the colonial era, suggesting the Peul had Middle Eastern origins.</note> during their settlement in **Tekrour** <note>An ancient state in the Senegal River valley that flourished from the 9th to the 13th century.</note>, and later with the Peul proper who arrived in the 16th century under the leadership of **Koli** <note>Koli Tenguella, a 16th-century warrior-king who founded the Denianke Dynasty.</note>. However, the results of this mixing were likely more noticeable among the Peul than among the Toucouleurs.

Another element of alteration, perhaps more significant, was introduced by the Soninke Sossé and by the Wolof. Not only did the latter conquer and rule Tekrour for a considerable period, but they also left behind a large number of families whose descendants still carry Wolof clan names today (**Ndiaye**, among others). On the eastern side, there were significant Soninke infiltrations among the Toucouleurs; contact with the Berbers and Arabs from the right bank of the river also exerted a serious influence. Finally, the foreigners who came to be educated by the <term>marabouts</term> <note>Muslim religious teachers and leaders in West Africa.</note> of the Fouta—who were numerous at all times—became naturalized <term>Tòrobé</term> <note>The Tòrobé (or Torodbe) are the scholarly and clerical social class among the Toucouleur and Peul people.</note> by virtue of their stay and the religious instruction they received there. Consequently, this clan contains a large number of families whose ties to the Toucouleurs are entirely artificial.

# THE PEOPLES

### VI. — **Songhai.**

Until about the end of the last century, the Songhai <note>A major ethnic group in the eastern Sahel, known for the Songhai Empire (c. 1464–1591).</note> had always been considered authentic Negroes. However, a work that had a certain impact (1), as much due to the timing of its publication as to the literary value of its author and the charm of his style, came to modify the ideas of several well-meaning ethnologists. One began to look to Egypt, or at the very least to Nubia <note>A region along the Nile river, encompassing northern Sudan and southern Egypt.</note>, for the cradle of the Songhai; much was said regarding the Songhai empire, the Songhai era, the Songhai civilization, etc. It was, I believe, doing a bit too much honor to this population of peasants and fishermen to seek for them such a distant and glorious past: the unfortunate Songhai certainly provided more slaves than princes, their influence on the development of the Sudan <note>In this historical context, "Sudan" refers to the *Bilad al-Sudan* or "Land of the Blacks," the broad geographical belt of the Sahel, rather than the modern nation-state.</note> has always been secondary, and their civilization only reached a relative brilliance through what was brought to it from the outside—by the Berbers first, the Mandé <note>Ethnic groups from the upper Niger and Senegal rivers, including the Bambara and Malinke.</note> next, and the Moroccans last. As for the contribution of Egypt, it appears to have been nearly nil, at least as a direct contribution.

On what basis has the attribution of an Egyptian origin to the Songhai been made? On their refined physical type, their degree of culture, and the architectural style of their buildings. Yet—a thing which is at the very least singular—none of these characteristics are found among the Songhai, except among those of the upper class, and this class is precisely only half Songhai. Furthermore, none of these characteristics can be attributed to an Egyptian origin or influence, but rather to a Maghrebi <note>North African.</note> and especially Moroccan influence, as history and an impartial examination of the facts abundantly demonstrate to us.

Where, then, does the error committed come from? Simply from the fact that Mr. Félix Dubois, on one hand, gratuitously attributed to Egypt influences that originated elsewhere and, on the other hand, he took the city of Djenné <note>An ancient trading city in present-day Mali, famous for its mud-brick architecture.</note> as his field of observation, which precisely does not contain Songhai people, or contains so few that it is in any case just as inaccurate to consider it...

(1) *Timbuctoo the Mysterious*, by Félix Dubois, Paris, 1897.

# ORIGIN OF THE SONGHAI

...as a product of Songhai civilization, just as it would be inaccurate to take the Peul <note>Also known as the Fula or Fulani, a traditionally pastoralist ethnic group spread across West Africa.</note> colony of Liptako as a type for Toucouleur civilization. Mr. Ch. Monteil (1) has perfectly demonstrated that in Djenné, at the time he resided there—that is to say, about eight years ago—there were only three families who had, among their ancestors, a few individuals of Songhai origin. The language of Djenné is the Songhai language, it is true, just as the language of Liptako is the Toucouleur language, and the language of the Marka or Soninke of Banamba is Bambara <note>original: "bamnana"</note>: but this is a phenomenon due to political and economic reasons, and has nothing to do with the ethnic origin of the people of Djenné.

The Songhai population, as a whole, is clearly of the Black African race <note>original: "race nègre"</note>, to which Berber elements first, then Arab, Jewish, and Peul elements, and finally and especially Moroccan elements were added, modifying the physical type of a certain number of families quite profoundly; these families, moreover—though their political and social influence was and still is considerable—constitute only a tiny fraction of the population from a numerical standpoint; the people, as a whole, have remained frankly Black African.

Everything leads me to believe that the primitive Songhai were indigenous to the lower Niger valley. I would willingly place the cradle of their people on the left bank of the lower Niger, in the regions generally designated by the names Kebbi, Maouri, and Zaberma <note>The Zarma or Zerma people, a group closely related to the Songhai today living primarily in Niger.</note>, between the Goulbi-n-Kebbi or Goulbi-n-Sokoto to the south and the Dallol Bosso to the north, with the Dallol Maouri and the Franco-British border forming roughly the center of this domain.

The advance of the Hausa from Katsina into Kebbi (2) must have, from a remote period, prompted a portion of the Songhai to cross the Niger and settle in Dendi, on the current border of the colony of Dahomey <note>Present-day Benin.</note> and the district of Say, while others moved toward the north and occupied the area east of Niamey

# THE PEOPLES

...and of Tillabéry, the region known by the name of Djerma-ganda (the country of the Djerma or Songhai).

It is probable that, before the 7th century of our era, the Songhai did not extend North beyond the approximate latitude of Tillabéry and had not yet penetrated the right bank of the Niger, except however in Dendi <note>A historical region located in the borderlands of modern-day Niger, Benin, and Nigeria</note>. Along the river itself, they must have moved a bit further upstream, likely as far as Bentia. A portion of the population devoted itself almost exclusively to fishing and occupied the banks of the river and especially the islands: these were the Sorko or Kourteï, currently called Kourtibé by the Peul <note>The Peul are also known as the Fulani or Fula, a large ethnic group spread across West Africa</note>. Thanks to the ease of communication provided by their pirogues <note>A type of traditional dugout canoe</note>, they had acquired a kind of political dominance which they used to the detriment of the Songhai farmers, known today as the Gabibi. Not cultivating the land themselves, the Sorko would wait until after the harvest to surprise the villages near the Niger, pillaging the granaries and carrying the stolen grain back to their island strongholds, thus supplying themselves at little cost. The peaceful farmers hated and feared them but could do nothing against them.

When the Lemta <note>A Berber tribal group from the Sahara</note> arriving from Tripolitania <note>A historical region in what is now western Libya</note> made their first appearance near Gounguia or Koukia—which must have been located, as I stated above, on the island of Bentia (1)—the Songhai farmers welcomed them with joy. Attributing to them a quasi-divine origin, which the newcomers did everything to encourage, they believed they had found allies who would protect them against the plunder of the Sorko.

The leader of the Lemta immigration, known by the name *Dia Aliamen* <note>Often interpreted as "He came from Yemen," a name reflecting the prestigious Eastern origins claimed by the dynasty</note>, indeed fought a battle against the Sorko of the island of Gounguia, drove them from the region, and settled in their place at Gounguia.

Naturally, I leave the responsibility for this legend to him; the fact that it was in circulation in Timbuktu in the 17th century proves, at the very least, that Gounguia had existed for a very long time by then.

### EXODUS OF THE SORKO TOWARDS THE NORTH
16

...with his companions (around the end of the 7th century). The Songhai farmers along the banks of the Niger, in gratitude, made Dia Aliamen <note>Also known as Za Alayaman, the legendary founder of the Dia or Za dynasty of the Songhai Empire</note> their king and swore an oath of obedience to him; soon his authority extended over all the Songhai living from Bentia to Kebbi.

A legend reported by Sa'di <note>Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di (1594–1656), a scholar from Timbuktu and author of the *Tarikh es-Sudan*, one of the most important historical chronicles of West Africa</note> tells that, upon Dia Aliamen’s arrival at Koukia, the natives were suffering under the yoke of a fish which, with a ring through its nostrils, would appear above the river waters at certain times of the year and dictate orders and prohibitions to the people; Dia Aliamen reportedly killed this fish with a harpoon strike and thus delivered the inhabitants from this bizarre tyranny. The author of the *Tarikh* <term>Tarikh: An Arabic word meaning "history" or "chronicle"</term> tries to explain this legend by saying that Dia Aliamen was undoubtedly Muslim and that his religious faith led him to destroy the idol personified in this strange fish; however, he felt the weakness of his explanation and had to offer the conjecture that Dia Aliamen’s successors later renounced Islam. In reality, Dia Aliamen and his companions must have been not Muslims, but Christians, and one might suppose that a religious motive did indeed lead them to destroy the idol of the natives. But it seems more rational to me to think that the legend simply symbolized, in the form of a tyrant fish, the predatory caste of Sorko fishermen, who might well have worn a ring in the nose—a frequent custom among the peoples of the Niger valley—and who indeed appeared as masters at harvest time, as I mentioned above.

In any case, a significant portion of the Sorko traveled up the Niger around this time and went to found Gao, where a fisherman named Faram-Ber (Faram the Great) created a sort of independent kingdom. This group of Sorko included two main clans: the *Faran*, who held preeminence and settled in Gao, and the *Fono*, who went to settle near Bamba, thus pushing the Songhai people upstream from the bend at Bourem.

The successors of Faram-Ber were almost constantly at war with the *Lemta* <note>The Berber tribal group from which the Dia dynasty originated</note> of Gounguia; one of them, Kobé-Taka,

Faran-Nabo or Nabonké, his son and successor, sought to avenge his father's death; however, after several successful victories over the Lemta <note>A Berber group, likely related to the Tuareg, who exerted significant influence in the Sahara and Sahel during this period</note>—*victories* that momentarily extended his authority south of Gao—he was pushed back and defeated. He was forced to leave Gao, yielding the territory to the successors of Dia Aliamen <note>The legendary founder of the Dia (or Za) dynasty mentioned on the previous page</note> (likely during the 9th or 10th century). It was at this time that the Songhai farmers, loyal subjects of the Lemta, advanced as far as Gao. A little later, probably at the beginning of the 11th century, during the reign of Dia Kossoi <note>Traditionally recorded as the first Songhai king to convert to Islam, around 1010 AD</note>, the capital of the Lemta-Songhai Empire was transferred from Gounguia to Gao (1).

Meanwhile, the Sorko <note>A specialized caste of fishermen and masters of the river</note>, continuing to act as scouts for the advancing Songhai movement along the Niger, soon reached Lake Débo.

The Faran, having been driven out of Gao, arrived at Bamba. In their capacity as a royal clan, they claimed the best fishing spots for themselves, to the detriment of the Fono. The Fono refused to be dispossessed in this manner and gave battle to the Faran; defeated, they moved back up the river and reached the lake region, where the Soninke and the Bozo then formed the bulk of the population. The Fono were authorized by the local chiefs to settle on the island of Koura, slightly upstream from Timbuktu, as well as at Gourao, on the northern shore of Lake Débo.

They were joined in this region by another Songhai clan, the Goou or Gow, composed mainly of hunters, who had been forced to emigrate from Djerma-ganda <note>The "land of the Djerma," located in present-day southwestern Niger</note> following conflicts with the Lemta. These Goou settled in Bara, on the right bank of the Bara-Issa <note>A branch of the Niger River in the Inland Delta region</note>, roughly halfway between Lake Débo and Niafounké.

However, the Bozo, who until then had been the masters of navigation on Lake Débo and the channels of the Niger, did not look favorably upon the competition that the Sorko were beginning to present...

### ESTABLISHMENT OF THE SORKO IN THE LAKE REGION

The Fono, having established a transport service between Mopti and Koura by way of Gourao, faced sabotage from the Bozo, who sought to ruin the enterprise. Near Kouna, between Mopti and Lake Débo, the Bozo constructed barriers using aquatic grasses known as *borgou* <note>A floating grass, *Echinochloa stagnina*, highly valued as fodder for livestock in the Niger delta</note>, creating a type of dam that halted the Fono’s vessels (1). The Fono, allied with Soninke merchants from Mopti, organized an expedition against the Bozo, but it proved fruitless. They then decided to call upon their cousins, the Faran, who had remained at Bamba, and sent messengers by water to request their assistance.

At this time (the end of the 12th century or the beginning of the 13th (1)), the authority of the Emperors of Gao had grown significantly. Their territory, expanding northward, had reached Bamba. The Sorko Faran, irreconcilable enemies of the Lemta <note>A Berber group whose influence the Faran sought to escape</note>, found the proximity of the latter difficult to endure and eagerly seized the opportunity to emigrate to new lands. They responded to the Fono's appeal and departed for the lake region, forming a veritable flotilla of canoes. When they arrived near the confluence of the Issa-Ber and the Bara-Issa, upstream from Koura, they encountered an armed force composed mainly of Soninke (2), who attempted to block their passage. The Faran easily overcame this obstacle and soon became the masters of the river. They established their primary settlement near the territory of the Goou, at the confluence of the Bara-Issa and the Koli, and built a village there which they called *Faran-Koïra* (meaning "Village of the Faran") in the Songhai language. The Peul <note>Also known as the Fulani or Fula people</note> translated this expression as *Saré-Faran*, which has the same meaning in their language, and from which we, in turn, derived the name *Sara-féré* (3).

# THE PEOPLES

Once firmly established at Saraféré, the leader of the Faran united under his authority all the Songhai of the lake region—namely the Fono of Koura and Gourao and the Goou of Bara—and organized an expedition with them against the Bozo of Lake Débo. He initially achieved only a questionable success, but during a second expedition, he completely defeated the Bozo, whom he forced to withdraw south of Lake Débo and to respect the freedom of navigation on the Bani River <note>The Bani is the principal tributary of the Niger River</note>.

Thus, towards the end of the 13th century—at the moment when the peak of the Mandinka Empire of Mali had begun at the expense of first the Soninke Empire of the Sosso, and then the Lemta-Songhai Empire of Gao—the situation of the Songhai was as follows: in the east, under the domination of the Lemta Berbers, they were spread all along the Niger from approximately the Dallol Maouri <note>A fossil river valley in modern-day Niger</note> to Bamba and occupied, on the left bank of the river, Zaberma and Djerma-ganda, and on the right bank, Dendi; in the west, roughly independent but placed under the at least nominal suzerainty <term>suzerainty: a condition where a region has internal autonomy but owes allegiance and tribute to a more powerful state</term> of the Emperor of Mali, they were spread out along the Niger and its main branches from Timbuktu to Lake Débo. The first group included farmers and fishermen (Gabibi and Kourtei); the second consisted almost exclusively of fishermen (Sorko), with a small group of hunters (Goou).

Around 1325, Kankan-Musa <note>Also known as Mansa Musa, famous for his pilgrimage to Mecca and his immense wealth</note>, Emperor of Mali, established his suzerainty over Gao, Timbuktu, and Massina, and consequently brought all the Songhai under his authority. Nearly a century and a half later, Sunni Ali Ber (Ali the Great), the penultimate Lemta prince of Gao, freed himself from Mandinka oversight and, pushing the boundaries of his empire far beyond Bamba, seized Timbuktu, Bara, and Djenné (1465 to 1492). One year after his death, a Soninke from the Silla clan-tribe, named Mohammed, son of Aboubakari Touré, arri- <note>The text likely intended to say "arrived at power," referring to the rise of Askia Mohammed</note>

# EXPANSION OF THE SONGHAI DOMAIN

managed to have himself proclaimed Emperor of Gao, replaced a Berber dynasty of the Lemta—the *sonni* <note>The Sonni or Si dynasty ruled the Songhai Empire before the Askia dynasty; they were of Lemta Berber origin</note>—with a Black dynasty—the *askia*—which had succeeded the *dia* <note>The Dia or Za dynasty was the first legendary dynasty of Gao</note> around 1335—and gave the Empire of Gao an even more significant expansion.

It was certainly from the time of Sonni Ali the Great and Askia Mohammed I—that is to say, from the final years of the 15th century—that the Songhai began to spread in greater numbers into the region of Timbuktu and the lakes. Although forming only a minority among the total population of peoples subject to the Emperor of Gao, and though the Emperor himself and his principal ministers and officers were generally not Songhai, the latter must have provided a notable contingent to the armies of Sonni Ali the Great and the Askias. As-Sa'di <note>Abd al-Sadi (1594–1656) was a Timbuktu scholar and author of the *Tarikh al-Sudan*, a primary historical source for this region</note> informs us that, during an expedition led by Mohammed I against the Bariba <note>An ethnic group located in what is now northern Benin and Nigeria</note>, a large number of Songhai from Zaberbanda (1) lost their lives, and among them were the best soldiers of the imperial army. We also know, thanks to the same author, that one of the main elements of the Askias' power was their fleet, whose crews were certainly composed mostly of Sorko <note>The Sorko are a specialized group of Songhai fishermen and masters of the river</note>.

However, while the political influence of the Empire of Gao was significant and if, thanks to its power and expansion, the Songhai language—which was, so to speak, the official language of the empire, even during the time of the Lemta—managed to spread as far as Djenné and to dethrone indigenous languages in many places, the Songhai people themselves likely did not establish numerically large colonies outside the banks of the Niger itself. In any case, these colonies did not extend past Lake Débo when traveling upstream. ### THE PEOPLES

Almost exactly a century after the accession of the first Askia, on **March 30, 1591**, the Moroccan army of Pasha Djouder—sent by the Saadian Sultan Moulay Ahmed-ed-Dehebi <note>Ahmed al-Mansur, known as "the Golden One" (ed-Dehebi) due to the wealth acquired from this conquest</note> and comprising three thousand warriors—reached the Niger at Karabara, a little to the west of Bamba. On the following April 12, the army of Askia Ishak II, 12,500 men strong, was routed in the blink of an eye near Tondibi (the black stone), 50 kilometers upstream from Gao on the left bank of the river, thanks to the Moroccans' muskets <note>Firearms were a technological novelty in the region at the time, giving the smaller Moroccan force a decisive advantage over the larger Songhai army</note>. Moroccan rule over the former Empire of Gao—with the exception of Dendi, which remained independent—was to last until toward the end of the 17th century. At that time, the last Pashas of Timbuktu saw what little authority they had left pass into the hands of the Tuareg in the East and North, and into the hands of the Fulani <note>Original: *Peuls*</note> and the Bambara <note>Original: *Banmana*</note> in the West (2). However, as early as 1612—that is to say, about twenty years after Djouder's victory over Ishak II—the Moroccan government had ceased appointing the Pashas and no longer exerted any direct influence over the Sudanese <note>Referring to the "Bilad al-Sudan" or the Sahel region, not the modern nation of Sudan</note> lands (3). From that date onward, the Pashas of Timbuktu and their local governors <note>Original: *caïds*</note> were recruited locally from among the officers who had come from Morocco with Djouder and his first successors, for as long as any remained, and then from among the descendants of these officers. These descendants were no longer Moroccans, strictly speaking: the governors and soldiers from Fez and Marrakesh had taken wives on the banks of the Niger, some among the Moors, others among the Tuareg...

(2) In reality, Timbuktu continued to have so-called Moroccan Pashas until the second half of the 18th century, but their purely nominal and fleeting authority hardly reached beyond the immediate surroundings of the city.

(3) Pasha Ammar was indeed sent from Marrakesh to Timbuktu—for the second time—in 1618, but without troops; he returned to Morocco less than three months after his arrival in the Sudan.

### MOROCCAN INFILTRATIONS AMONG THE SONGHAI

...or the Fulani <note>Original: *Peuls*</note>, the others among the Songhai, the Soninke, and other Black populations. As the years passed following the arrival of the first Moroccans, African ancestry became predominant among these people of mixed heritage, who had, moreover, adopted the Songhai language. These descendants gradually formed the noble and ruling class of the Songhai people, known as the *Arma* <note>Derived from the Arabic word *ar-rumat*, meaning "musketeers" or "shooters," referring to their ancestor's firearms</note>. Thus, this class was superimposed upon the original, purely African foundation, which was composed of the Gabibi <note>The commoner class, primarily farmers</note>, the Sorko <note>Masters of the river, primarily fishermen and boatmen</note>, and the Gow <note>Original: *Goou*; traditional hunters</note>.

According to the scholar Ahmed Baba, who received the information from Moulay Zidan—son of Sultan Ahmed al-Mansur <note>Original: *Ahmed-ed-Dehebi*, "the Golden One"</note>—twenty-three thousand soldiers were dispatched from Morocco to the Sudan <note>Referring to the "Bilad al-Sudan" or the Sahel region, not the modern nation of Sudan</note> between the times of Pasha Djouder and Pasha Sulayman <note>Original: *Slimân*</note>, specifically from 1590 to 1600. Most of these men died from battle wounds or, more frequently, from disease. Among the survivors, 500 returned to Marrakesh, while the rest settled in the Sudan. Mahmoud Lonko, who succeeded Sulayman and was the final Pasha sent directly from Morocco to Timbuktu, brought 300 soldiers with him; these were the last reinforcements ever sent from Morocco.

Nevertheless, a new group of Moroccan immigrants reportedly arrived in Timbuktu toward the end of the 17th century. Around 1670, Moulay al-Rashid <note>Original: *Er-Rachid*</note>, the first Alaouite <note>Original: *filalien ou hassanide*; the dynasty that still rules Morocco today</note> Sultan of Fez, conducted an expedition into the Sous region and besieged the *zaouïa* <note>A religious sanctuary or school</note> of a Muslim cleric named Ali-ben-Haidar. This man fled to the Sudan and sought protection from the Bambara <note>Original: *banmana*</note> Emperor of Segou, Biton Coulibaly <note>Original: *Biton Kouloubali*</note>, whose power was beginning to reach as far as Timbuktu. Ali presented Biton with two beautiful female captives of Spanish or Portuguese origin whom he had brought with him. Swayed by this gift, the Bambara prince authorized Ali to settle in Timbuktu with his family and disciples and promised him protection. Indeed, when Sultan al-Rashid pursued Ali, his forces clashed with the army of Segou between Timbuktu and Jenne <note>Original: *Dienné*</note>, in northern Massina. Facing Biton’s firm refusal to hand over the fugitive, the Sultan returned to Morocco.

Ali-ben-Haidar lived in Timbuktu for several months; he is said to have left descendants there, who became the ancestors of the *Haidara* clan of the Arma. Tradition relates that he left Timbuktu...

After staying in Timbuktu for several years, Ahmed returned to Morocco. As soon as he departed, Timbuktu ceased to recognize the—rather fleeting—suzerainty of the Sultan of Fez, and the garrison left behind by Ahmed dispersed among the locals and merged with them (2).

### THE ARMA

Since, on the other hand, the Songhai people themselves were not very numerous in this region, it is certain that their original physical type must have been quite profoundly modified by their mixing with the Moroccans. However, this modification hardly reached beyond the noble families and was limited to the cities: in Gao, Bamba, Koura, Tendirma, Kouna, and especially in Timbuktu. The Soninke families of Djenné also underwent identical modifications through a similar process of mixing. It is the results of this infusion of white ancestry <note>Referring here to North African and European genetic heritage</note>, which are still very visible today, that may have given some travelers the idea of attributing an Egyptian origin to the *Arma* <term>Arma</term> <note>An ethnic group of the Niger River valley descended from the 16th-century Moroccan invaders</note>.

But first, many of these people of mixed White and Black descent cannot be linked to the Songhai, and this is particularly the case for those in Djenné. Furthermore, one must not forget that, among the Songhai, the *Arma* form only a tiny part of the population, regardless of the political and social importance they may hold in the cities where they are found: the mass of the people, composed of the <term>Gabibi</term> <note>The commoner class of Songhai society, traditionally farmers</note> and the <term>Sorko</term> <note>A Songhai subgroup traditionally known as masters of the river, acting as fishermen and boatmen</note> of the lake region—and especially the entirety of the inhabitants of Djerma, Zaberma, and Dendi—has remained Black, setting aside Berber and Fulani influences. Finally, as we have seen, the white element that affected some Songhai families and produced the Arma came not from Egypt, but from the <term>Maghreb</term> <note>The region of Northwest Africa, including modern-day Morocco</note>; it is of recent importation and occurred after the period during which the so-called Songhai civilization reached its peak (1).
