# THE PEOPLES

It is the same with architecture as it is with racial mixing: the style known as "Djenné style" is in no way unique to the Songhai; it is a Maghrebian <note>From the Maghreb, the region of Northwest Africa including Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia</note> importation and is relatively recent. We know from the writings of Ibn Khaldun <note>A famous 14th-century Arab sociologist and historian</note> and from the *Tarikh al-Sudan* <note>original: "Tarikh-es-Soudan"; a 17th-century chronicle of West African history</note> that the first constructions of this type were built in Gao (a mosque) and in Timbuktu (a palace and a mosque) around 1325. These were built during the reign and by the order of the Mandinka emperor Kankan-Moussa <note>Commonly known today as Mansa Musa</note>, by a poet from Granada <note>Spain</note> who became an impromptu architect, Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, who died in Timbuktu and was buried there. Before this era, there were only cylindrical huts covered in straw in the Sudan <note>Referring here to the historical "Bilad al-Sudan" or "Land of the Blacks," the Sahelian region of West Africa, not the modern country of Sudan</note>, or shelters reminiscent of the *gourbis* <term>gourbis</term> <note>modest dwellings or huts found in North Africa</note> of the Bedouins or those of the Tuareg. Even the "palaces" of the emperors were no more comfortable or remarkable than the "huts" of their subjects; perhaps even flat-roofed houses of the most primitive type were unknown, for Arabic authors prior to the 14th century (Ibn Hawqal—who had traveled to the Sudan—al-Bakri, al-Idrisi, and Yaqut) mention no other dwellings than the conical-roofed huts of the Malinké and Mossi people seen today.

It was likely the Spaniard Abu Ishaq who was the first to inspire, in the western Sudan, these houses with trapezoidal porticos and these mosques topped with pyramids. Their appearance does indeed call to mind—though quite distantly—the monuments of ancient Egypt, but they are found everywhere from Algeria and Morocco across the entire Sahara to the edge of the tropical forest. This architecture, motivated by the necessities of the climate and the rarity of certain materials or the ignorance of certain techniques, is essentially Maghrebian and not Egyptian (1). It was spread throughout the Sudan, not—

---

—Islamized by their Moroccan masters and then entered the service of the Sultan of Marrakesh. Pasha Djouder himself, the conqueror of Gao and Timbuktu, a "small man with blue eyes," was a converted Christian <note>Judar Pasha was a Spaniard from Almería, captured as a child and raised in the Moroccan court</note>.

(1) It is possible, moreover, that Egyptian art was not without influence on Maghrebian art and that Abu Ishaq himself may have drawn some inspiration from Egypt when he passed through it returning from Mecca with Kankan-Moussa. ### FORMATION OF THE MODERN SONGHAI

...not by the Songhai—who are far from having all adopted it and who often live in hemispherical mat shelters copied from those of the Tuareg—but rather by the Moroccans of Timbuktu on one hand, and on the other, by the Soninke of Djenné and their close cousins, the Dioula. The people of Djenné have become masters of the art of Sudanese architecture; this is undeniable. However, they were initiated into this art by Moroccans and not by the Songhai, and they did not seek their models in Egypt.

The conclusion of the preceding points can be summarized as follows: the modern Songhai—especially those of the civil territories of *Upper Senegal and Niger* <note>A French colonial administrative territory in West Africa existing between 1904 and 1921</note>—form a very mixed people. Their primitive foundation and principal element consist of a Black population likely originating from the Tillabéry-Niamey-Dosso region on the left bank of the lower Niger; they include a caste of fishermen—the *Sorko*—, a caste of hunters—the *Goou*—, and a working and peasant class—the *Gabibi*. All three of these have remained almost entirely free of any white racial elements <note>original: "race blanche"; referring to Mediterranean or European ancestry</note>, though the primitive type has been more or less modified: among the *Sorko* by mixing with the *Bozo*; among the *Goou* by mixing with the *Bambara* <note>original: "Bambana"</note>; and among the *Gabibi* by mixing with the *Hausa*, *Gurmantché*, *Mossi*, *Tombo* <note>A name historically used by colonial authors to refer to the Dogon people</note>, *Soninke*, and *Bambara*, depending on the region. In the case of the *Gabibi*, it is also necessary to account for mixing with the Tuareg and the Fulani <note>original: "Peuls"</note> who have sometimes altered the primitive Black type. Finally, they include a noble class—the *Arma*—in whose composition the white racial element plays a fairly considerable part: this element was primarily provided by Europeans from the Iberian Peninsula and Arab-Berbers from Morocco and, to a lesser extent, by the Tuareg, Moors, and Fulani. As for the class of Muslim scholars—the *Alfa*—it is recruited from among all the peoples of the Su- <note>Likely "Sudan," referring to the historical Bilad al-Sudan region</note>

---

...absolutely no importance. If an Egyptian influence exists, which is not proven, it is through Morocco or, more generally, through the Maghreb <note>Northwest Africa</note> that it reached the Niger.

# THE PEOPLES

In the preceding pages, I have spoken only of the great migration or conquest movements that carried the Songhai as far as Lake Débo. Furthermore, a certain number of secondary movements occurred in various directions due to different causes: for example, after the capture of Gao by the Oulmidden <note>A powerful Tuareg confederation</note> in 1770, a certain number of Songhai emigrated from the Gao region to Djerma-Ganda and toward Niamey (a tradition collected by Commander Gaden <note>Henri Gaden, a French colonial officer and renowned linguist of West African languages</note>); similarly, according to Barth <note>Heinrich Barth, a 19th-century German explorer who traveled extensively in West Africa</note>, many Songhai from Bourem migrated toward Goundam around 1843. On the other hand, the Songhai have at all times provided a very large contingent for the slave supply of the Sahara and the Maghreb: a good portion of the Bella <term>A social group within Tuareg society, historically consisting of enslaved people or their descendants</term> of the Tuareg and the *Harratin* <term>Social groups in the Sahara and Maghreb who were historically sedentary or formerly enslaved</term> of the Kounta and Berabich Moors are of Songhai origin; descendants of slaves of the same origin are found in many places in southern Algeria and southern Morocco. Lieutenant Cancel, having recently studied the language of the Balbali or inhabitants of Tebalbalet, discovered that this language is a dialect that is simultaneously Songhai, Arabic, and Berber, but with a marked predominance of Songhai words in the vocabulary and the introduction of the principal rules of Songhai syntax (*African Review*, 1908).

### VII. Northern Mandé.

It appears indeed that the Mandé family, as a whole, is indigenous to the Western Sudan. Its original domain must have extended along the Niger, and principally on the left bank, from approximately Lake Débo in the North to near the sources of the Tinkisso in the South. # ORIGIN OF THE BOZO

Sansanding <note>A town on the Niger River in modern-day Mali</note> was the cradle of the Northern Mandé; the *Mandé* or *Manding* or *Mali* (upper Niger at the level of Bamako and the upper Bakhoy) was that of the Central Mandé; and the *Diallon* or *Fouta-Diallon* (from the upper Tinkisso to the upper Falémé) was that of the Southern Mandé.

Well before the start of our era, the Mandé family must have been spread throughout all these regions and formed their almost exclusive population.

1° *Bozo*.

The Bozo must have, at the beginning, constituted a caste of fishermen and navigators among the Northern Mandé, absolutely analogous to that of the Sorko among the Songhai and to that of the Somono among the Central Mandé. They mainly inhabited Lake Débo and the branch of the Niger known by the name of the Dia or Diaka channel <term>Originally "marigot," referring to a side-channel or seasonal stream common in the Niger Delta</term>. At a given moment, they must have spread a bit further north and south and reached the Bani river toward the east, near Mopti and Djenné. But the push of the Sorko from the north in the 12th to 13th centuries and that of the Somono from the south around the same time brought about the concentration of the Bozo in the region of their primitive cradle, which they have never left since except in isolation, and where they are still considered today as the owners of the soil and the waters.

While they remained thus fixed in their homeland of origin, the agricultural populations of the same family that surrounded them dispersed, on the contrary, throughout the Sudan, under the

---

<column-break/>

[-birth/origin] in Dia or the Diaka channel. The pronunciations *Diarha, Diagha, Diaga, Diaka, Diakha, Dia* and *Niarha, Niagha, Niaga, Niaka, Niakha, Nia* represent only one and the same word, of which they are only dialectal variants; the most widespread pronunciation in the Sudan <note>Referring to the "Western Sudan," a historical geographical region south of the Sahara, not the modern country of Sudan</note> is *Diaga*, with a slightly guttural *g*; the Songhai often pronounce it *Zaga*, especially those of the Southeast, and it is this spelling that has been adopted by most Arabic writers. Many names of countries, villages, or clans derive from the name of this region, famous above all others in the Western Sudan: such are the names of *Kaniaga* (south of Bagana) and *Gadiaga* or *Galam* (between Bakel and Kayes)—names which supposedly come from the phrase "let us call it Diaga" <note>original: "an ka niaga fo" or "an ga diaga fo"</note>—from the village of *Diara* (near Nioro), and the clans *Diara, Diakaté* or *Niakaté, Diakité*, etc. (those of Dia or Diaga, originating from Diaga).

name of Soninké, and reached, as a result of this dispersion and their mixing with very diverse peoples, a state of differentiating themselves quite notably from their fisherman kinsmen whose trade had tied them to the riverbanks. It is thus that today, by physical type, customs, and language, the Soninké are distinguished from the Bozo, although otherwise the similarities between the two peoples are also considerable. But their common origin does not seem doubtful.

Let us add to this that unions have occurred for centuries between the primitive Bozo and families belonging to the fishing castes of other nationalities, such as the Songhai caste of the Sorko, the Bamana caste of the Somono, and the Fulani <note>original: "peule"</note> caste of the Soubalbé. These unions resulted in somewhat altering the initial physical type of the Bozo and considerably modifying, no doubt, their primitive speech.

The Bozo are currently all Muslim: they have probably been so since the 14th century, having had to convert at the same time as the people of Djenné <note>A major historic commercial and religious center in the Inland Niger Delta</note>.

### 2° Soninké.

As I have just said, the Soninké, like the Bozo, had the Diaga or Massina (1) as their primitive habitat and, like the Bozo as well, they originally formed an exclusively Black population, much closer to the Central Mandé than it is currently (2).

---

(1) The name *Massina* is often given to the region of Bandiagara, but this is by error, or rather this region is only the extreme eastern limit of Massina; originally this name applied only to the Diaga properly so called, that is to say, to the left bank of the Dia channel <term>Originally "marigot," referring to a side-channel or seasonal stream common in the Niger Delta</term> (Western or true Massina); later the name was also extended to the country comprised between the Dia channel on the one hand and Mopti and Djenné on the other (Central Massina); later still, the region situated between Mopti and Bandiagara (Eastern Massina) was included in Massina.

(2) In the manuscripts brought back from Sokoto by Clapperton <note>Hugh Clapperton (1788–1827), a Scottish explorer of West Central Africa</note>, the Soninké (called *Sarankoli* or *Sarakolé*) are described as ancient "Persians": no doubt we must understand by this that they formerly practiced a religion somewhat analogous to that of the ancient Persians or Magism; Arabic authors often refer to non-Muslim Black people as *madjous* <note>original: "madjous," derived from the Arabic term for "Magi" or Zoroastrians, used here to denote "pagans" or practitioners of traditional religions</note>.

# FIRST SONINKÉ MIGRATIONS

From a very ancient era, by 200 BC at the latest, Soninké groups departing from the Diaga <note>A historical region in the Inland Niger Delta of modern-day Mali</note> moved toward the Northwest and founded agricultural colonies in the regions where Bas-ikounou, Néma, and Oualata are situated today. Perhaps even the foundation of *Néma* dates back to this distant period, as well as that of *Ghana* <note>Referring to the ancient Ghana Empire, not the modern nation</note>, which must have been very close to Néma and the site where Birou or Oualata was later built (1).

When, at the beginning of the 2nd century AD, the Judeo-Syrians coming from Cyrenaica <note>Modern-day Libya</note> by way of the Aïr <note>A mountainous region in northern Niger</note> settled in the Diaga, the Soninké fell somewhat under their influence, and from that moment, elements of the white race began to be introduced among them. We have seen how, toward the middle of the same century, they forced the Judeo-Syrians to leave the Diaga and how the latter, following the same path the Soninké had traced long before, went to settle in the Aoukar, alongside the Soninké colonies of Néma and Ghana. Some fifty years later, the Judeo-Syrians of the Touat <note>An oasis region in the Algerian Sahara</note> came to join them there, and toward the end of the 3rd century, a fairly powerful state was formed at Ghana, whose masters were these Judeo-Syrians or Proto-Fulani <note>original: "Proto-Peuls"</note>.

At that time, a certain number of Soninké from the Aoukar, fleeing the yoke of these foreigners, continued their migration toward the Northwest and moved as far as the Tagant and the Mauritanian Adrar, which the Berbers did not yet fully occupy. The current *Azer* <note>A specialized group among the Soninké</note> of Oualata (2), Tichit, and Chinguetti (3), etc., are merely the descendants, without

However, the bulk of the Soninké population had remained in the Diaga <note>The historical heartland in the Inland Niger Delta</note>. Toward the end of the 7th century, for unknown reasons, a fairly large group left this country and attempted a first effort at colonization near Dienné (1), then, retracing their steps toward the West, moved through the Kaniaga as far as *Kingui* and *Diafounou*, likely leaving behind small colonial groups along their route. Around 750, the majority of the emigrants, leaving Kingui to return almost exactly the way they came, arrived at *Ouagadou*, where they founded—under the leadership of *Maghan-Diabé Sissé*—the first Soninké state about which oral traditions have provided us some information.

A legend, still very much alive among all the Soninké of the Sahel <note>The semi-arid transition zone south of the Sahara</note> and reported more than once already by Europeans (2), recounts the story of this migration from the Diaga to Ouagadou via *Kaniagu* and *Kingui*, embellishing it with details bordering on the marvelous. According to this legend, the leader of the migration was a man named *Digna* or *Dinga*, son of Kiridion-Tagumanké, son of Yougou-Doumbessé (who was descended from Job, son of Solomon, son of David! <note>Oral traditions often linked local dynasties to Islamic and Biblical prophets to establish prestige and legitimacy</note>); this Digna, ancestor of the *Sempré*, *Soumpara*, or *Simbara* royal Soninké clans, had

Digna first stopped in the region of Dienné <note>Modern-day Djenné in Mali, a historic center of trade and Islamic learning</note> and there married a woman named Satakoullé Dafé; having remained there for 17 years (1) without this woman giving him any offspring, he repudiated her, left the country of Dienné, and returned to the Diaga, where he married *Assakoullé Soudouré*. She gave birth to three twins <note>The text likely means three sons, possibly including a set of twins, or simply three children in succession</note>, one of whom died at birth; the second, *Dia-Founè*, ancestor of the Dikéné or Dyikéné clan, went to settle in the country that was named *Diafounou* after him and colonized it; the third, *Diagabà-Founè* (2), father of the Souaré clan, remained in the Diaga.

Having arrived there, he sent people to draw water; these people perceived a spirit <note>original: "génie"</note> sitting at the edge of the well and returned in great haste to warn Digna. The latter went to the well and, thanks to the spells at the disposal of his priests, rendered the spirit blind, deaf, and paralyzed—which did not, however, prevent the spirit from doing the same to Digna. Then Garabara, the chief of the sorcerers, intervened; his magical procedures restored Digna’s use of his senses, while the spirit remained deprived of sight, hearing, and movement. No doubt he had retained the ability to speak, for he offered Digna—if the latter would heal him—an alliance and the hand of his three daughters in marriage; Digna accepted and restored to the spirit the free use of his senses and movements. Afterward, he married the three daughters of the spirit.

# FOUNDATION OF WAGADOU

...that of Téré-Kiné. Besides, are you not all my children?" In the meantime, Téré-Kiné returned from hunting with a buffalo he had killed. Upon learning of the trickery his brother had used, he flew into a violent rage and wanted to kill Maghan-Diabé. Digna calmed him by giving him a <term>talisman|a ritual object believed to hold spiritual power</term> which ensured that Téré-Kiné and his descendants would have the ability to make rain fall at will—a power that is still attributed today to the members of the <term>Sokhona|one of the founding clans of the Soninké people</term> clan.

Shortly after, Digna died. Garabara, having consulted the omens, predicted to Maghan-Diabé that he would one day reign in a place in the <term>Sahel|the semi-arid transition zone south of the Sahara</term> called <term>Koumbi|Koumbi Saleh, the site of the historical capital of the Ghana Empire</term> and located to the East. The small troop, marching eastward, arrived in a country inhabited by hyenas whose chief was named Tourougoulé Fadiga; Maghan-Diabé asked the latter to show him the way to Koumbi: the chief of the hyenas told him to continue toward the East. A little further on, the troop arrived at the country of the vultures, whose chief, Douga, demanded forty horse carcasses to show them the road to Koumbi. Maghan-Diabé therefore sacrificed his forty mounts, on which the vultures feasted. Then Douga began to fly ahead of the troop to show them the way, and, finally stopping on a tree near the place where Goumbou is located today, said:

"...I do not want you to come and disturb me here." However, Maghan-Diabé having proposed a transaction to the serpent <note>In Soninké oral tradition, this serpent is known as Bida, the guardian spirit of Wagadu</note>, the latter declared that he consented to let his brother settle in the country and to remain himself in his well without ever leaving it, on the condition that he be given one hundred virgins a year as prey. From the tree that had been felled there then emerged a drum that began to play all by itself; at the call of this magic drum, men came running from all directions: they were 9,999, all mounted on **bay horses**, and divided into four companies, each of which had a chief. These chiefs were: Ouagané Sakho, father of the **Sakho** clan; Diaméra Sogona, father of the **Diagouraga** (a branch of the **Diawara**); Makhan Doumbé, father of the **Silla**, and Goumaté Fadé, father of the **Yaressi** (also known as Diaressi or Diarisso).

When all this crowd was gathered, on the advice of Garabara, it was decided to elect as king the one whose arm would be exactly the same length as the drum (2). All the chiefs successively thrust their arms into the interior of the drum, but only Maghan-Diabé could fill it exactly with his arm and, in consequence, he was recognized as king by the entire assembly.

<header>DISPERSION OF WAGADU</header>

...the North-West and settled at *Diara* (near and to the North-East of *Nioro*); *Diaméra Sogona* received the East and settled at *Guesséné* in the South of *Kaniaga* (very close to *Sosso*); *Makhan Doumbé* received the South-West and settled at *Kamatingué* (between *Goumbou* and *Nioro*), from where he later went to *Kaarta*; finally *Goumaté Fadé* received the South-East as his share and went to live in *Bélédougou* (around the year 750).

Every year, at the harvest festival which is celebrated during the first rains, the four provincial chiefs came to pay homage to the King of Wagadu at Koumbi, and a virgin was sacrificed to the serpent <note>This refers to Bida, the mythical guardian serpent of the empire who provided rain and gold in exchange for the sacrifice.</note>.

When Maghan-Diabé died, his brother Maghan-Tané succeeded him; then reigned Maghan-Tané-Fankanté, then Maghan-Mamari, and finally Maghan-Kaya or Kaya-Maghan Sissé <note>Kaya-Maghan translates to "King of Gold."</note>, the last of the five sons of Katana Boro, under whose reign the ruin of Wagadu and the dispersion of its inhabitants took place (end of the 8th century).

Here is how tradition reports the motive and circumstances of this memorable event. A man named Mamari-Sité Dorhoté, originally from Kaniaga—a sort of magician remarkable for his silent character (he spoke only twice a year)—had come to reside in Diara with Ouagané Sakho, to whose clan he had affiliated himself, changing his original name to Mamari Sakho. He was in love with a young girl named Sia Yatébari who, that year, was chosen for her beauty to be offered to the serpent. When the day of sacrifice arrived, Mamari Sakho went to Koumbi, armed with a carefully sharpened saber, and, slipping through the crowd, placed himself near the sacred well. The serpent, according to custom, poked its head out twice to look at the virgin intended for it; at the moment it raised it a third time and prepared to seize Sia, Mamari rushed upon it and struck its neck seven times with his saber: at the seventh blow, the serpent's head detached, but instead of falling, it rose into the air, saying: "Mamari Sakho, you have destroyed Wagadu; for seven years, it will no longer rain in this country, for the rain I used to make fall will henceforth be transformed into gold and the..."

'Wagadu will no longer benefit from it.' <note>This refers to the curse uttered by the dying serpent Bida, the guardian of the empire, after being decapitated by Mamari.</note> And indeed, the head of the serpent flew off and fell to the south of Mandé, in Bouré, which became the region of the Sudan richest in gold.

The onlookers wanted to harm Mamari, but the latter, leaping onto his horse, succeeded in fleeing; Ouagané Sakho caught up with him, but because he belonged to the same clan as him, he did not dare kill him and let him go.

However, the serpent's threats were fulfilled; not a single drop of water fell in Wagadu for seven consecutive years; a great famine ensued, and the Soninké left this cursed land to disperse in all directions, in search of more fertile regions.

Some, under the leadership of *Alikassa Sempré*, son of Maghan Diabé, moved toward Tekrur, to Guidimaka and Galam, which they called Gadiaga; they founded the first Soninké colonies there—those of Yaressi and Silla, so named for the clans descended from Goumaté Fadé and Makhan Doumbé who established them; members of the royal Sempré clan who were part of the same migration founded *Galambou* (1). A tradition recorded by Mage <note>Eugène Mage (1837–1869) was a French explorer whose writings are a primary source for 19th-century West African history.</note> relates that Alikassa, having bathed one day in a tributary of the Falémé called *Bakili* which the indigenous people considered a sacred watercourse, and having suffered no ill effects from his recklessness, was regarded as a powerful sorcerer by the locals and became king of Galam. In memory of this circumstance, his descendants changed their name from Sempré to Bakili. The kingdom of *Galam* or *Gadiaga* had its capital at Galambou, also called Kounguel; it included Goye, Kaméra, and Guidimaka.

The Soninké, commanded by a man named Adyini Kounaté, reportedly settled near the Bozo of Dioboro; the Bobo, troubled by this neighborhood, reportedly emigrated shortly thereafter toward Bandiagara <note>The Bandiagara Escarpment is a famous geological feature in Mali, later home to the Dogon people.</note>.

Many Soninké who had remained in Diaga during the migration of Digna had since come directly into the Aoukar, so that the total number of Soninké spread through Ghana and its surroundings must have been considerable at the end of the <term>8th century</term>. Kaya-Maghan took advantage of this to overthrow the dynasty of the <term>Judeo-Syrians</term> <note>A theory held by some early 20th-century historians, like Maurice Delafosse, suggesting the first rulers of Ghana were of Middle Eastern origin; modern historians generally view Ghana as an indigenous African development.</note>, seize power, and establish Soninké supremacy over the Empire of Ghana: this was, as we have seen, the signal for the exodus of the <term>Proto-Fulani</term> <note>original: "Proto-Peuls" — the ancestors of the Fulani people.</note> toward Fouta-Toro (2).

<header>THE PEOPLES</header>

Aoukar and its capital, Ghana, <note>This refers to the ancient Ghana Empire, located in present-day Mauritania and Mali, not the modern nation-state of Ghana.</note> must have constituted the primary center of the Soninké, at least from a political perspective, from the early years of the 9th century until toward the end of the 11th. Alternating as rivals and overlords of the Leimtouna Berbers of Aoudaghost, the Soninké of Ghana established their supremacy at the end of the 10th century over the entire Hodh and at least part of Tagant, over Massina and Bagana, and over all the lands between the Niger River and Tekrour, where their compatriots had already founded colonies. This was the brilliant moment of their history. It was also the period when their ethnic formation was completed, through numerous and repeated mixtures with Berbers in the North and with Toucouleurs <note>A sedentary ethnic group from the Senegal River valley.</note> in the Southwest—mixtures added to those already experienced through contact with the Judeo-Syrians <note>This refers to a historical theory popular in the early 20th century suggesting that migratory groups from the Levant influenced West African cultures.</note> in Diaga and Aoukar. It is to these mixtures, in which the white racial element played a very significant part, that the Soninké owe their current physical and moral characteristics, and that their language likewise owes the particularities that clearly distinguish it from the Mandé dialects of the Center.

But the migrations and counter-migrations of the Soninké were far from having come to an end, and their dispersion across the entire Western Sudan was still only in its early stages. In 1076, the Lemtouna, led into holy war by Abdallah-ben-Yassine <note>The Almoravid leader who spearheaded the Islamic conquest of the region.</note>,

---

won a victory over the Whites. I must point out that many traditions place the dispersion of the Soninké from Wagadu only in the 14th century: this is because most legends transmitted orally only preserve the memory of major events and place them all one after another in an exact chronological order, but without concern for the periods devoid of history—though often very long—that unfolded between two facts retained by tradition. Thus, from the ruin of Wagadu—which must certainly be placed as early as the end of the 8th century since it preceded the Soninké conquest of Ghana and provided the occasion for it—the legends pass directly to the conquests of Soundiata <note>Sundiata Keita, the founder of the Mali Empire.</note> (13th century) and to the founding of Nioro by the Peuls Diawambé (beginning of the 14th). Dr. Tautain, in recounting the legend of the serpent, believed he could identify Wagadu with Ghana without, however, giving his reasons: in reality, the story of the serpent of Wagadu was simply the starting point for the Soninké takeover of Ghana.

<header>DISPERSION OF THE SONINKÉ OF GHANA</header>

...seized Ghana, plundered the city, massacred a portion of the inhabitants, and converted to Islam those who preferred their new religion over death or flight. <note>The Almoravids were a radical Berber Muslim movement that conquered the Ghana Empire around 1076.</note> Many Soninké remained in the Aoukar region where, having become Muslims, they lived under the Berber yoke until around 1090, at which point they regained their independence. However, many others also emigrated from Ghana toward the South, Southwest, and Southeast at the end of the 11th century, completing the formation of the Soninké states already beginning to take shape in Kaniaga, Bakounou, Kingui, and Galam, and bringing a new wave of population back to Diaga.

According to tradition, the Soninké families who fled Ghana during the Almoravid conquest were primarily descended from the first settlers who had remained in Aoukar during the time of the Judeo-Syrian domination <note>This refers to a now-discredited historical theory that early West African civilizations were founded by migrants from the Levant.</note> and belonged mainly to the following clans: the *Doukouré*, descendants of a man named Bentigui, who was in the service of a minister to the last Judeo-Syrian emperor of Ghana and whose son is said to have assassinated that emperor, likely at the moment of Kaya-Maghan Sissé's arrival in Aoukar; the *Soumaré*, descendants of another associate of the same minister; the *Diakaté* or *Niakaté* and the *Diarisso*, as well as the *Mangara*, the *Samoura*, and the *Koussata*, who were descendants of the vassals of the Judeo-Syrian emperors themselves; and finally the *Tounkara* who, for their part, consisted of the last remnants of the Sissé Soninké imperial family—that is, the descendants of Kaya-Maghan.

The *Diarisso* founded a kingdom in Kaniaga, where they reunited with people of their own clan in the form of the descendants of Goumaté-Fadé: this was the origin of the famous empire of *Sosso* or of the *Sossé*, which was to become celebrated some hundred years later under the *Kanté* dynasty. <note>The Sosso Empire would eventually become a major power under Soumaoro Kanté before being defeated by Sundiata Keita of Mali.</note>

The *Doukouré* founded a kingdom first in Bakounou, then in Goumbou, which in a sense corresponded to the ancient kingdom of Ouagadou. Their leader, Maré-Diago Doukouré, upon leaving Ghana, first moved into Guimbala on the northern bank of Lake Débo, went from there to Djenné, then to Diongoï in southern Bakounou, where he settled and died. Toumané and his younger brother Boubou, accompanied by all the notables of the kingdom, set out on horseback to scout the location; however, a diviner had predicted that the first of the two brothers to set foot on the ground would die immediately. Therefore, when they arrived at Goumbou, Toumané invited Boubou to be the first to dismount. Boubou, wishing not to disobey his elder, accepted the sacrifice of his life; but, before setting foot on the ground, he had the royal family’s treasure placed on one side and the country's notables gathered on the other. He then said to Toumané: "Choose between these two treasures: wealth or men; after my death, my children shall have that which you have disdained." Toumané chose the wealth. Boubou, having entrusted his children to the notables, then dismounted and died instantly. The notables declared to Toumané that, since he had preferred riches over them, they would no longer depend on him from that moment forward, but rather on Boubou’s eldest son, *Bouyagui-Toumbéli*, who was still only a child but nonetheless inherited the command of the kingdom. An elder, Diéroumfa Doukouré, was appointed tutor to the young king; after seven years, Bouyagui-Toumbéli Doukouré took up the reins of the State (late 12th or early 13th century). From that time until the present, the descendants of Boubou Doukouré have retained political command in Goumbou (1), while those of Toumané have never ceased to be regarded as the masters of the soil. <note>In many West African traditions, the "master of the soil" (maître du sol) holds a sacred, ritual connection to the land and its spirits, distinct from the political ruler or "chief."</note>

# THE DEFINITIVE FOUNDING OF DJENNÉ

...grated then <note>Continuing from the previous page: "A large number of Sossé emigrated then..."</note> toward Tekrour, the lower Senegal, and the Gambia, where their descendants are still found today, more or less mixed with the Toucouleur, the Wolof, the Serer, and the Malinke.

In 1240, Soundiata <note>Soundiata Keita, the legendary founder of the Mali Empire</note> definitively destroyed Ghana, established his residence near Niamina, founded a city there which was given the name of his country of origin (Mandé or Mali), and became the master of the entire upper Niger, from its sources to the lake region. The Soninké of Diaga <note>A historical region in the Inland Niger Delta</note> accepted Mandinka rule with some difficulty, and those of Nono in particular sought to escape it through emigration. Some descended the left bank of the Niger and went to found, between Niafounké and Bassikounou, a colony that also took the name Nono (or Nounou) and which has survived to this day; this colony is cited by the *History of the Sudan* <note>original: "Tarikh-es-Soudân," a primary historical chronicle of West Africa written in the 17th century</note>, which describes a woman named Bikoun-Kabi reigning there and speaks of the conquest of this country by Sonni Ali the Great <note>original: "Sonni Ali-Ber," the expansionist first king of the Songhai Empire</note> around 1473; today, the descendants of these Soninké-Nono—whom Sa'di <note>Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di, the author of the History of the Sudan</note> mistakenly calls "Sanhadja Nono" <note>Sanhadja refers to a Berber tribal confederation</note>—speak Songhai and are called *Dakouraré*; they inhabit *Nounou* (near Niafounké, south of Lake Gaouati) and a few neighboring villages of Soumpi near the road from Niafounké to Bassikounou.

Other Soninké from Diaga (the Komma or Koumba) traveled up the left bank of the river and went to found *Sansanding*.

But the greatest number of the Soninké-Nono, crossing the Niger at Diafarabé, occupied the country between this river and the Bani <note>A major tributary of the Niger River</note> generally spanning from Diafarabé to Mopti and San. They chose as the center of their new colony the location of *Djenné* <note>original: "Dienné"</note>, where Soninké had already settled since the beginning of the 9th century, but whose true founding can be placed at this time (around 1250). The spirits of the place demanded, to ensure the future prosperity of the new village, that a virgin be sacrificed as a burnt offering to them: a young girl was therefore provided by the Bozo of Dioboro to the patriarch of the Mana, the chief of the Soninké-Nono, who had her walled up alive in the ramparts then under construction, near what is known today as the Kanafa gate. Before the young girl took her last breath, she was heard, through the still-soft clay with which they had just covered her, telling the Soninké to always remember that it was to the Bozo that they owed the prosperity of their city (2). The Soninké of Djenné were primarily merchants: their continuous relations with Timbuktu and their travels on the river downstream from Mopti led them to adopt the Songhai language, probably starting in the 16th century, to the detriment of their own language. Their current descendants all speak Songhai, but those who inhabit the Pondori, between Djenné and Diafarabé, and who devote themselves primarily to agriculture, have preserved the use of the Soninké language. Shortly after the definitive establishment of the Soninké at Djenné, around 1300, Koumboro Mana, the twenty-sixth chief of the colony since its first foundation by the Kounaté, converted to Islam; from that time on, the people of Djenné were always fervent Muslims.

Around 1270, that is to say, about thirty years after the con—

### THE DIAWARA

Following the reconstruction of Jenne on its current site, a new fraction of the Soninké people was forming in Kingui <note>A historical region located in present-day western Mali</note>: the Diawara, who took the place of the Niakaté dynasty at Diara. The ancestor of the Diawara is said to have been a hunter of unknown origin named Daman-Guilé, the son of a certain Modi-Moussa Moumini. He arrived from the direction of the Hejaz <note>A region in the west of present-day Saudi Arabia; such claims of Middle Eastern origins were common in West African foundation myths to signify prestige</note>—that is, from the Northeast—into the Manding, accompanied by men named Ségui-Khéri, Dimbaüé, and Niagué-Maghan, the latter being the ancestor of the Kamara clan. Daman-Guilé reportedly arrived in the Manding during the reign of Sundiata Keïta <note>The founder of the Mali Empire</note>, specifically in the second quarter of the 13th century. A man of the *Garankè* <term>Garankè: a specialized social caste of leatherworkers and shoemakers</term> caste named Kaké-Kanédyi (1), who lived near Sundiata, went into the bush to look for mimosa bark to tan his leathers and encountered Daman and his companions. He asked them who they were and where they came from. Daman simply replied: "We are hunters from the East," and asked Kaké to inform the emperor of their arrival. Sundiata, notified by Kaké, summoned Daman-Guilé and his companions. When he asked them what their *diamou* <note>original: "diamou" — a Mandé term for a family or clan name</note> was, Daman replied: "*Dia wara*," which, according to legend, meant in the language of his country: "There are no clans among us" (2). However, this response was mistaken for the statement of their clan name, and they were henceforth called *Diawara*.

---

(1) One legend identifies this Kaké-Kanédyi as a Soninké, the ancestor of the Kanédyi or Kanté clan: I will only observe that this clan was already represented during the same period by the reigning family of Sosso, in Kaniaga.

(2) *Dia* or rather *dian* means in the Mandé language—among other meanings—"company, association, or clan," and *wala* in the Fula language <note>The language of the Fulani people</note> is the negative verb: one could therefore, strictly speaking, suppose that Daman was speaking Fula and said "there is no *dia*"; from *dia wala*, the Mandinka would have formed *diawara*, which is not at all impossible. Regardless of the value of this etymology, it is worth noting that the names *Diawara* in Mandé and *Diawambé* in Fula seem to stem from an identical root, which would be *diawa* or *diaw*. Among the Soninké, the Diawara form a group that is simultaneously a tribe, a caste, and a clan, very similar to the group formed by the Diawambé among the Fula. It would therefore not be absurd to suppose that both groups have an identical origin, if not from an ethnic perspective, at least from a social one.

Once provided with these precious instructions, Fié-Mamoudou shared them with his brother Niagué-Maghan, and both pressed their eyes until tears came out, which they collected in a gourd; then Niagué-Maghan went to steal a horse at Diara from the king's stables: they killed this horse, exposed its head to the sun until it was completely dried out, ground the bones, and prepared the talisman. Fassakoré having asked: "Where is the hand of the robust man?", Fié-Mamoudou presented his own hand, and, Fassakoré having coated his palm with the magic paste, he went to Diara, prostrated himself before the king to greet him, took Mana-Maghan’s hand in his, and returned. Immediately the king rushed out of his house like a madman, saddled his mare, galloped away, and never reappeared: no one ever knew what became of him. All the members of his family fled and disappeared as well, with the exception of a man named Sodoga who was sleeping at that moment and who later became the ancestor of the <term>griots</term> <note>traditional West African keepers of oral history, genealogy, and music</note> of the Daramé clan, who were called Sodogalé because of him.

These Diawara, whose ancestor—of unknown origin—was perhaps a Peul <note>Also known as the Fula or Fulani people</note>, were in any case formed from very diverse elements; but it seems that, since their installation in Kingui, it is the Soninké element that has dominated their final composition. Today, although they are regarded by the Soninké proper as forming a separate group—for reasons that are undoubtedly purely historical—the Diawara must be considered a fraction of the Soninké people.

At the end of the 13th century, the Soninké were therefore already dispersed and established in most of the provinces of the Western Sudan <note>The historical geographic region of West Africa, not to be confused with the modern nation of Sudan</note> where they are found today. However, this essentially mobile, traveling, migratory, and enterprising people had not yet finished their secondary movements, which they have probably not completely finished even in our own time. But, as had happened in Djenné, almost all the Soninké colonies that went to settle east of Diaga or south of Kaniaga and Gadiaga gradually lost part of their nationality and abandoned their language to adopt those of the peoples or countries within which they established themselves: Songhai in the Djenneri region, Dioula in the Niger Bend, Bamana <note>The Bambara people</note> near Ségou and Bamako, Malinké in Wassoulou, etc.

It is in this way that, from the 14th to the 19th centuries, Soninké coming from Diaga, Djenné, and Sansanding spread to San and the surrounding areas, then from there to Yatenga on one hand and Dafina on the other, spreading scattered colonies as far as Gao and Say toward the East and into the upper Ivory Coast (notably Samatiguila and Odienné) toward the South **(2)**. Some went as far as the very banks of the Niger at Niamina, where they mixed with the Koumba Soninké who had come from Sansanding; these Koumba had already founded the town of Niamina some time earlier, near the site where the capital of the <term>Mali Empire</term> was once located.

Other Soninké families from Galam (notably the Sakho and Silla) had also left the Senegal region toward the middle of the 16th century (**1534** according to João de Barros <note>A Portuguese historian of the 16th century</note>), following a war with the Toucouleurs of Fouta. in the south of Boundou and Bambouk and reached the upper Gambia, the Fouta-Djallon, and the Ouassoulou.

If we now look back at the circumstances—sometimes a bit tangled—that motivated or accompanied the different migrations and the formation of the Soninké people, we will see that this people, in its current state, is one of the most mixed in the <term>French Sudan</term> <note>A former colonial territory in West Africa, roughly corresponding to modern-day Mali</note>. No doubt very little different at the start from their congeners, the central Mandé, they are now notably distinguished from them by moral character, physical appearance, and language. Their long and intimate contact with the Judeo-Syrians, the Berbers, the <term>Fula</term> <note>Also known as the Peul or Fulani people</note>, and—more recently—the Beni Hassan Moors, has had sufficient influence on them—at least on the fraction of their people remaining in the Sahel—for <term>Leo Africanus</term> <note>A 16th-century traveler and diplomat whose writings provided Europe with its primary knowledge of African geography for centuries</note> to have considered them as being related to the Libyans, and for <term>al-Sa'di</term> <note>Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di, the 17th-century Timbuktu scholar and author of the historical chronicle Tarikh al-Sudan</note> to have confused some of their tribes with the Zenaga Berbers. On the other hand, those who underwent Songhai influence in the Djenneri and the lake region could be mistaken for Songhai, just as it is quite difficult at first glance to distinguish the Marka of the Niger Bend from the Dyula, those of the upper Niger from the Bamana, or those of the Ouassoulou from the Malinke or the Fulanke. However, even where they have abandoned their language, they still form a distinct ethnic unity where the primitive Mandé type dominates, but where the white racial element (and particularly the Semitic element) has left a strongly marked trace in their temperament, perhaps even more than in their physical features (1).

<header>THE ORIGIN OF THE DIOULA</header>

### 3. *Dioula.*

The Dioula certainly come from the same stock as the <term>Soninké</term><note>An ethnic group also known as the Sarakole, famous as the founders of the Ghana Empire</note>, but they separated from them before the latter were modified by their contact in the northern <term>Sahel</term><note>The transitional zone between the Sahara Desert and the Sudanian Savanna</note> with Judeo-Syrians and Moors. For this reason, they have better preserved the primitive <term>Mandé</term><note>A large group of West African peoples sharing linguistic and cultural ties, including the Bambara and Malinké</note> type, and their language differs very little from that of the <term>Malinké</term><note>Also known as the Mandinka people</note>; it is, in any case, much closer to the central Mandé dialects than it is to Soninké. They implicitly state this themselves by saying that their name, *Dioula*, means "from the bottom, from the primitive stock." <note>While the author cites this traditional etymology, the word is more commonly translated in Mandé languages as "trader"</note> However, regarding their origin, it is appropriate to link them to the Northern Mandé, as has been very well demonstrated by the man who first studied them and who knows them best, <term>Mr. Binger</term><note>Louis-Gustave Binger (1856–1936), a French explorer who traveled extensively through the Niger Bend</note>.

Doubtless, the formation of the Dioula people must go back to the first Soninké migrations that moved toward the <term>Djenneri</term><note>The region surrounding the city of Djenné</note> even before the founding of the short-lived kingdom of <term>Wagadu</term><note>The semi-legendary core of the ancient Ghana Empire</note>—migrations of which we traced the evidence in the legend of Digna at the beginning of the 8th century. The Kounaté family, who settled in Dioboro toward the end of the same century or the beginning of the 9th, after the dispersion of Wagadu, probably provided a second element to the origins of the Dioula. In any case, the latter—whom all their traditions claim came from <term>Djenné</term><note>An ancient center of trade and Islamic scholarship in present-day Mali</note>—were already spread throughout the Niger Bend and as far as the lower <term>Volta</term><note>A major river system in modern-day Ghana and Burkina Faso</note> before the final founding of Djenné by the Soninké-Nono in 1240, since we find them strongly established in **Bégho** (1), near the southern bend of the Black Volta and the edge

...Berber and not Songhai; 5. finally, the founder of the <term>Askia dynasty</term><note>The ruling dynasty of the Songhai Empire at its peak, starting with Askia Muhammad I in 1493</note> was precisely a Soninké, and the Songhai, in short, played only a passive role throughout this entire period of their history.

Great travelers and skilled merchants, even more so than their Soninké cousins, the Dioula are perhaps, of all the <term>Mandé</term><note>A large group of West African peoples sharing linguistic and cultural ties</note>, those who have provided the greatest number of pilgrims who visited Mecca: this fact may explain their ancient and rapid Islamization, an Islamization which has, moreover, slowed down during recent centuries. One must also take into account another phenomenon: with rare exceptions, the Dioula have only ever lived in towns, isolated amidst indigenous agricultural populations of animist religion; this allowed them to stick together more closely and to organize religious and economic centers that became all the stronger for being more isolated, and could only maintain themselves through the moral prestige the Dioula exercised over the indigenous people surrounding them.

In a more recent era—starting from the 15th and 16th centuries no doubt, and up to the present day—Soninké from Sansanding, San, and Ségou came to swell the Dioula colonies of the Bend <note>The "Boucle du Niger," or the Niger Bend, the region where the Niger River turns south</note>, which were already numerous in the <term>Mossi</term><note>An ethnic group primarily in modern-day Burkina Faso</note>, the Dafina, the Bobo and <term>Sénoufo</term><note>An ethnic group residing in the border regions of Mali, Ivory Coast, and Burkina Faso</note> lands, and the North of the Ivory Coast (Mankono, Kadioha, Bong, Kong, etc.). Most of the Dioula in the Samo country reportedly came there from Ségou around 1760, under the reign of the <term>nâba</term><note>A traditional title for a Mossi king or ruler</note> Kango; the leader of this migration, named Mamourou, supposedly left Toubara (in the modern-day district of Ségou) to go to Louta (in the modern-day district of Bandiagara), where he is said to have died. ### VARIOUS DIOULA ELEMENTS

The Samo; these people even protected them against the emperor of Ségou, Ngolo Diara, who, around 1780, led an expedition to Yatenga with the aim of bringing the Dioula back to Ségou—a goal that was not achieved.

Toward the end of the 19th century, Kong was a city of more than 15,000 souls, having become the primary center of the Dioula and the capital of a true federal state inhabited by highly diverse populations, though the Dioula held the government. The complete destruction of this city by Samori <note>Samori Touré, the founder of the Wassoulou Empire and a major resistor to colonial rule</note> in April 1895 triggered the exodus of most of the Dioula, under the leadership of their chiefs from the Ouatara clan, toward Bobo-Dioulasso, which had been a dependency of Kong since the time of Farama-Oulé (1860); near Bobo-Dioulasso, they founded several large villages, including that of <term>Dassalami</term><note>From the Arabic "Dar-es-salam," meaning House of Peace</note>, which quickly became flourishing. After the French occupation of the Kong region in 1898 and the pacification of the country, some Dioula families returned to settle on the ruins of their former capital with Yamoriba Ouatara, but most remained around Bobo-Dioulasso with Pinntièba Ouatara.

Despite the cohesion of their small groupings and their urban settlements, the Dioula could not avoid introducing many foreigners among them, especially when, having become wealthy, they acquired many slaves. Thus, today, the Dioula are heavily mixed with <term>Voltaic</term><note>A language family and group of peoples found primarily in Burkina Faso</note> elements from the Mossi and <term>Sénoufo</term><note>An ethnic group residing in northern Ivory Coast and southern Mali</note> elements in the regions of Bobo-Dioulasso and Sikasso. However, certain families seem to have remained more or less pure: these are generally those who are entirely Muslim and who have not adopted the custom of facial <term>scarifications</term><note>The practice of marking the skin to indicate ethnic identity or social status</note>; the others, more or less intermixed with indigenous peoples, practicing a somewhat lukewarm Islam and often even professing the local religion, are referred to by the "pure" Dioula by the name *Sonongui* or *Sorongui*, which interpreters often translate as "Muslims who drink *dolo*" (1), though its exact etymology is unknown to me.

## VIII. Central Mandé.

1. *Kâgoro*. — In ancient times, the Kâgoro were likely the indigenous inhabitants of Bagana. It is highly probable that the "savage *Bagama*" (1) noted by Al-Bakri <note>Abu Abdullah al-Bakri, an 11th-century Andalusian geographer and historian</note> to the southwest of Ghana <note>referring to the historic Ghana Empire, located in present-day Mauritania and Mali</note> and the *Baganes* mentioned by early Portuguese travelers were none other than the Kâgoro. Their territory likely extended to the west and southwest of Diagha (or Diaga), separating the cradle of the Soninké from that of the Malinké. Their land was invaded numerous times by Soninké migrations; it was the theater of conflicts between the Soninké Sossé and the Malinké; finally, it became one of the most active centers of Banmana colonization. All of this would explain why the modern Kâgoro—while faithfully preserving the physical and moral character of early Mandé farmers and thus closely resembling the Banmana—speak a dialect that shows undeniable affinities with the Soninké language.

Most of the original Kâgoro have, moreover, merged into the Soninké, Banmana, Malinké, and Foulanké peoples; those who have kept their ethnic individuality form only a very small group, scattered today across Bakounou, Kaniaga, Kaarta, and Bélédougou. However, because this small group has managed to preserve its original character and establish a distinct dialect, it is all the more interesting.

A descendant of Kossa, named Séguéba Makassa, reportedly reunited the two branches under his command in the 18th century. The conquests of the emperors of Manding <note>The Mali Empire</note>, starting from the beginning of the 13th century, by establishing the Malinké on the right bank of the upper Niger, must have forced the Banmana to confine themselves between the upper Baoulé and the upper Bagbé rivers, precisely where the Toron is located. Indeed, their highly marked character of independence and their attachment to their ancestral religion <note>Traditional West African beliefs, as opposed to Islam</note> did not dispose them to accept the yoke of the Mandingues, whose emperor and great chiefs then professed Islam <note>original: "islamisme"</note>, and it would be due to this circumstance that they owe their name, as I have already mentioned (*ban-ma-na*, meaning "refusal to the master").

Some, however, undoubtedly moved along the right bank of the Niger as far as Ségou as early as the 13th century, for the legends regarding Sundiata <note>Sundiata Keita, the founder of the Mali Empire</note> tell us of Banmana already inhabiting the banks of the river near Koulikoro between 1225 and 1250. Most likely, these precursors of the great Banmana migrations must have belonged to the caste of the Somono fishermen, who could not have found sufficient use for their special skills in the Toron and who preferred to accept the Malinké yoke and embrace Islam.

The agricultural faction of the Banmana people was also soon to head North; they were already very numerous and soon found themselves cramped in the Toron. The migration from which the Kulubali empire <note>The Ségou Empire, founded by the Kulubali (Coulibaly) dynasty</note> was to emerge is generally placed in the 17th century, but this migration had in reality begun much earlier, and the establishment of Kaladian Kulubali near Ségou in 1600 only constitutes the outcome of one of its most recent episodes. In fact, since at least the end of the 13th century and, it seems, without interruption, an ever-growing flood of Banmana descended the valleys of the upper Bani, advancing progressively from the Toron to the surroundings of Djenné, successively populating the region of Bougouni, the country located between the Baoulé (1) and Bamako, the Bendougou (on the right bank of the Bani), and all the territory between Djenné and Ségou from the left bank of the Bani to the right bank of the Niger.

(1) I mean, of course, the Baoulé which forms the western branch of the upper Bani and not the Baoulé that is a tributary of the Senegal River.

### THE KOULOUBALI

As I was saying just a moment ago, it is only from the 17th century onward that the legends become specific regarding the push of the <term>Banmana<gloss>The self-identifier for the people commonly known as the Bambara.</gloss></term> migrations; around this time, they took a new direction and, crossing the Niger, headed toward the West and Northwest, finally reaching Nioro in 1754.

Let us now look at the details of the principal legends among these.

In a very remote era, and most likely well before the 17th century, two Banmana brothers named Niangolo and *Baramangolo*—doubtless forming a lost fraction of a larger migration—arrived on the right bank of the Baoulé river, south of Barouéli (near the confluence of the Baoulé and the Bagbé). They were fleeing enemies who were pursuing them and driving them toward the Northwest. They wished to cross the river to escape these enemies but could find no canoes: it is in memory of this fact that their descendants took the name *Kouloubali*, a word which in the Banmana language does indeed mean "without a canoe" <note>original: "sans pirogue"</note> (*koulou* meaning canoe, and *bali* being a privative suffix). A fish with a large, flattened head, of the species called *mpolio* in Banmana <note>A type of catfish common to the region's rivers.</note>, took pity on their predicament and offered to carry them across the Baoulé on its back. It first carried the younger brother, Baramangolo, who advised the fish not to provide the same service to his elder brother Niangolo, as the latter was ungrateful and cruel. Nevertheless, the *mpolio* returned to the right bank, took Niangolo on its back, carried him across the river, and deposited him on the left bank beside his brother. Immediately, Niangolo seized the *mpolio*, killed it, and, cutting it into two pieces, offered one to Baramangolo; however, the latter refused to eat the meat of an animal that had saved his life and pronounced a curse against any of his descendants who should ever touch the flesh of an *mpolio* (1).

Meanwhile, the two brothers settled in the country between the Bani and the Niger rivers, and there they had children: such was—

---

(1) This is why the *mpolio* is still today the *téné* or *tana* <note>original: "animal sacré et prohibé"</note> <term>tana<gloss>A sacred animal or totem that members of a clan are forbidden to kill or eat.</gloss></term> of the Kouloubali who descend from Baramangolo, while the Kouloubali who descend from Niangolo have a different *téné* (the lion or the hippopotamus).

...the origin of the Banmana clan of the Kouloubali. One of the descendants of Baramangolo, named *Kaladian Kouloubali*, settled around 1600 on the right bank of the Niger, a short distance downstream from Ségou, at Markadougouba—a village where the lieutenants of the Mali Emperors had resided until toward the end of the 15th century and which, since then, had been placed under the at least nominal suzerainty of the Emperor of Gao first, and later the Moroccan <term>Caïd<gloss>A local governor or leader in Islamic North Africa and the Sahel.</gloss></term> of Djenné. His son *Danfassari*, leaving Markadougouba where *Notémé*, another son of Kaladian, had succeeded his father, went around 1620 to settle further upstream in a village that had been founded previously by a Muslim—likely a <term>Soninke<gloss>An ethnic group from West Africa, known for founding the Ghana Empire.</gloss></term>—named *Siékou* or *Sékou* (the Sheikh); this village was called Ségou after the name of its founder (1). We shall see in the fourth part of this work how the grandson of *Danfassari*, Fotigué, known as *Biton*, built a fortress there and made it the seat of the Banmana Empire of Ségou around 1670. This empire would soon extend its supremacy over the entire course of the Niger from Bamako to Timbuktu inclusive, thereby encouraging the migration movement of the Banmana toward the North as well as onto the right bank of the Bani river.

However, disagreements had broken out between the Kouloubali descended from Baramangolo, to whom *Kaladian* and his descendants belonged, and those descended from his elder brother Niangolo. The latter, who had taken the epithet *Massassi* (descendants of the king) because they represented the elder branch, saw themselves pushed away from power by the younger branch and bore this downfall with difficulty. Treated even more harshly by the Emperor *Biton* than by his predecessors, they crossed the Niger around 1670—that is to say, shortly after the accession of *Biton*—under the leadership of *Zié Kouloubali-Massassi* or, according to other traditions, under that of his brother *Sounsa* or *Sarhaba*. They went to settle in the Bélédougou and Kaarta regions, founding at Sountian, near Mourdia (Kaarta), a second Banmana empire which remained in constant rivalry with the Empire of Ségou.

<page-num>287</page-num>
<header>THE LAST BAMANA MIGRATIONS</header>

Many Bamana families belonging to other clans (*Taraoré* <note>original: "Taraoré"; today more commonly spelled Traoré.</note>, *Diara* <note>original: "Diara"; today usually spelled Diarra.</note>, etc.) also left the right bank of the Niger during the reign of *Biton*, fleeing the yoke of this despot and seeking uninhabited lands to pursue hunting and satisfy their desire for independence. Thus, the north of *Bélédougou*, which was then a wilderness, was colonized toward the beginning of the *18th century* by a hunter named *Bakoro Taraoré*, who had fled the court of the Emperor Biton; this Bakoro settled a few kilometers southeast of the current post of *Banamba*, in an uninhabited forest that he was the first to clear and where he founded the small village of *Gana*. Later, other Bamana emigrants, also coming from the right bank of the Niger, founded the village of *Touba* (meaning "the great forest") (1) in the same region, with the permission of Bakoro Taraoré, whose rights as the first occupant granted him ownership of the soil. *Monson* or *Mosson Diara*, who reigned in Ségou from 1792 to 1808 (2), came to raid these villages, capturing a large number of their inhabitants and taking them away to Ségou. However, the Bamana colonies of Gana and Touba managed to rebuild themselves and contributed, throughout the first half of the *19th century*, to the settlement of northern Bélédougou. During the wars of *El-Hadj Omar* <note>A leader of the Toucouleur Empire who launched a mid-19th-century jihad across West Africa.</note> (1860), many Bamana from the region of *Merkoya* and Gana emigrated to the south toward *Sanankoro* (3), only to return home starting in 1885 to rebuild their destroyed hearths (4).

(2) <note>*Mosson Diara* was reigning at the time of the two journeys of *Mungo Park* <note>A famous Scottish explorer who was one of the first Europeans to reach the central Niger River.</note>.</note>
(3) <note>This *Sanankoro* (or Sananko) is located north of the railway line, between that line and *Daba* (in the Bamako district).</note>

# THE PEOPLES

In the region comprised between the Niger and the Bani, a region of which they seem to have been almost the only occupants since their first settlement, the Banmana <term>Banmana: Now more commonly spelled Bamana or Bambara; they are one of the largest ethnic groups in Mali.</term> have remained almost pure of any mixture; the same is not true on the right bank of the Bani, where they have increased their domain at the expense of that of the Bobo and the Sénoufo, nor on the left bank of the Niger as well as in the Sahel and the Massina, where they have cohabited with Malinké, Kagoro, Soninké, Bozo, and Peuls <term>Peuls: Also known as the Fulani or Fula people, traditionally semi-nomadic cattle herders.</term>. Assuredly, even in these latter regions, the Banmana of the small rural villages must still be very close to the primitive type of their ancestors, but it is not the same for those who inhabit the towns. Many of the latter are only Banmana by the language they speak and by the customs they have adopted—while modifying them, moreover—only at a fairly recent date.

I will take as an example the inhabitants of Banamba and the Banmana of Bamako. The former are still considered today as Soninké <term>Soninké: A Mandé people known for their historical role in the Ghana Empire and their trade networks.</term>, but it is very possible that, in fifty years or so, they will be ranked among the Banmana, given that not one of them will then speak Soninké, which is already no longer understood by some of the old men: and yet their settlement in Banmana country only dates back to 1832 (1)! As for the principal Banmana families of Bamako—that of the Niarè, to which the current chief of the city belongs, and that of the Touré, to which the non-Somono <term>Somono: A caste of specialized river-faring fishermen on the Niger River.</term> Muslims belong—here is their history. At a relatively recent time which, in any case, cannot go back beyond the second half of the 18th century, since the Massassi <term>Massassi: The ruling dynasty of the Bamana Kingdom of Kaarta.</term> reigned in Kaarta, a Muslim Soninké originally from Diara near Nioro named *Sériba Niarè* (2), having left his native town following a family quarrel, asked the Massassi emperor of Kaarta

As for the Touré, who only arrived in Bamako at the start of the 19th century, they reportedly originate from the fusion of two families: one, the *Touâté*, descends from a Jewish blacksmith originally from Touat <term>Touat: A region in present-day Algeria, historically a major oasis and center for trans-Saharan trade.</term>, who came to settle in Bamako, where he reportedly married women from the blacksmith caste (*Noumou*) and the fishing caste (*Somono*); the other, the *Daraoué*, descends from a Muslim Arab originally from Dara (southern Morocco) and married in Bamako to a Soninké woman.

### 3. Khassonké.

We have seen, when speaking of the Peul <term>Peul: Also known as the Fulani; a large ethnic group spread across West Africa.</term> migrations, how the Khassonké people were born toward the end of the 11th century, as a result of the mixing of certain Peul groups with the indigenous people of the upper Senegal river. These indigenous people were likely Kâgoro on the north bank of the river, and Malinké on the south bank; the Soninké of Guidimaka and Galam must also have provided a significant element to the formation of the Khassonké, as well as, later, the Moors of the Sahel.

(1) The name Bamako (Bammako) was given to the village founded by Dia-Moussa either in memory of Bamma Sakho (*Bamma-ko*, behind Bamma, or beyond Bamma's village) or because of the local custom consisting of offering each year, at the beginning of the rainy season, a victim to the crocodiles <term>caïmans: Though the text uses the French word for caimans, these are biologically West African crocodiles.</term> of the Niger (*bamma-ko*, the "affair of the crocodile"). The etymology *bammako* "river of the crocodile," sometimes proposed, must be rejected due to the very closed pronunciation of the final *o* of Bamako (sounding almost like *ou*), while the *o* of *ko* meaning "river" is, on the contrary, very open.

According to the traditions currently circulating in Kayes, the ancestors of the Khassonké were a Peul <term>Peul: Also known as the Fulani; a traditionally pastoralist ethnic group spread across West Africa.</term> shepherd named Amadou Haoua and a Banmana woman belonging to a family whose herds Amadou Haoua tended. Since the origin of the Khassonké likely dates back to the 11th or 12th century, and at that time the Banmana <term>Banmana: The endonym for the Bambara people, the largest Mandé ethnic group in Mali.</term> likely had not yet reached the Kayes region, I would quite willingly replace the word "Banmana" in this legend with the word "Kâgoro"; this would lead to an explanation much closer to the truth, as proven by an examination of the dialect currently spoken by the Khassonké: it is a Mandé dialect closely resembling Kâgoro in its phonetics and containing a significant number of Peul roots in its vocabulary.

Séga Déoua, one of Amadou Haoua’s descendants, went to settle in Diomboko and built Koniakari there; one of his brothers settled in Séro, north of Koniakari, and founded a small rival kingdom whose sovereign bore the title of *sila-tigui* <term>sila-tigui: A Mandé title meaning "master of the road" or "leader."</term> like the emperor of Tekrour <term>Tekrour: An ancient state located in the Senegal River valley, influential from the 9th to the 13th centuries.</term>. Toward the end of the 18th century, a conflict broke out between the *silatigui* of Séro and the king of Koniakari, who was then named Demba Séga; after a series of minor struggles, the *silatigui*, aided by the Massassi Banmana of Kingui, gained the upper hand and, around 1810, forced Demba Séga to evacuate Diomboko and take refuge in Logo, between Kayes and Bafoulabé. After a brief flight <note>original: "fugue" — here meaning a temporary retreat or excursion due to conflict.</note> toward Boundou, Demba Séga settled permanently near and upstream of Kayes, at Médine, which became the capital of the Southern Khassonké and the province of Khasso or Khasson, where the ancestor Amadou Haoua had originally come from.

The Peul element which initially contributed to the formation of the Khassonké has become so diminished that today one can, without any issue, link the latter to the Mandé family.

# BEGINNINGS OF THE MANDING EMPIRE

Peuls of Massina <term>Massina: Here referring specifically to the "Manding-Mina" region in the upper Bakhoy basin, rather than the Inland Niger Delta region also called Macina.</term>, that is to say the region comprising the upper basin of the Bakhoy and the district situated between the upper Bakhoy and the Niger, south of Kita and southwest of Bamako. Their first capital must have been *Kangaba*, a village located a short distance from the left bank of the Niger, upstream from Bamako, about fifty kilometers from the point where the border of Upper Senegal-Niger crosses the river.

The foundation of the empire of Mali, or of the Malinké or Mandingues, is generally placed in the year 1213. In reality, this date has been preserved by Muslim traditions as being that of a pilgrimage to Mecca performed by the emperor *Allakoï Keïta* <term>Allakoï Keïta: Traditionally cited as the first Keita ruler to convert to Islam, though his historical details are often blended with legend.</term>, but it is quite probable that many Muslim and non-believing sovereigns had already succeeded one another on the throne of Mandé before Allakoï. In any case, it seems that at the beginning of the 13th century, the Malinké were already spread out, beyond Manding proper, into the Bouré, Sangaran, and Gangaran; they formed the entire population of these various provinces and had already founded several colonies on the right bank of the upper Niger (in present-day Ouassoulou), as well as in the north of Fouta-Djallon, Bambouk, the region of Kita, and the part of the Niger valley between Bamako and Ségou. It is this entire primitive domain of the Mandingues that was known in the North of the Sudan <term>Sudan: Historically referring to the "Bilad al-Sudan" or "Land of the Blacks," the Sahelian region of West Africa.</term> under the name of *Gangara* or *Ouangara* <term>Ouangara: A term used by medieval geographers to describe the gold-rich lands and the merchant networks of West Africa.</term> and which was universally famous because of the gold mines it contained, mainly in Bouré and Bambouk.

But it was starting from approximately 1230 that the conquests of the Mandingues began to considerably push back the limits of their territory toward the south, west, and north, and to turn the modest kingdom of Kangaba into the starting point of a true empire. The famous *Soundiata Keïta* <term>Soundiata Keïta: Sunjata Keita (c. 1217–1255), the epic hero and founder of the Mali Empire.</term>, known to Arab authors under the name of *Mari-Diata* (1) <note>original: "Mari-Diata"</note>, either directly—

Two of Soundiata's sons, Makan and Siétigui, settled in the same region, the former at Kayaba and the latter at Boko near Kouroukoto; Siétigui also married a daughter of Siéma Toulaba and had three sons: Dando, who took command of Birgo (the district of Mourgoula, between Kita and Manding proper); Massiré and Kouakourou, who settled northeast of Kita, toward the left bank of the upper Baoulé, in the region later called Fouladougou-Arbala.

One of Soundiata’s primary lieutenants, named Amari-Sonko, annexed Gangaran to his master’s empire, leaving the command to one of his servants named Sané-Nianga Taraoré; he seized the gold mines of Bambouk and continued his conquests—reinforced by a strong Mandinka immigration—through Boundou as far as Niani-Ouli (the Gambia River valley).

A little later, Soundiata defeated the Sosso <note>original: "sossé"</note> emperor Soumangourou at Kirina (1235), seized Kaniaga, Diaga, and all of Bagana, and advanced as far as the region of Oualata where he captured and destroyed Ghana (1240). Finding the position of Kangaba too remote from his new conquests, he founded his new capital not far from Niamina, which was given the name Mali or Mandé, in memory of its founder's homeland.

### DISMANTLING OF THE MANDING EMPIRE

At the death of Sundiata—that is to say, toward the middle of the 13th century—one of his best generals, *Moussa-Son-Koroma Sissoko*, came to settle west of the Bafing River, at Koundian (southeast of Bambouk), with a large number of warriors and partisans. There, he founded the Malinké kingdom of Bambougou or Bambouk which, while initially a vassal of the Emperor of Mali, later became independent.

Around the same time, another former general of Sundiata and a relative of the emperor himself, *Siriman Keïta*, passing south of Koundian, went to settle at Dékou in the mountains of Konkodougou. This country was still occupied at the time by the Diallonké <note>A Manding-speaking group, often considered the original inhabitants of the Fouta Djallon region</note>, but there were also Mandinka colonies there originating from Bouré and Sangaran. These were composed mainly of gold seekers who had been brought by migration leaders named *Kilia-Moussa Sissoko*, *Tira-Makan Taraoré*, and *Sori Doumbouya*, and who had founded the villages of Dindéra and Sintédougou. With the help of these Mandinka colonies, *Siriman Keïta* conquered Konkodougou from the Diallonké and turned it into a kingdom which was also a vassal of the Mali Empire.

It was in the 14th century, under the Emperor *Kankan-Moussa* <note>Better known in world history as Mansa Musa, famous for his immense wealth and his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca</note>, that the Manding Empire reached its peak. Having ascended the throne in 1307, *Kankan-Moussa* seized Gao and Timbuktu in 1325 and extended his authority to the borders of present-day Algeria. His successors entered into friendly relations with the sultans of Morocco and with the kings of Portugal (14th and 15th centuries). Never did an indigenous empire in West Africa obtain such renown or such power.

This singular fortune was destined to be of relatively short duration: as early as 1468, the Emperor of Gao, *Ali-Ber* <note>Also known as Sonni Ali, the founder of the Songhai Empire</note>, liberated the greater part of his states from Manding suzerainty, and the authority of the emperors of Mali, already diminished, was to be reduced to nothing toward the end of the 17th century by the conquests of the Banmana <note>The Bambara people</note> and the revolt of the vassal kingdoms. It is nonetheless true that, for nearly five hundred years, the Malinké laid down the law in the majority of the lands situated between the upper Niger and the Atlantic.

We should not be surprised, therefore, to see that they have

### 5. *Foulanké.*

I have sufficiently related, when speaking of the Peul migrations, how the various Foulanké groupings were formed to allow myself to be brief regarding them. I have also just stated that it is impossible today not to consider the Foulanké as Mandé, even though the importance of the Peul element that contributed to their formation was considerable and makes itself felt even today in their special <term>diamou</term> <note>A Mandinka term for a clan name or patronymic surname, which often indicates one's lineage and social status</note> as well as in certain secondary characteristics of their physical type and their customs.

One attributes to the Foulanké who inhabit *Ganadougou*, in the district of Sikasso, a somewhat special origin that dates back to a rather distant time: it is claimed that when the Soninké, under Kaya-Maghan <note>The title given to the kings of the ancient Ghana Empire; "Kaya-Maghan" means "King of Gold"</note>, seized power in Ghana (at the end of the 8th century), a few Judaeo-Syrian families <note>This refers to a historical theory, common in the colonial era, suggesting that the Fulani people originated from Middle Eastern or Levantine migrants</note>, separating themselves from the movement that drew their kin toward Fouta, reached Massina, retracing in the opposite direction the route that had brought them to Ghana six centuries earlier; without stopping for very long in Massina, they crossed the Niger,
