### IX. **Southern Mandé.**

#### 1. *Dialonke.*

As I have already stated, Fouta-Djallon—or rather the *Diallon (1)*—certainly seems to have been the original cradle of the Southern Mandé. But while the Dialonke <note>The Dialonke or Jalonke are a Mandé people closely related to the Susu</note> constituted the sole population of this country, it undoubtedly extended much further north and probably encompassed the entire region between the lower Bafing, the Senegal, and the Falémé rivers, touching the territory of the Mandinka to the east and the Kagoro to the north.

The first settlement of the Soninke in Gadiaga towards the end of the 8th century and the invasion of Khasso by the Peuls in the 11th century caused a retreat of the Dialonke toward the south. But it was especially in the 13th century, following the conquest of Gangaran, Bambouk, Konkodougou, and Labé by the Mandinka, that the major migratory movement of the Dialonke took shape: this movement carried them from that time as far as the shores of the Atlantic, near Conakry, through the coastal populations (Baga, Landuman, etc.) whom they began to partially absorb, becoming the Susu <note>original: "Soussou"</note> of Lower Guinea. However, it is far from being the case that all the original Dialonke or Susu were driven back by the Malinke <note>A subgroup of the Mandinka people</note> to the southwest of Fouta-Djallon: if they evacuated roughly—

<page-num>298</page-num>
<header>THE PEOPLES</header>

The Samo <note>The Samo are an ethnic group primarily located today in northwestern Burkina Faso and across the border in Mali</note> are said to be of Mandé origin and to have been formed by the mixture of several elements, one of which belonged to the Central Mandé group and another to the Southern Mandé group.

The first element was reportedly provided primarily by the Bambara <note>original: "Banmana"; the most populous Mandé ethnic group in Mali</note> of the Segou region; these people were said to have been driven from their country by the Malinké, most likely in the 14th century, after the arrival of the first Bambara migrations between the Bani and the Niger, but before the formation of the Empire of Segou. Under the leadership of a chief named Diyé, they crossed the Bani River and settled on the right bank of this waterway at Ninkiessa, between San and Djenné. From there, under the orders of Diougouri, the son of Diyé, they reached Toéré, between Koury and Ouahigouya. There, around the 16th century, they were joined by Samorho coming from the Southern Mandé migration current originating in Fouta Djallon; these Samorho had, moreover, mixed with Senufo and Bobo peoples while traveling from the Sikasso region to that of Koury. From the mixing of the Bambara and the Samorho, the Samo people emerged.

A portion of them remained in the vicinity of the northern bend of the Black Volta <note>Known today as the Mouhoun River</note> (the Samo of the Koury district); the others reached the southwest of Yatenga, where they were joined, during the reign of the *naaba* Kango <note>The Mossi ruler of the Yatenga Kingdom from approximately 1754 to 1787</note> (around 1770), by a few families of Bambara origin who, during Diyé’s migration, had pushed as far as Kaka, near Sofara, and had remained there.

Since that time, the Samo have been quite deeply influenced by the proximity of the Mossi and the Bobo and, although they have always lived more or less independently, the trace of their Mandé origins is no longer very perceptible. As for their current language—judging by the very scant information we possess—it seems to belong, at least in part, to the family of Voltaic languages <note>A major language family of West Africa, also known as Gur languages</note>.

Currently, the Samorho have adopted the religion and most of the customs of the Senufo <note>A group of related peoples living in northern Ivory Coast, southeastern Mali, and southwestern Burkina Faso</note>, but they speak a language that is generally agreed to be related to the Mandé languages.

### 4. Sia and various tribes.

The Southern Mandé, coming from the region of Kong <note>A historic city in modern-day northern Ivory Coast, once the capital of a powerful empire</note> after having given birth to the Lo of the Bandama toward the West and the Ngan of the Comoé toward the East, headed North and reached the Diébougou region. Driven back by the Bobo, they reportedly fell back toward the South as far as Lorhosso, finally moving toward the Northwest to reach the current site of Bobo-Dioulasso (*likely in the 16th century*). While some of them continued toward the West and contributed to the formation of the Samorho, the others, settling in Bobo-Dioulasso—or rather in Sia, which is the true name of this city—and, mixing there with the Bobo, gave birth to the Sia. Initially independent, these people were soon Islamized and conquered by the Dioula of Kong, whose dress and customs they partly adopted, while maintaining the use of a special dialect which, despite various influences and notably Bobo, seems indeed to belong to the Mandé family. From this comes the nickname *Bobo-Dioula* which has been given to the Sia, as well as the name Bobo-Dioulasso (village of the Bobo-Dioula) given to their main center.

The Sia left few traces of their passage through the current district of Gaoua <note>OCR: "Gahoua"; a town in southern Burkina Faso</note>, except perhaps at Diébougou and Lorhosso; but, once settled in Bobo-Dioulasso, they had

### 10. Senufo.

The Senufo seem indeed to be indigenous to all the lands where they are found today, both in Upper Senegal and Niger <note>A former colony in French West Africa, covering parts of modern Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso</note> and in the Ivory Coast: all collected traditions agree in making them the oldest known inhabitants of their current territory.

At most, it is permissible to suppose that this territory previously extended further toward the West. It is possible that the invasion of the Bambara <note>original: "Banmana"; the most populous Mandé ethnic group in Mali</note> from the right bank of the upper Niger into Toron and the lands between the Baoulé and Bagbé rivers—driven by the first Mandinka conquests—forced the Senufo then inhabiting those regions to migrate to the right bank of the Bagbé to join those of their compatriots already there. A tradition has been preserved in Sikasso relating that the Senufo, mostly elephant hunters, formerly inhabited the province of Massigui, in the current district of Bougouni. Having been driven out by overpopulation due to the Bambara invasion, they reportedly moved in search of new hunting grounds, some toward Sikasso, others toward Tengréla and the north of the Ivory Coast. Others were more or less absorbed by the Bambara, such as those who formerly populated the southeast of the Bougouni district, of whom only a few inhabitants of Niéné—

I do not know what credit should be given to these retrospective accusations of cannibalism, which are frequent in West Africa on the part of "civilized" peoples toward their more "backward" neighbors; it may well be, moreover, that they are well-founded regarding the Senufo (2), but I would not be far from admitting that they might be just as well-founded regarding the Banmana, the Diallonké, the Bobo, and the Gourounsi of former times. ### XI. Voltaic Peoples.

Like the Senufo, the peoples whose assembly constitutes the Voltaic family appear to be, as a whole, the oldest known inhabitants of the vast territory they currently occupy, which includes, generally speaking, all the regions belonging to the Volta basin, from the Hombori mountains in the North to the approaches of the forest zone in the South.

But it would not be accurate to say that each of these peoples has always inhabited the country they inhabit today: some seem not to have significantly changed locations since the most ancient times, like the Tombo <note>Often identified today as the Dogon people</note> and the Bobo; others on the contrary, although having originated in the current territory of the Voltaic family, owe their formation to sometimes prolonged migrations and occasionally multiple mixtures, like—

---

(1) Al-Bakri <note>original: "Bekri"; an 11th-century Andalusian geographer</note> (second half of the 11th century) says that, if one departs from the country of Gao following the "western edge of the river"—that is to say, the right bank of the Niger—and then moves away into the interior of the lands, "one arrives at the kingdom called the *Demdem*, whose inhabitants eat everyone who falls into their hands; they have a great king, who has viceroys under his orders; one sees in their country an enormous fortress on which is placed an idol having the form of a woman; the Demdem worship this idol and visit it on pilgrimage." It was thought that these Demdem of Al-Bakri could be the Tombo of Hombori, but perhaps they were rather the Mossi, whose empire had just begun at that time in Tenkodogo and who trace their origin to a famous princess <note>Yennenga, the legendary mother of the Mossi people</note>, buried in Gambaga: the tomb of this woman was for a long time a destination for pilgrimage (see further on).

### 1. *The Tombo Group (Tombo, Dogom, and Déforo).*

The Tombo and the Dogom <note>These groups are now more commonly known by the name Dogon</note> seem to have inhabited their current country from time immemorial. Arabic authors call this region either *El-hadjar* <note>original: "El-hadjar"; Arabic for "the land of stones"</note> or *Tombola* <note>original: "Tombola"; Mandé for "the land of the Tombo"</note> or even *Hombori* <note>Which has the same meaning in the Fula language</note>. Furthermore, they do not appear to have undergone major changes since their earliest origins, due to the unique nature of their geographic habitat. This environment protected them—better even than their own military prowess—against foreign invasions and the conquest attempts of the sovereigns of Mali, Gao, Yatenga, Ouagadougou, Massina, and the Pashas of Timbuktu. At most, it is reasonable to think that the Dogom of the plains were, in certain regions, more or less absorbed by invading populations, and that those who formerly lived in parts of Yatenga and Mossi country were forced to retreat northward under the pressure of the Mossi conquest.

Certain traditions seem to attribute a Mandé origin to the Tombo, or at least suggest that the Tombo—or a part of them—came from Mandé lands and took refuge in the cliffs of the Bend <note>The Niger Bend</note>. I believe these traditions concern only a small fraction of the current Tombo—those living near Bandiagara and San, between the mountains and the Bani River—and that they should be interpreted as meaning this fraction resulted from a mixture of the Tombo proper, the indigenous people of the mountains, and the Bozo people, who themselves came from Mandé country. Indeed, a legend relates that the Tombo of the Bandiagara escarpment, suffering from famine, sent a delegation to the Bozo of Mopti to implore their help; all the Bozo, men and women alike, went out to fish to provide the Tombo with food, leaving their children in the care of the Tombo envoys. It seems quite evident that by "Beni-Ham"—that is to say, "Hamites"—the author of the manuscript simply meant the Negroes, as opposed to the Peuls, the Arabs, and the Tuareg, to whom he collectively attributed a Semitic origin: his Beni-Ham of the mountains of the Bend were obviously the Tombo, while his Beni-Ham of the left bank were the Songhai. ### 2. *Mossi Group (Mossi, Yansi, Nankana, Gurma, Dagari, and Birifor).*

The group I have called Mossi contains a certain number of peoples who have very close affinities with each other from the point of view of physical type and language, but whose respective civilizations offer rather notable differences depending on whether they have undergone more or less political influence from the Empire of Ouagadougou or have escaped it entirely. In the nomenclature of the peoples of this group, I have mentioned only those who inhabit the Upper Senegal and Niger <note>A French colonial territory covering parts of modern Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger</note> in its entirety (Mossi, Yansi, Gurma, and Birifor) or in part (Nankana and Dagari); but the Mossi group also contains four other peoples whose habitat belongs to the British colony of the Gold Coast <note>Modern-day Ghana</note>: the *Gbanian* or *Gonja* or *Nta* (Bole region), the *Dagomba* or Dag-

If this hypothesis seems a bit bold, it is in any case almost certain that the country of the Dagomba and the Mampoursi was the starting point for invasions that headed toward the Northeast, North, Northwest, and West, establishing powerful states in Fada-n-Gourma, Ouagadougou, and Ouahigouya. These invasions, thanks to their conquests, greatly favored the extension of the Mossi group within the Niger Bend and the formation of the Mossi people proper, as well as the Gurmantché <note>original: "gourmantché"</note>, Yansi, Dagari, and Birifor <note>original: "birifo"</note> peoples.

According to several traditions collected in Ouahigouya, Ouagadougou, and Tenkodogo—traditions which present very remarkable agreements with one another—the oldest invasion of which memory has been preserved occurred at the beginning of the **11th** century of our era. These traditions, in fact, all count **22** generations (1) from this invasion until the present time: by estimating the average duration of each generation at forty years, one obtains the date of 1030 for the first event mentioned. <header>THE LEGEND OF THE DAGOMBA PRINCESS</header>

Thus, probably at the very beginning of the 11th century, a Dagomba chief named *Nédéga* reigned in Gambaga; he had united the Dagomba, the Mampoursi, and the Nankana under his scepter. One of his daughters, called *Yennenga* by some and *Poko* by others, was a remarkable warrior and led her father’s soldiers on raids. The latter, considering her more as a man than a woman and believing, moreover, that if she became a mother she could no longer march at the head of the armies, did not want her to marry—a situation that did not suit the young woman. One day, while she was conducting a raid against the Boussansé <note>An ethnic group living in what is now southeastern Burkina Faso</note> between Bitou and Tenkodogo, her horse bolted and carried her far from her troops. Having entered a thick forest, the animal was forced to slow its pace and eventually stopped in front of a hunter's hut. This hut was inhabited by a man named *Rialé* or *Riaré*, who, according to legend, was the son of a Malinké chief. Cheated out of his father’s succession by his brother, this Rialé had supposedly struck out alone into the bush to hunt elephants; traveling always toward the East, he had arrived in the vicinity of Bitou, where he had provisionally settled. Attracted by the gallop and neighing of Yennenga's horse, he emerged from his hut, steadied the animal, helped the princess to dismount, and offered her hospitality in his cabin. Yennenga fell in love with the hunter’s charms, gave herself to him, and did not wish to leave him.

They had a son; in memory of the equestrian adventure to which she owed her motherhood, Yennenga named her child *Ouidiraogo*—which means "stallion" <note>literally "male horse"</note> in the Dagomba and Mossi languages. When Ouidiraogo had become a young man, Yennenga dispatched a messenger to Gambaga to inform Nédéga that he had become a grandfather. Upon hearing this news...

Yennenga thus went to Gambaga with Rialé and Ouidiraogo; Nédéga received his daughter, son-in-law, and grandson very well and wished to keep them near him, but Rialé refused, saying that he would die if he lived anywhere other than in the forest. Nédéga let him depart with regret, along with Yennenga and Ouidiraogo, while giving him a gift of four horses and fifty oxen and entrusting the young Ouidiraogo with a large army of Dagomba soldiers so that he might march worthily in the footsteps of his mother and his grandfather.

Rialé returned to the forest near Bitou, where he continued to divide his life between elephant hunting and marital pleasures. After many years, Yennenga died: her body was transported to Gambaga, where she was buried. Her tomb became an object of great veneration and was a place of pilgrimage for the sovereigns of the Mossi until a recent era; upon the death of each <term>naba</term> <note>The title for a traditional king or chief among the Mossi people</note> of Ouagadougou, one of his horses and one of his wives were sent to Gambaga to be sacrificed to the spirits <note>original: "mânes," referring to the ancestral spirits</note> of Yennenga (1).

As for Ouidiraogo, at the head of his army, he seized the country from the Boussansé and established his residence in a place he called *Tankourou*, which has become the current *Tenkodogo*. Other Dagomba, attracted by his rising fame, constantly came to swell the number of his followers and increase the strength of his troops; the indigenous populations, who were sparse and very divided, soon recognized his authority. He had several sons, three of whom are known to us: *Zoungourana*, *Raoua*, and *Diaba*. He entrusted each of them with the command of one of the provinces of his nascent empire: Zoungourana received the government of the West, Raoua that of the North, and Diaba that of the East, and this was the origin of the—

All these regions, much less populated than today, were occupied mainly by the Gourounsi (the Boussansé in the Tenkodogo region, the Nounouma and Nioniossé near Ouagadougou, and the Nioniossé near Ouahigouya), the Dogom (in the regions of Ouahigouya, Ponssa, and Fada-n-Gourma), and some Bariba in the southeast of the current administrative district <note>The author uses the colonial term "cercle" to describe this administrative division</note> of Fada-n-Gourma. However, as we have seen, Zoungourana, the eldest son of Ouidiraogo, had remained at Tenkodogo, which was initially the seat of an empire of which the provinces of Oubritenga, Zandoma, and Fada-n-Gourma formed the vassal kingdoms: after some time, the province of Oubritenga became the Mossi empire

When Diaba took possession of the province of Fada N'Gourma, it was likely very sparsely inhabited: however, the Dogom <note>Likely referring to the Dogon people</note> must have been spread throughout the North and the Bariba in the East and South-East; the former were largely driven out toward Aribinda and became the Déforo, as we have seen previously; the others were partly pushed back toward the South but also partly absorbed by the Dagomba invaders, and from their mixture with the latter emerged the Bimba or Gourmantché people.

The Nankana people, who formed the leading edge of the group prior to the Dagomba invasion, do not seem to have considerably changed their character since ancient times.

As for the Birifo and the Dagari, they are the product of another push by the Dagomba, but in a westward direction this time, a push undoubtedly much later than the one from which the Mossi, the Yansi, and the Gourmantché emerged: according to traditions collected in the Gaoua district, it was only at the beginning of the 19th century that the Birifo and the Dagari finished occupying their current territory.

The Birifo are said to have originated from the mixture of a Dagomba invasion with the Lobi, which would explain why they closely resemble the latter in terms of character and customs, while they speak a language almost identical to the Dagomba language and very different from the Lobi language. This Dagomba invasion undoubtedly had its starting point on the banks of the White Volta, in the north of the Gold Coast <note>The colonial name for modern-day Ghana</note>: arriving at the Black Volta and having crossed it—perhaps toward the end of the 18th century—it infiltrated through the Pougouli and the Dian, dispossessing the latter of a portion of their

# ORIGIN OF THE BIRIFO AND THE DAGARI

Birifo people resulting from this Dagomba invasion had remained on the eastern bank of the Black Volta, where they are still found today, mixed with Dagari; the English call them, rather improperly, Lobi-Dagarti.

The Dagari appeared west of the Black Volta only after the Birifo, but they must have already existed for a long time east of the same river and likely originated from a Gbanian <note>Likely referring to the Gonja people</note> migration rather than a Dagomba one—a migration caused specifically by the conquests carried out by the Dagomba in the eastern Gbanian territory. The Dagari invasion did not, in fact, possess the warlike and conquering character of the various Dagomba invasions to which we owe the Mossi, the Yansi, the Gourmantché, and the Birifo; the current physical type of the Dagari is remarkably close to the Gbanian type. As for their language, it is barely distinguishable from Gbanian, which itself is very similar to Dagomba. In any case, the Dagari immigration to the west of the Black Volta was peaceful and slow, but irresistible; it undoubtedly began in the 18th century and continues even today: weaving through the Birifo, the Dagari settled wherever they found an open space, without however moving very far from the Volta, on the eastern side of which the bulk of their people remain. But one of their factions, that of the *Oulé*, more warlike in character than the others, advanced westward as far as the Diébougou district, pushing the Pougouli toward the northwest, and even penetrated the Koury and Ouagadougou circles until they met the Nounouma and the Soninké of Dafina. More recently, around 1850, a few Oulé families, called upon by the southern Dagari to support them against the Birifo, pushed a point southward along the Volta, settling in Goumparé (near Gaoua) and its surroundings.

THE PEOPLES

### **3. The Gourounsi Group** (*Nioniossé, Nounouma, Sissala, and Boussansé*).

As we saw earlier, it appears that prior to the 11th century, the peoples forming the Gourounsi group occupied almost all the territory between that of the Tombo and Dogom <note>Likely referring to the Dogon people</note> to the north and that of the Dagomba group (the future Mossi group) to the south. The warrior invasions coming from Dagomba <note>An ethnic group from present-day northern Ghana whose migrations led to the founding of several kingdoms</note> and the resulting formation of the Mossi, Yansi, and Gourmantché peoples significantly restricted the reach of the Gourounsi group and fragmented it. This fragmentation, as well as the absorption of many Gourounsi subgroups by the invaders, was made easier because the Gourounsi peoples lacked cohesion; they lived in small, scattered tribes prone to anarchy <note>In this context, "anarchy" refers to a decentralized or "acephalous" society without a single ruling king</note> and consequently offered no organized resistance.

The *Nioniossé* (also known as the Lilsé, Youlsé, Nimsé, etc.) inhabited the north of the current Ouagadougou district and the majority of the current Ouahigouya district. They had the Dogom as neighbors to the north and the Nounouma, Sissala, and Boussansé—three peoples very similar to their own—to the south. They seem to have been the first inhabitants of the triangle formed by Koury, Ouagadougou, and Ouahigouya. From a very remote era, they expanded outside this triangle (the ancient Kipirsi <note>A historical region in central Burkina Faso</note>) toward the northeast: well before the 11th century, a few Nioniossé families, under the leadership of a chief named *Ouéto*, had gone to settle in Djilgodi at Loroum (near Pobé). They did not remain there long, and Ouéto soon moved to settle in Bougouré (in the current Ouahigouya district), while his brother Ziguiri settled in Gambo and one of his sons in Rounga or Ronga (to the northeast and east of Ouahigouya). These families, who were the northernmost of the Nioniossé people, settled peacefully among the Dogom, who gave them land and lived with them in good understanding. Thus, little by little, the *Nioniossé* occupied the majority of the country that would later be called the Yatenga. We have seen that, during the formation of the Mossi empires, certain subgroups of the Nioniossé accepted the rule of the invaders while keeping their language and their

This is why today one encounters Nioniossé scattered among the Mossi from Yatenga <note>One of the oldest and most powerful Mossi kingdoms</note> to Kipirsi.

The *Nounouma*, before the Dagomba invasion, probably advanced further North and East than they do today: a large number of them were absorbed by the conquerors and provided their contingent to the formation of the Mossi people; the others, pushed back or maintained in their current country on the banks of the Black Volta <note>A major river flowing through Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, and Ghana</note> downstream from Koury, have remained more or less intact.

The *Sissala*, a small people of little importance, must have formerly joined the Boussansé toward the East: a push by the Nankana toward the North, following the expansion of the Dagomba, separated them from the Boussansé and restricted their territory to a very small province.

Finally, the *Boussansé*, as we have seen, allowed themselves to be conquered and assimilated by the Dagomba invaders North of Tenkodogo <note>A city considered the cradle of the Mossi kingdoms</note> (regions of Koupéla, Béloussa, Boussouma, etc.) to form the *Yansi*, while South of that same point they succeeded in preserving their nationality.

But many Nioniossé or Nounouma families wanted neither to accept the suzerainty of the Mossi nor to confine themselves to the small territory of Kipirsi, which was undoubtedly too narrow to hold all the migrants coming from the North: thus, exoduses occurred, the most important of which gave rise, as we shall see in a moment, to the Lobi group and the Koulango people, and others, less considerable, led to the formation of small isolated tribes of Gourounsi origin found in the Ivory Coast: that of the *Siti*, between Bouna and the Black Volta, and that of the *Dégha* (also called *Mo* or *Diammou*), between Bondoukou and the English border <note>Referring to the border with the Gold Coast, present-day Ghana</note>.

### 5th *Lobi Group (Pougouli, Dian, Gan, and Lobi).*

The *Pougouli* say they came from Kipirsi. Their traditions report that they originally belonged to the same group as the Nounouma—that is, the Gourounsi group—and that they emigrated from Kipirsi when this refuge of the independent Gourounsi became too narrow to contain them all, but following the emigration that gave rise to the Koulango (see further on), which is to say at the earliest toward the end of the 12th century. Crossing the Black Volta near the confluence of the Manouan-mâné (river of Manouan), which was called *Pougouliba* or *Bougouriba* <note>Meaning "River of the Pougouli"</note> by the Dioula because of them, they settled along the banks of this waterway. In the 18th century, under pressure from the Dagari and especially the Oulé, they moved further upstream and away from the Volta.

The *Dian*, who are hardly encountered today except in Diébougou and the surroundings of that town, came from Kipirsi like the Pougouli but after the latter, likely toward the end of the 13th century. They reportedly settled first in the region of Djifango, then, under the leadership of a chief named Konkouné, in the region of Loto, which they still occupy; they are said to have driven out the *Padorho*, of whom only a few representatives are found today in the west of the district of Gaoua and who were perhaps the indigenous people of the country (1).

***

(1) The identification of the *Padorho* has not yet been possible: they are generally linked to the Dorhossiè; some make them Sénoufo, others consider them Bobo.

-># THE DIAN, THE GAN, AND THE LOBI 317<-

Troubled in the 18th century by the invasion of the Oulé, the Dian called upon the Dioula of Bobo-Dioulasso, who sent them a small army commanded by Bé-Bakari Ouatara; the latter occupied Loto; some Dioula remained there, established lineages <note>original: "firent souche"</note>, and introduced Islam among the Dian. However, their overlordship was only effective in the region when a military column came from Bobo-Dioulasso to raid the country. Around 1820, a Dian family who had remained on the left bank of the Volta, at Lorha, had cause for complaint against the Dagari and came to seek refuge with their compatriots in Loto: it was this family that founded the present-day Diébougou.

The Gan were reportedly part of the same migration as the Dian and settled south of the Pougouli, in the center of the current district <note>original: "cercle," a French colonial administrative unit</note> of Gaoua. One of their principal villages was specifically Gaoua, which the natives still call *Gan-oura* today, which is said to mean "the Gan are here." They were supplanted in this region by the Lobi at a date that is difficult to specify, but which is certainly after the 13th century (the probable date of the Dian and Gan immigration) and before the formation of the Birifo people (17th century). Thus pushed toward the south by the Lobi, the Gan moved toward Lorhosso, which they occupied at the expense of the Lorho, the ancestors of the Koulango. These events must have taken place in the 14th century: this date would agree with the traditions that the administrator Mr. Benquey and I collected at Bondoukou (Ivory Coast) concerning the founding of a quarter of that city by Lorho fleeing the Gan, prior to the arrival of the Dioula from Bégho, which occurred in the 15th century. Currently, the Gan territory is reduced roughly to the town and the canton of Lorhosso, and their original physical type has been heavily altered, like that of the Dian, by mixing with the Dioula of Bobo-Dioulasso.

The Lobi, as I have just said, likely made their first appearance in their current country during the 14th century, also coming from Kipirsi. Having a more warlike character than the Pougouli, the Dian, and the Gan, it was by force of arms that they occupied the mountainous and gold-bearing <term>auriferous: containing gold</term> regions that border

### 6th Group or *Koulango* people.

This was the first of the Gourounsi migrations coming from Kipirsi which, toward the end of the 11th century, gave rise to the *Lorho* and subsequently to the *Koulango* or *Pakhalla* people. Crossing the current district <note>original: "cercle," a French colonial administrative unit</note> of Gaoua, the Lorho reportedly moved toward the southwest of this district and established themselves at a spot they named Lorhosso. When the Lobi invasion pushed the Gan toward this point in the 14th century, most of the Lorho emigrated south and went on to found Bouna and Bondoukou, spreading into the northeast of the Ivory Coast from the Black Volta to Kong and south to the edge of the dense forest, even penetrating the forest in certain places and forming the *Koulango* people. Some Lorho, however, remained in Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A French colonial territory in West Africa existing under this name from 1904 to 1921.</note>, notably at Lorho-péni, near and to the east of Lorhosso.

### 7th *Bariba* Group.

This group, which primarily concerns Dahomey <note>Modern-day Benin.</note>, nevertheless has some representatives in the district of Fada-n-Gourma; these representatives belong to two different peoples: the *Bariba* proper and the *Soumba*; the latter are, moreover, very few in Upper Senegal-Niger.

It appears that the Bariba were the ancient indigenous inhabitants, not only of their current country but also of a large part of the current district of Fada-n-Gourma: many merged with the Dagomba invaders to form the *Gourmantché* people; others moved further south and have roughly preserved their original characteristics, although the influence of the *Mossi* group on their civilization is quite perceptible.

# CHAPTER III

## Descriptive Ethnography.

I intend, in this chapter, to briefly address the primary external and moral characteristics of the various peoples of Upper Senegal-Niger <note>Haut-Sénégal-Niger; a former administrative territory of French West Africa, encompassing parts of modern-day Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger</note>, without having any intention of either exhausting the subject or even entering into great detail, which would require a long monograph for each group. I wish only to attempt to sketch in broad strokes the distinctive character of each people and the aspects common to several, from the triple perspective of physical appearance, housing and costume, and finally, mentality and lifestyle. I will not speak here of customs, which are the subject of the fifth part of this work: "Civilizations."

### I. — Physical Characteristics.

1° *Skin Coloration.* — The skin color of the natives of Upper Senegal-Niger is exceedingly variable, even within a given group, and can hardly provide useful indications regarding the ethnic affiliation of individuals. Assuredly, white coloration—or what is called such—is only found among the peoples of the white race, namely the Moors <note>original: "Maures"; refers to the Arab-Berber populations of the Sahara</note> of Azawad and Hodh, the Tuareg, and the Fulani <note>original: "Peuls"; a traditionally nomadic pastoralist group spread across West Africa</note>, but it is rare, even among individuals pure of any interbreeding with Black Africans, for this coloration to present the same appearance as in Europeans, or at least Europeans from the North or even the Center: apart from a few maraboutic <note>original: "maraboutique"; referring to families of Muslim religious scholars or leaders</note> fami-

<vocab>Ethnography, Upper Senegal-Niger, Moors, Azawad, Hodh, Tuareg, Fulani, coloration, physical characteristics</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces an ethnographic survey of the Upper Senegal-Niger region, focusing on the diversity of physical and moral traits among its peoples. The author notes that skin color is a highly variable and often unreliable indicator of ethnic origin, even among the "white" groups like the Moors, Tuareg, and Fulani.</summary>
<keywords>ethnography, physical anthropology, skin color, Moors, Tuareg, Fulani, Upper Senegal-Niger, Azawad, West African history</keywords>

--- Page 348 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on physical characteristics, specifically focusing on skin pigmentation as a factor of environment and interbreeding among the Moors, Tuareg, Fulani, and various Black African groups.</meta>

<header>THE PEOPLES</header>

...those who live in a sedentary state and inhabit houses from which they rarely emerge, the Moors and the Tuareg of pure Arab or Berber origin are all more or less swarthy <note>original: "basanés"</note>—no more so, however, than many peasants from Mediterranean countries. However, it should be noted that the relatively dark tint of their skin is due primarily to the effects of the sun and the open air, for the parts of their body usually covered by clothing are notably lighter than those generally exposed. Among the Fulani <note>original: "Peuls"; a traditionally nomadic pastoralist group</note>, whose poverty has prevented them from acquiring Black slaves and has thus preserved them from interbreeding <note>original: "métissage"; a term used historically to describe the mixing of different ethnic groups</note>, the tint is perhaps a bit darker than among the Moors and Tuareg of pure race, yet this tint does not differ significantly from that of many Southern Italians.

But the number of mixed-race individuals is naturally considerable among these various peoples, especially among the Moors and the Fulani, not to mention the Harratin <note>Social group of the Sahara and Sahel, often traditionally agricultural workers for Moorish masters</note>, Bella <note>A social class of the Tuareg, traditionally of servile origin</note>, and Rimaibe <note>A social class of the Fulani, traditionally of servile origin</note> of purely Black origin who live among them. Consequently, every coloration is encountered, from the lightest to the darkest, and many Moors, Tuareg, Fulani—or those claiming to be such—are as black as the Bambara <note>original: "Banmana"</note> or the Mossi.

Among the peoples of the Black race—setting aside albinos as representing a purely pathological case—skin coloration is also quite varied. First of all, one must take interbreeding into account for them just as with the peoples of the White race: certain Arma <note>The "Arma" are descendants of the Moroccan invaders who conquered the Niger Bend in the late 16th century</note> of Timbuktu, certain Soninké, and Toucouleurs owe a relatively light tint to Moroccan, Moorish, or Fulani ancestors. This leads them to be given the same name of "red men" that the natives of the Sudan <note>The term "Sudan" here refers to the "Bilad al-Sudan" (Land of the Blacks), a broad geographic region south of the Sahara, not the modern country of Sudan</note> generally apply to Moors and even to Europeans. But outside of this special circumstance, the coloration of purely Black groups is far from homogeneous. Generally speaking, the Black populations of the Sahel and the Sudanese zone, when they have not been influenced by White populations, have a notably darker complexion than those of the forest zone; it would not be impossible for this difference to be due to the effects of the sun, which must naturally be more...

**3º Hair.** — The *Moors*, the *Tuareg*, and the unmixed *Fulani* <note>original: "Peuls"</note> have straight hair; the other peoples of the Upper Senegal-Niger all have tightly curled <note>original: "crépus"</note> hair: here, the distinction between populations of the white race and populations of the black race is very clear, much clearer than that resulting from pigmentation or facial features. I believe that if one encounters a Black person whose hair is straight or nearly straight, one can say with certainty that they had ancestors of the white race, and conversely, any White person having somewhat curled hair had ancestors of the black race.

It is especially in the way of wearing the hair that one can note differences—no longer natural, but acquired—between the various peoples or ethnic groups. Regarding the men, one generally finds the hair shaved or worn short among the *Moors* of the *Azaouad*, the *Tuareg*, the *Toucouleur*, the *Songhai*, the *Bozo*, the *Soninke*, the *Khassonke*, the *Mossi*, and the *Yansi*; the *Moors* of the *Hodh* — except in a few Maraboutic <note>relating to Muslim religious leaders or scholars</note> families — wear their hair long and bushy; the *Fulani* generally braid their hair, as do the *Malinke* and the *Foulanké*; among the other peoples of the Upper Senegal-Niger, some (*Dyula, Kagoro, Bambara, Dialonke, Samo, Samorho, Sia*) usually shave their heads but often also wear braided hair; others (*Senufo, Tombo, Dogon <note>original: "Dogom"</note>, Deforo, Bobo*) sometimes shave and sometimes wear their hair long, either loose or braided or plaited into a crest; still others shave it while keeping a tuft at the top of the head (*Nankana, Gourmantché, Dagara*) or else braid it into thin plaits or parallel ridges adhering to the skull (*Birifor, Gurunsi, Lobi*).

### 4° *Mutilations.* — The excision of the clitoris <note>a form of female genital cutting</note> among women is, I believe, absolutely universal among all the white and black populations of the Upper Senegal-Niger, except perhaps among the Tuareg, regarding whom I do not possess precise information on this matter, and also among a few rare Fulani subgroups. The age at which it is practiced varies according to the people: among the Moors, girls are operated upon on the seventh day after birth; it is done around the age of three among the Fulani and the Soninke; slightly later (around four years old) among the Toucouleur; and generally at the time of puberty (around ten or twelve years old), or even only at the time of their marriage, among other peoples.

The circumcision of boys, although very widespread, is not universal like the excision of girls; it is practiced among the Moors and the Tuareg around the age of 7; among the Fulani, the Soninke, the Toucouleur, the Songhai, the Bozo, the Jula, the Kagoro, the Bambara, the Khassonke, the Malinke, the Foulanke, the Jalonke <note>original: "Diallonké"</note>, the Samo, the Samorho, the Sia, the Dogon <note>original: "Tombo"</note>, the Dogom, the Deforo, the Mossi, the Yansi, and the Gourmantche, it is practiced between 8 and 12 years of age, roughly at the time of puberty. Furthermore, the mark of a people or a tribe has often been adopted by members of another people or tribe, or imposed upon slaves of foreign origin, so that an individual’s tattoo is not an absolutely certain indication of the ethnic group to which they belong.

**The tent**, made of wool or cotton cloth, sometimes of skins, is used only by the Moors and occasionally by the Tuareg, though the latter hardly use it except when traveling as a temporary shelter.

**The hemispherical hut**, which is merely an intermediate stage between the tent and a proper house, is found among the Tuareg, the Fulani <note>original: "Peuls"</note>, and the Songhai. Among the former, it is built using skins or mats resting on a framework of branches; among the second, it is made of grass or mats also held up by branches; among the third, it is made primarily of mats, sometimes covered with straw at the top. The fully sedentary Fulani also make use of cylindrical huts with conical roofs, as do certain Songhai; the noble class in the cities of the latter generally live in terrace houses. It is also worth noting that the straw hemispherical hut, often in the shape of a beehive, is used by all populations of the Sudan <note>In this context, "Sudan" refers to the broad Sahelian and savanna region of West Africa, not the modern nation of Sudan.</note> to construct the provisional villages built in the middle of plantations during the farming season, as well as to serve as shelter for hunters, charcoal burners, ferrymen, etc. Everywhere it has the character of a temporary dwelling. In regions where palmyra palms <term>roniers: African fan palms (Borassus aethiopium)</term> are found, the straw is often replaced by palm fronds.

**The cylindrical hut**, built of clay—either raw or shaped into crude bricks—and topped with a conical straw roof with a framework of wood, bamboo, or raffia ribs, is certainly the most widespread type of dwelling throughout the Western Sudan. It is adopted almost exclusively by the Toucouleur, the Kagoro, the Khassonke, the Mandinka <note>original: "Malinké"</note>, the Foulanke, the Jalonke <note>original: "Diallonké"</note>, the Mossi, the Yansi, the Gurma <note>original: "Gourmantché"</note>, the Dian, the Gan, and the Lorho, and it is also found very frequently alongside other modes of construction among the sedentary Fulani, certain Songhai, and many...

# THE DWELLINGS

The *double-cylindrical hut with an egg-shaped <note>ovoid</note> roof*, actually composed of two cylindrical huts joined at their center, is only found, I believe, among the Sénoufo: very frequent among the portion of this people inhabiting the Ivory Coast, it is rarer among the Sénoufo of Upper Senegal-Niger, who generally prefer either the ordinary cylindrical hut, the terrace house, or the rectangular flat-roofed house.

The *rectangular house with a flat roof* is distinguished from the terrace house in that its roof—very often slightly rounded—is not intended to serve as a place of residence, even temporarily, although it sometimes consists of a true terrace supported by a frame of wooden logs. This type of dwelling varies enormously depending on the location and the people. This house is found among the Tombo of the mountains, where it is generally built of dry stone, often supports a second story, is adorned with carved doors and windows, and frequently utilizes a natural cave or a cliff face to form one or more of its sides, and sometimes its roof, just as is practiced among us in certain regions of Touraine <note>A historical province of France famous for its "troglodyte" homes carved into limestone cliffs</note>; it is also found: among the Dogom <note>likely the Dogon</note>, with walls made primarily of rectangular bricks; among the Déforo, whose villages are perched on rocks or hillocks, with a slightly rounded roof; among the Bobo and some of the Sénoufo, with a roof composed of a layer of wood, a layer of straw, and a layer of clay laid one on top of the other, and with a kind of veranda on one of its sides; among the Dian, with a straw roof that is sometimes no longer flat but has two slopes.

These terrace houses form almost the exclusive type of dwelling in the few towns or villages of the Hodh and Azawad <note>regions in the Saharan-Sahelian transition zone</note> and in the large cities near the Niger in the Saharan and Sahelian regions, regardless of the composition of their population (Timbuktu, Djenné, etc.); they are generally more comfortable and elegant in these latter cities than in the Hodh and Azawad and often feature a second story. They are also very common in all towns, even modest ones, inhabited by the Bozo, the Soninké, or the Dioula, and have often been adopted by the Samorho, the Sia, and the Sénoufo; finally, they constitute, alongside cylindrical huts, the most widespread type of dwelling among the Bamana <note>also known as the Bambara</note>.

The main dwelling is generally low, sometimes with the floor situated below the level of the surrounding ground; it serves primarily as a food store, a stable, or a refuge in case of rain or danger. The Moors of the Azawad are generally recognizable by the fact that they cover their heads with a piece of fabric rolled into a turban, while the Moors of the Hodh almost always go bareheaded, with the exception of certain marabouts <note>Muslim religious leaders or scholars</note>; both groups, at least when traveling, are usually dressed in a fairly short *boubou* <note>A flowing, wide-sleeved robe</note>, often tightened at the waist by a belt, frequently reduced to a simple sleeveless blouse, and generally do not wear trousers. — The Tuareg are characterized by the veil worn by the men <note>The *tagelmust*, an indigo-dyed litham that serves both practical and social purposes</note>, which allows only the eyes and part of the nose to be seen, and by their long trousers ending at the ankles. — The Fulani <note>Original: "Peuls"</note> generally wear a blouse tightened at the waist, with or without trousers, or a simple *pagne* <note>A length of fabric wrapped around the body; a wrapper</note> with one end thrown over the left shoulder; they go bareheaded or wear a white cotton frustum-shaped cap <note>A cap shaped like a cone with the top cut off</note>; their women wear the *pagne* tied around the hips. — The Toucouleurs are generally very well-dressed: a large *boubou* and trousers, and a white frustum-shaped cap; their women wear the *pagne* and, in addition, a very loose blouse. — The Songhai generally wear trousers and a blouse, and often the turban and the Tuareg veil; their women, at least in the poor and middle classes, wear only the *pagne*. — The Bozo and the Soninké dress much like the Toucouleurs. — The Dioula wear a short blouse or a *boubou* in addition to trousers; their cap generally has the shape of a Neapolitan cap <note>A soft, conical stocking cap</note> and their hats have a base that is sometimes conical and sometimes hemispherical; their women wear the *pagne*. — The Kâgoro, the Bambara <note>Original: "Bannmana"</note>, the Khassonké, the Malinké, the Foulanké, the Diallonké, the Samo, the Samorho, and the Sia generally wear a short blouse, trousers, and a cap surmounted or not by a...

3. *Adornment.* — Adornment, especially among women, is more varied than clothing and is also more specialized according to country and tribe. However, the scope of this work does not permit me to treat this subject exhaustively, and I must content myself with pointing out certain particularly characteristic customs relating to tattoos or mutilations that are ornamental rather than ethnic.

Among the peoples of the North (**Moors**, **Tuareg**, **Fulani** <note>original: "Peuls"</note>, **Toucouleur**, **Songhai**, **Bozo**, **Soninké**), as well as among the **Dioula**, the women very frequently blue their lips and eyelids with antimony <note>original: "antimoine"; a mineral-based pigment used similarly to kohl for cosmetic and protective purposes</note>. — Among the **Songhai**, many men and women wear rings in their ears and in the nasal septum. — Among the **Bambara** <note>original: "Banmana"</note>, a large number of women have a copper or silver ring passed through the nasal septum, and many men have a pierced ear. — The same fashions exist among the **Senufo**; furthermore, among the latter, the women frequently wear in their ears either a simple leather cord decorated with cowries <note>original: "cauries"; small seashells used throughout West Africa as both currency and decoration</note>, or a whole series of small copper rings covering the entire rim and the lobe; often they also have a small copper loop in each nostril and a quartz cone, set point-down, in the lower lip. — Among the **Dagari**, the women insert a small stick or a simple stalk of straw into the upper lip, and sometimes into both; the same is true among the **Nunuma**, the **Sissala**, and most of the **Bobo**. — Among the **Birifor** <note>original: "Birifo"</note> and the **Lobi**, it is a disk of ivory or stone that the women lodge in each lip.

I must add that, independently of the facial scarifications of which I spoke above, and even among peoples who do not wear them, it is exceedingly common to encounter, on individuals of both sexes, small scars in the form of raised dots that decorate the back of the neck, the chest, the belly, the lower back, the arms, or the thighs. 4. *Weaponry.* — The flintlock rifle <note>original: "fusil à pierre"</note> has been imported in such quantities into West Africa since the 17th century, either through Morocco or from the coasts, that it is currently spread almost everywhere. Percussion rifles <note>original: "fusils à piston"; a more modern firearm for the time, using a percussion cap rather than flint</note>, though rarer, are nonetheless found in fairly large numbers. Despite this, many populations, especially in the Niger Bend <note>the great curve of the Niger River as it flows through modern-day Mali</note>, have remained faithful to the weapons of their ancestors. These weapons are: the lance, still widespread today among the **Tuareg**, the **Fulani** <note>original: "Peuls"</note>, the **Songhai**, and the **Bariba**, and also among many other peoples for whom it is now little more than an ornament or an insignia of command; the bow and arrows with tips of hardwood or iron, poisoned or not, still in use among the **Bambara** <note>original: "Banmana"</note>, the **Senufo**, and the **Mossi**, but especially among the **Samo**, the **Dagari**, the **Birifor** <note>original: "Birifo"</note>, the various **Gurunsi** peoples, the **Bobo**, the **Lobi**, the **Bariba**, and the **Soumba**; the war club <note>original: "casse-tête"</note>, in use primarily among the **Senufo** and the peoples of the Voltaic family <note>referring to groups speaking Voltaic/Gur languages around the Volta River basin</note>; the wooden throwing knife, which is hardly encountered—at least I believe so—except among certain **Senufo** of the **Bobo-Dioulasso** district (and the **Korhogo** district of the Ivory Coast), and iron throwing knives still in use among the **Bariba**. As for swords and sabers, they exist almost everywhere, but hardly constitute true weapons except in the hands of the **Tuareg**: among the other peoples of the Upper Senegal-Niger, they are primarily objects for parade or display, although a certain number of murders are committed using the saber, as they also are, for that matter, with the woodcutter's axe or the simple hoe of the farmers.

But many also bear the stamp of the ethnic origin of each people or of the geographical, economic, political, social, and religious environment in which they have evolved and which has contributed powerfully to their formation. And this is of considerable importance, particularly for those who are called upon to administer these various peoples.

I will seek, in the lines that follow, to summarize in a few words the most striking characteristics of each of the groups or peoples of the Upper Senegal-Niger, from the dual perspective of the intellectual and the moral, while further indicating their way of life and special aptitudes. I have no illusions about how flawed or incomplete this sketch may be, but I do not believe, however, that I am straying far from the truth as a whole. It remains understood that my observations apply only to the mass of each group or people and that it is necessary to take into account, there as elsewhere, local, tribal, and individual exceptions.

The ***Moors of Azawad*** <note>The Azawad is a vast desert region north of Timbuktu</note>, more distinctly Semitic <note>The author uses "Semitic" here in a nineteenth-century racial sense to denote groups with Arab linguistic and cultural heritage</note> than those of the Hodh, are also more exclusively nomadic; primarily herders and <term>Marabouts</term> <note>Muslim religious leaders and teachers who often wield significant social influence</note> in the case of the **Kounta**, and mainly guides and caravan escorts or salt merchants in the case of the **Bérabich**, they easily transform into warriors or highwaymen when their needs or circumstances demand it. The Bérabich, who are considered to have the most predatory instincts of all, are perhaps nonetheless more easily disciplined and will more readily transform themselves into constables on the day—soon to come—when they find it in their interest; meanwhile, the Kounta, who have never ceased to have political designs, will find it more difficult to accept no longer playing an active role in the destinies of the Timbuktu region.

The ***Moors of the Hodh*** <note>A region spanning the border of modern-day Mauritania and Mali</note> form an amalgam as variegated from a moral point of view as from a physical one: the Arab element, represented by the **Beni Hassan**, seems to have no other goal than war—holy war <note>original: "guerre sainte"</note> against the infidels or simple <term>razzia</term> <note>A rapid raid or plundering expedition</note> carried out with a view to appropriating the harvests of sedentary populations or the herds—

# MOORS, TUAREG, AND FULANI

...the skins of the shepherds; the Berber element, certainly more numerous but generally reduced to a more or less marked state of <term>vassalage</term> <note>A social hierarchy similar to feudalism, where "vassal" groups provide tribute or services to dominant "warrior" groups</note>, is primarily engaged in livestock raising and trade. Finally, the mixed element, which constitutes the <term>Maraboutic</term> <note>Religious families descended from Islamic teachers and scholars</note> families—often possessing a higher intellectual culture than one might be inclined to believe—relies sometimes on the warriors and sometimes on the shepherds, depending on the interests of the moment. They contribute, moreover, to the general wealth through their numerous serfs, who are cultivators and artisans. Fervent Muslims for the most part, the Moors of the Hodh <note>A region in present-day southeastern Mauritania</note> are nevertheless generally monogamous, by tradition rather than by necessity.

Practicing a very mitigated form of Islam <note>The author implies that their religious practice was less orthodox or strictly followed than in other regions</note>, except within the Maraboutic families or sub-tribes, the Tuareg are characterized above all by a spirit of independence and a touchy pride that has become legendary. Even more exclusively monogamous than the Moors, they show a deference toward women that results in giving them a very considerable social importance; from this, no doubt, comes their reputation as a chivalrous people—a reputation which, in other respects, has not always been verified in practice. The Tuareg are, it seems, nomadic only by necessity and not by atavistic instinct; it is permissible to suppose that, should political events lead to a modification of economic conditions, a great number of them would return, as soon as they are able, to the semi-pastoral and semi-agricultural life led formerly by their ancestors in North Africa, and which is still led today by their cousins in the Algerian and Moroccan Atlas Mountains.

The ***Peuls*** <note>Commonly known in English as the Fulani or Fula people</note> are equally remarkable for their independent character, but their pride is not such that it has not bent many times, even to the point of making them accept a life as servants and almost pariahs among the Negroes <note>The author uses "Nègres" in the nineteenth-century sense to refer to the sedentary, dark-skinned agriculturalist populations of the region</note>. It seems that, provided they are left to live as they please and that there is no intervention in their internal affairs, the Fulani accept any social or political situation. The most devout Muslims among them feel no repugnance at hiring themselves out as shepherds in the service of an infidel <note>A non-Muslim</note> owner, nor even at providing warrior contingents to a pagan prince.

More intelligent than the <term>Peuls</term> <note>The Fulani people</note> regarding material matters, they have, on the other hand, a much less developed capacity for the conception of abstract ideas, and they could neither elaborate upon nor perhaps even understand certain poetic reveries to which the Fulani are accustomed. <margin>----</margin>
The *Songhai*, by the way they present themselves today, contradict the brilliant role that some have attributed to them in the history of the Sudan. In truth, this history unfolded in their land but almost without them: they contributed little to making it and played hardly more than a passive role. If one excepts the <term>Sorko</term> caste <note>A group traditionally known as masters of the river, specialized in fishing and boating</note> and the—admittedly small—caste of hunters, both of whom have always possessed predatory and conquering instincts and provided useful contingents to the emperors of <term>Gao</term> <note>The capital of the Songhai Empire</note>, the Songhai have never constituted a warrior or dominant people. The so-called Songhai Empire was governed in turn by <term>Berber</term> princes and <term>Soninké</term> princes, to say nothing of the eras when it paid tribute or ransom to the <term>Mandingues</term>, the <term>Mossi</term>, and the <term>Tuareg</term>. The rare powerful sovereigns who gave some prestige to this empire owed their strength to an army recruited from all over—even among the Songhai, but mainly among captives of <term>Mossi</term>, <term>Bariba</term>, and <term>Banmana</term> <note>Bambara</note> origin. It was enough for <term>Pasha Judar</term> <note>A Moroccan military leader of Spanish origin who led the 1591 expedition that toppled the Songhai Empire</note> to appear with a few hundred muskets to see this famous Songhai Empire vanish into thin air, whereas later, Sultan <term>Er-Rachid</term> <note>Moulay al-Rashid, a 17th-century Sultan of Morocco</note> did not even dare to measure himself against the army of the rising Bambara Empire. The mass of the Songhai people, composed of defenseless farmers of mediocre intellectual value, was constantly the unfortunate plaything of invasions, <term>razzias</term> <note>Rapid military raids or slave-raiding expeditions</note>, and palace revolutions that desolated the banks of the lower and middle Niger until...

The fact that their language became the commercial language of the middle Niger—the language of Timbuktu and Djenné—is in no way due to a dominating or "civilizing" character (which was never a trait of the Songhai); it is primarily due to the extraordinary simplicity of this language <note>The Songhai language is noted by linguists for its relatively simple grammar compared to neighboring languages, which facilitated its use as a "lingua franca" or trade language</note> and also to the fact that it was the idiom of the boatmen, through whose hands all commercial transactions of the region necessarily had to pass.

The *Northern Mandé* form, from a mental and social point of view, a nearly homogeneous group, in which the *Bozo* <term>Bozo</term> <note>An ethnic group traditionally specializing in fishing and river transport, often called "masters of the river"</note> constitute a special fraction—of little numerical importance, moreover—a fraction that became a distinct people but which was likely, in the beginning, only a sort of caste of navigators and fishermen analogous to that of the *Somono* <term>Somono</term> <note>An ethnic group or caste of river-dwellers, often associated with the Bambara people</note> among the *Central Mandé*. # THE MANDÉ PEOPLES

->347<-

The Soninke and the Dioula are called upon, more than others, to contribute to the spread of new ideas and, because of this, they can be either useful or harmful to us, depending on the nature of the current <note>Referring to social, political, or religious movements</note> they believe they have an interest in spreading.

It is with them that the list of the peoples of the Upper Senegal-Niger <term>Haut-Sénégal-Niger</term> <note>A French colonial territory in West Africa existing in the early 20th century, covering parts of modern Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso</note> who have been won over by Islamic influence ends; a list which, in reality, includes only the Moors, the Tuareg, the Toucouleur, the Songhai, and the majority of the Peuls <note>Also known as the Fula or Fulani</note> and the Northern Mandé. One certainly still encounters a few Muslims among the Central Mandé and, here and there, among other populations, but these are nothing more than tiny groups or even individual exceptions. Generally speaking, one can say that Islamic civilization has never deeply touched the peoples we are now going to review, and that, most of the time, it has not even grazed them. They therefore represent more of the primitive Sudanese <note>In this context, "Sudanese" refers to the "Bilad al-Sudan" or "Land of the Blacks," the historical geographical region south of the Sahara, rather than the modern nation of Sudan</note> type, both morally and physically.

*The Central Mandé* as a whole offer a less perfect homogeneity than the Northern Mandé, perhaps simply because they are much more numerous and had to separate, from the very beginnings of the historical period, into various currents of political and social development. All of them, however, have in common—along with all the other non-Islamized Blacks of the Sudan—a very deep attachment to their native soil and, whatever their differences of character, all are first and foremost farmers; those who have remained the most primitive and the most individualistic, like certain Malinké, are also hunters. Trade seems to be held in little honor among them and generally does not exceed the limits of purely local exchanges necessitated by daily food needs; on the other hand, manual professions—whether they remain the privilege of special castes or are open to all—absorb a notable part of their activity. Deeply attached to the soil, patient and methodical workers, with simple and unrefined tastes, resigned with fatalism, they submit easily to the orders of authority as to the blows of fate when they cannot do otherwise, but evade them through flight or passive resistance <note>original: "force d'inertie"</note> when they have the opportunity. They are subject to fits of wild anger, as often happens to people who are usually cold and calm; they possess an intelligence generally below average but are capable of being cultivated and progressing in contact with a favorable environment. While very backward in terms of external civilization, they are skillful with their hands and apt for industrial <note>In this context, manual crafts and manufacturing</note> as well as agricultural work. On the other hand, they are less suited to commercial operations. Above all calm and patient, they constitute a people eminently suited to provide a labor force that lacks initiative but is easily directed, which is what the development of a new country needs most of all.

# CHAPTER ONE

## **Classification and distribution of the languages of Upper Senegal-Niger**

### **I. — Nomenclature and classification**

I have spoken sufficiently, I believe, regarding the historical formation of the various languages of Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A former administrative territory of French West Africa (1904–1921), covering parts of modern-day Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.</note>, while treating the origins of the peoples, so as not to have to return to it here; for the moment, I shall content myself with examining these idioms as they currently exist and researching how they ought to be classified.

As I had the opportunity to state above, a linguistic classification is much easier to establish than an ethnic classification; if the one I am about to propose regarding Upper Senegal-Niger can only be considered a provisional draft, this is solely due to the still too rudimentary state of our documentation regarding a certain number of languages and dialects.

I thought it necessary to adopt a terminology that corresponds, at least in the majority of cases, to that used in my ethnic classification. I have therefore divided the various idioms into several *linguistic families* which may be subdivided into *groups*, the latter being composed of *languages* which, in turn, include *dialects* and *sub-dialects*.

By “*linguistic family*,” I mean a set of languages

<note>original: "Haut-Sénégal-Niger, classification linguistique, classification ethnique, idiomes, familles linguistiques, groupes, langues, dialectes, sous-dialectes"</note>

<summary>The author introduces a systematic framework for classifying the languages of the Upper Senegal-Niger region, modeling the linguistic hierarchy after his previous ethnic classifications. <keywords>Upper Senegal-Niger, linguistic classification, West African languages, language families, dialects, colonial linguistics</keywords>

--- Page 376 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's definition of a "linguistic family," establishing a hierarchical system for classifying speech that mirrors his ethnic classifications of West African peoples.</meta>

->THE LANGUAGES<-

which, although often very different from one another from a grammatical point of view and especially in terms of vocabulary, can nevertheless all be traced back to a common origin and present clearly defined shared principles. It may happen that a family has never ceased to maintain a perfect homogeneity; it can also happen that, over the course of the ages—either as a result of differences in the environments in which its various branches evolved, or because of foreign influences that have exerted more or less pressure depending on the location—various currents have formed within the same family. The outcomes of these currents constitute what I call "groups": the initial origin of the various groups within a family is common, but the formation of each has been accomplished according to a specific process.

I call a "language" an idiom <note>Here, "idiom" refers to a specific form of speech or a distinct language variety.</note> that has sufficient characteristics to maintain its own existence among neighboring languages and form a separate unit; the different languages of the same group, and even those of two groups of the same family, are obviously related, both by their vocabulary and by their syntax and morphology. However, they nonetheless constitute distinct idioms, to such a point that an individual speaking one of these languages will not understand—unless they have undertaken special study or had prolonged contact—people speaking one of the others. But two idioms presenting between them only superficial differences—differences consisting of expressions or phrases of a purely local specialization and, above all, phonetic variations—do not constitute two distinct languages: they are no more than "dialects" of the same language; two individuals speaking each one of these dialects will be able, with more or less ease, to understand each other, at least in general terms, from their first contact. Finally, even less profound and even more localized differences only manage to constitute simple "sub-dialects."

Generally speaking, though not absolutely, a linguistic family most often corresponds to an ethnic family, a linguistic group to an ethnic group, a language to a people, and a dialect to a tribe or a geographic fraction.

<vocab>linguistic family, groups, language, dialects, sub-dialects, ethnic family, people, tribe</vocab>

# CLASSIFICATION TERMS

of a people, a sub-dialect to a sub-tribe or sub-fraction. But I cannot stress enough that such a correspondence is currently subject to many exceptions: indeed, a given people or a fraction of a people, belonging as a whole to a specific ethnic family, may perfectly well have abandoned its own language to adopt that of a people belonging to another family. I will cite only two typical cases: that of the Peuls <note>Also known as the Fulani or Fula people.</note> of Semitic origin who today speak a Negro language <note>The author uses the historical term "langue nègre" to refer to the languages of Sub-Saharan Africa.</note>, and that of the Soninké of Djenné who now speak only Songhai. On the other hand, an originally single people may have subdivided into several now-distinct peoples, without the mother tongue having subdivided into anything more than simple dialects: this is the case with the Banmana <note>The Bambara people.</note>, the Malinké, and the Dioula, who together constitute three different peoples from an ethnic point of view, even though the idioms spoken by them are merely dialects of the same language. Finally, it can happen that two tribes not belonging to the same people speak two sub-dialects of the same dialect, while two tribes of the same people may speak two dialects so different that they almost deserve to be considered two distinct languages: some Malinké of Wassoulou, for example, speak—with barely perceptible differences—the same dialect as the Dioula, while certain Malinké of the Gambia speak a dialect clearly distinct from the Malinké of the upper Niger. There is a whole series of quite complex phenomena here in which historical, geographical, and especially economic reasons have played a far more significant role than purely ethnic causes.

I must also point out that a linguistic family, like an ethnic family, may very well consist of only a single group; sometimes it even comprises only a single language. Other times, we will encounter families which, although rich in groups and languages, are represented in the region we are considering by only one of their groups or by one of their languages.

All are Negro languages, but that is their only common bond. ### LINGUISTIC FAMILIES

In any case, my personal studies have led me to distribute among seven distinct linguistic families the languages currently spoken by the natives of the civil colony of Upper Senegal-Niger <note>A former administrative territory of French West Africa, covering much of modern-day Mali, Burkina Faso, and southern Niger.</note>. This total may seem enormous, but it will not surprise those who have studied the question on the spot and who know what a Tower of Babel West Africa is. Furthermore, the colony of Upper Senegal-Niger is relatively less richly endowed, in terms of language diversity, than certain other neighboring colonies; the Ivory Coast in particular, to which barely more than two million inhabitants are attributed, is home to six distinct linguistic families on its own, without counting foreign languages.

(1) I have distinguished the three groups of the Mandé family by giving each as a name the word most generally used in the languages of that group to express the number "ten"; I do not mean to suggest at all that these different ways of saying the number "ten" are the defining characteristic of the differences separating the three groups: these are simply names that seemed convenient to me and likely to objectively represent the thing they are intended to represent, in the same way that the names <term>langues d'oc</term> and <term>langues d'oïl</term> <note>Historical names for the southern and northern dialects of France, named after their respective words for "yes" (*oc* vs. *oïl*).</note> are used in our country.

B. *mossi group* (four languages spoken in <term>Upper Senegal-Niger</term> <note>A former administrative territory of French West Africa, covering parts of modern Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger.</note>: *môrhé* or *mossi* (to which the mossi dialect spoken by the *Samo* and the dialect of the *Yansi* are linked), *gourmantché*, *nankana*, and *dagari* (to which the *birifo* dialect is linked) (1);
C. *gourounsi group* (three languages spoken in Upper Senegal-Niger: *nounouma* (to which the dialect of the *Nioniossé* is likely linked), *sissala*, and *boussansé*) (2);
D. *bobo group*, containing only one language, *bobo* (four dialects: *kian*, *tara*, *boua*, and *niénigué*);
E. *lobi group*: two languages, *lobi* and *dian*, plus two dialects, *gan* and *pougouli*, which are likely related to the dian language;
F. *koulango group*: a single language, *koulango*, represented in Upper Senegal-Niger by the *lorho* dialect;
G. *bariba group*: two languages spoken in Upper Senegal-Niger, *bariba* and *soumba*, the latter represented by the *takamba* dialect (3).
8º the *Senegalese family*, represented by one of its groups, the *wolof group*, which itself includes only one language, *wolof*, spoken in Upper Senegal-Niger by fairly numerous wolof settlements (4);
9º the *Niger-Logone family* (5), represented by the main—

(1) Outside of Upper Senegal-Niger, the mossi group possesses on the <term>Gold Coast</term> <note>The British colony that became modern-day Ghana.</note> *dagomba*, *gbanian*, *boura* or *frafra*, and *mampoursi*; it is probable that the first two of these four idioms are dialects belonging to the same language as dagari and that the other two are dialects belonging to the same language as nankana — I have reasons to believe that the Samo, in addition to a dialect of the mossi language, possess a special idiom that should perhaps be linked to the Mandé family.
(2) Belonging to the same group are the *siti* and the *dégha* of the Ivory Coast.
(3) This group is primarily represented in <term>Dahomey</term> <note>Now the Republic of Benin.</note> and Togo, as much by bariba and soumba as by other languages or dialects (*kaouri* or *kabré*, *kotokoli*, *pila-pila*, *ouindji-ouindji*, etc.).
(4) The other group or *Serer group* includes *kéguem* or Serer proper and *none*, spoken only in Senegal.
(5) I give it this name because its domain extends, in a general manner, from the lower Niger to the Logone, a tributary of Lake Chad.

## II. — **Geographic, Ethnic, and Numerical Distribution (1).**

We will now examine which ethnic groups the languages and dialects listed above serve as national idioms, and at the same time, the specific geographic range of each family or linguistic group; we will also seek to define the actual range of certain languages spoken by indigenous people other than those for whom they constitute the mother tongue.

1st **Semitic Family (Arabic).** — Arabic is spoken in the Azawad, the Hodh, and the northern Sahel: there it is the mother tongue, not only of the Moors of Arabic origin (Kounta, Berabich, and Beni-Hassan), but also of almost all Moors of Berber origin, who long ago abandoned the use of Zenaga <note>Zenaga is a Berber language of Mauritania that has largely been replaced by Hassaniya Arabic.</note>, as well as all the <term>Haratin</term> <note>Historically sedentary populations of the Sahara and Sahel, often of diverse ethnic origins.</note>. Furthermore, Arabic is spoken, in addition to their own language, by the Soninke Azer living in Saharan localities and by many Songhai and Tuareg of Timbuktu and its surroundings; it is also understood by a certain number of Soninke, Soninke <note>This repetition appears in the original text, likely a printer's error.</note>, Fula, etc., living in the vicinity of the Moors and maintaining commercial relations with them. However, the range of Arabic, at least as a spoken language, is very limited in Upper Senegal-Niger; if its—
