### ARABIC, BERBER, AND FULA

While the geographic area is extensive, we must not forget that it mostly covers nearly uninhabited regions; it is also worth remembering that it is rare to find people speaking Arabic in the <term>Sudan</term> <note>In this colonial context, "Sudan" refers to the "French Sudan" (modern-day Mali), not the modern Republic of Sudan.</note> outside of the Moors. One can estimate at a maximum of **120,000** the number of indigenous people in the colony who speak Arabic, including 104,000 Moors and <term>Haratin</term> <note>A social group in the Sahara and Sahel; historically sedentary and often associated with the Moorish communities whose language they speak.</note> for whom it is the mother tongue, 10,000 Soninke of the Saharan zone, and 6,000 individuals from various ethnic groups. — It should be noted that the Moors of the Hodh give the language they speak the name *Hassaniya* or *Hassani* (the language of the Beni-Hassan) and not the name *Arabia* (the Arabic language); they reserve this latter expression for literal Arabic <note>Original: "arabe littéral"—referring to Classical Arabic used in religious and scholarly texts.</note>.

**2°** *Hamitic Family (Berber Group).* — *Zenaga* is still spoken by some groups of Moors in Mauritania, notably in the <term>maraboutic</term> <note>Relating to Muslim religious leaders or scholars (marabouts) who often formed distinct social or tribal classes.</note> sub-tribes of the Oulad-Dayman and the Idao-el-Hadj; however, in the part of the Hodh belonging to Upper Senegal-Niger, families that have preserved the use of Berber are very rare. Some are nonetheless encountered among the Idao-Aich and perhaps among other tribes, though the number of people speaking Zenaga in Upper Senegal-Niger likely does not exceed **3,000** to **4,000** individuals at the absolute maximum. But, if Zenaga has almost disappeared from the Sudanese Sahara as a living language, its mark there has remained deep: it is found in place names, which are almost all Berber, and in the numerous terms it passed into Hassaniya Arabic, as well as—though to a lesser degree—into some Black <note>Original: "langues nègres"—a historical classification for Sub-Saharan African languages.</note> languages (notably Soninke).

*Tamacheq* or *Tamacherht*, on the contrary, has not disappeared: it is still spoken by all the Tuareg and their <term>Iklan</term> or <term>Bella</term> <note>Historically servile groups living among the Tuareg who adopted the Tuareg language (Tamacheq) and culture.</note>. Outside of the people for whom it constitutes the mother tongue, it seems to be understood only by very rare individuals. We can therefore estimate at 60,000 at most (including 57,000 Tuareg and Bella) the number of indigenous people in Upper Senegal-Niger speaking Tamacheq.

**3°** *Tekrurian Family (Fula).* — Fula, which it would perhaps be more logical to call <term>Toucouleur</term> <note>The French often used "Toucouleur" to distinguish sedentary Fula-speaking populations from the nomadic "Peul" (Fula/Fulani).</note>, is spoken at once by

The domain of this language is geographically very extensive due to the scattering of the Fula across the <term>Sudan</term> <note>In this 1909 context, "Sudan" refers to the "French Sudan," a colonial territory encompassing much of modern-day Mali.</note>, but it is, like the domain of this people itself, excessively fragmented. Furthermore, it is quite rare for Fula to be understood by people for whom it is not their mother tongue: it is a language widespread in many regions of the Sudan because Fula people are encountered nearly everywhere, but it is not a trade language <note>Unlike Dyula or Hausa, which served as regional "lingua francas" for commerce, Fula remained largely restricted to its ethnic community.</note>. The number of individuals speaking Fula in Upper Senegal-Niger can be estimated at approximately 450,000, including 443,000 for whom it constitutes their mother tongue.

Although the Fula language is one, it contains, by the very nature of the dispersion of the people who speak it, a rather considerable number of dialects: the purest of all seems to be that spoken by the Tukulor, who observe much more scrupulously than the generality of the Fula the most characteristic morphological and syntactic rules of the language; among the special dialects that have emerged among the Fula of Upper Senegal-Niger, one may cite those of the Sahel, <term>Massina</term>, the Upper Black Volta, the <term>Mossi</term> countries, <term>Liptako</term>, etc. Finally, it is worth mentioning a sort of "common dialect," sharing a little with all the others, employed by Fula and Tukulor who travel often; this common dialect allows them to make themselves easily understood in the various regions they traverse.

**4º Songhai Family (Songhai language).** — Songhai presents itself under a completely different aspect than that of Fula: the <term>Songhai</term> people proper (<term>Arma</term> <note>Descendants of the 16th-century Moroccan expeditionary force that conquered the Songhai Empire.</note>, <term>Sorko</term> <note>Historically the river-faring and fishing clan of the Songhai.</note>, and <term>Gabibi</term> <note>Historically the agriculturalist social class of the Songhai.</note>) hardly exceed 100,000 in Upper Senegal-Niger (101,582 according to the 1909 censuses). But I do not believe I am overstepping by saying that they form barely a quarter of the population speaking their language. First of all, Songhai has become the mother tongue of a significant number of <term>Soninke</term> in Djenné and in the Massina region; furthermore, it is spoken and understood, in addition to their...

5º *Mande family.* — *Bozo* is undoubtedly hardly spoken by anyone other than the Bozo themselves, that is to say, by approximately 15,000 individuals. It is, however, divided into several dialects, notably those of Dia, Massina, and Pondori, plus a dialect mixed with Banmana and Songhai which is spoken in the Bara region and near Niafounké.

The *Soninké* language is not only virtually unspoken outside of the Soninké people, but it is not even spoken by all Soninké: of the 245,392 individuals representing this people in Upper Senegal-Niger, more than 40,000 have abandoned their language for Dioula <note>Also spelled Dyula or Jula; a major trade language of the Mande family.</note> (those of the Niger Bend and notably Dafina), at least 10,000 have abandoned it for Songhai (districts of Djenné, Mopti, Niafounké), more than 30,000 for Banmana (districts of Koutiala, San, Ségou, Bamako, etc.), and about 10,000 for Malinké (notably the south of the Kayes district); so that there remain hardly more than 135,000 who have retained the use of their language. A noteworthy fact is that those who find themselves isolated among the Moors <note>Refers to the Sahrawi or Hassaniya Arabic-speaking populations to the north.</note> have remained more faithful to their national idiom than those who have spread into the South and East of the Sudan.

*Kâgoro* is only spoken today by ten thousand individuals at most; most Kâgoro, moreover, speak the Banmana dialect (Kaarta and Kaniaga), and some speak Soninké (Bakounou), in addition to their own language.

As for *Mandinka* <note>The author uses "mandingue" to refer to the broader Manding language continuum.</note>, comprising the four dialects of Khassonké, Banmana, Malinké, and Dioula, it is the mother tongue of approximately 1,070,000 natives of Upper Senegal-Niger: 11,191 Khassonké, 598,450 Banmana, 146,733 Malinké, 106,066 Fou...

[Ma]linké speaking the Malinké dialect, 218,820 Dioula, 8,450 Boron, and more than 40,000 Soninké speaking the Dioula dialect. But that is not all: in all the regions where the Central Mandé or the Dioula form the majority of the population—that is to say, in the districts <note>The French "cercle" was the primary administrative unit in French West Africa, here translated as "district."</note> of Sokolo, Ségou, Bamako, Kita, Bafoulabé, Kayes, Satadougou, Bougouni, and Sikasso—the Manding language has spread with such force that it is understood and spoken by the immense majority, if not the totality, of the other inhabitants, in addition to their own respective idioms (Arabic, Fula, Soninké, Kagoro, Susu, Samogo, Senufo); moreover, the Banmana <note>Bambara</note> language has spread across numerous districts of the Sahel and the right bank of the Bani where, however, the Banmana people are only relatively few in number. Therefore, I believe I am still underestimating the truth by estimating at 1,500,000 at a minimum the number of natives in Upper Senegal-Niger who use the Manding language—that is, nearly one-third of the total population of the colony.

The *Susu* <note>original: "soussou"</note> language is only spoken by the 9,824 Jalonke of the Satadougou and Kita districts; *Samogo* <note>original: "samorho"</note> by the 23,705 Samogo of the Sikasso and Bobo-Dioulasso districts; *Sia* by 6,000 individuals; *Blé* by 1,035; *Natioro* by 2,745; *Wara* <note>original: "ouara"</note> by 7,000; and *Sembla* by 8,000; these last five idioms are localized in the Bobo-Dioulasso district.

7. *Voltaic Family.* — The languages of the Tombo <note>The Tombo group refers to the Dogon people, famous for their complex cosmology and cliff-side villages in the Bandiagara Escarpment.</note> group are, it seems, strictly limited to the specific territory of the peoples of the corresponding ethnic group—that is to say, the mountainous region of the Northwest of the Bend <note>The "Niger Bend" or "Niger Curve" refers to the great arc the Niger River makes through the Sahel.</note> and the plains immediately adjacent to it. *Tombo* is spoken there by approximately 120,000 individuals, *Dogom* by 5,000 to 6,000, and *Déforo* by 12,000.

Among the languages of the Mossi group, *Môrhé* <note>Now usually spelled Moore, the language of the Mossi people.</note>, or the Mossi language proper, has spread not only among the **1,262,277** natives who today constitute the Mossi people, but also—with dialectal variations that are quite subtle—among the **48,707** Yansi and the majority of the **75,232** Samo (1): it is therefore currently the mother tongue of more than 1,387,000 individuals. Furthermore, it serves as the common language in all the regions where the political influence of the Yatenga and Ouagadougou empires reached. It is spoken, in addition to their mother tongue, by nearly all the Dioula of the districts of Ouahigouya and Ouagadougou (approximately 105,000), by the Silmimossi <note>A group of mixed Mossi and Fulani heritage.</note> (at least 15,000), by a large number of Fulani and Rimaïbé <note>Rimaïbé are historically a social class of settled agriculturalists of diverse origins within Fulani society.</note> (approximately 20,000), of Nioniossé (approximately 20,000), and of Boussansé (approximately 25,000). Outside the zones inhabited or governed by the Mossi themselves, their language is still understood by many Soninke, Dioula, and Hausa traders, and by many natives whose national idioms are very close to Mossi (Gourmantché, Nankana, Dagari). One can therefore estimate at approximately 1,600,000 the number of inhabitants of the colony speaking Mossi, which places this idiom, by order of numerical importance, at the same rank as Manding and even slightly above the latter.

However, from the point of view of its geographic range and its importance as a language of international exchange, *Mandinka* <note>The Manding or Mandinka language group includes various dialects like Bambara and Dioula, which served as the primary trade languages across West Africa.</note> unquestionably holds the first rank. — *Gourmantché* is spoken by approximately 150,000 individuals, *Nankana* by 20,000, and *Dagari*, including the *Birifo* dialect, by more than 105,000.

The various dialects related to the *Nounouma* language (the dialects of the Nioniossé, the Kipirsi, the Nounouma proper, etc.) are spoken as a national language by more than 150,000 individuals; furthermore, in addition to their own languages, it is spoken by a certain number of Dagari and Pougouli. The *Bobo* language has not spread much beyond the Bobo people themselves; the number of individuals speaking this language can therefore be estimated at approximately 228,000. The *Tara* dialect leads the group, spoken by more than 102,000 Bobo-Oulé <note>Original: "Bobo-Oulé" or "Red Bobo," today more commonly identified as the Bwa people.</note>; *Boua* comes next with more than 62,000 Bobo-Fing <note>Original: "Bobo-Fing" or "Black Bobo," considered the Bobo proper.</note>, then *Kian* with 36,666 Bobo-Gbê <note>Original: "Bobo-Gbê" or "White Bobo."</note>, and finally *Niénigué* with 24,817 Bobo-Niénigué.

The languages and dialects of the *Lobi* group are scarcely understood by anyone other than the peoples or tribes for whom they constitute the national idioms, namely 62,050 individuals for *Lobi*, 5,950 for *Dian* proper, 5,350 for *Pougouli*, and only 1,100 for *Gan* (district of Gaoua).

The *Lorho* dialect of the *Koulango* language is represented only by the 4,000 Lorho in the district of Gaoua <note>The "Cercle" or district was the primary administrative unit in French West Africa.</note>.

The languages of the *Bariba* group are spoken in Upper Senegal-Niger by only about 5,000 natives, including 4,497 *Bariba* and 540 *Takamba* of the *Soumba* language.

The dialects of the unclassified tribes of the Bobo-Dioulasso and Gaoua districts are of relatively minor importance: *Toussia* is spoken by 10,045 individuals, *Dorhossié* by 3,700, *Vigué* by 2,790, *Tiéfo* by 2,000, and *Padorho* by 500.

9th Niger-Logone family (*Hausa*). — It is quite different for Hausa: the Hausa people permanently established in the colony are not numerous, but those who travel there for business and who are generally called *Maraba* <note>Derived from the Hausa greeting "Maraba," meaning "welcome," this term became a nickname for the itinerant Hausa traders.</note> in the Bend of the Niger are far more so, whether they come from Hausaland proper by crossing the Niger near Say, or from their very important colonies on the Gold Coast <note>The Gold Coast is the historical name for modern-day Ghana.</note> and upper Togo. Their language, in any case, has spread widely in the Southeast of the Bend, where it follows Mandinka as a language of exchange, the boundary between the two zones of extension passing roughly through the meridian of Ouagadougou. Hausa is the language of the markets and the idiom of travelers in a part of Gourounsi, in eastern Mossi, and especially among the Boussansé and in the districts of Fada N’Gourma and Say. Evaluating the number of natives in Upper Senegal-Niger who understand Hausa is quite difficult; I believe, however, I can estimate this number at a minimum of one hundred thousand individuals.

### III. — Written Languages and Spoken Languages

1. *Written Arabic.* — Of the 31 languages in use in Upper Senegal-Niger, only one deserves the title of a written language: Arabic. And yet, it would perhaps be more accurate to say, however paradoxical it may seem, that none of the 31 languages spoken in Upper Senegal-Niger, including Arabic, deserves the title of a written language, but that, in addition to and outside of these languages, there exists a 31st that is written and not spoken: *written Arabic*. Indeed, it would be difficult to claim that Hassaniya Arabic, which the Moors speak, is a written language; in the Sudan <note>The "French Sudan," a colonial territory roughly corresponding to modern-day Mali, not the modern Republic of Sudan.</note> as in the Maghreb and elsewhere, there are in reality two types of the Arabic language: the spoken language, which differs quite significantly by region in terms of both vocabulary and phonetics and which cannot be rendered through writing, and the written language, which is the same everywhere, aside from a few local idioms, and which is never spoken, except by a few pretentious scholars during the lessons they give to their disciples. We know that spoken Arabic elides almost all short vowels, suppresses most case endings <term>flexions désinencielles: the suffixes at the end of words that indicate their grammatical role, such as subject or object</term> and consequently declensions and almost all verb tenses and moods, and employs only a limited number of words and derived forms, whereas written Arabic, even under the pen of the commoner, remains faithful to most of the morphological and syntactical rules of the literary language. In the Sudan perhaps more than elsewhere, the differen- <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("différence").</note>

<header>WRITTEN ARABIC</header>

The difference is profound between the two languages, not only from the point of view of grammar and lexicology, but also regarding the special use that is made of each of them.

The Moors <note>Historically, the nomadic Berber and Arab populations of the Sahara and Sahel.</note>, the *Haratin* <note>A social group within Saharan society, often composed of freedmen or sedentary agriculturalists.</note>, and the few thousand Soninke that I mentioned earlier as speaking Arabic, use only *Hassaniya* <note>The specific Arabic dialect of the western Sahara region.</note> in their conversation. This is an impure spoken dialect, heavily mixed with Berber words, but otherwise not vastly different from the dialect used in southern Oran <note>A region in western Algeria.</note>. The vast majority of them can neither read nor write, and for them, Arabic exists only as a spoken tongue. As for the scholars, the marabouts <note>West African Muslim religious leaders and teachers.</note>, and their disciples, they speak the same *Hassaniya* as the others, but they use correct Arabic for writing, for which they reserve—as I have previously stated—the name *arabia* <note>Refers to *al-Arabiyyah*, the literary or classical form of the language.</note>. It is not uncommon to hear a Moor say in excellent spoken Arabic: *La 'dref el-'arbia* <note>original: "La 'dref el-'arbia," meaning "I do not know Arabic."</note>, which in his mind means: "I do not know how to write Arabic" or "I would be unable to understand written Arabic."

As for the Black Muslims spread throughout the colony of Upper Senegal-Niger, there are very few among them capable of sustaining a conversation in Arabic, yet a very large number read written Arabic with ease and write it themselves fluently and correctly. I would not even be surprised if the number of literate individuals were proportionally higher among Black Muslims—the Soninke and the Dyula in particular—than among the Moors. Those among these Black scholars who have acquired extensive practice in written Arabic and have assimilated a considerable number of words and forms—and these, I repeat, are much more numerous than is commonly believed—manage to speak Arabic, with some difficulty, it is true, but expressing what they wish to say. However, the Arabic they speak is *written* Arabic, and native Arabic speakers—the Moors in this case—do not understand them, unless they are professional scholars themselves.

While spoken Arabic is localized roughly to the country of the Moors and occupies only the tenth rank on the scale of distribution—

<page-num>376</page-num>
<header>LANGUAGES</header>

In contrast to its low numerical distribution among the languages of Upper Senegal-Niger, written Arabic possesses a considerable importance: known and practiced by Muslim scholars of all races, it is the true and only literary language of the Sudan <note>In this context, "Sudan" refers to the historical region of the Western Sudan, specifically the French Sudan, modern-day Mali and surrounding areas.</note>; its knowledge allows a great number of natives living in an environment of ignorance to acquire a relative but quite appreciable level of instruction; it develops their mentality all the more because, to be acquired, it has required considerable mental gymnastics and prodigious efforts of memory and application: it must not be forgotten, indeed, that Sudanese students have no dictionaries or grammars at their disposal, and it is only through repeated readings and exercises that they manage to accumulate their store of literary knowledge; however meager this store of knowledge may be, I for my part cannot help but admire the efforts that must have been deployed to acquire it. It is only regrettable that the libraries of Sudanese scholars contain little more than treatises on religious exegesis or works relating to prayer formulas, stories of miracles, or discussions on insignificant points of canon law <note>original: "droit canonique," referring here to Islamic jurisprudence or Sharia.</note>; history occupies only a very secondary place, and the sciences and literature proper are completely excluded from them.

From a practical point of view, the knowledge of written Arabic allows scholars of different languages to correspond easily with one another and to recommend to each other, via a sort of safe-conduct, those of their friends who are traveling to distant lands. This ease of correspondence is certainly one of the principal strengths of the Muslims of the Sudan, both in relation to the animists <note>Followers of traditional African religions.</note> who are deprived of this means of communication, and also in relation to the European authority. Furthermore, it appears well-established that all the intellectual and moral benefits sometimes attributed to the influence of the Islamic religion are due, not to this religion in itself, but solely to the fact that it was the occasion for the diffusion among Black Africans of the knowledge and use of a literary language.

2° ***Are there written languages in Upper Senegal-Niger besides Arabic?*** — I have already answered this question in the negative. However, it would be inaccurate to say that Arabic is the only language of Upper Senegal-Niger that is written: I have only said, and I maintain, that Arabic is the only language of the colony deserving the title of "written language." One does indeed encounter some written specimens of four other languages—Tamacheq, Zenaga, Fula <note>original: "peul"</note>, and Hausa—but they are too few in number and of too specialized a character for these languages to claim the title of written languages, at least regarding Upper Senegal-Niger.

*Tamacheq* <term>Tamacheq: The Berber language spoken by the Tuareg people.</term> possesses a special alphabet, well known today, whose geometric characters (circles, rectangles, straight lines, and dots) bear the name of *Tifinagh* <note>original: "tifinarh"</note>. Knowledge of these characters is only very slightly widespread among the Tuareg in general, and it is exceedingly rare among the Tuareg of the Sudan and the Sudanese Sahara <note>In this context, "Sudan" refers to the French colonial territory "Soudan Français," primarily modern-day Mali.</note>. Only a few women still maintain the use of it, using it to trace mottos on drums, leather shields, or other objects; one sometimes finds inscriptions in *Tifinagh* on rocks, but the descendants of those who carved them are unable to read them. This alphabet, which possesses no means of representing most vowels and proves inferior in this respect even to the Arabic alphabet, is otherwise exceedingly defective. If there exist some scholars

### THE LANGUAGES

Among the Tuareg, at least within the maraboutic families <note>Marabouts are Muslim religious leaders and teachers who often serve as the primary educators and scribes in West African society.</note>, they use the Arabic language and alphabet for writing.

The Moors who still make use of *Zenaga* <term>Zenaga: An endangered Berber language once widely spoken in Mauritania and northern Senegal.</term> have completely forgotten how to use the Libyco-Berber characters <note>Referring to the Tifinagh script used by Berber peoples since ancient times.</note> that the Tuareg still employ, albeit in a restricted manner. Like the Berber-speaking tribes of Algeria and Morocco, they use Arabic characters to transcribe their language; however, this practice itself is almost unheard of in Upper Senegal-Niger. The few Zenaga-speaking Moors encountered in this colony are either completely illiterate or know written Arabic, and it is this latter language they use when they wish to commit something to paper.

As for Fula <note>original: "peul"</note> and Hausa, it happens that Muslim scholars speaking these languages write them using the Arabic alphabet, by giving certain characters of that alphabet a special conventional value or by modifying the value of a particular character using additional diacritical marks <note>Small signs, like dots or strokes, added to a letter to indicate a different sound.</note>. In this way, they roughly adapt the Arabic alphabet to the phonetics of these languages. They have even invented a special sign—a thick dot placed below the line of writing—to represent the vowel *é*, which has no corresponding sign in Arabic and is frequently used in Fula and Hausa. But even thus modified, the Arabic alphabet is still quite inadequate for rendering the sounds of languages as different from Semitic languages as Fula, Hausa, and indeed all the Black languages. The frequency of vowels, their variety, their morphological importance, and the quantity and value of nasal sounds <term>Phonemes: The distinct units of sound in a specified language that distinguish one word from another.</term> constitute obstacles that are very difficult to overcome with an instrument as poorly suited to expressing vowel and nasal phonemes as the graphic system of the Arabs. Furthermore, there exists no agreement, nor any possibility of agreement, among the Fula or Hausa scholars of the various regions of the Sudan <note>Referring to the historical "Bilad al-Sudan" or the Sahelian region, rather than the modern country of Sudan.</note> regarding the methods to be used to remedy the drawbacks of the system. Consequently, apart from a few practices that have become generalized almost everywhere—such as the representation of the vowel *é* by a thick dot and that of the special *d*

Since, on the other hand, it is practically necessary to already know written Arabic itself to be capable of transcribing Fula or Hausa into Arabic characters, most scholars prefer to simply use the latter language; they are all the more inclined to do so because, if they must write to a correspondent speaking a language other than their own, a letter written in Fula or Hausa would *not* be understood by that correspondent, whereas a letter written in Arabic always will be. However, as I was saying, one encounters some specimens of Fula and Hausa transcribed in Arabic characters: these are mostly short poems imitated or translated from Arabic; they are also sometimes letters exchanged between two Fula or two Hausa people, one of whom resides in a country where his language is not understood, and who can, by using this system, better preserve the secrecy of their correspondence than by using the Arabic language.

None of the other languages of Upper Senegal-Niger, to my knowledge, are written *even occasionally* (1). This is not to say that scholars do not exist among the Songhai, the Mandé, the Wolofs, etc.; but, when these scholars wish to commit something to paper, it is always the Arabic language they use and not their own language. At most, they might transcribe words from their mother tongue in the course of a letter written in Arabic, using Arabic characters sometimes modified in the manner of the Fula and Hausa.

### 3. *Oral Literature.* — If no language of the Sudan <note>The author uses "Sudan" to refer to the "Bilad al-Sudan" (Land of the Blacks), the historical geographic region of the West African Sahel, rather than the modern nation-state.</note> other than Arabic deserves the title of a "written language," and if Sudanese Arabic literature itself has produced very little—with a few rare exceptions (1)—in the way of truly original works beyond a few diaries, obituaries, and unremarkable correspondence, one should not conclude that no literature exists in the Sudan. On the contrary, there exists in this part of Africa a popular literature of extraordinary richness, but it is entirely oral.

This literature is not only rich; it is varied and touches upon every subject. History and epics are represented by very curious traditions regarding the origins of peoples and tribes, and the deeds and gestures of famous heroes or warriors: the legends reproduced or simply summarized—

<header>ORAL LITERATURE</header>

in the second part of this work can give an idea of the genre and the large share given therein to symbolism and the marvelous. Fables are legion in the Sudan; one could create voluminous collections that would recall at once our old *fabliaux* <note>Short, humorous, and often satirical medieval French verse tales.</note>, our *Renard the Fox* <note>original: "Roman de Renard," a medieval cycle of animal fables featuring a trickster fox.</note>, and the good old La Fontaine; it is generally the hare who is the hero of these fables and who plays the same sorts of tricks on other animals—the hyena in particular—that are the specialty of the fox in our tradition. The morality of Sudanese fables is no more "moral" than our own, but it most often exalts cleverness and cunning at the expense of brute strength. Alongside fables exist proverbs, which are generally more truly moral and frequently steeped in the most marvelous common sense, as well as riddles which serve to pass the evenings and which sharpen the wit. Poetry proper is widely represented, whether by interminable epic songs, by satirical or licentious songs, or by simple love songs: these last are the most widespread among the common people and are sung especially by women during their dances, while epic and satirical songs are instead recited by those professionals whom we call <term>griots</term> <note>Traditional West African storytellers, musicians, and oral historians who maintain the genealogies and oral traditions of their communities.</note> (1). To be complete, one would also need to add to this enumeration a sort of religious literature, including liturgical chants, formulas for sacrifice, incantation, and initiation, legends relating to the spirits <note>original: "génies," referring to local spirits or djinns.</note> and their action upon the world, and so on.

All the peoples of the Sudan do not shine equally from a literary point of view. The Mandé, though superior in other respects, hold only a rather mediocre rank in this regard and rarely escape ordinary banality; the poetic side, in any case, is generally lacking in them. The Senufo show—

But it is especially the Fulani <note>The author uses the term "Peuls," the French name for the Fulani or Fula people.</note> who distinguish themselves by the poetic allure of their songs. To give some idea of this, I take the liberty of translating here two Fulani songs collected in the Niger Bend by Captain Figaret, of the colonial artillery, who very kindly shared the text with me. As a translation cannot preserve the elegant and harmonious allure given to them by the assonances of the Fulani language, I reproduce the text itself below, transcribing it to the best of my ability according to the ordinary rules of French pronunciation.

->Love Song<-

->(collected among the Bari Fulani of Boromo, district of Koury).<-

*The sky darkens with the dark blue of guinea cloths,* <note>original: "Kâmou balni balnougol bouguédyi"</note>
*The mist lets drip a dew of fresh milk;* <note>original: "Misso missi missougol birâdam"</note> (2)
*The hyena howls, the elder of the bush answers...* <note>original: "Fowrou oulli, diko laddé dyaboké..."</note> (5).
*It is then that it is good to whisper with a fair-skinned friend.* <note>original: "Ndén é danédyo wéli goundiddâdé."</note>

The sky darkens with the dark blue of guineas (3),
The mist lets drip a dew of fresh milk (4);
The hyena roars, the elder of the bush responds... (5).
It is then that it is good to whisper with a fair-skinned friend.

---

(1) See the specimens of Mossi literature published and translated by Mr. Froger, deputy of indigenous affairs, in his *Study of the Mossi Language*.
(2) Variant: *The mist lets a trickle of fresh milk slip away* <note>original: "Bâdé sokki tyokkougol birdam"</note>.
(3) This refers to those dark blue cotton fabrics, almost black, similar to the tint the sky takes on at nightfall. <note>Guinea cloth was a staple of West African trade, often dyed with deep indigo.</note>
(4) Allusion to the evening dew which often takes on a milky hue in the gathering darkness.
(5) The "elder of the bush" is one of the nicknames for the lion.

### War Song
#### (collected among the Fulani of Djilgodi). (1)

> *At Djibo there is a pond:* <note>original: "Djibo ouendou"</note>
> *He who brings peace may drink and bathe there, he who brings evil will drink blood.* <note>original: "Ardi dyam yara loto, ardi boné yara dyidyam."</note>
> *It has been surrounded by stallions:* <note>original: "Ndou filirâma kaï goudyi"</note>
> *God watches from evening until morning, and spears watch from morning until evening.* <note>original: "Alla doma fa ouéta, gaoué doma fa hira."</note>
> *Its banks will be covered in guts, they will no longer be covered in women’s clothes.* <note>original: "Lîlèté ndou dyadyâli, ndou lilatâké goudé rèoubé."</note>
> *The whole pond has been surrounded;* <note>original: "Ouendou paté filâma;"</note>
> *Treacherous spears are in the pond, weapons are in the pond;* <note>original: "Gaoué bonndé ndèr ouendou, dyoga dyokâdyi ndèr ouendou ;"</note>

> *How bitter is the arrival of those who would make us leave!* <note>original: "Méti ngardo kala dilla !"</note>
> *The pond is full to the brim!* <note>original: "Yoppa tyoppi ouendou ndèr ouendou !"</note>

At Djibo there is a pond:
He who brings goodness can quench his thirst and bathe there,
but he who brings evil will drink blood there.
It has been surrounded by stallions (2):
God watches from evening until morning, and spears watch from morning until evening.
Its banks will be covered in entrails, they will no longer be covered in women's pagnes <term>pagne: a wraparound garment or sarong common in West Africa</term> (3).
Around the pond, hedges of thorny mimosa have been arranged;
Treacherous spears are in the pond, there are weapons in the pond;
It will be planted with the heads of the dead, it will no longer be planted with water lilies.

---

(1) Relating to a raid made by Boukari Koutou, the Mossi emperor of Ouagadougou <note>Wobogo, the 30th Moro Naba of the Mossi</note>, into the Djilgodi region around 1890, a raid during which he was repelled by the Fulani near the pond of Djibo.
(2) An allusion to the Fulani cavalry sent to withstand the shock of the Mossi army.
(3) Usually, the banks of the pond are covered with the cloths that the women have washed there and which they spread on the sand to dry.

### CHAPTER II / Comparative Linguistics

The scope and general character of this work do not allow me to attempt a detailed comparative study of the numerous languages in use in the <term>Upper Senegal-Niger</term> <note>A major French colonial territory in West Africa, established in 1904, which encompassed parts of modern-day Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso.</note>. Furthermore, it would be difficult for me to successfully complete such a study, given the still precarious state of knowledge currently acquired regarding many of these languages. I would like only to try to sketch in broad strokes, in a brief and precise form, the main characteristics of each linguistic family, sticking to generalities. I have arranged these details in successive tables to facilitate comparisons and to allow one to see, at a single glance, how the various families differ from one another and where, conversely, some share points of contact and affinities.

For the <term>Semitic</term>, <term>Hamitic</term> <note>A historical and now-obsolete linguistic classification formerly used for various North and East African languages; here the author uses it to categorize Berber languages.</note>, <term>Niger-Logone</term> <note>A historical classification used by the author to group certain West African languages; today, Hausa is classified as a Chadic language within the Afroasiatic family.</note>, and <term>Senegalese</term> families, I have used as types for comparison the only languages of these families represented in Upper Senegal-Niger—namely <term>Arabic</term>, <term>Tamasheq</term> <note>The language of the Tuareg people.</note>, <term>Hausa</term>, and <term>Wolof</term>. Since the <term>Tekrurian</term> <note>A term referring to the languages of the Tekrur region, specifically Pulaar or Fula spoken by the Fulani.</note>, <term>Songhai</term>, and <term>Senufo</term> families each possess only a single language, it was naturally that language which was chosen as the point of comparison. Regarding the <term>Mande</term> and <term>Voltaic</term> <note>Also known as Gur languages, spoken across the savanna regions of the Volta River basin.</note> families, the observations apply to all the languages within each of these two families.

<vocab>Comparative Linguistics, Upper Senegal-Niger, Semitic, Hamitic, Niger-Logone, Senegalese, Tekrurian, Songhai, Senufo, Mande, Voltaic, Arabic, Tamasheq, Hausa, Wolof</vocab>

->THE LANGUAGES<-

# I. — Word Composition and Formation.

## 1. Usual Composition of Roots (excluding pronouns and particles).

*Arabic*: three consonants without a vowel; sometimes four consonants <note>The author refers to the "triliteral" and "quadriliteral" root systems characteristic of Semitic languages, where meaning is carried by consonants and modified by vowels.</note>.
*Tamasheq* <note>The language of the Tuareg people.</note>: one consonant; two consonants; two consonants with an <term>intercalated</term> <note>Inserted or placed between other elements, such as a vowel between consonants.</note> vowel; some roots end in a vowel.
*Hausa*: one consonant followed by a vowel; two consonants with an intercalated vowel; one consonant followed by a vowel then two consonants.
*Wolof*: two consonants with an intercalated vowel (the second consonant may only be a semi-vowel); sometimes one consonant followed by a vowel then two consonants.
*Fula* <note>original: "Peul"; also known as Fulani or Fulfulde.</note>: two consonants with an intercalated vowel; one consonant followed by a vowel then two consonants.
*Songhay*: one consonant followed by a vowel; two consonants with an intercalated vowel; one consonant followed by a vowel then two consonants; perhaps also one consonant, one vowel, one consonant, one vowel (doubtful).
*Mande*: one consonant followed by a vowel; one vowel between two consonants (rare); perhaps also one consonant, one vowel, one consonant, one vowel (doubtful).
*Senufo*: one consonant followed by a vowel; one vowel between two consonants (rare); perhaps also one consonant, one vowel, one consonant, one vowel (doubtful).
*Voltaic* <note>original: "Voltaïque"; a group of languages now commonly referred to as the Gur languages, spoken across the Volta River basin.</note>: one vowel between two consonants; one vowel preceded by a consonant and followed by two consonants; also one consonant followed by a vowel.

## 2. Use of Isolated Roots.

*Arabic*: the root cannot be used alone (certain pronouns and particles excluded).

<summary>This page provides a comparative structural analysis of linguistic "roots" across several West African and Semitic languages, detailing the specific combinations of consonants and vowels used in each.</summary>
<keywords>linguistics, morphology, root composition, Arabic, Tamasheq, Hausa, Wolof, Fula, Songhay, Mande, Senufo, Voltaic languages, phonology</keywords>

<page-num>389</page-num>
<header>WORD FORMATION</header>

*Tamasheq* <note>The language of the Tuareg people.</note>: certain roots can be used alone.
*Hausa*: most roots can be used alone.
*Wolof*: the root can be used alone.
*Fula* <note>original: "Peul"; also known as Fulani or Fulfulde.</note>: the root cannot be used alone (with the exception of certain pronouns and particles, as well as imperatives and a few common abbreviations).
*Songhay*: the root can be used alone.
*Mande*: the root can be used alone.
*Senufo*: some roots can be used alone, while others cannot.
*Voltaic* <note>A group of languages found in the Volta River basin, today often categorized as "Gur" languages.</note>: the roots can only be used alone in certain specific cases and only when they have a vocalic ending (except for a few otherwise doubtful exceptions).

->3. *Methods of word formation.*<-

*Arabic*: internal and <term>desinential</term> <note>Relating to the "desinence" or the ending of a word that indicates its grammatical function, such as case or number.</note> <term>inflection</term> <note>The modification of a word to express different grammatical categories, such as tense, case, or gender.</note>; <term>agglutination</term> <note>A process where complex words are formed by stringing together distinct morphemes (prefixes, infixes, or suffixes) that each carry a specific meaning.</note> through prefixes, infixes, and suffixes.
*Tamasheq*: internal and desinential inflection; agglutination through prefixes, infixes, and suffixes.
*Hausa*: internal and desinential inflection; agglutination through prefixes and suffixes.
*Wolof*: no inflection; agglutination by suffixes only.
*Fula*: no inflection; agglutination by suffixes only.
*Songhay*: no inflection; agglutination by suffixes (with a single example of a prefix: *i* before the <term>attributive adjective</term> <note>An adjective that ascribes a quality to a noun, acting as the predicate of a sentence, e.g., "The water is *cold*."</note>); <term>juxtaposition</term> <note>Placing words or roots side-by-side without modification to create new meanings.</note> of roots or stems.
*Mande*: no inflection; agglutination by suffixes and very rarely by prefixes (used to form <term>causative</term> <note>Verbs expressing that a subject causes someone else to perform an action.</note> or <term>factitive</term> <note>Verbs that indicate the object is being made to be something.</note> verbs); juxtaposition of roots or stems.
*Senufo*: no inflection; agglutination by suffixes only; juxtaposition of pure roots placed before other roots or stems.
*Voltaic*: same methods of formation as for Senufo.

### 4. *Morphological modifications of root consonants (dialectal or euphonic modifications aside).*

*Arabic*: no modification, except through doubling.
*Tamasheq*: no modification, except through doubling.
*Hausa*: no modification, except through doubling.
*Wolof*: very numerous cases of morphological modification of certain root consonants.
*Fula* <note>original: "Peul"; also known as Fulani or Fulfulde.</note>: regular morphological and syntactic modification of certain root consonants.
*Songhay*: no modification.
*Mande*: no modification (except for a few cases in the Mande-Tamu group).
*Senufo*: a few cases of morphological modification of root consonants.
*Voltaic* <note>Commonly referred to today as "Gur" languages.</note>: numerous cases of morphological modification of certain root consonants.

## II. — Morphology and Syntax.

### 1. *Genders and classes.*

*Arabic*: two genders distinguished in both numbers <note>Referring to singular and plural forms.</note> in pronouns, nouns, adjectives, participles, and verbs (by means of suffixes or <term>desinential inflections</term> <note>Changes at the end of a word that indicate its grammatical function, such as case or gender.</note> in nouns, adjectives, and participles; through prefixes and suffixes in verbs).

*Tamasheq*: two genders distinguished in both numbers in pronouns, nouns, participles, and verbs (by means of prefixes and suffixes in nouns and participles, as well as in verbs).

*Hausa*: two genders distinguished in the singular only in pronouns, nouns, adjectives, and participles, but not in verbs, with the exception of one feminine verbal form for the verb "to be": *tchê* (by means of desinential inflections in nouns and participles; by means of desinential inflections or prefixes in adjectives).

<header>NUMBERS</header>

*Wolof*: no genders, but a large number of noun classes <note>Noun classes are categories—such as "people," "tools," or "liquids"—that function similarly to grammatical genders like masculine or feminine.</note> distinguished by special articles or suffixed determining particles.
*Fula* <note>original: "Peul."</note>: no genders, but a large number of noun and participle classes distinguished by special suffixes, the use of different pronouns, and the modification of certain root consonants.
*Songhay*: neither genders nor classes.
*Mande*: neither genders nor classes.
*Senufo*: no genders, but noun classes distinguished by special suffixes.
*Voltaic* <note>Known today as the Gur languages.</note>: no genders, but noun classes distinguished by special suffixes.

### 2° Numbers.

*Arabic*: three numbers <note>Singular, plural, and the "dual" number used for exactly two people or things.</note> distinguished in pronouns, nouns, adjectives, participles, and verbs (by means of inflections, <term>infixes</term> <note>A word element inserted into the middle of a root, rather than at the beginning or end.</note>, and suffixes in nouns, adjectives, and participles, and prefixes and suffixes in verbs).
*Tamasheq*: two numbers distinguished in pronouns, nouns, participles, and verbs (by means of inflections, prefixes, and suffixes in nouns and participles, and prefixes and suffixes in verbs).
*Hausa*: two numbers distinguished in pronouns, nouns, adjectives, and participles, but not in verbs (by means of internal or <term>desinential inflections</term> <note>Changes made specifically to the ending of a word.</note> in nouns and participles, and inflections or prefixes in adjectives).
*Wolof*: two numbers distinguished only in pronouns and in articles or determining particles of the noun, through special forms for each number.
*Fula*: two numbers distinguished in pronouns, nouns, participles, and certain verbs (in nouns and participles by means of suffixes special to each number and by the modification of certain root consonants; in verbs by a similar modification and—in some cases—by special suffixes).

<header>THE LANGUAGES</header>

*Songhay*: two numbers <note>Singular and plural.</note> distinguished in pronouns and nouns only (in nouns, by the addition of a suffix to the singular form).

*Mande*: similar to Songhay, with the difference that in certain languages or dialects, the suffix indicating the plural can replace the final vowel of the singular form; additionally, in the Mande-Tamu group <note>A classification used by the author to group specific Mande languages, likely including Samo and Tougan.</note>, there are cases where the first root consonant <note>The core consonant of a word that carries its basic meaning.</note> is modified.

*Senufo*: two numbers distinguished in pronouns and nouns (in nouns, by adding a suffix to the singular form or by using suffixes unique to each number, and sometimes by modifying certain root consonants).

*Voltaic* <note>Known today as the Gur languages.</note>: two numbers distinguished in pronouns and nouns (in nouns, by using suffixes unique to each number and sometimes by modifying certain root consonants).

*Remark.* — In the Arabic, Tamasheq, Hausa, Fula <note>original: "peule"</note>, and Voltaic languages, nouns always take a plural marker, even if plurality is already indicated by a number or a word expressing quantity (such as "many"). Conversely, in the Songhay and Mande families, the plural marker disappears if the plurality is indicated elsewhere, even if only by context. In Senufo, both of these patterns can be found occurring at the same time.

### 3. Modifications of the verbal idea (persons, tenses, moods, voices, forms).

*Arabic*: persons, tenses, moods, passive voice, and <term>derived forms</term> <note>Variations of a basic verb root that change its meaning, such as making it causative (to "cause" something to happen).</note> are indicated by <term>inflections</term> <note>Changes to the form of a word, like "sing" to "sang."</note>, prefixes, infixes, and suffixes.

*Tamasheq*: persons, tenses or moods, and derived forms are indicated by prefixes, infixes, and suffixes; it possesses only one voice.

*Hausa*: persons are indicated by subject pronouns; tenses or moods are indicated by particles or auxiliaries <note>Helping words, like "have" or "will" in English.</note> placed before the verb, and sometimes by suffixes or <term>desinential inflections</term> <note>Changes specifically made to the end of a word.</note>, or even by the use of special subject pronouns; the passive voice is indicated...

<header>THE VERB AND NEGATION</header>

...by a prefix (*a*) and by the inversion of the subject pronoun; a fairly large number of derived forms indicated by suffixes or inflectional endings <note>These are specific endings added to the root of a word to change its grammatical function.</note>.

*Wolof*: persons indicated by subject pronouns; tenses or moods indicated by suffixes or by prefixed auxiliaries, or sometimes by the position of the subject pronoun relative to the verb; a single voice; numerous derived forms indicated by suffixes.

*Fula* <note>Also known as Fulani or Pulaar.</note>: persons indicated by subject pronouns and sometimes, in the imperative, by suffixes; tenses or moods indicated by suffixes and occasionally by prefixed auxiliaries; three voices (active, passive, and middle or reflexive), indicated by special suffixes; very numerous derived forms indicated by suffixes.

*Songhay*: persons indicated by subject pronouns; tenses or moods indicated by prefixed particles or auxiliaries; a single voice; two derived forms (the intensive, marked by simple reduplication <note>Repeating a word or part of it to add emphasis or change meaning.</note>, and the factitive or causative <note>A form indicating that the subject is causing an action to happen.</note>, indicated by a suffix).

*Mande*: persons indicated by subject pronouns; tenses or moods indicated by prefixed or suffixed particles or auxiliaries; passive voice indicated by a suffixed particle or simply by the absence of a direct object <note>original: "régime direct"</note>; a few derived forms indicated by prefixes or suffixes.

*Senufo*: persons indicated by subject pronouns; tenses or moods indicated by prefixed particles or auxiliaries (perhaps also occasionally by suffixed particles); voices (?); forms (?).

*Voltaic* <note>Known today as the Gur languages.</note>: persons indicated by subject pronouns; tenses or moods indicated by suffixes and by prefixed particles or auxiliaries; a single voice (?); derived forms indicated by suffixes.

### 4. Negation.

*Arabic*: indicated by a particle prefixed to the verb (various particles depending on the tense: *lâ*, *mâ*, *lam* <note>original: "lâ, mâ, lam" — these are standard Arabic negative particles used for different temporal contexts.</note>).

*Tamasheq* <note>The language of the Tuareg people.</note>: the same system (using a single particle: *our* or *ou* <note>original: "our" or "ou"</note>).

*Hausa*: indicated by the particle *ba* placed at the beginning and the end of the clause (in the imperative by the particle *kada* at the start of the clause).

*Wolof*: indicated by a suffix placed between the root of the verb and the conjugation suffix, or by a negative auxiliary <note>A "helping verb" used to express grammatical meaning, like "do" in "I do not know."</note> prefixed to the verb.

*Fula* <note>Also known as Peul or Fulani.</note>: indicated by special conjugation suffixes and, in the imperative, by a negative auxiliary or a negative particle prefixed to the verb.

*Songhay*: indicated by a particle prefixed to the verb (*na* for the past, *si* for the future).

*Mande*: indicated by a negative particle or auxiliary prefixed to the verb (various particles and auxiliaries according to the tense, mood, or voice: in Mandinka *tè* for the present, *ti* for the future, *kana* for the injunctive <note>A grammatical mood used for commands or expressing a desire that something happen.</note>, *ma* for the past and the passive).

*Senufo*: indicated by a particle prefixed to the verb (various particles according to tense or mood) and often specified by the addition of another particle suffixed to the verb.

*Voltaic* <note>A group of languages (also called Gur) spoken in parts of West Africa like Burkina Faso and Ghana.</note>: indicated by a particle prefixed to the verb or to the conjugation auxiliary (various particles according to tense or mood) and often specified by the addition of another particle suffixed to the verb.

5° *Interrogation* (excluding cases where the clause contains a pronoun or adverb that marks the interrogation on its own, such as "who? what? when? where? how? etc.").

*Arabic*: interrogative particle at the beginning of the clause or (in the colloquial language) an interrogative word suffixed to the verb, or else a particle meaning "or not" <note>original: "aou-lâ"</note> placed at the end of the clause.

*Tamasheq* <note>The language of the Tuareg people.</note>: interrogative particle meaning "or else" <note>original: "mirh"</note> placed at the end of the clause.

*Hausa*: interrogative particle or formula meaning "or else" <note>original: "ko"</note> or even "or else not so" <note>original: "ko ba hakka ba"</note> placed at the end of the clause; use of special verb forms.

<summary>This page outlines the grammatical rules for forming negative sentences and questions across several West African and Semitic languages, highlighting the use of particles, suffixes, and auxiliary verbs.</summary>

"to be," depending on its meaning, in interrogative sentences.

*Wolof*: an interrogative particle placed at the start of the clause.

*Fula* <note>Also known as Peul or Fulani.</note>: an interrogative particle at the start of the clause (*yalla*) or, more frequently, an interrogative particle at the end of the clause (*nâ*), or both used simultaneously. Alternatively, inversion may be used (where the subject is placed after the verb, with morphological modifications <note>Changes in the form or structure of the words.</note> to both in certain cases).

*Songhay*: an interrogative particle meaning "or else" (*ouala*) placed at the end of the clause.

*Mande*: the same system (the particle *ouala*, *ouô*, or *â* in Mandinka).

*Senufo*: the same system.

*Voltaic* <note>A group of languages (also called Gur) spoken in parts of West Africa like Burkina Faso and Ghana.</note>: the same system.

**Note.** — In all these linguistic families, intonation alone, without the use of any special particle, can be enough to express a question.

### 6. The Adjective.

*Arabic*: true adjectives exist apart from participles <note>Words derived from verbs that function as adjectives, like "broken" or "shining."</note>.

*Tamacheq* <note>The language of the Tuareg people.</note>: no adjectives; participles and qualifying verbs <note>Verbs that describe a quality or state, such as "to be red" or "to be tall."</note> take their place.

*Hausa*: true adjectives, compound adjectives made of a noun or a verb preceded by a prefix, and participles and passive infinitives used as adjectives.

*Wolof*: no adjectives or participles; qualifying verbs take their place, either conjugated or preceded by a kind of relative pronoun which is essentially a special defining particle attached as a suffix to the noun.

*Fula*: no adjectives, but participles take their place, along with qualifying verbs that are either conjugated or preceded by a type of demonstrative acting as a relative pronoun.

*Songhay*: true adjectives and adjective-participles formed from a verb by adding a suffix.

*Mande*: no true adjectives, but qualifying verbs

*Senufo*: proper adjectives and qualifying verbs <note>Verbs that express a quality, such as "to be large."</note> acting in their place, either conjugated or used adjectivally in the infinitive.
*Voltaic*: proper adjectives, participle-adjectives formed from a verb by the addition of various suffixes, nouns used adjectivally, and conjugated qualifying verbs.

### 7° Placement of the noun complement.
<note>This section describes how languages express a relationship between two nouns, such as "the head of the man" or "the man's head."</note>

*Arabic*: the noun complement <note>The "possessor" noun.</note> follows the main noun without a linking particle (the noun that is defined by its complement loses its definite article).
*Tamacheq*: the noun complement follows the main noun, with a linking particle (*n* or *en*) placed between the two.
*Hausa*: the noun complement follows the main noun, with a linking particle (*n* for both genders or else *na* for the masculine and *ta* for the feminine) placed between the two.
*Wolof*: the noun complement follows the main noun without a linking particle (the noun defined by its complement generally retains its definite particle).
*Fula*: the noun complement follows the main noun without a linking particle (the noun defined by its complement retains its class suffix <note>A suffix that categorizes the noun into a group, such as humans or tools.</note>, except in certain very common phrases acting as compound nouns).
*Songhay*: the noun complement comes before the main noun without a linking particle (generally only the complement can take the definite particle) (1).
*Mande*: the noun complement comes before the main noun without a linking particle, or with a linking particle indicating either possession or location.
*Senufo*: the noun complement comes before the main noun without a linking particle (the noun acting as the complement frequently loses its class suffix).

### *8° Placement of verb objects.*
<note>In linguistics, the "regimen" or object is the noun or pronoun that completes the meaning of a verb, such as "the book" in "I read the book."</note>

*Arabic*: all objects are placed after the verb; the direct object generally comes first and the indirect object second (however, a pronominal indirect object <note>An object consisting of a pronoun, like "to him."</note> is placed before a nominal direct object <note>An object consisting of a noun, like "the bread."</note>).

*Tamacheq*: all objects are placed after the verb; the indirect object is generally placed before the direct object (unless the latter is a pronoun) and sometimes even before the verb.

*Hausa*: all objects are placed after the verb; the indirect object generally precedes the direct object.

*Wolof*: the direct object generally follows the verb; however, if this object is a pronoun and the subject pronoun is placed before the verb, the direct object pronoun is inserted between the subject pronoun and the verb; the indirect object is always placed after the verb, sometimes after and sometimes before the direct object.

*Fula*: all objects are placed after the verb; an indirect object not accompanied by a preposition always precedes the direct object; however, an object one wishes to emphasize is placed at the beginning of the clause, and in that case, the subject is placed after the verb.

*Songhai*: all objects are placed after the verb; the indirect object generally precedes the direct object.

*Mande*: the direct object is always placed immediately before the verb, between the conjugation auxiliary <note>A "helping verb" used to indicate tense or mood.</note>—if one exists—and the verb itself; the indirect object, by contrast, always follows the verb.

*Senufo*: the same rule as in Mande.

*Voltaic*: the direct object and the indirect object generally follow the verb; the direct object is most often placed first, sometimes inserted between the verb itself and the

### 9º *Possessives*.

*Arabic*: possessive adjectives are rendered by means of pronominal suffixes which are, in reality, personal pronouns acting as objects of the noun <note>In many Semitic and African languages, saying "my book" is grammatically structured as "book-of-me."</note> and placed after it according to the general rule; the noun does not take the article.

*Tamacheq*: the same system, but with the ordinary use of the linking particle *n* or *en* <note>A "linking particle" or "particule d'union" acts like the word "of" to connect two related words.</note> between the noun and the pronoun.

*Hausa*: the same system, using the linking particle *n*.

*Wolof*: for the first and second persons singular and plural, and the third person plural, there are true possessive adjectives (formed from a root *s* indicating possession and followed by the pronoun), which are placed before the noun; (in the singular, the noun does not take a determination particle <note>A "determination particle" functions like "the" or "a" to specify a noun.</note>; in the plural, the determination particle is placed either after the possessive or after the noun; a possessive modifying a noun that is the object of another noun is placed before the latter: 'your horse's feet,' *sa tank-i fas* <note>original: "ton pieds cheval"</note> "your feet-of horse";) for the third person singular always, and exceptionally for the other persons, the possessive adjective is rendered simply by the pronoun suffixed to the noun.

*Fula*: <note>The original French uses "Peul," the name for the Fula or Fulani language and people.</note> our possessive adjectives are rendered by means of the pronoun suffixed to the noun, with a particle *ma’* or *m* indicating possession inserted between the two (except in the first person singular).

*Songhai*: our possessive adjectives are rendered by means of the pro-

### 10° *Relative*. <note>The relative pronoun, such as "who," "which," or "that."</note>

*Arabic*: the relative exists after a determined noun and immediately follows its antecedent; if the relative is an object, a corresponding object pronoun, called a "resumptive pronoun" <note>A "pronom de rappel" or resumptive pronoun is used when a language repeats the object in the sentence, like saying "the book that I read *it*."</note>, is expressed after the verb; there is no relative after an indeterminate noun: this is supplemented by the personal pronoun.

*Tamacheq*: no relative; it is supplemented by the demonstrative, with frequent use of a resumptive pronoun in the case of a relative object.

*Hausa*: there is a relative (*nda* or *da*), which immediately follows its antecedent; whether it is the subject or the object, it requires a resumptive pronoun.

*Wolof*: no relative; it is supplemented by the determination particle of the noun, increased if necessary by a demonstrative.

*Fula*: no relative properly speaking; it is supplemented by a kind of invariable demonstrative (*ko* or *no*) or, most often, by the personal pronoun.

*Songhai*: a relative exists (*ka*, plural *ka-yo* or *ki*), which follows its antecedent either immediately or with the insertion of the determination particle; when the relative is an object, the use of the resumptive pronoun is necessary.

*Mande*: no relative; a demonstrative generally takes its place (*mi* or *min* in Mandinka), with the use of the resumptive pronoun if one is dealing with a relative object.

*Sénoufo*: ?

### 11° *The infinitive following a verb.*

*Arabic*: no infinitive; both verbs are placed in a personal mood <note>Meaning the verb is conjugated to a specific person (e.g., "I want that I go" instead of "I want to go").</note>.
*Tamacheq*: no infinitive; both verbs are placed in a personal mood.
*Hausa*: the infinitive immediately follows the verb of which it is the object, or it is replaced by a personal mood.
*Wolof*: the infinitive follows the verb with a linking particle (*a*) inserted between the two.
*Fula*: the Fula infinitive is a noun and can, like any noun, be the object of a verb and follow it directly; if it is not strictly the object of the verb, it is replaced by a personal mood.
*Songhay*: the infinitive follows the verb, with a linking particle (*ka*) inserted between the two; however, if the logical subject of the infinitive is not the same as that of the preceding verb, the infinitive is replaced by a personal mood.
*Mande*: the same rules as in Songhay (the linking particle varies by language; it is *ka* in Manding).
*Senufo*: the same rules as in Songhay and Mande (the linking particle is generally *sa*).
*Voltaic*: the same rules as in Songhay, Mande, and Senufo (the linking particle varies by language; it is *n* in Mossi).
Note.—In Mande and Senufo, the infinitive used as a noun precedes the verb of which it is the direct object, according to the general rule.

### 12° *The object of particles replacing our prepositions.*

*Arabic*: the object follows the particle.
*Tamacheq*: the object follows the particle.

### 13° *Position of the subject.*

*Arabic*: before or after the verb.
*Tamacheq*: before or after the verb.
*Hausa*: before the verb; if the subject is a noun, it is generally followed by a resumptive pronoun <note>A pronoun that repeats the subject, e.g., "The man, he speaks."</note>.
*Wolof*: before the verb if it is a noun; after the verb—except in certain tenses—if it is a pronoun.
*Fula*: before the verb in general; however, in common expressions, in poetry, in certain interrogative sentences, and when one wishes to draw attention to the object by placing it at the beginning of the clause, the subject follows the verb. In the 1st and 2nd persons, the subject pronoun then takes a special form or merges with the conjugation suffix of the verb; the latter behaves, even in the singular, as if it were in the plural.
*Songhay*: subject before the verb.
*Mande*: subject before the verb.
*Senufo*: subject before the verb.
*Voltaic*: subject before the verb.

### 14° *Position of the predicate.*

*Arabic*: after the subject or the expression serving as the verb "to be," as the copula <note>A "copula" is a word like "is" that links a subject to a predicate.</note> does not exist.
*Tamacheq*: the noun predicate is placed after the verb "to be" or before the subject of the verb "to be"; the adjective predicate is generally translated by a participle directly following the subject, without expressing the verb "to be."
*Hausa*: the predicate is placed between the subject and the verb *ne* <note>original: "né"; this is the Hausa copula for masculine and plural subjects.</note> (femi- <note>The word is cut off; likely "féminin" (feminine), referring to the feminine copula "ce".</note>

### 16º Articles.

*Arabic*: an invariable definite article (<note>original: "el"</note>) precedes the noun; there is no indefinite article.
*Tamacheq*: no article, but the <term>demonstrative<gloss>a word like 'this' or 'that'</gloss></term> can play the role of a determinative article, and the numeral can serve as an indefinite article.
*Hausa*: no definite article; a special adjective plays the role of an indefinite article and precedes the noun.
*Wolof*: no article strictly speaking, but various <term>particles of determination<gloss>small words that specify or limit a noun</gloss></term> play the role and are placed after the noun: they all consist of a consonant or a semi-vowel followed by a vowel; the consonant varies according to the <term>class<gloss>a grammatical category similar to gender but often based on characteristics like 'human' or 'liquid'</gloss></term> or according to the initial consonant of the noun, and the vowel varies according to the nature of the determination.
*Fula*: no article; the third-person personal pronouns, used as demonstratives after the noun, often have a value similar to that of our definite article; a participle expressing the number "one" plays the role of an indefinite article and follows the noun.
*Songhay*: a determination particle (<note>original: "di"</note>) suffixed to the noun plays exactly the same role as our definite article; the numeral can play the role of an indefinite article.
*Mande*: no definite article; an indefinite article exists, distinct from the number "one" (<note>original: "do"</note> in Mandinka).
*Senufo*: no article.
*Voltaic*: no article.

### 17º Verb of non-existence.

*Arabic*: several verbs of non-existence exist, but, in the spoken language, the verb of existence used negatively is more frequent.
*Tamacheq*: the idea of non-existence is expressed by the negation of the verb of existence.

### 18° Numeration <note>The system of naming and using numbers.</note>

*Arabic*: <term>decimal<gloss>a base-10 counting system</gloss></term>; the number precedes the noun, which remains singular from the number 11 onwards.
*Tamacheq*: the same system and the same rules.
*Hausa*: decimal; the number follows the noun, which can be plural starting from 2 or remain singular.
*Wolof*: <term>quinary<gloss>a base-5 counting system</gloss></term>; the number precedes the noun but takes the plural <term>determination particle<gloss>a small word used to specify the noun</gloss></term> (<note>original: "i" or "yi"</note>) after it from 2 onwards, while the noun remains invariable and takes no determination particle.
*Fula*: quinary; the number follows the noun, which is put in the plural.
*Songhay*: decimal; the number follows the noun, which remains singular.
*Mande*: decimal or quinary, depending on the language; the number follows the noun, which remains singular.
*Senufo*: quinary; the number follows the noun, which remains singular.
*Voltaic*: decimal or quinary, depending on the language; the number follows the noun, which can be plural or remain singular.

<summary>This page catalogs the grammatical methods for expressing non-existence and the mathematical bases of various West African and Semitic numbering systems. It highlights the distinction between decimal (base-10) and quinary (base-5) systems and their respective rules for noun agreement.</summary>

<header>VOWELS AND CONSONANTS</header>

### III. — Phonetics

#### 1° Vowels (semi-vowels *w* and *y* not included, as they are classified among the consonants).

*Arabic*: pure vowels only (at least in the spoken language).
*Tamacheq*: pure vowels and nasalized vowels (1).
*Hausa*: pure vowels and nasalized vowels.
*Wolof*: pure vowels (including the vowel *eu* <note>a sound similar to the 'u' in 'burn'</note>), nasalized vowels, and some nasal vowels (2).
*Fula*: pure vowels only.
*Songhay*: pure vowels and nasalized vowels; some nasal vowels, though not very distinct.
*Mande*: pure vowels (including the French *u* <note>a tight, rounded vowel sound not found in standard English, similar to the 'ue' in German 'über'</note>, which is actually quite rare); nasalized vowels and numerous nasal vowels.
*Senufo*: pure vowels (including *eu* and *u*) and nasal vowels.
*Voltaic*: pure vowels (including *eu* and *u*), nasalized vowels, and nasal vowels.

#### 2° Consonants (presence or absence of certain special consonants).

*Arabic*: possesses the semi-vowels *w* and *y*, the *hamza* <note>a glottal stop, like the catch in the throat in 'uh-oh'</note> (hiatus), the *'ain* <note>a deep, constricted sound made in the throat</note>, two kinds of *h*, the *kh* (or *jota*) <note>the raspy 'ch' sound in 'Loch' or Spanish 'Jose'</note>, the *rh* or *gh* (a "gargled" or uvular *r*), <term>sibilants<gloss>hissing or shushing sounds</gloss></term> (*sh* and *j*), <term>interdentals<gloss>sounds made with the tongue between the teeth</gloss></term> (the hard and soft *th* of English), and additionally a special *d*, *t*, *s*, *z*, and *k* (emphatic or "clicking" <note>these are "heavy" consonants produced with the back of the tongue raised</note> sounds); no *v* nor *ñ* <note>the 'ny' sound as in 'onion' or French 'dignité'</note>.
*Tamacheq*: possesses the semi-vowels *w* and *y*, the *rh* or *gh*, sibilants (*sh* and *j*), interdentals (hard and soft *th*), a *d*,

(2) I call "nasal vowels" vowels ending in an unvoiced *n*, like the groups "on, en" in the French words "bon" <note>good</note> and "mien" <note>mine</note>; some give these phonemes the name "nasalized vowels," which seems less logical to me.

*Hausa*: possesses the semi-vowels *w* and *y*, half-shushing sounds (*sh* and *zh*), and the *ñ*; (no *hamza*, *'ain*, *kh*, *rh*, no hissing sounds <note>original: "zézayantes"</note>, no *v*, nor any emphatic or "clicking" letters <note>referring to glottalized or implosive consonants</note>).

*Wolof*: possesses the semi-vowels *w* and *y*, the *kh* <note>a raspy 'ch' sound like in 'Bach'</note>, the *ñ*, the *v*, and a special *p* and *k*; (no *hamza*, *'ain*, *rh*, no shushing sounds, no hissing sounds, nor the letter *z*).

*Fula*: possesses the semi-vowels *w* and *y*, the *hamza*, the *ñ*, the velar *n* <note>the 'ng' sound as in 'singing'</note>, and a special *b* and *d* <note>likely implosive consonants</note>; (no *'ain*, *kh*, *rh*, no shushing sounds, no hissing sounds, nor the letter *z*; the *v* is rare and only dialectal, replacing the semi-vowel *w*, which is also sometimes replaced by a semi-vowel *u*).

*Songhay*: possesses the semi-vowels *w* and *y* and the *ñ*; (no *hamza*, *'ain*, *kh*, *rh*, no shushing sounds — except for a very rare *sh* found only in a few foreign words —, no hissing sounds, no emphatic or clicking letters, nor the letter *v*).

*Mande*: possesses the semi-vowels *w*, *u*, and *y*, the *kh* (dialectal), the *rh* or *gh*, the *ñ*, the velar *n* (rare), the *v*, the half-shushing *sh* (rare and dialectal), and <term>labial-velar stops<gloss>consonants produced by simultaneously closing the lips and the back of the throat</gloss></term> (*gb* and *kp*); (no *hamza*, *'ain*, no true shushing sounds, no hissing sounds, nor any emphatic or clicking letters).

*Senufo*: possesses the semi-vowels *w*, *u*, and *y*, the *'ain*, the *rh* or *gh*, the *ñ*, the *v*, half-shushing sounds (*sh* and *zh*), and labial-velar stops; (no *hamza*, *kh*, no true shushing sounds, no hissing sounds, nor any emphatic or clicking letters).

*Voltaic*: possesses the semi-vowels *w*, *u*, and *y*, the *rh* or *gh*, the *ñ*, the *v*, emphatic or clicking consonants (special *b*, *p*, *d*, and *g*), plus aspirated consonants; (no *hamza*, *'ain*, *kh*, no shushing sounds, nor hissing sounds).

Note. — The Arabic, Tamacheq, and Hausa languages do not, strictly speaking, possess <term>nasalized consonants<gloss>consonant clusters where a nasal sound like 'm' or 'n' precedes another consonant</gloss></term> or <term>palatalized consonants<gloss>consonants modified by moving the tongue toward the hard palate, often called 'yodized'</gloss></term>; all the other languages of the Upper Senegal-Niger region, on the contrary, make frequent use of nasalized consonants (*mb*, *nd*, *ñg*, in particular) and palatalized consonants (*dy* or *gy*, *ty* or *ky*, in particular).

<header>TERMINAL SYLLABLES OF WORDS</header>

### 3° *Terminal syllables of words.*

**Arabic:** vocalic and consonantal endings (consonantal endings are more frequent).
**Tamacheq:** vocalic and consonantal endings (consonantal endings are more frequent).
**Hausa:** vocalic endings are the most frequent; consonantal endings are rarer and only appear as a dental <note>sounds made by the tongue touching the upper teeth, such as t, d, s, z, r, l</note> (*t*, *d*, *s*, *z*, *r*, *l*) or a nasal (*n*, *ñ*) or even a semi-vowel.
**Wolof:** vocalic and consonantal endings.
**Fula:** vocalic and consonantal endings; apart from cases where the root is used alone, consonantal endings are only found as *l*, *m*, *n*, *ñ* or the semi-vowel *y*.
**Songhay:** vocalic and consonantal endings; the latter, less frequent than the former, only appear as *l*, *m*, *n*, *ñ*, *r*, *s* or a semi-vowel.
**Mande:** exclusively vocalic endings (using either pure or nasal vowels).
**Senufo:** exclusively vocalic endings (except in cases where the root is used alone, and in those instances the root actually forms only the first part of a compound word).
**Voltaic:** vocalic and consonantal endings; the latter, being less frequent, only appear as a labial <note>sounds made with the lips, such as p, b, or m</note> or a dental (except for the cases mentioned for Senufo).

## CHAPTER III

### **General characteristics of each of the four main languages.**

1° *Mossi*. — My competence is quite limited regarding the Mossi language <note>also known as Mòoré, the language of the Mossi people of modern-day Burkina Faso</note> and, although it is the most important of all those spoken in French Sudan <note>a colonial territory in West Africa that encompassed much of the interior, roughly corresponding to modern-day Mali and parts of its neighbors</note> in terms of the number of individuals who use it, I will necessarily be very brief on the subject. I would not have even permitted myself to speak of it here, had the fine work of Mr. Froger, published last year, not arrived just in time to provide me with the information I was lacking.

It is enough to browse his work to be convinced that the Mossi language is remarkably rich, both in vocabulary and in forms, and that it is perfectly adapted to the needs of the current Sudanese civilization and even to those of a more developed civilization whose advent one may foresee. However, I doubt that this language is destined for a very significant expansion, and I believe that as the center of the Niger Bend <note>the geographical region where the Niger River turns south, a historical crossroads of trade and culture</note> moves further away from the state of isolation in which it has confined itself until now, Mande, Songhay, and Hausa will spread there more and more, while Mossi will remain more or less localized to the countries where it is currently spoken and will even lose ground instead of gaining it. This is because this language presents rather great difficulties, especially from a phonetic point of view, for foreigners who might be tempted to adopt it: if it is spoken by such a large number of people, it is solely due to the population density of the Mossi countries and to the political hegemony exercised
