But it is easy to observe that it has not spread significantly outside the actual habitat of the Mossi or the tribes that the Mossi have assimilated.

The frequency of consonants, which often follow one another in groups of two, three, or even more without a distinct supporting vowel, makes the pronunciation of many words very difficult and requires a particularly trained ear to hear and understand them; I will content myself with citing, as examples, words like *pabrhdba*, *sikkdba*, and phrases such as *t f kyi*, *t b yell t h wa t h leb*, *t m gnangh fo*, etc.

The difficulty of assigning the appropriate suffix to a root according to the class and number of nouns is also an obstacle—certainly surmountable, but somewhat confusing and of a nature to make the study of Mossi more difficult than that of languages with very few rules and even rarer exceptions, such as Songhay and Mandingue <note>Mandingue refers to the Mande language family, including Bambara, Malinké, and Jula</note>.

2° *Mandingue*. — This latter language presents a very different appearance from that of Mossi: no phonemes that are difficult to articulate, nothing but syllables with vocalic endings, rarely two consonants following one another without an intervening vowel (when this occurs, the second consonant is almost always a liquid <note>a "liquid" is a consonant like 'l' or 'r'</note> or a semi-vowel, or the first is a nasal); an extremely simple morphology, consisting simply of the judicious use of a limited number of suffixes and particles—about twenty—which serve to form compound nouns, diminutives, augmentatives, adjectives, participles, and nouns derived from verbs, the plural in nouns, and the tense, mood, and voice in verbs, without any modification ever occurring in the root of the word; finally, a syntax reduced to roughly two rules: the object of a word is always placed before that word, and the adjective is always placed after the noun. A complete explanation of Mandingue grammar can fit into about twenty pages.

The very widespread ability to use the same radical <note>the fundamental part of a word that contains its primary meaning</note> as a noun, an adjective, and a verb further assists foreigners who possess only a limited portion of the vocabulary.

All of this sufficiently explains the expansive power of this language and helps one understand how it tends to spread more and more outside its own proper domain, to the point of becoming almost the official indigenous language in the Western Sudan <note>The "Western Sudan" refers to the broad savanna region of West Africa, stretching from the Atlantic to Lake Chad, rather than the modern nation-state of Sudan</note>, the one to which people first resort when they encounter an individual whose origin is unknown.

To be impartial, I must say, however, that Mandingue <note>A major language family of West Africa, including Bambara, Malinké, and Jula</note> presents some difficulties. The main one comes from the large number of homonyms <note>words that sound the same but have different meanings</note> and paronyms <note>words with similar but not identical sounds</note>: in a language where the majority of roots consist of a single consonant followed by a single vowel, it is not surprising that many of these roots resemble each other phonetically or are even completely identical, and this phenomenon contributes quite a bit to making certain propositions obscure which, grammatically, are otherwise of a limpid simplicity. This phrase is often cited: *a ko a bè fani ko ko ko* "she says that she is washing the laundry on the other side of the river," in which the syllable *ko* represents four very different words: to say, to wash, river, behind. In truth, when *ko* means "river," it is pronounced with an open *o*, while the *o* is closed in *ko* meaning "to say" and in *ko* meaning "behind," and both closed and lengthened in *ko* meaning "to wash." But how many exactly similar sounds represent very distinct meanings! For example: *kan*, which means "to be equal, neck, language, and on top of"; *di*, which means "to give, to be pleasant, how? and honey"; *bon*, which means "to be large, to spread, and house"; *sama*, which means "to pull, to present, and elephant"; *kono* or *konon*, which means "to wait, belly, bird, and pearl," etc.

Another difficulty lies in the relatively large number of dialects and sub-dialects; certainly, the differ—

### MANDINGUE DIALECTS

The differences between the various dialects, apart from rare exceptions, are primarily phonetic in nature, but they are often sufficiently pronounced that it is difficult for the uninitiated to recognize the same word under its various dialectal aspects. Thus, "hand" will be said *bourou* in Dioula, *boulou* in Malinké, and *bolo* or *blo* in Banmana <note>The Banmana are more commonly known today as the Bambara people</note>; "sun" will be said *téré* in Dioula, *télé* in Malinké, and *tlé* or *klé* in Banmana; "name" will be said *torho* in Dioula, *torho* or *togo* in Malinké, *tokho* in Khassonkè, and *toua* in Banmana; "similar" will be said *nyorhon* in Dioula, *nyorhon* or *nyohon* in Malinké, and *nyouan* in Banmana; "one" will be said *kélé* in Dioula, *kélé* or *kélen* in Malinké and in Banmana, and *khélé* in Khassonkè; *koro* "beside" becomes *koto* in Malinké and *sorho* "meat" becomes *soubo*; "white" will be said *gbé* in Dioula, *gouè* or *guè* in Malinké, *dyè* in Banmana, etc. Certain dialectal modifications also affect the use or value of a few conjugation particles: *ka*, for example, marks the past tense in Dioula and the injunctive <note>A grammatical mood used to express a command, wish, or exhortation</note> in Banmana, etc.

But it should be observed that with a little study and experience, one very quickly gains the key to these modifications, which generally occur according to very regular and constant patterns. Furthermore, it is very rare that, among the different forms a given word takes depending on the region, there is not one whose use has become so generalized that it is understood even in countries where it is not habitually used; thus, although "name" is usually translated as *toua* in Banmana, I believe that nine out of ten Banmana will understand without hesitation someone who says to them: *i torho bè di?* "what is your name?" Even for grammatical forms, when they differ by dialect, it is rare that at least one of them is not understood everywhere: for instance, the Banmana use *yé* as a past tense particle, some Malinké prefer to use *li* in the same case, while other Malinké and all the Dioula generally use *ka*; however, the phrase *a ka sô san kounou* <note>original: "a ka sô san kounou"</note> will be understood everywhere as "he bought a horse yesterday." It is in this way that this "white language" <note>The author uses "white" (gbé) here in the sense of "clear," "pure," or "universal"</note>, this *ce kan gbé*, was formed, which is the Mandingue of everyone and that all...

**3º Peul.** — The Peul language <note>The language of the Fula or Fulani people.</note> has acquired a reputation as a harmonious language that is certainly not overrated: it has been called "a language of birds," the "*Italian of Africa*", etc., and not without reason. The absence of any harsh sounds, the extreme abundance of dentals and especially soft liquids <term>liquids: consonants produced with a fluid, vowel-like quality, such as "l" or "r"</term>, the frequency of the vowels *i* and *é*, as well as the musical intonation so characteristic of this language, make it pleasant to hear, even when one does not understand it, especially when spoken by women.

Although its morphology and syntax are based on very simple principles, the considerable number of its suffixes and the delicacy of the modifications that each brings to the meaning of a given root make Peul one of the most difficult African languages to master thoroughly and to handle with precision. On the other hand, these same factors ensure it an indisputable superiority over the idioms spoken around it: I do not believe there exists a nuance of thought that cannot be rendered with exactitude in the Peul language.

Its vocabulary is one of the richest I know. The number of roots is extraordinarily abundant and, if one considers that from almost every root, one can derive six to ten verbs, and that each of these derived verbs can be used in three different voices (active, passive, and middle or reflexive), and that each voice of each verb can produce...

-># THE PEUL LANGUAGE<-

...rise to at least three participles with different meanings and an almost unlimited quantity of nouns <note>The author refers to "substantifs," the formal term for nouns.</note>, all of this, moreover, by the simple addition to the root of suffixes, each of which has its own specific value; one will not be surprised at the favor in which I hold this language.

One of the most unique characteristics of Peul lies in the phenomenon of classes into which nouns are divided. There are eleven for the singular—or seventeen if one takes sub-classes into account—and five for the plural. Each class or sub-class possesses a special pronoun to represent the nouns it contains, and each is characterized morphologically <term>morphologically: relating to the form and structure of words</term> by a suffix identical to this pronoun or derived from it. Furthermore, certain root consonants undergo a very special modification or transformation in certain classes: for example, the root *rèw* becomes *dèbb* in six singular classes and in three plural classes, while it retains the form *rèw* in the other classes. From the perspective of how beings or objects are categorized by class, there is less precision; however, certain classes have a very clear categorization: for instance, the singular class using the pronoun *o* and the plural class using the pronoun *bé* contain only the names of human beings (1). The singular class with the pronoun *ngèl* (with a hard *g*) and the plural class with the pronoun *koñ* (pronounced like the French imperative "cogne" <note>This sounds roughly like the "ny" in the English word "canyon."</note>) contain only...

---

(1) From this comes the designations of "human gender" and "common gender" (common to both sexes) given respectively to these two classes by General Faidherbe <note>Louis Faidherbe (1818–1889), a French colonial administrator and linguist who studied West African languages.</note> and by de Guiraudon. These same authors placed all other words into a single class that the former called "brute gender" and the latter "neuter gender." Such a division is entirely defective, for there is no reason to group together classes that are each as distinct from one another as they are from the class using the pronoun *o*. Faidherbe and de Guiraudon also claimed that the modifications of root consonants occurred in opposite directions depending on whether the word belonged to the human/common gender or the brute/neuter gender; this assertion is inaccurate, as many nouns that do not refer to human beings undergo the same modifications as human names, at least in the singular. This is a matter of multiple classes rather than a simple binary of human and non-human genders.

# THE LANGUAGES

...diminutive names (diminutives of human beings, animals, or any objects), the singular class with the pronoun *dam* contains only the names of liquids or substances that are easily liquefied; the singular sub-class with the pronoun *mba* (*nga* in the dialects spoken east of the lower Niger) contains only the names of animals that feed on plants; but, for each of the other classes and sub-classes, there generally exists a more or less large number of diverse categories: the singular class with the pronoun *ngal* contains augmentatives <term>augmentatives: words modified to express a larger version or greater intensity of the original noun</term>, the names of instruments, and the names of birds; the singular class with the pronoun *ngol* contains the names of elongated objects, abstract nouns, etc. However, even when the specialization of categories is not absolutely distinct, it nonetheless exists.

The fact that each class or sub-class possesses its own special pronoun and its own special endings, and that adjectives (or participles qualifying nouns) take an ending similar to that of the class to which the qualified noun belongs—along with the treatment undergone by certain radical <term>radical: the core part or "root" of a word before prefixes or suffixes are added</term> consonants depending on the word's class—gives the Peul language a very particular character <note>original: "physionomie"</note> that has not always been understood but has been noticed by everyone.

These various peculiarities of Peul, while making it an interesting, harmonious, rich, and powerful language, also make it a language that is difficult to master. Thus, it is very rare to hear it spoken by any natives other than those for whom it is the mother tongue, and it has no chance of becoming a language of exchange <note>A "lingua franca" or trade language used between different ethnic groups.</note>. By a reverse phenomenon, the Peuls who find themselves in small numbers within a population other than their own are forced to learn the language spoken around them; this is how one encounters a considerable number of Peuls who speak Soninké, Manding, Songhai, Mossi, Hausa, etc., while it is exceedingly rare to find Mandé, Songhai, Mossi, or Hausa people who speak Peul.

Furthermore, those who, due to special circumstances, have managed to learn Peul generally speak it very poorly. The Rimaïbé <note>A social class within Peul society, historically consisting of descendants of enslaved people or serfs who adopted the Peul language and culture.</note>, although they often know no other language...

# THE PEUL LANGUAGE OF THE TOUCOULEURS

that Peul, which is the language of their masters, is spoken by them only in an incorrect manner. The same observation has been made regarding people belonging to special castes, particularly the Laobé <note>The Laobé are a specialized caste of woodworkers and artisans within Peul society</note>. The Peuls proper themselves are far from always observing all the rules of the language and take liberties, notably in applying the principles relating to the distinction of classes and the modifications of radical <term>radical: the core root of a word before it is modified by grammar</term> consonants. Only among all the Peul-speaking people do the Toucouleurs <note>The Toucouleurs are an ethnic group from the Senegal River valley, closely related to the Peul</note> speak in a completely correct manner.

This fact is not the least of the arguments in favor of the theory I maintained above—a theory according to which the ancestors of the Peuls, during their stay in Fouta-Toro from the 8th to the 11th centuries, abandoned their language of Asiatic or North African origin to borrow from the Black populations of Tekrour <note>Tekrour was an ancient state located in the Senegal River valley</note> the Toucouleur language, which we call today the Peul language (1). We have seen that all indigenous traditions agree in identifying Fouta-Toro as the starting point for the various migrations that carried the Peuls eastward as far as the Nile basin; however, it is easy to observe that, as one moves away from Fouta-Toro in an easterly direction, the language spoken by the Peuls deviates more and more from the fundamental rules that give it its specific character, while the Toucouleurs, even when permanently established very far from their country of origin—for example, those of Ségou, Bandiagara, or Say—continue to scrupulously apply these same rules. All this tends to prove, it seems to me, that Peul is truly the national language only of the Toucouleurs and that its true homeland of origin must be placed in ancient Tekrour, that is to say, in the Senegalese Fouta.

Another phenomenon further supports my hypothesis. An examination, even a superficial one, of the Serer language <note>The Serer are an ethnic group primarily found in modern-day Senegal and the Gambia</note> shows that a considerable number of radicals in this language, and—

notably those expressing the most common ideas, such as “to leave, to accept, to buy, to sell, to light, to bring, to have, to beat, to be beautiful, to be white, to be black, to be brave, to cook, to sleep, to drink, to eat, to ask, to send, to walk, to be able, to laugh, to fall, to kill, to steal, etc.”, are identical or analogous to the corresponding Peul <term>radical: the core part of a word that contains its primary meaning</term> radicals, while the general character of the Serer language is very different from the general character of the Peul language and closer instead to the appearance of Wolof. On the other hand, one encounters in Serer—and although on a much more limited scale, in Wolof—phenomena of radical consonant mutations and elements of derivation that singularly recall the corresponding phenomena and elements of Peul. And yet Serer, by its general morphology, and Wolof especially, by its vocabulary and grammar, distance themselves quite considerably from Peul. It is known that the Serer have not always inhabited their current country, that they were formerly established further to the East and North, and that they were, for centuries, neighbors with the inhabitants of Tekrour <note>Tekrour was an ancient state in the Senegal River valley, often associated with the ancestors of the Toucouleur people</note> and part of their empire; it is also known that the Wolof were by turns subjects and suzerains of the same empire: it is therefore not surprising that borrowings were made by the Serer and the Wolof from the language of Tekrour and that the trace of these borrowings is still visible today. One might even claim, though it is more daring, that it was Serer that influenced the language of Tekrour, or even—which would perhaps be closer to the truth—that a language of the lower Senegal, now vanished, contributed to the formation of the Toucouleur language, the Serer language, and, to a lesser extent, the Wolof language. Whatever the case may be, as the analogies observed between Peul on one hand and Serer and—to a much lesser degree—Wolof on the other are just as visible in the dialect of the Peuls of Baguirmi <note>A region in modern-day Chad, thousands of miles from Senegal</note> as in that of the Toucouleurs of Fouta-Toro, it must be admitted that the Peuls of Baguirmi and elsewhere took their language from the lower Senegal, given that the influence of the Serer has never, to my knowledge, reached as far as Lake Chad. This is therefore a first point which seems to me definitively established:

# THE ORIGIN OF THE PEUL LANGUAGE

the current language of the Peul was spoken in Tekrour <note>An ancient state located in the Senegal River valley</note> before the era of the first Peul migrations toward the South and toward the East.

But, one might say, this would not prevent the Peul from having brought their current language from Asia or from Northeast Africa: they would have introduced it with them to Tekrour, where it would have passed some of its <term>radicals: the primary roots of words</term> to Serer and would have become the language of the Toucouleurs <note>An ethnic group from the Senegal River valley, closely related to the Peul</note>, and they would have subsequently transported it throughout the western and central Sudan <note>Referring to the "Bilad al-Sudan" geographic region, the broad belt south of the Sahara</note>.

Certainly, such a hypothesis is not materially absurd, and it will even remain historically defensible as long as we possess no document allowing us to know what language was spoken in Tekrour before the arrival of the Peul in that country; yet it is likely that we will never have a document of this nature at our disposal.

We do indeed have the name for "gorillas": when the Carthaginian navigator Hanno reached the coasts of Guinea, he saw hairy savages who did not seem to him to have human features and whom his interpreters designated to him by a name which—having passed into our language through the Greek translation of the Punic text—has become "gorilla." As it is likely, according to Hanno's account, that his interpreters had been taken on board at the mouth of the Senegal River, one could link the word "gorilla" to the Wolof expression *gór yi* <note>original Wolof: "gór yi"</note> "these are men," which would allow us to suppose that, as early as the 6th century B.C., Wolof was already being spoken at the mouth of the Senegal and that the name used to designate men in Wolof already belonged to a root which, precisely, also serves to designate them in Peul (*gór-ko*, root *gór* or *wór* depending on the case). But I certainly do not wish to rely on an argument based on a single word, transmitted through a Punic text that we do not possess.

The argument drawn from the fact that Peul is spoken more correctly by the Toucouleurs than by the Peul themselves seems to me to have much greater value. Still others exist in support of my thesis. The Peul or Proto-Peul did not only stay in the Fouta <note>Referring to Fouta Toro or Fouta Djallon, key highland regions of Peul settlement</note>: before arriving there, they were forced to pass through some—

If we leave the realm of history to approach that of pure linguistics, the matter will appear even more certain: the Peul language, by its purely <term>agglutinative: a linguistic type where words are formed by joining distinct morphemes together without changing them</term> type, by its noun classes, by its conjugation suffixes, by its phonetics, by the very nature of its radicals, and by the form of its roots, presents all the fundamental characteristics of Black African languages <note>original: "langues nègres"; a historical term used by the author to categorize sub-Saharan language families</note>; it constitutes a separate family within Black Africa, it is true, but this family should be grouped with the other Sudanese families and with the Bantu family, which it resembles in certain respects, whereas the differences separating Peul from <term>Semitic and Hamitic: language families including Arabic, Hebrew, and Berber, formerly used as a racial-linguistic category</term> languages are such that I cannot manage to conceive how anyone was able, even for a

A very authoritative English linguist regarding African idioms, Mr. Migeod <note>Frederick William Hugh Migeod (1872–1952), a colonial official and linguist who wrote extensively on West African languages</note>, raised a single objection to my theory: "How can we accept," he said to me, "that a people of the white race and of superior mentality could have abandoned its language to adopt a Negro language?" <note>The author is navigating the "Hamitic Hypothesis," a 19th and early 20th-century theory that attributed African cultural achievements to "whiter" or "Hamitic" peoples from the North or East.</note> This objection is not of a nature to frighten me. First of all, it is not demonstrated that the mentality of the Judeo-Syrians <note>A reference to the legendary origin of the Peul people, whom some early ethnographers believed descended from migrants from the Levant</note> and their civilization, at the moment of their arrival in the Fouta, was notably superior to that of the Blacks of Tekrour <note>An ancient state in the Senegal River valley</note>; furthermore, it is very probable, as I have hinted, that the language they spoke then was not *their own language*, but rather a borrowed language gathered in Egypt or Cyrenaica <note>The eastern coastal region of modern Libya</note>, perhaps a bastardized Egyptian, perhaps simply Berber: since their departure from Syria they had undoubtedly changed languages more than once, and they must not have held excessively to the one they spoke at the time of their arrival on the banks of the Senegal, which suited their national genius no more than the language of the Toucouleurs <note>The sedentary inhabitants of the Senegal River valley, closely related to the Peul</note>. Finally, the fact of a group of the white race adopting a Negro language does not seem to me otherwise surprising: reasons drawn from racial pride have nothing to do with the development of languages; the Kel-Oui Tuareg have almost abandoned Tamashek to speak only Hausa, and yet it was their serfs, the Bugadie, who taught it to them; the descendants of the Moroccan conquerors of Timbuktu speak no language other than that of the Songhay Negroes, whom their ancestors had enslaved and regarded as a race of slaves.

4° *Songhay*. — I place the Songhay language after the Peul language because of its slight inferiority in terms of the number of its speakers, but it would be more logical, in this sketch of the general characters of the main languages of the French Sudan <note>The colonial name for the territory that became Mali</note>, to place it alongside Mandinka. It has its simplicity and power of expansion, precisely because of this simplicity.

than *Manding*: its pronunciation is even easier, for it has neither the guttural *rh* nor the somewhat specific nasal vowels of *Manding*; its morphology, very similar to that of the latter language in terms of the applied principles, is even more rudimentary; as for its syntax, it is almost non-existent. If *Manding* grammar can fit in twenty pages, ten pages would be more than enough for *Songhay* grammar: the grammatical section of the Hacquard and Dupuis manual <note>Augustin Hacquard (1860–1901) and Auguste Dupuis (1867–1945), known as Dupuis-Yakouba, were French missionaries who published a pioneering grammar and dictionary of the Songhay language in 1897.</note>, which is, I believe, complete, contains forty pages, more than three-quarters of which are filled with examples. Furthermore, homonyms <term>homonyms</term><note>Words that sound the same but have different meanings.</note> are only limited in number, and their presence does not present the real difficulty they cause in *Manding*. Dialectal variations appear insignificant, with the exception of the difference in the pronunciation of the *palatalized* or *yodized d* <note>A 'y'-like sound added to the 'd', similar to the 'di' in 'adieu'.</note> which distinguishes the speech of Timbuktu and Djenné from that of the *Djerma* <note>Also known as Zarma, a major ethnic group in modern-day Niger who speak a variety of Songhay.</note>; in the latter country it is pronounced *z*; for example, one would say *Zenné* instead of Djenné.

While *Songhay* is an easy language, it is otherwise a poor language: its vocabulary is much more restricted than that of *Manding*, and the number of derivatives that can be formed from a given radical <note>The basic form or root of a word.</note> is not considerable. Thus, it has borrowed heavily from foreign languages—from *Arabic*, from *Tamasheq* <note>The language of the Tuareg people.</note>, and especially from *Fula* and *Manding*. These borrowings, moreover, consist only of words that *Songhay* has adopted as-is, without concern for their formation. Quite naturally, foreign words are often only of local use: many *Arabic* expressions commonly used in Timbuktu are almost unknown in Say <note>A town on the Niger River in modern-day Niger.</note>; numerous *Manding* words are current in Djenné that are not understood in Gao; but many have also definitively and everywhere acquired right of citizenship <note>A French idiom (*droit de cité*) meaning they have become officially accepted and integrated.</note> and are today part of the *Songhay* vocabulary, of which they constitute nearly a quarter.

# CHAPTER IV

## **Linguistic Bibliography.**

I do not intend to establish a complete list here of publications relating to Sudanese languages <note>In this context, "Sudanese" refers to the "Western Soudan," a historical geographic region in West Africa comprising the Sahel and savannah belts, rather than the modern nation of Sudan.</note>: such a bibliography, while very sparse for certain idioms, would on the contrary be extremely extensive regarding Manding, Fula, and especially Hausa. But among everything that has been published on these languages and others, many works or memoirs are now of little interest except to collectors and scholars.

I would like to provide only the indication of the most recent works and those which offer the most guarantees and facilities for the study of the languages spoken in Upper Senegal and Niger <note>French: *Haut-Sénégal-Niger*, a large administrative territory in French West Africa existing from 1904 to 1921.</note>. Indeed, I believe this information to be very useful, judging by the large number of people who have approached me to find out where they could study this or that language of the colony.

The same [Author]. — *Wolof-French Dictionary*, new edition. <note>original title: "Dictionnaire wolof-français, nouv. édit."</note> — Saint-Joseph de Ngazobil, 1875, octavo.
P. H. GREFFIER. — *French-Wolof Conversation Guide.* <note>original title: "Guide de la conversation français-volof."</note> — Saint-Joseph de Ngazobil, 1907, thirty-twomo <note>original: "in-32," a very small pocket-sized book format.</note>.

*Peul.* <note>Peul, also known as Fula, Fulani, or Fulfulde, is a major language spoken across West and Central Africa.</note>
Dr. TAUTAIN. — *Contribution to the Study of the Fula Language* <note>original title: "Contribution à l’étude de la langue foule."</note> (*Review of Linguistics and Comparative Philology*, Paris, 1889-90, 82 pages).
T. G. de GUIRAUDON. — *Manual of the Fula Language.* <note>original title: "Manuel de la langue foule."</note> Paris (Welter), 1894, eighteenmo <note>original: "in-18," a small book format.</note>, 144 pages.
H. GADEN. — *Note on the Fula Dialect Spoken by the Fula People of Baguirmi* <note>original title: "Note sur le dialecte foul parlé par les Foulbé du Baguirmi." Baguirmi was a historical kingdom in what is now Chad.</note> (*Asiatic Journal*, Paris, Jan.-Feb. 1908, 70 pages).
D. WESTERMANN. — *Handbook of the Fula Language.* <note>original title: "Handbuch der Ful-Sprache." Translated from German.</note> — Berlin, 1909, octavo, 274 pages.

*Songhai.* <note>Songhai (or Songhay) refers to a group of closely related languages spoken along the Niger River.</note>
A. HACQUARD and A. DUPUIS. — *Manual of the Songhai Language.* <note>original title: "Manuel de la langue songay."</note> — Paris (Maisonneuve), 1897, eighteenmo, 254 pages.
A. DUPUIS-YAKOUBA. — *The Gow, Hunters of the Niger* <note>original title: "Les Gow, chasseurs du Niger."</note> (Songhai text and French translation). — Paris (Leroux), 1911, octavo, approximately 300 pages.

*Mande Languages: General Study.* <note>The Mande languages are a large family spoken in several countries across West Africa, including Mali, Guinea, and Ivory Coast.</note>
H. STEINTHAL. — *The Mande-Negro Languages.* <note>original title: "Die Mande-Neger-Sprachen." Translated from German.</note> — Berlin, 1867, octavo, 344 pages.
M. DELAFOSSE. — *Essay on a Practical Manual of the Mande Language* (Part IV). <note>original title: "Essai de manuel pratique de la langue mandé."</note> — Paris (Leroux), 1901, large octavo, 304 pages.

*Bozo.* <note>Bozo is a Mande language spoken by the Bozo people, who are traditionally known as "masters of the river" along the Niger.</note>
M. DELAFOSSE. — *Comparative Vocabularies* <note>original title: "Vocabulaires comparatifs."</note> (Chapter IV contains a short Bozo vocabulary and some grammar notes). — Nothing else has been published to my knowledge regarding the Bozo language.

*Soninke (no complete study of the Soninke language has appeared until now).* <note>Soninke is a Mande language spoken by the Soninke people of West Africa; they were the founders of the ancient Ghana Empire.</note>
General FAIDHERBE. — *Senegalese Languages.* <note>original title: "Langues sénégalaises."</note> — Paris (Leroux), 1887, eighteenmo, 266 pages (includes a short grammatical notice and a vocabulary).
Dr. TAUTAIN. — *Note on the Three Languages: Soninke, Bambara, and Malinke* <note>original title: "Note sur les trois langues soninké, banmana et mal-linké." Bambara and Malinke are major languages within the Mande family.</note> (*Review of Linguistics and Comparative Philology*, Paris, 1887).

<page-num>425</page-num>
<header>LINGUISTIC BIBLIOGRAPHY</header>

### *Senufo.* <note>The Senufo languages are a group of about 15 languages spoken by the Senufo people in northern Ivory Coast, southern Mali, and western Burkina Faso.</note>

**MR. DELAFOSSE.** — *Comparative Vocabularies* <note>original title: "Vocabulaires comparatifs." Maurice Delafosse was a French colonial administrator and a pioneer in African ethnology and linguistics.</note> (chapter V: dialects of the Minianka, the Folo, and several tribes of the Ivory Coast). — To my knowledge, nothing else has been published on the Senufo language.

### *Voltaic languages: general study.* <note>Now more commonly known as the Gur languages, this family includes Mossi and many other languages of the West African interior.</note>

**MR. DELAFOSSE.** — *The Voltaic Languages (Niger Bend).* <note>original title: "Les langues voltaïques (Boucle du Niger)." The "Niger Bend" refers to the great curve the Niger River takes through the Sahel.</note> (*Memoirs of the Linguistic Society of Paris*, volume XVI, issue 6, Paris, 1911).

### *Tombo, Dogon, and Deforo: none recorded.* <note>Tombo and Deforo are dialects of the Dogon language family, spoken primarily in Mali.</note>

### *Mossi.* <note>Also known as Moore, the language of the Mossi people and the most widely spoken language in Burkina Faso.</note>

**F. FROGER.** — *Study of the Mossi Language*, followed by a vocabulary and texts. <note>original title: "Etude de la langue des Mossi."</note> — Paris (Leroux), 1910, large octavo <note>original: "gr. in-8," a standard book size about 10 inches tall.</note>, 260 pages.

### *Gurma.* <note>The Gurma (Gourmantché) language is spoken in Burkina Faso, Togo, Benin, and Niger.</note>

**F. DUBOIS.** — *Gurma Vocabulary* <note>original title: "Vocabulaire gourma."</note> (*Bulletin of the Committee of French Africa*, Paris, July 1898). — Nothing else.

### *Nankana: none recorded.* <note>Nankana (or Gurenne) is spoken in northern Ghana and southern Burkina Faso.</note>

### *Dagaare and Birifor.* <note>Two closely related languages within the Gur family, spoken in Ghana and Burkina Faso.</note>

**MR. DELAFOSSE.** — *Comparative Vocabularies* (chapter VII). — Nothing else.

### *Nounouma.* <note>A Gurunsi language group in Burkina Faso.</note>

**MR. DELAFOSSE.** — *Comparative Vocabularies* (chapter VII, *Gurunsi* <note>original: "gouressi," a variant of Gurunsi, a group of related languages.</note>). — Nothing else.

### *Sissala.* <note>A language spoken in northern Ghana and Burkina Faso.</note>

**F. W. H. MIGEOD.** — *The languages of West-Africa* (counting on page 144 and some phrases on page 284 in *Isala* and *Ajolo*).

### *Bissa: none recorded.* <note>Bissa (referred to here as Boussansé) is a Mande language spoken in Burkina Faso, Ghana, and Togo.</note>

### *Lobi, Dyan, Puguli, and Gan.* <note>These are specific ethnic groups and languages in the Gur family, located near the borders of Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, and Ghana.</note>

**MR. DELAFOSSE.** — *Comparative Vocabularies* (chapter VII). — Nothing else.

### *Bobo.* <note>The Bobo people speak several distinct languages; the author identifies specific dialects below.</note>

**MR. DELAFOSSE.** — *Comparative Vocabularies* (chapter VII, vocabularies of the Kian and Tara dialects and grammatical notes). — Nothing else.

### *Kulango.* <note>A language spoken primarily in the Ivory Coast.</note>

**MR. DELAFOSSE.** — *Comparative Vocabularies* (chapter VII). — Nothing else.
